Prācyavidyāsaṃśodhanālayagranthamālā-114:
*Saundaryalaharī*, composed by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya.
The Bhāvanopaniṣad, adorned with the commentary of Lakṣmīdhara, accompanied by a translation into the Karṇāṭaka language and with appendices, together with the commentary of Śrī Bhāskararāya.
The editor of the *Devīpañcastavī* is the scholar En. Es. Veṅkaṭanāthācārya.
Srinivasa Research Assistant, Oriental Research Institute,
Mysore.
The Oriental Research Institute,
Mysore University,
Mysore.
Oṃ.
The *Saundaryalaharī*, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda,
together with the commentary titled *Lakṣmīdhara* composed by the teacher Lakṣmīdhara.

Śiva, when joined with Śakti and accompanied by her exposition, becomes capable of manifesting; for if it were otherwise, the Lord would indeed not be able even to move. Therefore, you are to be worshipped.
How can one who has not performed meritorious deeds be capable of bowing down to or praising [him] even by Hari, Hara, Viriñca, and the others? The commencement of the commentary:
We pay homage to the most exalted one, who bears a mass of thick, hanging matted locks.
The jingling sound of the bracelets is itself the science of grammar.
Adorned with the entirety of the remaining utterances, smelling the fragrance of the treatises of Kaṇāda and Caraka,
tasted by the boldness of Bhaṭṭa’s speech, and flourishing with the expansion of the most profound compositions of the Guru (Kumārila),
they are free from doubt regarding the words of Śaṅkara and are the upholders of the doctrine of Paśupati.
The compositions of whose speech shine forth like the number of the Sāṃkhya system, he is the jewel among the wise, the illustrious Lolla Lakṣmīdhara.
Thus, I, Lakṣmīdhara, have composed this commentary named Lakṣmīdharā;
may the wise, with concentrated minds, study it constantly.

Though there may indeed be some fault here or there on my part due to indolence or dullness of intellect, there is no cause for any suspicion; for the innate power of the virtuous, ever skilled in bringing out excellence,
truly triumphs forever upon this earth.

In this work, the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpūjyapāda, who is a knower of the reality of the Samaya doctrine, introduces the digit of the moon known as Samaya in a hundred verses, beginning with the word "Śiva.
"Śiva" refers to the principle of Sadāśiva, endowed with all auspiciousness. [The root] *vaś* means "to desire" or "to be beautiful."
From this root, the word *śiva* is derived. As it has been said:
"The word *siṃha* is formed from the root *hiṃs* (to injure); *śiva* is traditionally known [from the root] *vaś* (to desire).
Just as *paśyaka* and *kaśyapa* are established through the transposition of syllables."

Thus: the root *vaś*, meaning "to desire," is included as belonging to both the *tudādi* and *adādi* classes. For the *vaśati* of the *tudādi* class, the meaning is "radiance" (*dīpti*); radiance is [the same as] splendor (*kānti*).
For the *vaṣṭi* of the *adādi* class, the meaning is "desire" (*kāmanā*), because it is the locus of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

The nature of Śiva belongs to the Lord (Īśvara). He is called Śiva because he dwells (vaśati) as self-luminous light, or because he illumines the phenomenal world within himself; or else, the word Śiva is derived from the verbal root *śīṅ* meaning "to sleep," in the sense that he blows away (vāti), that is, casts off, [the state of] sleep.

*Śiva* means free from dullness (*jāḍya*), that is to say, liberated from ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, *śiva* is so called because he "goes to" (*vāti*) or enters into ignorance as if it were a dream; this implies he is conjoined with the *kalā* known as Sādākhyā.
It will be explained later that such a being alone is denoted by the word *śiva*. Such is Śiva.

Endowed with *śakti*, that is, the power of creating the universe; "limited" (*avacchinna*), because it is precisely Brahman as consciousness limited by ignorance (*avidyā*) that possesses the capacity for the creation of the universe.
If it exists, then indeed it is capable—that is, empowered—to bring [the world] forth.
To manifest conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
3) "If not thus" means: if he were not endowed with such power; that is the meaning of "if."

The "Deva" is the aforementioned Sadāśiva, so called because he "shines" (divyati). The particle *nakhalu* is used here in the sense of negation and possibility. He is not at all capable—meaning not even able—to stir or move, for he is formless, all-pervading, and equal to space.
The meaning intended here is "because of the impossibility of vibration."

The explicit meaning, however, is that according to the analogy of husband and wife, if Śiva is joined with Śakti as his consort, he is able to create the continuous stream of the phenomenal world; if he is separated from her, he is not able to do so.

As for the secret meaning of the scripture, by the word *śiva*— [in the middle of the Śrīcakra, which consists of nine *yoni*s as will be described, namely "the four Śrīkaṇṭhas related to the two Śivas"— Ma.]— it is indicated.

In the midst of the wheel of nine wombs (*navayonicakra*), the half-wheel consisting of four wombs is spoken of; by the word "power" (*śakti*), the remaining half-wheel consisting of five wombs is spoken of. Thus, the two halves joined together constitute the wheel consisting of nine wombs.

It will be explained further on that the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe proceed from this very wheel (*cakra*) alone. And it has been said: "By means of the four wheels of Śiva and the five wheels of Śakti..."
The Śrīcakra, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, should be known as the very body of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus [it is said]. It will be explained later that the union of Śiva and Śakti is a distinct principle (tattvāntara), the twenty-sixth, which transcends all principles. Furthermore, it will be stated that the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe proceed from this very union alone, and not from either one individually. As it has been said:

In the *Vāmakeśvara-mahātantra-catuḥśatī*: "Even the Supreme [Lord], if devoid of Śakti, would be incapable of performing creation, maintenance, and dissolution; however, when joined with Śakti, he is indeed empowered."
And this we shall explain more thoroughly on the occasion of commenting on the verse beginning with "etacca caturbhiḥ śrīkaṇṭhaiḥ" (verse 11).
Therefore, for that reason, you— the venerable one worthy of being propitiated and worshipped by Hari, Hara, Viriñca, and others (where Hari is Viṣṇu and Hara is Rudra)— [are to be honored].
Virincha is Brahmā; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), Indra and others are included.

These are persons of limited authority who fall within the sphere of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca). It is therefore entirely appropriate that the Blessed Lady, the progenitor of the phenomenal world, should be the object of their salutation. Thus it has been stated.

Therefore, one should understand that "you are to be propitiated" is not a figurative praise; or rather, the word *nigama* includes the *Ādi* (etcetera) because the Blessed Lady is served by the Vedas (*nigama*),
as will be clarified later in the verse beginning with "the heads of the Śrutis" (verse 84).

The word *viriñca* ends in the vowel *a*. The particle *api* embellishes the sense of the word *katham* (how). "To prostrate" (*praṇantum*) means to pay homage. The prefix *pra-* denotes the threefold salutation—bodily, verbal, and mental. [And] "to praise" (*stotum*).

The meaning is: "or even to perform mere praise. One who has not performed merit (*akṛtapuṇya*) is one for whom no accumulation of merit has been gathered in previous births; one other than that is "one who has performed merit" (*kṛtapuṇya*).
Such a person prevails, rules, or is capable [of doing so].
Here the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady, if the god Śiva is joined with Śakti, then he is able to manifest power;
if it were not so, he would certainly not be capable even of moving.
Therefore, [I worship] you, who are to be propitiated even by Hari, Hara, Viriñca, and the others.
How can one who has not performed meritorious deeds be able to bow down or offer praise? || 1 ||

Virinchi, gathering even the smallest particle born from the lotus-feet of Your feet, constructs the worlds without fail; Śauri carries it somehow upon his thousand heads; and Hara, having crushed it, bears it [upon his head].
He practices the rite of smearing himself with ashes. || 2 ||
The exceedingly minute, most subtle particle of dust arising from the lotus-feet of you, the Goddess— feet which are like two lotuses— from those [feet].

The Lord Viriñci is Brahmā; for in the *Amaraśeṣa* it is stated that the word *viriñci* ends in the vowel *i*, as in "Viriñci and Viriñcana. "Accumulating" means bringing about or making into vessels (*bhāṇḍīkurvan*); he "fashions," meaning he creates various worlds—those which are perceived.

Thus, "the worlds" means the manifold universe consisting of both the stationary and the moving; or alternatively, the seven upper worlds beginning with Bhūr and the seven lower worlds beginning with Atala—
these fourteen worlds in their entirety.
In such a way that they remain mutually unmixed; or rather, in such a way that no deficiency occurs among them until the final dissolution (*pralaya*);
she carries, brings, and protects this particle of dust as being composed of the fourteen worlds.

[It was] situated there. Śauri is the offspring of Śūra and Yadu; Śauri refers to Balabhadra, who indicates Śeṣa because Balabhadra is an incarnation of Śeṣa. Alternatively, Śauri is the king of serpents (the serpent-king), namely Śeṣa, so called because he "destroys" (śṛṇāti) or "bites" (daśati). Or else...
Śauri is Viṣṇu. Thus it is stated in the *Catuḥśatī*: "In the form of Śiṃśumāra, Viṣṇu supports the seven worlds situated below; as Śeṣa, he supports the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ situated above."

Even in the remaining alternative, Śeṣa alone is Viṣṇu, because the office of protection belongs exclusively to Viṣṇu. "Hara" refers to one who seizes (harati) the phenomenal world at the time of dissolution; somehow, by some means, even with a thousand heads—having thoroughly crushed and ground him down, he [seizes it].
He worships—that is, he serves and relies upon—the single grain of dust from his feet, which exists as the essence of the fourteen worlds;
[the meaning is that he lives by it].
He performs the rite of smearing with ashes, which is the act of smearing or anointing with ashes.
The application of body-unguents refers to the method or performance thereof; that is what is meant by that expression.
p.
6) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady, Viriñci, gathering the minute particles of dust produced from your lotus-feet, [creates] the worlds.
He fashions it in its entirety. O Blessed One, Śauri somehow carries this upon his thousand heads. O Blessed One, having crushed this, Hara resorts to the practice of smearing himself with ashes.

The meaning is this: the agency of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the phenomenal world depends upon the greatness of the dust from the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lady. || 2 ||
He praises that very dust:
it is an island-city for the inner darkness of ignorance,
a stream of cascading nectar from the blossoms of consciousness for the dull-witted, and [a treasure] for the destitute...
For those submerged in the ocean of birth, the tusk of the Boar, the enemy of Mura, becomes a collection of wish-fulfilling gems.

This dust belongs to those who possess ignorance—meaning those whose minds are permeated by ignorance and who are ignorant; it does not refer to those for whom knowledge (*vidyā*) is non-existent, because ignorance (*avidyā*) is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśas-* group, such that "those possessing ignorance" (*avidyāvantaḥ*) are called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

Thus [it is said]. Or alternatively: even those whose minds are pervaded by ignorance are metaphorically called "ignorance. For them, there is the "inner darkness" (*antastimira*)—that is, the ignorance situated within. The attribution of "darkness" (*timira*) to ignorance is due to the similarity in their quality of being obscuring, just as in the following example: [the city of the island of the sun that dispels inner darkness].

Just as darkness veils external objects, so too does ignorance veil the internal object, which is the Self. Of that darkness, the city on the island of Mihira— the island (*dvīpa*) of Mihira, the Sun,
being the region of sunrise in the midst of the ocean— is the city, the port (*pattana*).

That is to say, the bedchamber. For the dull-witted, the slow, and the foolish, there is a stream of flowing nectar from the cluster of blossoms of consciousness; "consciousness" (*caitanya*) itself is the meaning, with the suffix *ṣyañ* used in its own sense.

Volition (*cetanā*) is a certain power consisting of the expansion of the mind that awakens the objects within oneself; that itself is the cluster, a bunch of flowers from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*);
its nectar is the floral juice; its flow is the trickling forth, its exudation. Of that...

A cascade is a stream. For the poor and the wretched, it is a multiplication of the *cintāmaṇi*—that is, a repetition or, in other words, a multitude of that particular jewel. In the ocean of birth, birth itself is the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

The superimposition of the nature of an ocean upon *saṃsāra* is due to the similarity of being shoreless (*apāratva*). "Sunk therein" means those who are utterly submerged, lacking any emergence. "Tusk" (*daṃṣṭrā*) is clear.
The enemy of the demon named Mura is Viṣṇu; he is the "Boar-form of the Enemy of Mura" (*muraripu-varāha*). This...

The word *muraripu* (enemy of Mura), although denoting a qualifier, denotes the qualified object, Viṣṇu himself, due to the inherent nature of the word. Nor is there a contraction of its power (*śakti*) here, as in the case of words like *paṅkaja* (lotus), because this word denotes a substance (*dravya*). Of him [Viṣṇu], there is the Boar (*varāha*), a particular incarnation (*avatāra*). Of that...
Thus it is said; it exists.
Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady, this dust of Your lotus feet is a sun for the island-city of the inner darkness of the ignorant;
a stream of cascading nectar from the cluster of blossoms of consciousness for the dull-witted; and a collection of wish-fulfilling gems for the destitute.
For those submerged in the ocean of birth, the tusk of the Boar, the enemy of Mura, becomes [a means of rescue].

Here, the figure of speech is *pariṇāma* (transformation), because that which is superimposed exists by way of having the nature of the object of superimposition. Accordingly, Maṅkhaka’s sūtra states: "When that which is being superimposed serves the purpose of the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma*. The meaning of this very [sūtra] is that the superimposed element must serve the purpose of the subject at hand.
It is stated with the intention of the result that [the superimposition] is indeed the basis for persistence by virtue of having the object of superimposition as its nature (p.
Alternatively, it is the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description), because the dust is described in the form of a city and so forth.
Or let it be a metaphor; its application to the subject at hand is not intended to be expressed. || 3 ||

The host of deities other than you bestows the boons of fearlessness with their two hands; you alone, however, manifest the gestures of granting boons and dispelling fear. O Refuge of the worlds, it is your two feet alone that are truly skillful in protecting from fear and in granting even the most desired fruit.

Other than you, [there is] another who, with both hands (pāṇibhyām), grants fearlessness (abhaya) and boons (vara); "fearlessness" means freedom from fear—that is, protection from fear—and a "boon" refers to a desired object; thus he is "the giver of fearlessness and boons," being a giver of fearlessness with one hand.

The meaning is "by another," namely, the Giver of Boons (*varada*). The term *daivatagaṇaḥ* means the host of deities; *daivata* is derived from *devatā* with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the base itself, according to the rule beginning with *vinayādi*.
Suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) may deviate from the gender and number of the base word, just as *caitanya* (consciousness) is derived from *cetana* (a conscious being). Of these...

The *gaṇas* are Indra and others, as well as the Ādityas and other deities of the *gaṇas*. You, the Blessed One (*bhavatī*), are not even one—the primary, or that which is numbered by the number one; you simply do not exist [in that sense].
You manifest the gestures of the *vara* (boon) and *abhaya* (fearlessness). "Manifested" means made clearly visible.
The word "with both hands" is to be supplied [to the verse]. "Vara" means a desired object; "abhīti" means fearlessness, that is, protection from fear.
She whose expressive gesture (*abhinaya*)—the manifestation (*abhivyañjana*)—of these two consists of the granting of boons and fearlessness with her two hands is described thus.
The granting of boons and fearlessness with both hands is common to all deities; such is the case for her.

He describes the uncommon manner of granting the boon of fearlessness: to protect from fear, to guard from saṃsāra, to grant a fruit corresponding to the desired object, and moreover— as indicated by the conjunction *api ca*— even more than what is desired, that is, exceeding one's longing or wish.

"Properly more" (*samyagadhikam*) means more than the desired object. "In the refuge-worthy" (*śaraṇye*) means worthy of being a refuge for the worlds, that is, for the fourteen realms of existence (*caturdaśabhuvana*). "Of you" (*tava*) refers to you, O Lady (*bhavatyāḥ*). The word *hi* is used in the sense of "thus," meaning "having reflected. "Feet" (*caraṇau*) refers to the two feet. The particle *eva* [is used for emphasis].
In the sense of restriction; "nipuṇau" means capable or competent.
p.

9) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! O Refuge of the worlds! Other than you, the host of deities grants the boons of fearlessness and boons with both hands; you alone [grant them] with both hands.

Thinking thus— that you do not indeed manifest the gestures of the "Vara" (boon) and "Abhaya" (fearlessness)— your two feet alone are skillful in protecting me from fear and in bestowing even the most abundant fruit of my desire.

The meaning is this: since the granting of the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and boon-granting (*varada*) by the two hands is common to all [deities], your two feet themselves are spontaneously engaged in such granting of fearlessness and boons;
therefore, you need not perform the granting of fearlessness and boons with your two hands.
For [if it were so], there would be an absence of purpose, the consequence of it being common to all, and a contradiction of the fact that the world has only one refuge; such is the instruction.

Here, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is clear; the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), based on the sentence as its mark, is also clear. There is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of these two through the relationship of the subordinate and the principal. || 4 ||
In ancient times, Hari, having become a woman, worshipped you— who generate the good fortune of those who bow before you—
and even brought the enemy of the cities (Śiva) to agitation. Smara too, having bowed to you with a body to be licked by the eyes of Rati, indeed possesses the power to delude even the sages.
Of the great ones. || 5 ||
Hari, Viṣṇu, having worshipped, honored, recited, and meditated upon you— the Goddess in the form of the discus and in the form of knowledge— for this very reason,
among the various expansions (*prastāra*) of Tripurasundarī, Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of one such expansion.
An "ṛṣi" is a mantra situated within the Veda by whom it was seen; for this very reason they say, "He is called an ṛṣi because of his vision. This [mantra] consists of fifteen syllables.

This Vidyā is recorded in the Ṛgveda in such passages as: "The four bear him, seeking security" (ṚV 5.47.4). Nor should it be argued that there are three *īṃ* sounds here, since only three instances of *hṛllekhā* are heard; for this refers to the Śrībīja consisting of sixteen kalās.
Since that which is to be known exists by virtue of the lineage of the Guru, the four *īṃ* syllables are established; thus, the presence of the Root-Vidyā within the Veda is proven.
In this regard, some who are well-versed in the conduct of the Kula tradition maintain four *īṃ*s.
They say that there are three *hṛllekhās* together with the syllable *ī*, these four *ī*-sounds being indicated by such Vedic texts as "kṣemayantaḥ" (*Ṛgveda* 5.47.4).
This is incorrect, because it is improper to speak of the syllable *ī* as being the syllable *īṃ*, and because the root-mantra consists of sixteen phonemes.

And the fact that [the root-vidyā] consists of sixteen phonemes is because it is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the sixteen *Nityās*. This was explained on the occasion of commenting upon the two verses beginning with "The sixty-four tantras" [verse 31] and "Śiva, Śakti, Kāma" [verse 32].

We shall establish this more thoroughly later on. Furthermore, it will be explained that the Vedic basis of this mantra is established by the *saṃjñāna-anuvāka* (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.1) and the *iyaṃ vāva saraghā* (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10) anuvāka.

Let us return to the subject at hand: she who gives birth to the good fortune of those who bow down—those who have bowed down intensely (praṇatāḥ), meaning those people or devotees who possess physical, verbal, and mental salutations;
[we shall praise] her, the mother and progenitor of their good fortune, as she was in the past.

Formerly, having been a beloved woman and assuming the form of a woman, she brought about *kṣobha*—that is, a mental agitation—in the Enemy of the Cities (*puraripu*), the Destroyer of Tripura (*tripurāntaka*). The word "even" (*api*) suggests his mastery over the senses. [This is understood] by the rule beginning with *gatibuddhipratyavasāna...* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).

It has two objects [of the verb]. *Smaro'pi* means "even Smara" (the god of love). The word *api* (also/even) includes the previously mentioned attributes of Viṣṇu; that is, just as Viṣṇu is the *ṛṣi* of your mantra, so too is Smara. Having bowed to you—that is, having approached you for refuge—...
Having properly worshipped the Śrīcakra and having thoroughly practiced your root-mantra,
one whose being has been transformed by your power—
"By that which is to be licked by the eyes of Rati"— meaning, by that which is fit to be licked by the eyes of his own wife Rati,

or rather, by that which is to be gazed upon solely with the eyes of Rati; or else, since Rati is exceedingly beautiful, [it means] "to be drunk in by her eyes," thereby indicating the extreme beauty of Kāmadeva’s body.
With his body—that is, with his physical form—[he overcomes] even the sages, those whose senses are conquered; the word "api" (even) is used here in the sense of possibility.
He prevails—that is, he is capable—within, that is, within the internal mental state. The particle "hi" indicates well-known fact. [He is capable] for the sake of delusion.

In order to arouse the desire for objects such as sound and the like, [it is said]: "Of the great ones, the high-souled ones. Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! Having formerly propitiated you—the mother of good fortune to those who bow before you—Hari, having become a woman, brought even the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) to agitation.
Even Smara, having bowed to you, is indeed capable of inciting inner infatuation even in great sages with his vast body that is to be licked by the eyes of Rati.

It is said that in ancient times Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a woman, lured and slew Kanakasvāmin; one should recall the story of how, being entreated by Śambhu, he showed him such a female form and deluded him. Manmatha, too—
It proceeds, causing agitation in the minds of all sages.
And this has been described in the *Vāmakeśvara-mahātantra* in the *Catuḥśatī*:
"Having previously worshipped [having previously meditated upon] this very Vidyā, the Enchantress of the Three Worlds..."

The Blessed Lord Hari deluded the Enemy of Kāma (Śiva) throughout the three worlds. And even Kāmadeva, having propitiated the Goddess Tripurasundarī, the Queen of the Gods, became the most beautiful and fortunate being in the world. Thus it is said.

Therefore, this undertaking by the poet is intended to declare that wherever there arises a disturbance of the mind rooted in passion, each such instance is obtainable through the grace of the Blessed Goddess. || 5 ||

(p. 12) Although the boldness of Manmatha, acquired through the grace of the Blessed Lady, was described in the preceding verse, nevertheless, regarding Manmatha’s science of the bodiless one (anaṅgavidyā)...
Since Manmatha (the God of Love) is a seer (*ṛṣi*), his extreme audacity is dependent upon him; thus [the author] says:
"His bow is made of flowers, his string consists of bees, his arrows are five, Vasanta is his vassal, and the Malaya breeze is his war-chariot; and yet, he alone [conquers] everything."
Having obtained some indescribable grace from the side-glance of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, the Bodiless One (Kāma) triumphs over this world.

In this verse, there is the ellipsis (adhyāhāra) of *yat* and *tat*. The ellipsis of both [relative and demonstrative pronouns] is established by the convention of all poets. For example, in the *Raghuvamśa*, in the line "vāgarthāviva saṃpṛktau" ("like word and meaning joined together"), [the sense is] "I salute those two who are joined. Likewise, in the phrase "ye nāma kecid iha naḥ... [the same principle applies].

In passages such as *Mālatīmādhava*, "they display contempt," this effort is directed toward him who will be born. The bow (*dhanuḥ*) is the instrument for battle; it is a bow made of flowers (*pauṣpa*), consisting of blossoms. This is because flowers are exceedingly delicate and cannot endure touch.

The intended meaning is that [the bow] is unfit for the functions of a bow, such as bending and drawing. "Maurvī" means a string; "madhukaramayī" means abounding in *madhukara*s, that is, composed of rows of bees (*bhramara*). [This refers to] those which are not mutually connected.

The intended meaning is that it does not connect with the state of being a bowstring (*śiñjinītva*). There are five arrows, that is, five in number. The intended meaning is that for the discharge of these five, remaining silent is the only recourse. Furthermore, five...

By the word *viśikhāḥ*, since these arrows are well known to consist of flowers, the intended meaning is that they lack the capacity to perform the function of [ordinary] arrows. *Vasantaḥ* refers to a particular season, according to the lexicon stating "Vasanta consists of Madhu and Mādhava. *Sāmantaḥ* means a minister. Of him...
The intended meaning is that because it is of the nature of time (*kālātmaka*), its capacity to act as an auxiliary (*sācivyakāritva*) is not logically consistent. *Malayamarut*.

The southern wind (dakṣiṇānila) is the chariot for battle (āyodhanaratha), meaning a vehicle that serves as the means for battle (āyodhana). Because the Malaya breeze resides on Mount Malaya, it is not universal;
even if it were universal, it would not exist at all times; and even if it existed at all times, [it would not be constant].

The intended meaning is that because it lacks form (*nīrūpatva*), it lacks the capacity to perform the function of a chariot. Nevertheless, even though the aforementioned principle is established as common knowledge for all people, [the Lord], being a solitary hero (*asahāya-śūra*)—one without a second—[subdues] the entire (*sakala*) phenomenal world (*prapañca*). "Himagirisute" refers to the daughter of Himagiri; *Himagiri* is a mountain (*giri*) characterized primarily by snow (*hima*).

The word is correct by virtue of belonging to the *śākapārthiva* (and similar) class of compounds. "Her daughter" refers to Nandinī; this is its vocative form. "Whom" means an indescribable one. The particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility.
"Compassion" means pity. "Having obtained" means having received from your *apāṅga*, that is, from your sidelong glance.

The world (*jagat*) consists of that which is moving, since there is no possibility of it being stationary. This refers to what is currently perceived. "Anaṅga" means bodiless; by this, the weakness of the seeker is also indicated. Precisely because of the absence of hands, [the acts of] drawing the bow and fixing the arrow [are impossible].
Even that which is impossible: because of the absence of feet, standing upon a chariot and the like is also impossible;
and because of the absence of a face, eyes, and so forth, conversing with, gazing at, and sitting together with one's friend Madhu are likewise impossible.
The intended meaning is this: the reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "the root *ji* takes the reflexive voice when preceded by *vi* or *parā*."

Here is the word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*): O daughter of the Snowy Mountain! although that bodiless one (*anaṅga*) has a bow made of flowers, a bowstring consisting of bees, five arrows, the spring as his vassal, and the Malaya breeze as his war-chariot—nevertheless, that single bodiless one [is surpassed] by your side-glance.
Having obtained some measure of compassion, one conquers this entire world.
Here, the figure of speech is *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit of the extraordinary), because victory arises even in the absence of the means for victory;
the definition is: "the production of an effect in the absence of its cause. (6)

In order to introduce the nature of the Goddess's manifestation as it appears within the *maṇipūra*— by virtue of the power of the practitioners' contemplation on the fourfold unity, which serves as the basis for the subsequent verse beginning with "In the midst of the ocean of nectar"— he proceeds as follows:
Jingling with a girdle of bells, her breasts like the frontal globes of a young elephant, slender at the waist,
with a face like the full autumn moon— she [holds] a bow, arrows, a noose, and even a goad.
May the self-aggrandizement of the Destroyer of Cities stand before us, held in her palms—
she who wears jingling girdles and tinkling jeweled belts,
whose breasts are like the frontal globes of a young elephant, and who possesses two breasts resembling the frontal globes of a young elephant.

"Slightly bent by her breasts" means that her waist is slightly curved. "Emaciated in the middle" means that her waist (avalagna) is slender; thus, she has a thin waist. "Her face like the full autumn moon":
the autumn moon is the moon in the season of autumn (*śarad*), which is full in all its digits; her face is like that.

She who [possesses these]: a bow, arrows made of flowers, a noose, a cord, and a goad— the word "api" (also) includes exactly what has been mentioned— bearing [these] with her four lotus-hands, that is, with the palms of her hands, in front.
"Having emerged from Maṇipūra into the heart-lotus"—this is the ellipsis. "May she sit"—let her be seated.
"Of us"—of our own. "Of the Destroyer of the Cities"—of Tripurāntaka;
or else, he who churns the three cities—the three syllables that are the seed-mantras of Tripurā—and having churned them, produces the butter (navanīta) within [the heart].

In the Rudrayāmala, that Rudra is called "Puramathita. *Āhopuruṣikā* [is explained as follows]: the word *āho* expresses wonder (*āścarya*), while the word *puruṣa*, which denotes the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is indicated as being denotable by the word *aham* (I). Therefore, *āho* refers to the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*), and this is *āhopuruṣikā*.

This refers to what is called *ahaṅkāra* (ego). That Rudra has the nature of *ahaṅkāra* has been explained in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning with "The Lord is Śiva through Śakti" [Śloka 1], and will be further elaborated upon.
Herein is the construction of the words: She whose girdle and string of bells jingle, whose breasts are like the frontal globes of a young elephant,

who is slender at the waist, whose face is like the full autumn moon, and who holds in her palms a bow, arrows, a noose, and even a goad— she is the self-aggrandizement of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva).
May they be before us.
p.

15) Whatever is to be said on this matter will be explained more thoroughly at the conclusion of the commentary on the six verses beginning with "That which resides in your wheel of command" (verse 36); therefore, one should look there for it.
This is how it must be understood. || 7 ||

In the midst of the ocean of nectar, on an island of jewels surrounded by groves of celestial trees and lush thickets of *nīpa* flowers, within a palace of wish-fulfilling gems, upon a couch in the form of Śiva—
there, on the bed of Paramaśiva, some fortunate ones worship you.
The wave of the bliss of consciousness. || 8 ||

In the midst of the ocean of nectar (*sudhāsindhu*), surrounded by groves of celestial trees (*suraviṭapivāṭī*)— that is, encircled by clusters of *kalpa* trees— on a jewel-island (*maṇidvīpa*) consisting of precious gems, which possesses groves of *nīpa* trees (*nīpopavana*). [Of the *nīpas*...]

In a garden filled with *kadamba* trees, in a palace made of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), in a temple in the form of Śiva, whose nature is Śiva and whose form is Śakti— that is, in a triangular dais or couch— [she who] dwells upon the bed of Paramaśiva.

The fortunate ones— only a few rare individuals who have achieved their life's purpose through your grace— worship and serve you, she whose abode and dwelling place is that couch, the Supreme Śiva himself; [they worship] the wave of consciousness-bliss, where "consciousness" (cit) means knowledge.
That form is bliss, the unsurpassed happiness; its "wave" is in the form of an overflowing abundance.

The construction of the words here is as follows: O Blessed One! in the midst of the ocean of nectar, on a jeweled island surrounded by groves of celestial trees and possessing gardens of *nīpa* trees, within a palace of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*).
On a couch in the form of Śiva, you who reside upon the supreme Śiva-couch as a wave of consciousness-bliss— only a few fortunate ones worship you.

16) Here, this should be kept in mind: the venerable teachers (Bhagavatpādācāryas), who have reached the further shore of the Samaya doctrine and are devoted to the conduct of the Samaya, offer praise to the Blessed Lady in the form of the Samaya.

The secret is this: "conduct according to the *samaya*" means delighting in internal worship; "conduct according to the *kula*" means delighting in external worship. And this [was stated] during the explanation of the verse beginning with "in your foundation, at the root, together with the *samaya*" [verse 41].

We shall establish this more thoroughly. The Śrīcakra has another name, "Viyaccakra" (the Sky-Cakra). Its status as Viyaccakra, however, arises from its being worshiped by the sky (*viyat*). This worship by the sky is twofold: that born of the internal space (*daharākāśa*) and that born of the external space (*bāhyākāśa*). [The latter is] that born of the external space...
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark, a clean cloth, or a plate of gold, silver, and so forth, within the space of the external sky or upon a seat and the like, one performs the worship.
The elders say that this very practice is "Kaula-pūjā. This will be explained further below.

It is explained: the worship of the wheel within the space of the heart-cavity, which is called "born of the small ether" (*daharākāśaja*), is precisely what the observers of the *samaya* call "the *samaya*-worship. This too will be further elaborated upon later. Therein, above the four *yoni*s situated below that consist of Śiva, [is the following].
The name of the station of the Bindu (baindavasthāna), which is the lower region of the fivefold Yoni consisting of the upward-abiding Power (ūrdhvasthitaśakti), is Sudhāsindhu (the Ocean of Nectar).
The abode of the *bindu* is an ocean of nectar; there are five wombs and celestial trees.

Right there is a row of *nīpa* trees, and in their midst is a jeweled pavilion. Within that is the supreme temple of the Goddess, fashioned from wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*). Upon a great couch whose essence is Śiva, with Maheśāna as its pillow, [the Goddess resides].
In that most delightful place, Sadāśiva is the couch, the four-legged animals are the servants,
and Mahendra is the spittoon; there dwells the Supreme Sovereign,
Mahātripurasundarī, having pierced the solar orb of Śiva.
Causing the lunar orb to melt, she— delighted by the supreme bliss flowing from the nectar produced therein—
that woman of the Kula, having abandoned her own lineage, reaches the supreme rain.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhairavayāmala*, the great tantra of the *Vāmakeśvara*,
within the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka-vidyā*: "The supreme abode of the Goddess."
The meaning of this is as follows: the temple of the Goddess is called the Śrīcakra, which consists of forty-three triangles.
Therefore, it is said [to be] "on the couch in the form of Śiva," because the Bindu-abode is a constituent part of the Śrīcakra composed of triangles.

The secret point is this: because the station of Bindu (Baindava) is primary, and because a subordinate element is included within the primary, its inclusion therein has been stated. The meaning of the word *bhṛtakāḥ* is "servants" (*bhṛtyāḥ*); [these] are Druhiṇa, Hari, Rudra, and Īśvara. And these have departed.

The meaning of the phrase "having pierced the solar orb of Śivā" will be explained in the commentary on the verse beginning with "the state of Mañca, O Druhiṇa" (verse 92). Regarding this, "Śivā" is the power named Kuṇḍalinī; she pierces the "solar orb," which is situated above the heart-lotus.

"Having divided," meaning having separated and covered; having closed the Brahma-door situated above the solar orb (arka-maṇḍala), one "devours," that is, causes to melt, the lunar orb (indu-maṇḍala) situated within the thousand-petaled lotus. Therefore...

The noble woman, the Kuṇḍalinī power, having abandoned the *kula*— the path of the *kula*, the path of the *suṣumṇā*— and having taken her stand right there in the lunar orb, performs the supreme rain, the most excellent showering,
raining down upon the seventy-two thousand channels.

The word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The intended meaning is that Kuṇḍalinī, having returned to her own place and reached Svādhiṣṭhāna, sleeps there. [Furthermore,] Śiva and the others assume the states of being a couch, a pillow, a spittoon, and a resting place.
[The justification for its being a couch is because it serves as a *patadgraha* (receptacle) for the gods.
Because the gods can assume any form at will (*kāmarūpatva*), it is suitable for the purpose of their extremely close service.
Sadāśiva has stated this very point in brief:
In the Nandana garden within the ocean of nectar, she dwells in the center of a jeweled pavilion;
she has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, possesses four arms, and has three eyes.
Having meditated upon the Auspicious One (Śivā), who is the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) and who holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow,

and having visualized the wheel-diagram (yantra) situated within the heart, one established in the vow should perform the recitation (japa) while contemplating the Supreme Goddess through the previously described method of meditation. Having thus reflected, he should perform the recitation.
One should practice meditation. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that by this [commentary], the two verses beginning with "anena kvaṇatkāñcīdāmā" and "sudhāsindhormadhye" have been explained as a single unit.
Having pierced the earth at the *mūlādhāra*, the fire situated somewhere in the *maṇipūra*,
the wind in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the ether above in the heart, and even the mind between the eyebrows—
having thus broken through the entire path of *kula*— she remains in secret with her Lord in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
You dwell [in this state]. || 9 ||
The earth is the *pṛthivī-tattva* (earth-element) located in the *mūlādhāra*, that is, at the root in the region of the anus;

it is the wheel (*cakra*) that serves as the foundation for all, hence it is called the *mūlādhāra*. In that *mūlādhāra*, the earth exists as the support of all because it stands there as the *mūlādhāra*. However, in its absence:
There may be either the falling away or the emergence of the body.

Thus it is stated in the *Rudrarahasya*. The meaning is that in the absence of the *mūlādhāra*, which consists of the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*), the body would either go upward or fall downward. "Ka" refers to the water element (*udakatattva*).
The word "api" (also) includes the fire mentioned in relation to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. [This occurs] in the *maṇipūra*.

The Maṇipūra-cakra is so called because the Goddess resides there and fills that region with jewels; it is the third lotus where, during the occasion of the internal worship of the Samayins, various ornaments inlaid with clusters of diverse gems are offered to the Goddess.
This is the secret: that the fire-element (hutavaha), which abides as the *pratiṣṭhā* principle,
having itself presided over [by its own will] the knot in the wheel named Svādhiṣṭhāna, belonging to the Blessed Lady Kuṇḍalinī.
Having established oneself, one performs the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). As it is stated in the *Yogadīpikā*:
"This Rudra-knot [is located] at the limit of the tip of the power of self-consecration."
(p. 19) Although the Svādhiṣṭhāna should be described as being above the Ādhāra-cakra, nevertheless,
following the sequence of the arising of the principles (tattvas) beginning with space, it is treated here in reverse order.
It should be understood that the description of the Maṇipūra Cakra has been completed.
This has been fully explained during the commentary on the six verses beginning with "And this [is located] in your Ājñācakra" (verse 36). [In the] heart...

In the heart-space, in the cakra named Anāhata, it is called "Unstruck" (anāhata) because it is the locus of the unstruck sound (anāhatanāda). Above the wind— the wind-element— and above the space— the space-element— [it resides] in the Viśuddhi-cakra, which is like pure crystal.

Its name is Viśuddhi. "Manas" refers to the principle of the mind; the word "api" (also) serves to include what has been previously mentioned. It is located in the *bhrūmadhya*, the space between the eyebrows, at the *ājñācakra*. Here, the prefix *āṅ* signifies "slightness"; *jñā* means knowledge; thus, it is where "slight knowledge" (*īṣaj-jñāna*) arises.

This concerns the subject matter of the Goddess for practitioners (*sādhakas*). Because of the intense agitation caused by the piercing of the *brahmagranthi*, the Goddess remains in the *ājñācakra* for only a moment;
because she then manifests to the practitioners in the form of a streak of lightning, this [center] is named the *ājñācakra*. Thus it is established.

The verb ending is to be supplied everywhere by means of a transposition (*tiṅ-vyatyaya*). Having broken through the entire path of the *kula*— that is, the entire *suṣumnā* path— even while uniting with the thousand-petaled lotus in the *sahasrāra*, you sport in secret solitude with your husband, Sadāśiva.
You play.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! You are present as the Earth (Mahī) in the Mūlādhāra, as Water (Ka) in the Maṇipūra, and likewise as Fire (Hutavaha) in the Svādhiṣṭhāna; as Air (Marut) in the Heart, as Space (Ākāśa) above [in the Viśuddha], and as Mind (Manas) in the space between the eyebrows (Bhrūmadhya).
Thus, You abide even as Space.
The change of gender applies everywhere by ellipsis: even having pierced the entire path of the Kula, you sport in secret with your Lord in the thousand-petaled lotus.
In this regard, the following should be considered:
there are six chakras consisting of the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā. These...
The principles (tattvas) consisting of earth, fire, water, air, ether, and mind reside within those cakras in the form of subtle elements (tanmātras).
The subtle elements (*tanmātra*), however, consist of smell, form, taste, touch, and sound.
The group of eleven sense organs is subsumed by the principle of the mind (*manastattva*) situated in the *ājñācakra*.
Thus, twenty-one principles have been explained. [This was done] in private with the Lord (*pati*).
By the phrase "you dwell upon the thousand-petaled [lotus]," the fourfold reality (*tattvacatuṣṭaya*) is indicated;
that fourfold reality consists of *māyā*, *śuddhavidyā*, *maheśvara*, and *sadāśiva*.
Thus, combined, there are twenty-five principles (*tattva*) extending up to *māyā*.
[As previously explained, those are] called "prākṛta" (natural) because they are joined with *māyā*.
*Māyā*, when conjoined with Maheśvara, brings about his state as the individual soul (*jīva*). That *jīva* is indeed *prākṛta*. But *Śuddhavidyā*, when conjoined with Sadāśiva, [is different].

She is conventionally designated as the "Kalā called Sādākhya. Therefore, the Blessed Lady, having transcended the twenty-four principles (tattvas) along with Śiva, and sporting together with Sadāśiva as the twenty-fifth, has attained the nature of the twenty-sixth principle and is thus the Supreme Self (Paramātman).

It is sung [in scripture]: this is what is meant—the *sādākhyā* category, when united with Sadāśiva, who consists of twenty-five principles, becomes the twenty-sixth; for their union constitutes a distinct ontological principle (*tattva*).
Nor is the union of the two itself composed of both, because it takes the form of identity (*tādātmya*).
The secret is that it is indeed a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*). As for the Vedic statement, "The self becomes the twenty-fifth" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.6),
it should be understood that this is intended to establish the principle of Sadāśiva, and not to signify a merging [of the principles].
Now, one might object: the station of Bindu is situated in the center of the Śrīcakra because it lies above the four Śiva-cakras and below the five Śakti-cakras;
furthermore, since the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra-padma) is located at the crown of the head, it exists above all of them.
If it is argued that its status as the location of the *bindu* is not tenable—
listen then to the secret of the Bhāgavata doctrine:
"By means of the four *śiva-cakras* and the five *śakti-cakras*..."
The Śrīcakra, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, should be known as the body of the two, Śiva and Śivā.
In such passages as these, there are five wheels of power (*śakticakra*), consisting of a triangle, an octagon, two decagons, and a fourteen-sided figure.

Regarding the wheels (*cakras*): the *śivacakras*, however, consist of an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, three girdles (*mekhalā*), and three enclosures (*bhūpura*). Therefore, the *śivacakras* are situated outside the *śakticakras*; for it is impossible for Śiva to be outside of Śakti, and thus they are called *śivacakras*.

Having drawn [the elements] in the form of the *bindu*, they are established within the circle of power (*śakticakra*). For this very reason, some say that the *bindu*—which consists of the four circles of Śiva (*śivacakra*)—is completed by pervading the five circles of power; thus, there is the identity of Śiva and Śakti.

Others, however, say that the identity of Śiva and Śakti occurs through this manner: the identity of the *bindu* and the triangle; the identity of the eight-cornered [figure] and the eight-petalled lotus; the identity of the pair of ten-spoked [figures] and the sixteen-petalled lotus; and the identity of the fourteen-spoked [figure] and the *bhūpura*. Here, by the word *bindu*, [the following is meant].

What is perceived as a circular form is a representative of the four wheels of Śiva (*śivacakra*), and not the bindu situated in the center of a square; rather, that [bindu] resides within the thousand-petaled lotus and is the primordial source of the support (*ādhāra*) and the self-established (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) ten-petaled [lotuses].

The body entered into the union of Śiva and Śakti is the twenty-sixth principle, called Sādākhya. With that [Sādākhya], there is no identity for Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, because it transcends Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. This will be explained in detail further on. Therefore:

The nectar-ocean situated within the lunar disc at the center of the thousand-petaled lotus is indeed the place where the Blessed Lady sports; thus, the two verses— "you sport in secret with your husband in the thousand-petaled lotus" and "in the midst of the nectar-ocean"— have one and the same meaning.
The Secret: Regarding this very matter, Śiva spoke to Pārvatī in the *Candrajñānavidyā* of the *Bhairavayāmala*:
"By means of the four wheels of Śiva and the five wheels of Śakti—by these nine wheels..."
The perfected Śrīcakra is the body of Śiva and Śivā.
The triangle, the octagon, the two decagons, and the fourteen-spoked [figure]—
these are the five wheels of Śakti.
The Bindu, the eight-petalled lotus, the sixteen-petalled lotus, and the square— these are the four Śiva-cakras in successive order.
The Bindu is joined to the triangle; the eight-petalled lotus is in the eight-spoked [cakra];
the sixteen-spoked [cakra] is in the two ten-spoked [cakras]; and the earth-mansion is in the fourteen-cornered [cakra].
Who knows the relationship of inseparable concomitance between the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the *cakras*? He alone is a knower of the *cakra*.
The triangular, the eight-cornered, the two ten-cornered, the fourteen-cornered,
and the four-cornered— these are the six corner-wheels in sequence.
The wise know the Mūlādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Maṇipūraka, the Anāhata,
the one called Viśuddhi, and the Ājñā-cakra.
O Pārvatī, the corner-wheels (koṇacakrāṇi) are the essential forms of Your support; Śakti is remembered as being triangular in form, and Śiva as being of the nature of the Bindu.
"Therefore, there is a relationship of inseparable concomitance between the bindu and the triangle."
Prior to this— [the practitioners] know [the seat] to be downward-facing, quadrangular, and consisting of the Śiva-cakra.
Accordingly, it should be understood that the statement "four downward-facing triangles are of the nature of Śiva" intends to show that the external Śiva-cakras exist in that very form.
Alternatively— according to the Kaula tradition, there are four downward-facing triangles representing Śiva and five upward-facing triangles representing Śakti.
In the Kaula system, when drawn according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), the Śrīcakra consists of nine triangles.

Although all of this should have been explained during the commentary on the verse beginning with "by the four Śrīkaṇṭhas" (verse 11), it is stated here because it must necessarily be addressed in the context of the phrase "you sport in secret with your Lord upon the thousand-petaled lotus," as it is useful for both parts.
Only a small portion has been stated here; the full detail, however, should be understood from that very source. || 9 ||

Sprinkling the phenomenal world once more with the streams of nectar flowing from between Your pair of feet— streams that possess the splendor of the traditional lore of aesthetic rasa— You sleep, having returned to Your own ground and made Yourself Your own bed, coiled like a serpent.
In the hollow of the family-pit. || 10 ||
(23) By means of the showers— that is, the downpours— of streams of nectar (*sudhā*).
Here, the word *āsāra* alone signifies a "downpour of streams," as is evident from its association with the word *dhārā*.
Since the word *āsāra* denotes merely a "downpour," there is no tautology. Alternatively, the *āsāras* are streams of nectar that serve as its receptacle;
by these, which have fallen between the pair of feet—that is, between the two lotus-feet—...

The sprinkler, flowing with [nectar] trickling from within— that is, streaming from the middle region— sprinkles the *prapañca*, the network of seventy-two thousand channels; furthermore, even after that sprinkling, [she does so] from the moon, which is the splendor of the tradition of nectar (*rasāmnāya*).
The term *rasāmnāyamahaḥ* is well-known in the *Yāmalas* and the *Kalānidhi*.

According to its etymology, it refers to one whose splendor (*mahaḥ*)—that is, radiance—is of the nature of *rasa*, meaning nectar (*sudhā*), which signifies an abundance of qualities (*guṇānām ādhikyam*). Having attained [this], that is, having reached it.
Having made one's own ground— the *ādhāra-cakra*— which resembles a serpent (*bhujaga*),
possessing three and a half coils (*adhyuṣṭavalaya*) characterized by a specific state of coiling,
and having taken up, maintained, and dwelt within that as one's own self, relying upon one's true nature.
"You sleep"—you are asleep—in the *kulakuṇḍa*. *Ku* is the earth-element (*pṛthivītattva*) wherein [the seed] dissolves;

that *kula* is the *ādhāra-cakra*. By metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*), the path of the *suṣumnā* is called *kula*. For this very reason, the *kaulas* are worshippers of *kula*, meaning they serve the *ādhāra*; such is their state as *kaulas*.

"This" refers to their secret; this will be further elucidated later. At the base of the *suṣumnā*—the path of the *kula*—there is a *kuṇḍa* (pit) shaped like the bulb of a lotus, which is the *ādhārakanda* (foundation-bulb).
Within that hollow space, there is a cavity similar to the pore situated in the center of a lotus bulb.

The "vessel" (kuṇḍa) is described as such; the intended meaning is that the Kuṇḍalinī power resides there within the hollow situated in the center of the supporting bulb (ādhārakanda), resembling a lotus fiber.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! sprinkling the phenomenal world with showers of streams of nectar flowing from between Your pair of feet, You have once again attained Your own ground from the presence of the light of the tradition of Rasa.
Having made yourself a coiled serpent resting within a circle,
you sleep in the hollow of the primordial womb (kulakuṇḍa).
In this regard, the following should be considered: that the lunar orb is situated at the head is established in all yoga treatises.
In the view of those who observe the *samaya*, that [moon] is indeed the *Śrīcakra*.

Since the lunar orb consists of sixteen digits (*kalā*), and because the increase and decrease of these digits during the sixteen days beginning with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) will be explained regarding Śrīvidyā, this very [cakra] is the lunar orb.

It has been demonstrated in the *Subhagodayavyākhyāna* that even the lunar orb situated externally is indeed the Śrīcakra; however, that is a great secret. Therefore, [the worship] is performed within the center of the lunar disc, which consists of the Śrīcakra located inside the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the crown of the head.

Having bathed the entire body of the practitioner with the nectar-like waters used for washing the lotus feet of the standing Bhagavatī, that Bhagavatī again enters the Ādhāra-kuṇḍa in the form of a serpent and takes hold of the Suṣumṇā.
"She sleeps," as it is said in the *Vāmakeśvara-mahātantra*: "The power named Kuṇḍalinī, auspicious and resembling a lotus fiber, rests in the *mūlādhāra* in the form of a coiled serpent."
The meaning is that she is impure, momentary, and like lightning.
Having bitten the root-tuber with the tip of her hood as if it were a lotus-root, and having grasped the tail with her mouth,
she has taken refuge in the *brahmarandhra*.
Seated in the lotus posture, composed, contracting the anus, the practitioner, with his mind fixed on *kumbhaka*, causes the vital air to move upward.
By the force of the impact of the wind, the fire situated in its own locus blazes;
and by the impacts of that blazing fire and the wind, the sovereign serpent is awakened.
Then, having pierced the Rudra-knot, one pierces the Viṣṇu-knot;
and having pierced the Brahma-knot, one pierces the six lotuses.
"In the thousand-petaled lotus, Śakti rejoices together with Śiva; that state should be known as the supreme, and it alone is the cause of liberation. Thus [it is said].
(25) Scripture also establishes the sprinkling of the phenomenal world with the showers of the nectar-streams from the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lady. For instance:

The gate of the world, radiant, pure, luminous, shining, and glorious; yielding the stream of immortality in many ways—may it establish us, well-established, in the world of the living. [Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.1.32]

The meaning of this is as follows: it is the door—that is, the means of attaining—for the world, for one’s own place of residence, for *sāyujya* (union), for *sārṣṭi* (equality of power) and so forth, or for the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
"Radiant" (*arcimat*) means that rays (*arciṣ*)—that is, beams of light—are present in it; thus, it means "possessing radiance" (*arciṣmat*).

The elision of the letter *s* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). "Mayūkhas" means rays. "Pavitra" means that which is itself exceedingly pure and the cause of purity for others. The repetition of the words "jyotiṣmat," "bhrājamānam," and "mahasvat" is for the purpose of praising "arciṣmat. Alternatively—
The *mātṛkā*-wheel is threefold (*trikhaṇḍa*), consisting of the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire;
this will be explained [later]. By the term "radiant" (*arciṣmat*), the one hundred and eight fiery rays are denoted. By the term "luminous" (*jyotiṣmat*)...
One hundred and thirty-six lunar lights (*jyotis*) are indicated;
by the word "luminous" (*mahaḥsvat*), one hundred and sixteen solar rays (*mahas*) or beams are comprised. And this [total] on earth is fifty-six [as stated in verse 14].

We shall explain this more skillfully on the occasion of commenting upon the verse. [The Lord] is sprinkling— that is, pouring out— in manifold ways, through the seventy-two thousand channels, streams of nectar, that is, flows of ambrosia.
The meaning is that he should rain down streams of nectar situated within the lunar orb, purified by his own ablution; such is his foot.
The word *caraṇa* is neuter; as Amara states: "pada, aṅghri, and caraṇa are not feminine.

May He establish us—us practitioners—in this world, in the phenomenal realm (*prapañca*), making us well-situated and satisfied, or rather, making us wise (*sudhiyaḥ*) by generating the light of understanding (*buddhiprakāśa*), and thus nourish us.
But surely this mantra is prescribed as the *yājyā* (offering verse) for the *apāghā* sacrifices;
and since mantras have the nature of manifesting the meanings present [in the ritual]— namely, their respective deities—
it is only the word accompanied by the dative case, as in "to the movement, *svāhā*," that [is appropriate].
If it is argued that this explanation is inconsistent because [the word] is joined with a dative ending and thus functions as a deity,
it is said in reply: regarding this, the venerable Bhagavatpāda says— having abandoned the prepared food—
"The evil-minded one wanders for alms.
This is the intended meaning: since the authorship of the Veda is unestablished, it is accepted by all learned people as being capable of bestowing its fruits.

In the mantra "svāhā to the feet for the sake of [attaining] feet," it is the very feet of the Blessed Lady— distinguished by such qualifiers as "the door to the world whose power is determined through the usage of the elders"—
that are denoted by the word "feet. || 10 ||
In the preceding verse, it was stated that the Śrīcakra consists of the lunar orb; he now teaches that very Śrīcakra:
"By the four Śrīkaṇṭhas and also by the five Śivayuvatis..."
The nine root-natures (mūlaprakṛtis) of Śambhu, having been differentiated,
have transformed together with the forty-four petals, the eight digits (kalās), the four triangles, the three circles, and the three lines into the corners of your sanctuary.

(27) By the four Śrīkaṇṭhas, who are numbered as four; [the term] "Śrī" (glory) is so called because it "destroys" (śṛṇāti) or "slays" (hinasti); he who has poison (viṣa) in his throat is Śrīkaṇṭha—[namely], Hara. They...

The corners are also Śrīkaṇṭhas; because of identity with them, they are designated as such, and for this very reason the use of the plural number is established. The meaning is "by those whose nature is Śrīkaṇṭha. By the Śivayuvatīs, that is, the Śaktis, the establishment of the plural number is as before. The meaning is "by those whose nature is Śakti."
[The phrase] "by five" [is used]. The word *api* (also/even) indicates differentiation; [it means] by those that are "distinctly differentiated," that is, intensely differentiated.
This intensity, however, arises because the station of *bindu* exists in the center of the wheel of Śiva and Śakti.
And this should be understood according to the system of the *Samaya*, in the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), when drawing the five wheels.

According to the Kaula doctrine, when drawing the wheel of nine triangles (*navayonicakra*) by means of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should understand that there is a state of separation due to their being positioned with faces turned upwards and downwards. By this, the meaning is that both [the upper and lower sets] remain distinct from one another.
In the word "of Śambhu" (*śambhoḥ*), the fifth case ending is used; by the word *śambhu*, four [triangles] are indicated.

The Śrīkaṇṭhas are said to be nine, that is, numbering nine; the word "api" (also/even) includes the great multiplicity that will be described hereafter. They are the root-natures (*mūlaprakṛtis*), the fundamental causes of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); for this very reason, they are designated by the term "source" (*yoni*). Nine.
The sources (yonis) consist of nine elements (dhātus). Thus it is said in the Kāmika:
"The elements of skin, blood, flesh, fat, and bone have Śakti as their root;
the elements of marrow, semen, vital breath (prāṇa), and the individual soul (jīva) have Śiva as their root. These are the nine elements."
The body arises from nine sources. The "vital element" (*jīvadhātu*) is so called because it is the substratum of life;
indeed, it is the element of *ojas* (vital essence) that is termed the vital element. As stated by Vāgbhaṭa:
"Among the elements beginning with *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and ending with *śukra* (semen), the *prasāda* (pure essence) is the most excellent."
"The element that serves as the support for the living soul is *ojas*"; this reading, which is an additional explanatory form, is seen in the *ta*-manuscript. "The tenth source is indeed one;
the tenth element is indeed one" is an alternative reading. "She is the supreme power, the sovereign of that. Thus [it is said].
The tenth source is the station of Bindu; the meaning is that its mistress is the mistress of that body.
Thus, once the single *piṇḍāṇḍa* (the microcosmic egg) had arisen, the *brahmāṇḍa* (the macrocosmic egg) likewise came into being.
The five elements belonging to Śakti, beginning with Māyā, belong to Śiva; and Māyā...
Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva— these twenty-five principles are included within that very [category].
The eleven sense organs and the subtle elements beginning with sound are referred to by the word "tat" (that).
Know this entire world of moving and non-moving things to consist of Śiva and Śakti;
the meaning is that the "moving" refers to the microcosmic body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) and the "non-moving" refers to the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Some, however, assert fifty-one principles (*tattva*). For instance:

the five gross elements (*bhūta*), the pentad of subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), and likewise the five organs of action (*karmendriya*); the seven constituents (*dhātu*) beginning with the skin, and the five...
The vital breaths and other winds; the mind, ego, intellect, and the qualities (guṇas);
primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa); attachment, knowledge, limited agency (kalā), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla);
as well as illusion (māyā), pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti.
And they know the Śiva-principle and the [other] principles in their proper sequence. Thus [it is said].

These fifty-one principles (*tattvas*) are expounded in all the *Śaiva Purāṇas*, such as the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*. The meaning of this is as follows: the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—exist in the form of both effects and causes.
The five subtle elements (tanmātras)—namely, smell and the others—are the causes of earth and the other gross elements.
The organs of knowledge consist of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
The organs of action consist of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. These are the constituents (dhātus).
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; the vital airs—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna; the mind (manas), which is the power consisting of thought;
the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti), which is the power that generates the sense of "I"; discernment (khyāti), which is knowledge; and the qualities (guṇas).
Sattva, rajas, and tamas;
prakṛti is the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti); puruṣa is the individual soul (jīva); rāga is desire; vidyā is knowledge.
The knowledge consisting of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) produced by the scriptures. The *kalās* are three hundred and sixty in number. *Niyati* is the power that governs or restricts.
*Kāla* is the power of withdrawal or dissolution. *Māyā* is the knowledge of illusionists and the like.
[Kādyajñāna is also a reading. Śuddhavidyā is the liberating knowledge.
Maheśvara, permeated by the quality of rajas, is the agent of creation. Sadāśiva is the agent of both creation and maintenance. Śakti belongs to both Maheśvara and Sadāśiva.
The power of protection and creation; by the word "and" (ca), the power of destruction in the form of time is also included. The Śiva-tattva is of the nature of being pure, awakened, and liberated.
Among all these principles (tattvas), several principles are subsumed within some of them.
The seven constituents, beginning with the skin, are included within the elements. The vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, are included within air. Thus, their inclusion is indeed within the elements.
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is included within the mind (manas). Manifestation (khyāti), which is knowledge (vidyā), is included within [the category of] knowledge.
The qualities (guṇas) are included within primordial nature (prakṛti), while primordial nature itself is included within power (śakti).
The person (puruṣa) is included within Maheśvara. Limited agency (kalā) is included within pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), while necessity (niyati) is included within power alone.

Kāla (Time) is included within Maheśvara and Sadāśiva; Śakti is included within Śuddhavidyā; and the Śiva-tattva is included within the Sadāśiva-tattva. Thus, the principles (tattvas) are exactly twenty-five.
The five elements, the pentad of subtle essences (*tanmātra*), the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the principle of the mind (*manas*),
and the four consisting of Māyā, Viśuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva— these [are the categories].
The twenty-five principles (tattvas) are accepted by all because they are supported by the Śruti.
Thus, the Śruti states: "The Self is the twenty-fifth" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.2.6).
Therefore, alternative enumerations of principles, such as the thirty-six principles and so forth, are also in accordance with the Śruti.

It should be understood that he is beyond the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Therefore, [the ultimate reality] is the union of Śiva and Śakti, transcending all principles; from that alone arises the manifestation of the universe. As it is said in the *Subhagodaya*:
"Even the Supreme, if devoid of Śakti, is not capable of accomplishing anything; [only when endowed with her] is he capable."
O Supreme Goddess, this may be so if he should be joined with Śakti. Thus it is said.

30) There is much that could be said on this point; however, we have already established it more thoroughly during the course of our commentary on the *Subhagodaya*. Therefore, enough with excessive detail.
Let us return to the subject at hand.

By these forty-four [elements], namely the eight petals (*vasudala*), the sixteen digits (*kalā*), the four circles (*valaya*), and the three lines (*rekhā*)— wherein "vasu" refers to the number eight,
as the word *vasu* indicates the number eight— the term *vasudala* signifies the eight petals.

*Kalāśra* means sixteen *kalās*; by the word *kalā*, the number sixteen is indicated. By the word *aśra*, a petal (*dala*) is indicated. Therefore, *kalāśra* means a sixteen-petaled [lotus]. *Trivalaya* refers to three enclosures (*valayas*).

"Samāhāraḥ" means a triple circle, that is, a triple girdle. "Trirekhāḥ" means lines in the form of circular enclosures, that is, three square enclosures (bhūpura). And these three square enclosures are provided with gates on the four sides. Thus it has been said:

Endowed with a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, a pair of ten-cornered figures, a fourteen-cornered figure, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and a sixteen-cornered figure, together with circles and three protective walls, and possessing four gates on all sides— this is declared to be the Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity.
Thus also says the Śruti:
"The city of yours has seven gates and four entrances" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka).
The meaning of this is: "having seven gates" means having four entrances.

There is also the elision of the vowel *a* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). "Aṭṭāragamaṃ" means [the city] that is difficult to access (*agama*) due to the three encircling walls (*aṭṭāra*, i.e., *prākāravalaya*). "Tā" refers to those very elements (*bhūtāni*).
O Blessed One! Your city, the fortress consisting of the Śrīcakra, is to be withdrawn.
The meaning is "that which effects withdrawal. The intended sense is that the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Maheśvara dissolve right there.
Some explain it thus: "saṃhārya" means it should be written according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
That is not correct, because according to the Kaula doctrine itself, the cakra is to be drawn according to the sequence of withdrawal. Let us return to the subject at hand.
p.

31) Together with them, [there are] "your refuge-corners": a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the refuge" (*śaraṇa*), meaning the house or abode, namely the *bindu*-mandala, and the "corners" (*koṇāḥ*).

Therefore, the meaning is that there are forty-four corners. Now, one might object: according to the sequence beginning with "the point (bindu) and the triangle," if one includes both the triangle and the point, there would be forty-six corners; if the point is excluded, there would be forty-five corners.
If this is argued— true, by virtue of the arrangement, the two lower corners of the triangle are contained within the octagon;
therefore, there are indeed only forty-three corners.
The explanation is that "koṇā" is a *dvandva* compound meaning "with Śaraṇa.

Alternatively, there is a variant reading, "trayaścatvāriṃśat" (forty-three); in that case, the meaning is quite clear. "Pariṇatāḥ" means having reached transformation (*pariṇāma*). This is the meaning.
The Śakticakras consist of triangles, octagons, pairs of decagons, and fourteen-sided figures;
there are four [other cakras] consisting of an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, three girdles, and three enclosures (bhūpuras).
The Śiva-cakras: within the triangle is the eight-petalled lotus; within the eight-cornered [figure] is the sixteen-petalled lotus;
within the pair of ten-spoked [figures] is the triple girdle; and within the nine-cornered [figure] is the earth-house (bhūgṛha).
This is said to be "internally contained" (*antarbhūta*) and "transformed" (*pariṇata*). And this has already been explained previously.

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! the corners of your shelter are formed by the five young wives of Śiva—emerged from Śambhu through the four Śrīkaṇṭhas—and by all nine root-natures (mūlaprakṛtis).
Together with the eight petals, the sixteen digits, the four triangles, the three circles, and the three lines, they total forty-four.
In this regard, the following should be considered: in this wheel (cakra), there are twenty-eight locations of vital points (marmasthāna) and twenty-four joints (sandhi).
Now, one might ask: "Are there not only twenty-four vital points (*marmāṇi*), so how can there be twenty-eight?
32) The point where two lines meet is designated as a joint (*sandhi*).
"Those who know the vital points (marman) recognize the junction where the three lines meet as a vital point. Thus [it is said].

It is said: although the three lines of the three Śiva-cakras—the eight-petalled, the sixteen-petalled, and the three girdles with the three enclosures—do not constitute a point of intersection, they are designated as "marmas" (vital points) by scriptural authority. As it is stated in the *Candrajñānavidyā*:
"Four circles with sixteen, twenty, eighteen, and eight spokes;
twenty-eight vital points (marmas) and twenty-four joints. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: by counting the points where three lines intersect in the fourteen-angled, the pair of ten-angled, and the eight-angled figures, there are twenty-four vital points (*marmasthāna*); together with the four circles that constitute the Śiva-cakra, there are twenty-eight.

Since it is difficult to understand all of this without knowing how to draw the *cakra*, the method of drawing the *cakra* is now described. That method is of two kinds: by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) and by way of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Drawing according to the sequence of withdrawal belongs exclusively to the Kaula path.
Nevertheless, that method is examined for the sake of fully understanding the nine sources.
First, having drawn a circle in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), and having drawn nine lines within that circle,
one should produce a triangle from the two ends of the western line and join it with the sixth line relative to itself; likewise from the two ends of the eastern line.
Having produced a triangle from one's own perspective, one should join it with the seventh line.
Having produced a triangle from the two ends of the second western line, one should join it from one's own perspective with the eighth [line]. From the two ends of the second eastern line...

Having produced a triangle, one should join it with the eighth [line] relative to itself. Then, from the two ends of the first and third lines— east and west— one should draw a hexagon [having produced the hexagon, one should join it with a circle, according to the Pa manuscript].

Having formed a triangle from the two ends of the western line among the three short lines situated in the center of the hexagon, one should join it with the fifth [line] relative to itself. Likewise,
having formed a triangle from the two ends of the eastern line, [one should join it] with the fifth relative to itself.
One should join [the lines];
having produced a triangle from the two ends of the very short line situated in the center.

One should join it with the third line relative to itself. In this way, there are twenty-four vital points (*marmas*) and twenty-four joints; this is the *navayonicakra*. This is the secret of the Kaula doctrine.

The sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), however, is the path of the convention (*samayamārga*). That is described as follows: first, having drawn a triangle and placed a dot (*bindu*) in its center, one draws another triangle above the dot, piercing through it, and then draws another triangle within that one with its apex pointing east.
From the tip of the first triangle, one should draw another triangle facing westward.
In this manner, the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭakoṇacakra*) is produced. From this very [wheel], one should produce the ten-spoked wheel (*daśāra*).
It is as follows: from the two ends of the eastern and western lines of the eight-spoked [wheel]...
Having produced a hexagon, one should produce four triangles from the four points located at the vital spots (marmasthāna) situated in the intermediate directions;
then, above the source (yoni) located within the octagon, one should join a line extending from south to north across the three triangles in the northeast and southeast corners. Thus.

One should join [the spokes] from the west; thus there comes to be a ten-spoked [wheel]. From this very ten-spoked wheel, one should again produce another ten-spoked wheel according to the method described above. From this very ten-spoked wheel, one should produce a fourteen-spoked [wheel]. It is as follows:

One should produce a hexagon from the two endpoints of the eastern and western lines of the first decagon. From the four points located at the vital spots (*marman*) within that hexagon, one should produce a set of four triangles. Then, from the four upper vital spots...
Having produced a set of four triangles according to the method of the ten voids (*daśāranya*), one should join the eastern and western lines.
Thus, there are forty-three angles, twenty-four junctions, and twenty-four vital points (*marman*). This is the secret of the *Samayamata*. In this wheel—
A triangle facing upwards should be drawn. In the *kaulacakra*, there is a drop (*bindu*) situated in the center of the triangle.
In the *samayacakra*, there is a drop situated in the center of a quadrangle [in some readings, "hexagon"]. In the *kaulacakra*, there is no fixed number of corners.
Because it consists of nine triangles, when these nine triangles are joined together, only vital points and junctions arise; this is a great secret.

Above this, the construction of the Śrīcakra is to be understood as follows: common to both wheels [is] an eight-petalled lotus, then a sixteen-petalled lotus, then three girdles, and then three enclosures (bhūpura) provided with four gates.
p.
34) Here, three types of arrays (*prastāra*) are possible: the Meru-array, the Kailāsa-array, and the Earth-array.
The Meru-array refers to the identity with the sixteen Nityās. The Kailāsa-array...

The identity with the *mātṛkā* is called the "Name," while the identity with the *Vaśinī* group and others is called the "Expansion of the Earth" (*bhūprastāra*). We shall explain all of this more thoroughly on the occasion of commenting on the verse beginning with "by means of the sixty-four tantras" (verse 31).
