Regarding this, a specific detail is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"The sages named Pṛśnis all took refuge in the Cakra;
they practiced the Cakra-vidyā, which is worshipped by gods and Gandharvas, [and which is] of the nature of Agni and Soma."

The wheel is composed of Agni and Soma; it is the world. The radiance shone within Agni, and it is remembered as being composed of Agni and Soma. The Mātṛkā-cakra consists of three sections and is of the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. It comprises the triangle, the Bindu, the lunar [sixteen-petaled lotus], and the eight-cornered [lotus].
The Mixed [Mandala]: A wheel consisting of the moon, likewise two sets of ten spokes, a fourteen-spoked wheel for Fire, and four wheels for the Sun.

By the grace of this [Cakra], Indra and the others, the eight Vasus, and the hosts of Maruts— whosoever in this world are prosperous, they are all servants of the Tripura-cakra. Furthermore, the three cities of the Cakra, consisting of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, as well as the city and cakra of Mahālakṣmī, reside right there.
Sadāśiva. Thus.

The Śruti also expresses this very same meaning in the Aruṇa Upaniṣad of the Taittirīya school, beginning with "May we overcome these worlds" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.27) and ending with "given by the speckled seers" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.27). It is called the Aruṇa Upaniṣad because it belongs to Aruṇā.
The *Upaniṣad* that expounds the *Bhagavatī* begins with "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious" (*Tai.
Ā. 1.1*) and ends with "The ascetic becomes meritorious" (*Tai. Ā.
1.2*); this *Aruṇopaniṣad* teaches the *Aruṇā* herself.
The seer Aruṇaketu perceived this meaning. The sense of the Śruti passage is as follows:
"May we indeed bring these worlds to fulfillment."

The meaning of this is as follows: the sages named Pṛśni converse among themselves regarding this *cakravidyā*. The word *nukam* expresses a deliberation (*vitarka*). The word *bhuvanā* means "the worlds. The phrase *sīṣadhema* means "we shall understand. [They say this because] it is only by relying upon the *cakravidyā* that the worlds remain stable.

The meaning is "we deliberate. Alternatively, "May we accomplish this wheel-vidyā as the very self of the world (bhuvanātmatayā) for the sake of [the world]?"—here *nukaṃ* is used in the sense of an inquiry (*pṛcchā*). According to Amara, *nu* is used in the sense of an inquiry and in deliberation (*vitarke*). [In the phrase *nukaṃ*, *nu* signifies an inquiry. For what purpose? As the self of the world.
The meaning is: "having asked, we understand. According to Amara’s lexicon—printed in the Kārveṭinagara edition—"anu" is used in the sense of inquiry and deliberation.
Thus: Indra and the Viśvedevas.
The meaning of this sentence is indeed clear; the ellipsis is "they remain only by relying upon the Cakra-vidyā."
May Indra, together with the Ādityas, bring our sacrifice, our body, and our progeny to fulfillment.

The meaning of this is as follows: Indra, together with the Ādityas and the hosts of Maruts, [bestows] upon us the sacrifice—such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—the body (tanu), that is to say, the wife who is half of one's own person; offspring, that is, progeny; and by the word "and" (ca), all forms of prosperity.

Having attained supreme sovereignty through the worship of the Cakra-vidyā, Indra instructed us in that Cakra-vidyā and said, "May he bring it to fulfillment" (sīṣadhātu). The imperative mood (*loṭ*) is used here because the time for its accomplishment has arrived.
"May Indra, together with the Ādityas and the host of Maruts, be the protector of our bodies.
36) The meaning of these two mantras is as follows: "protector of our bodies," that is, of sons, friends, wives, and so forth.
"May he be our protector"—this is the meaning. The sense is that Indra alone is the provider of our acquisition and security (yogakṣema).
Plunge in! Swim out!

The *pṛśni* [mantras] proclaim the knowledge of the wheel: perform a leaping from head to foot, sprinkling the flow of nectar; perform an intense leaping, sprinkling [the nectar] throughout the paths of the seventy-two thousand channels.
O egg-born one, do not be born again and again.
*Āṇḍī*, *piṇḍāṇḍam*, and *brahmāṇḍam* end with the suffix *cvipratyaya*.
O Bhava, [enter] in the form of our *piṇḍāṇḍa* and in the form of the external *brahmāṇḍa* belonging to you; obtain union with the Lord (*bhavatsāyujyam*)—this is the meaning. O Ja, understand this!
"Understand me repeatedly"—this means "favor me. [The form] *aja* is derived from the root *aj* (to go);
the elision of the vowel *a* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
[She is] the one who brings about the end of suffering for those beginning with happiness.

The meaning of this is as follows: *sukhādi* means that which eats (*atti*) and bestows (*adayati*) happiness; thus, it refers to the moon (*indu*), the bringer of bliss, situated in the *baindava* station. *Khanidhanām* means her whose wealth (*dhana*) is entirely (*nitarām*) the void (*kham*), namely the *baindava* station itself. Alternatively, *sukhādīm* may mean "beginning with happiness."
"Sukhātmikām" means having happiness as its nature. "Duḥkhanidhanām" means the end or destruction of suffering therein;

the meaning is that it is devoid even of the scent of suffering. Alternatively, "sukhādīm" means having a beautiful "kha"—that is, the sense organ of the mind—as its beginning; the meaning is that it is the first thing to be known by the mind.
It is the destruction of suffering, and it is beyond the range of the afflicted faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
Release your own city.
Release your own Bhāgavata city, the body— the word ending in the letter *ra*— and preside over it.
The rays belong to Svayambhū.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Bhavas" refers to the rays or beams produced from the Blessed Lady herself; the ellipsis of the sentence is that they exist pervading all the worlds. This [is] the illuminating power of the sun, moon, and fire.
That it is "solely by the grace of Svāyaṃbhuva Marīci" will be explained later.
Those who fashioned the bodies.

The meaning of this is as follows: those rays, numbering three hundred and sixty, which constitute the bodies that are of the nature of time—namely, the days numbering three hundred and sixty—are themselves the year; for the year is indeed Prajāpati (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa).
Thus says the Śruti.
May they fashion their respective bodies.
May those rays fashion your body, O Blessed Lady; may they take refuge in your body.
By the word "body" (deha), the movement of the limbs of the body is meant; the meaning is that they are produced from the feet of the Goddess.
And let it not fail you; may it bring you across.
May your renown—your fame, which is knowledge—not fail us; that is to say, may the knowledge concerning you never abandon us, but be ever accomplished for us.
From this point on, the Pṛśnis, hastening to practice the science of the wheel, address one another:
"Arise! Do not sleep! O Bhāratas, seek fire from the king!"
Satiated with Soma, the Dawns are united with the Sun.

The meaning of this *ṛc* is as follows: "O Bhāratas," those who are devoted (*ratāḥ*) to *bhā*, that is, to the wheel-knowledge (*cakravidyā*) which is of the nature of light (*bhārūpa*), of the nature of radiance (*jyotīrūpa*), and so forth; [those] who are devoted to its worship.
Alternatively, they are the worshippers of Bhāratī—that is, Sarasvatī, the Śrīvidyā.
Because the general suffix [denoting "worshippers"] here conveys a specific meaning, they are called "Bhāratas.
Arise! Begin your worship! Do not sleep; remain vigilant.
"Seek the fire; kindle the fire residing in your own seat.
[This refers to] King Candra. Soma is accompanied by Umā.
Because she resides in the station of the *bindu* within the lunar orb, she belongs to Candra.

The establishment of [the deity] being denoted by the word *soma*. "Satiated" means satisfied by the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of that moon. "By the sun" means by the sun situated between the *anāhata* and *viśuddhi* cakras;
the meaning is that it is conjoined with the sun, which resides between fire and the moon. Alternatively:

The syntactical connection is: "We are satisfied by the King who is united with the Sun. Of what nature are they? They are those for whom the afflictions consisting of the illusory nature of existence have been scorched away by the dawn; or alternatively, they are those devoted to meditation at the time of dawn (uṣas), because the practice of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) upon the Blessed One is prescribed specifically for that time.
From here on, the *pṛśnis* instruct upon the materials for worship: "The youth, well-attired;
the youth with firm limbs, healthy; well-attired means wearing bright garments. This...
This is an indicator of bright ornaments, auspicious garlands, and so forth; the ellipsis is that being in such a state, one should perform worship.
They first describe the essential nature of the Śrīcakra:
it has eight wheels and nine gates.

She is the one who possesses eight wheels (*cakras*), consisting of an eight-cornered, two ten-cornered, and a fourteen-cornered [wheel], as well as an eight-petaled, a sixteen-petaled [lotus], three circles (*valayas*), and three lines. For this very reason, she has nine gates (*navadvārā*), meaning nine doors in the form of triangles.
That which has these is the nine-gated one.
Ayodhyā is the foremost city of the gods.
The city (*pūḥ*) belonging to the gods (*devānām*), such as Indra and others, by virtue of being their object of worship,
is Śrīvidyānagara. Alternatively, they are called *devas* because they "shine" (*dīvyanti*).

The city (*pūḥ*) is the foundational substratum of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). Alternatively, it is the city of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, because the Śrīcakra consists of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; since it is the unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) of those three cities, the singular form "city" (*pūḥ*) is established—this is how it should be understood.
Ayodhyā is unattainable for those of meager fortune; this is the implied meaning.
Its sheath is golden; it is the heavenly world, enveloped in light.
The meaning of this is as follows: in that city, within the center of the Śrīcakra, there is a golden sheath;
the meaning is the sheath of the thousand-petaled lotus, because the sheath of the thousand-petaled lotus exists in the location of the Bindu (Baindava-sthāna). By the light of that sheath...
The heavenly world is covered; "the world of light" means the heavenly world.

Then the Pṛśnis state the fruit of the worship of the knowledge of the wheel: "To him who indeed knows that city of Brahman, which is enveloped by immortality— for him Brahman and Brahmā grant long life, fame, and progeny."

The meaning is this: [one should meditate upon] that aforementioned city in the form of the Śrīcakra, which belongs to Brahman— that is, the Blessed Lady who is the very nature of Brahman— and which is enveloped by nectar, being covered by streams of ambrosia falling from the lunar orb.

To that wise worshiper who knows the city of Tripurā and performs its worship preceded by knowledge, both Brahmā— the Lord in the form of Brahmā— and Brahman— the Goddess whose nature is Brahman— [bestow their grace]. The two *ca*s (and-s) signify the conjunction and union of both.

Because they both reside together in the place of Bindu, within the ocean of nectar in the Sahasrāra, on the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa) in the palace of the wish-fulfilling gem (Cintāmaṇigṛha); the meaning is that these two together bestow—shall grant—longevity, life, fame, glory, progeny, and offspring. There is a grammatical inversion [of the verb].
The word "bahulam" (frequently) indicates a transposition of the grammatical rule.
p. 40) They say that Śiva and Śakti dwell right there—
in the city that is radiant, golden-hued, and completely surrounded by glory.
Brahmā entered Aparājitā, which was made of gold.

The meaning of this *ṛc* is as follows: "shining forth" means manifesting with infinite millions of rays—this is the ellipsis. "Harinīm" means golden-colored (*hiraṇyavarṇā*), according to the *Śruti* in the *Śrīsūkta*: "The golden-colored one is Harinī. By her glory...
The meaning is that those who are famous in the world, being completely surrounded by fame, are all possessed of fame obtained through the grace of the Blessed Lady. May that city of Bindu,
the abode of the wish-fulfilling gem, which is Brahmā and Sadāśiva— that Brahmā and Śiva— be mine.
From the Śruti text, "Sadāśivo" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 4.29),

it is understood that the masculine word *brahman* and the word *sadāśiva* have one and the same meaning. By means of two sentences, [it is shown that] the Aparājitā, the Sādākhyā, entered the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*).

The demonstration of the difference between the two modes of entry [into the *bindu*] is as follows: Sadāśiva is eternally present in the wish-fulfilling gem-house (*cintāmaṇigṛha*) of the *bindu*, while the invincible Kuṇḍalinī energy, having pierced the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), enters again and again; such is the meaning.
In order to make known.
They describe the manner in which Śiva and Śakti abide within that wheel: "The Supreme (Parā) consists of the non-departing and the non-aging; the Supreme (Parā) is the non-perishing."
The meaning of this is as follows: she who is turned away, facing downward, and having the form of a wheel [or the form of the moon];

the Śakti situated between Śiva and Śakti; "ajyāmīyī" means devoid of decay (*jyāni*), that is, devoid of destruction, eternal, free from suffering, and consisting of bliss—this is the meaning. Thus it goes.
It proceeds. Alternatively, *ajyāmayī* means "not consisting of *jyā*"; since *jyā* signifies the earth (*bhūmi*), this indicates the five elements (*pañcabhūtāni*).
Thus, it does not consist of those, but rather consists of the principle of the mind (*manastattva*) and so forth.
That is to say, she consists of the four *yoni*s that are the essence of the *śivacakra*;

because the *śivayoni*s are situated below the *bindu* station (*baindavasthāna*) with their faces turned downward (*avāṅmukhatayā*). She is *anāśakī*, meaning devoid of destruction, and consists of the five *yoni*s that are the essence of the *śakticakra*. She is *parāṅ*, meaning facing downward.
This is because even the Śaktiyonis are downward-facing in relation to the Śivayoni. Thus,
the mutual downward-facing nature of the Śivayoni and the Śaktiyoni is understood from the sequence of drawing the wheels (cakras).
They say that the fruit of the wise man follows him both here and in the hereafter; the wise man [overcomes] both gods and asuras.

They are called *devas* because they "shine" (*divyanti*); these are the eleven organs. *Asuras* are the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*), that is, the five winds beginning with *prāṇa*; those which "seize" (*rānti*) or take them away are said to be the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) [in some readings, *mahadādayaḥ* is additionally seen].

The wise one who, having understood the group of twenty-five principles as being encapsulated by Śiva and Śakti, perceives both Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva as present in both categories— namely, among both the gods and the asuras— [attains liberation].
He who knows the twenty-sixth principle, which is distinct from the twenty-five principles,
is a wise man; and by virtue of the gradations of worship in this world, he attains in the next world the fivefold liberation consisting of *sārṣṭi*, *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*.
One follows and is joined with liberation (*mukti*). The nature of *sārṣṭi* and the other states will be explained in detail later, in the commentary on verse 99.
Then they spoke of the means for both gods and asuras to gain knowledge:
"Whatever a maiden utters in a low voice, whatever a woman devoted to her husband [utters], and whatever auspicious act is performed— Agni penetrates all that."

The meaning is this: there are three states of the power Kuṇḍalinī. In which wheel (cakra) the maiden, having entered the state of childhood, first awakens from sleep and "sighs" (mandrayate)—that is, she makes a low, rumbling sound—because Kuṇḍalinī has the nature of a serpent; for a serpent indeed...

The meaning is that it produces a low, resonant sound (*mandrasvara*) upon waking from sleep; likewise, [the text says] "if" (*yady*), meaning that in whichever wheel the woman—the *kulayoṣit*—goes as far as the Viṣṇu-knot (*viṣṇugranthi*), she gives pleasure (*rāti*). This is the ellipsis to be supplied. (p. 42)

"A woman of noble family, having abandoned her family, finds rest in the piercing of Viṣṇu"—so says the word of Sanatkumāra. "In which wheel" means in that thousand-petaled lotus, where the devoted wife (pativratā) sports together with her husband, Sadāśiva. Riṣṭaṃ... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Since it is stated that "inauspiciousness (*ariṣṭa*) is the absence of the auspicious (*śubha*)," and "in safety (*kṣema*) there is the absence of the auspicious," anything other than that inauspiciousness is "auspicious," meaning it is the "taste of the nectar of immortality" (*amṛtāsvāda*).
Whatever is performed, the fire residing in one's own seat (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) penetrates it and acts as its assistant. And therefore—
By the power of practice, having kindled the fire with the vital breath (*vāyu*),

one may realize that the Supreme Goddess transcends the twenty-five principles upon experiencing the stream of nectar (*pīyūṣa*) dripping from the lunar orb, which has been melted and pierced by the crest of the flame.
The instruction is that it is easily accomplished.
Intending to show that the worship of the wheel of Cakra bestows fruits upon those in the stages of life (āśramins), those of various classes (varṇins), and both the wise and the ignorant, they say:
"Whether they have cooked [offerings] or have not cooked, whether they are performers of sacrifice or non-performers of sacrifice."
Those going to heaven have no expectations.

The meaning is as follows: *aśṛtāsaḥ* means uncooked, that is to say, those whose internal impurities (*antaḥkaraṇakalmaṣa*) have not been destroyed. *Śṛtāsaḥ* means cooked, that is to say, those whose internal impurities have been destroyed; the form *śṛtāsaḥ* takes the augment *asuk* according to the rule *ājjaserasuk*. *Yajvānaḥ* means those who are habitually performers of sacrifice.

The *traivarṇikas* are those belonging to the [three] stages of life (*āśramins*). The "non-sacrificers" (*ayajvanas*) are those devoid of sacrifice, such as Śūdras and others. Regarding this, there is the Vedic revelation (Śruti): "Therefore, a Śūdra is unfit for the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1).
The word *yajña* (sacrifice), which denotes the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites restricted exclusively to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), refers [only] to those;

however, since there is an injunction for Śūdras to practice the *cakravidyā*, their eligibility is established—just as in the case of the *niṣādasthapati*—and thus there is no contradiction regarding their eligibility for Vedic ritual action. [The root] *iṇ* means "to go."
Those who understand the Wheel-Vidyā do not look toward their own heaven.
(43) They state that there is an undesirable consequence in the worship of another deity apart from the worship of the Cakra-vidyā:
"Those who know Indra and Agni come together like grains of sand by means of their rays."
They have been proclaimed from this world and from that world.

The meaning is this: those who [worship] Indra and Agni as being distinct from the Cakra-vidyā— the lotus-feet of which are worshipped by the leaders of gods and asuras, which is the inner ruler of all beings, all-pervading, and the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe— [are mistaken].

By the word "and" (ca), those who know the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Sadāśiva, as well as the world-protectors such as Yama, as objects of worship— they fall apart like grains of sand (*sikatā*),
meaning they become scattered and separated from one another. Furthermore, by means of the rays...

The meaning is that they would be summoned, restrained, and bound by the nooses of Yama, as set forth in the *Uttaraprabandha* in the passage beginning with "depart, go away" (*apeta vīta*). Furthermore, the ellipsis is that they would fall from both this world and the other world; for this very reason...
Another scriptural passage states:
"Those who worship ignorance enter into blind darkness" (Īśa Upaniṣad 9).
The meaning of this is that "ignorance" refers to that which is opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*), being contrary to the path of wisdom.
"Those who perform worship by superimposing [divinity]—thinking, 'One should worship speech as a cow that serves Indra and the other gods' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 7.8.1)—they are ignorant;
they enter blind darkness, meaning they enter the blinding gloom (andhatāmisra). The word 'and' (ca)..."
This indicates the conclusion of the section.
The seers gave with the dappled cows.

By the sages named Pṛśni, all this was given; "was given" (*adāyi*) is in the passive voice, with the *luṅ* suffix used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*), involving the elision of the passive suffix and the substitution of the active suffix.
The meaning is that it was spoken thus by the Pṛśni sages; or else, [it was spoken] by the Pṛśnis.
The assembly of sages, together with the individual sages, spoke these words; "spoke" is the sense, with "thus" being the understood object of the speech. || 11 ||
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, even the lords of poets, such as Viriñci and others, can somehow manage to compare your beauty; for out of eagerness to behold it, the celestial nymphs go forth.
Even the state of union with Giriśa, which is difficult to attain even through mental discipline and austerities.

"Belonging to you" (tvadīyam) means related to you, that is to say, residing in your body. "Beauty" (saundaryam) refers to loveliness. "O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain" (tuhinagirikanye): a mountain where snow (tuhiṇa) predominates is the Himālaya;
[the term refers to] her, the daughter, and is used as a vocative. "To weigh" (tulayitum) means to equalize with a balance.

The lords of poets, the best among the learned, somehow—by any means whatsoever—are unable; that is, they are not capable. Viriñciprabhṛtayaḥ refers to those headed by Viriñci (Brahmā), namely Hari, Indra, and the others. *Yat* means for which reason.

Out of longing for the light— that is, out of the eagerness regarding the sight of your beauty— the celestial nymphs (amaralalanāḥ), the wives of the gods, go— that is, they reach— [you] with their minds (manasā), that is, with their inner faculties (antaḥkaraṇena). [The ablative case is used here either because of the elision of a word ending in the suffix -lyap (meaning "having resorted to"), or as the ablative of cause.]
Even by means of austerities— such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances— which are difficult to attain and impossible to reach,
even the state of union with Giriśa [is unattainable].
Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain! the lords of poets, beginning with Viriñci, are somehow able to equal your beauty;
for this reason, the celestial damsels, out of a longing to behold it, [perform] penances.
They reach, even in their minds, the state of union with Giriśa, though it is difficult to attain.

The meaning is this: even for those such as Vāṇīpati and Vācaspati, it is impossible to describe your beauty by imagining a similar counterpart, because there exists no other beautiful object comparable to you.
The entry of celestial nymphs such as Urvaśī and Tilottamā even into a ten-millionth part of the comparison with a fraction of your beauty is cast far aside; for it is because,
upon seeing your beauty, these celestial nymphs pray for the state of being male.

Regarding the reality of your beauty, which is difficult for other men to comprehend and accessible only to Sadāśiva, they exist with the longing for the rare attainment of union (sāyujya) with Sadāśiva.
The sense is that the Apsarases themselves felt loathing for their own beauty.
Here, the figure of speech *ananvaya* (self-comparison) is suggested, because since no object equal to it exists anywhere in the world, there arises the realization that it is its own equal. || 12 ||

Hundreds of women— whose braids are falling loose, whose garments have slipped from their jar-like breasts, whose waistbands are forcibly snapping, and whose silk cloths have fallen away— run after a man who is older than themselves, whose eyes are harsh, and who is dull-witted in jest, the moment he falls within the range of your sidelong glance.
Young women.
A mere man, exceedingly aged and advanced in years, with eyes rendered insipid—
meaning afflicted by visual defects such as cataracts and opacities— and dull in his amusements, that is, utterly ignorant in the arts of love and pleasure, [beholds] you, O lady.

The meaning is: "fallen within the range of her side-long glances" (apāṅgāloke kaṭākṣavīkṣaṇe patitam), that is, having become the sole object of her sidelong looks; "they pursue" means "pursuing," numbering in the hundreds—the word "hundred" (śata) being indicative of a number exceeding a hundred.

The meaning is that all those residing in the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar [are meant]. "With their braided hair coming loose" means those whose braided hair (veṇībandha) is slipping down. "With the hems of their garments falling from their jar-like breasts" means the hems (sicaya)—that is, the edges of the cloth—have slipped loose and become disheveled from their jar-like breasts (kucakalaśa).
Those young women whose waist-bands— their girdles and strings of bells— were suddenly snapping and falling away, and whose fine silk garments were slipping off as their knots loosened.

Herein is the construction of the verse: O Blessed Lady! hundreds of young women—with their braided hair loosened and the garments on their jar-like breasts slipping away—[rush toward] a man who has fallen within the range of Your sidelong glance, even if he be very old, harsh to the eyes, and dull in amorous sports.
With their waistbands forcibly snapping and their silk garments slipping away, the women run after such a man, thinking— this is implied— that he is the God of Love himself.
(46) We shall explain such methods for intoxication more skillfully on the occasion of commenting on the verse beginning with "making the face the drop" (mukhaṃ binduṃ kṛtvā), verse 19. || 13 ||
Those which are fifty-six on earth, fifty-two in water, sixty-two in fire, fifty-four in air,
thirty-six in heaven, and sixty-four in the mind— these [are the kalās].
Above even those rays is the pair of your lotus feet.
On the earth— that is, in the *mūlādhāra* which is associated with the earth element—
there are fifty-six (fifty-two plus two) in number;
in the water— that is, in the *maṇipūra* location which is associated with the water element— there are fifty-two.

In the *hutāśa* (fire) [cakra], which is endowed with the fire-element (*vahni-tattva*), there are sixty-two in the *svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra*— that is, two and sixty, making sixty-two. According to the rule *vibhāṣā catvāriṃśatprabhṛtau sarveṣām*, the vowel *i* of the word *dvi* is replaced by *ā*.
Fifty-four means fifty increased by four;
in the *anāhata-cakra* associated with the air element (*anila*), and in the *viśuddhi-cakra* associated with the space element (*divi*),
there are thirty-six doubled, that is, numbering seventy-two.

The meaning is that they are seventy-two in number. In the *ājñācakra*, which is joined with the principle of the mind—[whereby the word "mind" includes the eleven sense organs]—there are sixty-four. Thus are those well-known in the scriptures.
These rays are well-known among yogins as being self-evident in the Āgamas;
and even above those rays, in the ocean of nectar known by the other name of *bindu*, which consists of the lunar orb situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, you, O Bhavati, reside.

The pair of lotus feet exists; that is, the tradition of the *samaya* exists—this is the ellipsis. Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Bhagavatī! those rays which are fifty-six on earth, fifty-two in water, and sixty-two in fire.
In the wind [element] there are fifty-four (p.
47), in heaven thirty-six, and in the mind sixty-four; above these is yours.
The pair of lotus feet exists—this is the ellipsis.
In this context, because words expressing numbers such as "fifty-six" and so forth refer to the objects being numbered,
they remain in the singular even when the rays to be numbered are many.
For example:
The numbers beginning with twenty are always singular in form, whether they denote the counted object (*saṅkhyeya*) or the number itself (*saṅkhyā*).
When denoting the number itself, they take dual and plural endings.

But because of the restrictive rule that [the number] does not apply to the things numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), the use of the plural ending is established, since no restriction would otherwise apply to the rays themselves, which are the things numbered. Herein lies the essential point:
although numbers such as "fifty-six" and so forth function as qualifiers of the things numbered, [they do not restrict the rays].

Regarding the equality of qualities such as "white" and so forth, as the author of the *Padamañjarī* has stated: "Numbers such as twenty and the rest cannot possess the same properties as qualities such as 'white' and the like;
for numbers such as twenty reside in substances that possess separateness (*pṛthaktva*)."
But qualities such as whiteness and the like have distributive occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) and terminate in each individual instance.
Herein lies a profound secret: when numeral words denoting a number greater than [five] are used in the plural, as in the case of "fifty-six rays," [the rule] would otherwise apply.
They would number three thousand one hundred and thirty-six;
therefore, the accomplishment of the intended meaning is the fruit of the rule.
In this regard, the following should be considered:
the Śrīcakra consists of the six cakras— Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā— and is composed of three sections, embodying the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
The two wheels, the Mūlādhāra and the Svādhiṣṭhāna, constitute one section.
The two wheels, the Maṇipūra and the Anāhata, constitute one section.
The two wheels, the Viśuddhi and the Ājñā, constitute one section. Here, above the first section...

The location of Agni is called the Rudra-knot. Above the second section is the location of Sūrya; that is called the Viṣṇu-knot. Above the third section is the location of Candra; that is called the Brahmā-knot.
The phrase "consisting of Soma, Sūrya, and Anala" is to be understood according to the order of descent (avarohaṇakrama).
In that regard, the Fire situated above the first section envelops the first section with its own flames; [and] the Sun situated above the second section...
With its own rays, it covers the second segment;
situated above the third segment, the moon covers the third segment with its digits.
In the *ādhāra-cakra*, which consists of the earth element (*mahī-tattva*), there are fifty-six flames of fire;
in the *maṇipūraka*, which consists of the water element (*udaka-tattva*) and is situated above it, there are fifty-two flames.

Thus, there are one hundred and eight flames of fire. Of the sun, there are sixty-two rays in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* cakra, which consists of the fire element (*agnitattva*), and fifty-four rays in the *anāhata* cakra, which consists of the air element (*anilatattva*). [The sun's rays] exclude the *maṇipūra* cakra.

The entry into the *svādhiṣṭhāna* occurs because of the unity of the sun and fire, and because fire is contained within the sun. However, between the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and the *maṇipūra*, which are the locations of the sun and fire respectively, there is an entry of the sun into the place of fire, and [the entry] of fire into the place of the sun.
The "Entry into Fire" (*agnipraveśa*)— which is also read as "the extinguisher of the fire that burns the world"—

is for the purpose of generating rain produced by the rays of the sun in the form of the *saṃvarta* clouds. This, however, will be discussed on the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "endowed with lightning, by means of Śakti" (verse 40).

We shall establish this more precisely. Thus, the sun has one hundred and sixteen rays. As for the digits of the moon: there are seventy-two in the *viśuddhicakra*, which consists of the element of space (*ākāśa*), and sixty-four in the *ājñācakra*, which consists of the element of mind (*manas*). Thus...
The moon has one hundred and thirty-six digits (*kalā*). As it is stated in the *Bhairavayāmala*, in the section concerning the eight Bhairavas:
"One hundred and eight for Fire, and one hundred and sixteen for the Sun."
And the determination of the moon is one hundred and thirty-six. Thus [it is said].

Thus, the Moon, Sun, and Fire exist pervading both the microcosmic body (piṇḍāṇḍa) and the macrocosmic universe (brahmāṇḍa). Because of the identity of the microcosmic body and the macrocosmic universe, the very pervasion of the microcosmic body is the pervasion of the macrocosmic universe; this is the secret. Thus, having transcended—and pervaded—the microcosmic body...
[This is also the reading. There exists the Thousand-petaled Lotus (*sahasrakamala*). And that is the world consisting of moonlight (*jyotsnāmaya*).
The moon situated there is eternally full. This was stated during the commentary on the verse beginning with [verse 36]: "And this is located in your *ājñācakra*," and so forth.

We shall establish this more precisely. As for what was stated—that the moon is situated above the *ājñācakra*—that refers merely to the location of the lunar digits (*kalā*), not to the location of the moon itself.
This is because it is stated in the *Subhagodaya* that the sixteen digits consist of the nature of the sixteen *Nityās*.
Since those [days] consist of the lunar dates (tithi) of the waxing and waning phases beginning with the first day (pratipad),
increase and decrease do indeed occur for the moon as well, even when it resides within the thousand-petaled lotus.
49) However, that [moon] does not undergo increase or decrease;
rather, there are sixteen lunar digits (kalās), which consist of the sixteen Nityās [and are thus called "moons"].

In some readings, it says: "those that initiate the lunar days starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (pratipad) up to the full moon (paurṇamāsī), and likewise those that initiate the lunar days starting from the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pratipad) up to the new moon (amāvāsyā)— in many manuscripts, the reading is 'starting from the new moon up to the first day of the dark fortnight'."
"By means of the concealment and non-concealment of one's own nature"—this is the secret of the knowers of Mantra.

This is to be understood here: since Śrīvidyā, whose alternative name is Candrakalāvidyā, consists of the fifteen lunar days (tithis), it possesses three hundred and sixty rays in the form of days; therefore, it is the year.
It is observed that because this year— which consists of the power of time— is of the nature of Prajāpati,

and because Prajāpati is the creator of the world, the Marīcis possess the quality of effecting the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. And those Marīcis [reside] within this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
And within a single *piṇḍāṇḍa*, there are three hundred and sixty [rays].
Likewise, this applies to infinite millions of *piṇḍāṇḍas* and *brahmāṇḍas*. In exactly this same way, within every *brahmāṇḍa* and every *piṇḍāṇḍa*, there are three hundred and sixty rays.
Therefore, there are infinite rays;

and those rays, joined with the sun, moon, and fire, born from the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lady, illuminate various worlds. And this is the radiant, purifying door of the world (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.6).
By the scriptural passage [Brāhmaṇa 3.12.3],
it is stated that the rays originate from the lotus-feet of the Blessed One; and likewise,
by the scriptural passage [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.27], "the Marīcis of Svāyambhuva," their...
It has been stated that rays possess the power of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. What is meant by this is as follows:
among the infinite millions of rays emanating from the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady, the sun, moon, and fire constitute only a few.
Having drawn forth rays [of light],
they illuminate the worlds by virtue of the power to reveal the universe obtained through the grace of the Blessed Lady; and for this reason, the circle of lunar digits transcends all worlds.
Regarding the phrase "the station of the bindu": it refers to the lotus-foot residing there.
Since its rays extend beyond even the countless millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) and elemental eggs (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), your lotus-foot transcends even those.
It should be understood that this is a restatement of what is already established, and not a figurative praise through superimposition.
As it has been stated by Maheśvara to Gaurī in the *Candrajñānavidyā* section of the *Bhairavayāmala* (p.

Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You have asked well, O beauty of the three worlds. This knowledge, the most secret of secrets, has not been revealed anywhere. The *kalā-vidyā* of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*)—[the reading *śaktiḥ* also occurs]—has the form of the Śrīcakra.

In the center of that is the station of Bindu; there dwells the Supreme Goddess, united with Sadāśiva, the virtuous one who transcends all principles (tattvas). O Īśvarī, the wheel of Tripurasundarī has the form of the cosmic egg and consists of the five elements.

She consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra), likewise consists of the sense organs, and similarly consists of the principle of the mind (manas). She has the form of the principles beginning with Māyā, and she is beyond the principles (tattvātīta) as the Bindu.
Within the Bindu, she brings about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and is eternally united with Sadāśiva.

The Great Goddess transcends all principles; she is the form of light, possessing a supreme aspect, from whose body, O Śiva, thousands, two thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, and a hundred million rays emanate—
there is no higher number than these.

Having entered into that very [power], she illumines the world of the moving and the unmoving; O Great Goddess, by the light of that Goddess everything shines forth. There is nothing whatsoever that shines without her light, nor is there anything that manifests apart from her. And as for that Śiva-Śakti, whose nature is consciousness—[meditate upon] her consciousness.
"O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, without those infinite millions of rays, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings would surely fall into blindness. Among those [infinite] rays,
O Śivā, these three hundred and sixty rays sustain the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)."
Pervading [the universe] through their nature as Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, they [offer] one hundred and eight oblations to Agni and one hundred and sixteen to Ravi.
O Śivā, one hundred and thirty-six rays of the moon illuminate the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) as well as the individual body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), O Consort of Śaṅkara. Likewise, during the day the sun,
at night the moon, and at the two twilights the fire illuminate those times.

Therefore, the three are of the nature of time; and three hundred and sixty days indeed constitute a year. Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), is of the nature of the year—such is the Vedic revelation.
Prajāpati, the creator of the worlds, creates the sages headed by Marīci; these [sages] create...

They are the world-protectors, all of them guardians of the world. Withdrawal depends upon Hara; creation is fashioned by Bhava. Protection, however, is linked to Mṛḍa. Śiva is appointed by the Supreme Goddess for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world]; thus the universe proceeds. Thus it is said.

By the words "having entered into that very [Self]" and so forth, the meaning of the Śruti passage, "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15), is restated.
There is much that needs to be said on this matter, which we shall properly explain further on.
He states the ritual application for Sarasvatī:
[One should meditate on her] pure as the autumnal moonlight, wearing a crown of matted locks joined with the moon,
and holding a lute, a protective amulet, and a crystal rosary (or, according to another reading, a crystal *ghuṭhikā*).
O you who hold a book in your hand! How indeed could the sweet compositions of the virtuous—possessing the sweetness of honey, milk, and grapes—not abide within them once they have bowed to you? 15.
Pure as the autumnal moonlight— pure like the moonlight (jyotsnā) that occurs in the season of autumn, exceedingly white; she whose crown is a mass of matted locks joined with the moon— that is,
she whose diadem is a coil of matted hair accompanied by the moon.
The meaning is "she who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel.
(She is) one whose hands hold a leather thong, a protective amulet, a crystal rosary, and a book.
The *vara* is the mudrā of granting desired boons; the *trāsa-trāṇa* is the mudrā of granting fearlessness.

A *sphaṭika-ghaṭikā* is a crystal drinking vessel. Some say it is a rosary of crystal beads (*sphaṭikākṣamālā*). According to that view, the reading is *sphaṭika-gulikā* (or even *ghuṭikā* as a variant).
The term *pustakavidyāmudrā* (or *pustakavā*) refers to one whose hands are joined with these—namely, a book and the gesture of knowledge (*vidyāmudrā*).

This is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term according to the rule beginning with *śākapārthiva*. It is not, however, a locative *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has crystal, a rosary, and a book in her hands."

Because of the rule "there is an addition [of the suffix] after words such as *praharaṇa*," it is restricted to those very words beginning with *praharaṇa*. The letter *na* occurs once, in one instance, for the purpose of negation;
*tvā* means "you" (*tvām*); *natvā* means "having performed salutation"; *kathaṃ kathaṃcit* means "somehow" or "in some way."

In the presence of the great lords of poets, who are the ornaments of speech, [these] compositions attain their proximity; for these compositions possess the sweetness of honey, milk, and grapes— where "madhu" is honey, "kṣīra" is milk, and "drākṣā" is the grape (*mṛdvikā*).

*Madhurimā* means sweetness; *dhurīṇāḥ* refers to those who bear the burden (*dhuraṃ vahanti*), that is, leaders or foremost ones; thus the meaning is "as sweet as that. *Phaṇitayaḥ* refers to eloquent speech or the art of expression.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! having bowed but once to You—whose crown is a mass of matted hair joined with the moon, pure as the autumnal moonlight, and whose hands hold a water-lily, a protective amulet, a crystal rosary, and a book.
How could the refined delicacies, as sweet as the sweetness of honey, milk, and grapes, not be set before the virtuous?

This is the meaning: here, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is indicated that even a single act of salutation produces the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the seed of poetic genius; for in its absence, there is no arising of that seed by any other means whatsoever. (15) [Salutation] to the lords of poets.
Those few virtuous ones who resort to you, who possess the ruddy luster of the morning sunlight upon the forest of the lotuses of the mind,
delight the wise with words profound with the surging waves of the most youthful passion of Brahmā’s beloved. (16)

Those who resort to— that is, serve— the morning-red glow of the forest of lotuses of the minds of the lords of poets, the sovereigns of poets; for "minds" are themselves the "lotuses," and their "forest" is a grove, and its "morning-red glow" is the dawn-hue of crimson light.
Only a few virtuous and noble persons, being rare indeed, recognize you— who are Aruṇā by name and red in color—
as the beloved of Viriñci’s consort;
for Viriñci is Brahmā, and his beloved is Sarasvatī.

"Profound with waves of exceedingly fresh erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). "Exceedingly fresh" means extremely youthful; or rather, it refers to the "exceedingly fresh" *śṛṅgāra* itself, and its "wave" (*laharī*) is the surging flow. Or else, by the word "wave," one may refer to [the swelling of] the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Such is what is called "overflowing" (utseka). By means of words— meaning speech characterized by waves, that is, exceedingly profound linguistic embellishments—
these [poets] effect the delight, the enchantment of the hearts, of the virtuous members of the assembly.
The virtuous reflect thus:

here the construction of the words is as follows—O Blessed One! You, who possess the luster of the morning sun to the forest of lotuses that are the minds of the lords of poets, and who are indeed ruddy (aruṇā)—those few [who...]
These virtuous ones worship the beloved of Viriñci; with words profound with the waves of youthful amorous grace, they bring delight to the virtuous.

The meaning is this: meditating upon the Goddess Aruṇā within the lotus of the heart, they have attained manhood and, like Sarasvatī, delight the assembly with playful expressions of speech characterized primarily by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa). Of the Goddess...
Because she is of the nature of the *mātṛkā*, she bestows the *sārasvata* [attainment] precisely by virtue of being the form of Sarasvatī.

Through the power of meditating upon her as having a ruddy complexion, or through the predominance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), the activity of the play of speech (*vāgvilāsa*) proceeds. As it has been stated in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*:
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady named Aruṇā, who has the luster of dawn;
the auspicious Goddess holds a noose and a goad, and she bears a bow and arrows.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, and endowed with a book and a rosary, she has eight arms and three eyes;
sporting in the ocean of nectar,
she always makes all the members of the assembly greedy for the tasting of the sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
"The supreme practitioner [should be seated] in the assembly hall. Thus it is said.

(54) Here, the figure of speech is *paramparita-rūpaka* (chain-metaphor), because the attribution of the quality of having the luster of morning sunlight is the cause for the attribution of lotus-ness to the mind; thus, it is a *rūpaka-hetu-rūpaka*.
This is because of the definition [of metaphor] as being "successive" (paramparita). || 16 ||
O Mother, he who meditates upon you together with Vaśinī and the other [Śaktis], whose splendor is like the fragments of moonstone and who are the generators of all speech—
he becomes a creator of great poems through his graceful and radiant compositions.
With words as sweet as the fragrance from the lotus-face of the Goddess of Speech.
By the mothers who give birth [to them], by means of words and songs possessing the luster of fragments of moonstones—
having a splendor equal to shards of moon-gem— and which have crushed the moonstone itself.
Extreme whiteness is established in the world. By "Vaśinyādyābhiḥ" (by those headed by Vaśinī), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the inclusion of the quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*);
that is, those eight powers (*śaktis*) of whom Vaśinī is the first are the "Vaśinyādyāḥ," and the yoginīs are twelve.

The four beginning with Gandhākarṣiṇī are Vaśinī and the others. Here, there is an elision of one of the two initial words [of the compound], meaning "the first among those beginning with Vaśinī. The group of eight Vaśinīs consists of Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, and [Kaulinī].

O Mother! O Janani! That practitioner who meditates upon you together with these [energies], including Kaulini, becomes capable and empowered as a creator and author of poems and literary compositions. [He becomes one] among the great, the high-souled ones.
By means of the graceful turns and lusters of Kalidasa and others— by means of words that are sweet with the beauty of their stylistic turns and lines, which are the playful manifestations of speech,
and which are as fragrant as the lotus-face of Vagdevi (the Goddess of Speech).
The meaning is: by the sweet and indistinct fragrances— the *parimala*— of the lotus of her face,
these [words] create the illusion that they are the playful expressions of the goddess Bhāratī who has assumed a male form.
p.

55) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Mother! he who [worships] you together with Vaśinī and the others, who are the progenitors of speech and possess the luster of fragments of moonstone—
He reflects with the graceful splendors of the great,
and through words as sweet as the fragrance from the lotus-face of the Goddess of Speech, he becomes a creator of poems.

In this regard, the following should be considered: in the phrase "I [worship] you" (*tvāṃ*) by means of [the powers] Vaśinī and the others, the word "you" (*tvām*) denotes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Goddess. The essential nature of the Goddess, however, is indeed the Mātṛkā consisting of the fifty phonemes. This, moreover, is Śiva, Śakti, and Kāma.
This will be explained in detail during the commentary on the verse beginning with [32 ślokaḥ].
This *mātṛkā*, consisting of fifty phonemes, comprises eight groups (*varga*).
These eight groups are those beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya,* and *śa*. The sixteen vowels beginning with *a* [are as follows]:...
The vowels constitute the first group; the five beginning with *ka* constitute the second;
the five beginning with *ca* constitute the third; the five beginning with *ṭa* constitute the fourth;
the five beginning with *ta* constitute the fifth; the five beginning with *pa* constitute the sixth; and there are four beginning with *ya*.

The seventh [group] consists of the five beginning with *śa*; the eighth consists of [the remaining letters]. Thus, the Goddess Mātṛkā, Tripurasundarī, who consists of eight groups, is joined respectively with the powers beginning with Vaśinī within the groups of *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, and va*.

When joined with and meditated upon within the eight wheels— consisting of the four Śiva-wheels composed of the *bindu* and triangle, the eight-spoked wheel, the two ten-spoked wheels, and the fourteen-spoked wheel—
she brings about the perfection of being a poet. By the word "and others" (*ādi*) in the phrase "with Vaśinī and others," [the remaining powers are included].
It is stated that the inclusion of the eight [goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī,
the inclusion of the twelve Yoginīs beginning with Vidyā, and the inclusion of the four beginning with Gandhākarṣiṇī have been accomplished.
The group of eight Vaśinīs has been described. As for the twelve Yoginīs, they are:
Vidyāyoginī, Recikāyoginī, Mocikāyoginī, Amṛtāyoginī, Dīpikāyoginī, Jñānayoginī, Āpyāyanīyoginī, Vyāpinīyoginī, and Medhāyoginī.
The Yoginī whose form is space, the Yoginī whose form is accomplishment, and the Lakṣmī-Yoginī— thus, together with these twelve Yoginīs and the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī,
there are twenty digits (kalās). These are the twenty digits.
Resembling pure crystal, they are to be visualized within the corners of the pair of ten spokes;
they bestow the aforementioned fruits. This is a variation of the *bhūprastāra*.
Regarding the *bhūprastāra*, it will be explained during the commentary on the verse beginning with "by means of sixty-four tantras" [31].
It is examined more precisely: Gandhākarṣiṇī, Rasākarṣiṇī, Rūpākarṣiṇī, and Sparśākarṣiṇī are assigned to the four gates (p. 56).
[The Yājñikī Upaniṣad, Section 1] These bestow the aforementioned fruits. And so says the Śruti:
"I invoke here Śrī, the goddess who has fragrance as her door, who is invincible, eternally nourishing, rich in sacrificial offerings, and the sovereign of all beings."
[The meditators bestow the respective fruits mentioned].

The meaning of this is as follows: "Gandhadvārām" (the one whose door is fragrance) refers to smell, taste, form, and touch, all of which are subsumed under the word "gandha" (fragrance/smell). Therefore, the presiding deities are Gandhākarṣiṇī and the others.

They are comprised of the attractor of fragrance, the attractor of taste, the attractor of form, and the attractor of touch. That [city] which possesses four gates endowed with these is "Gandhadvārā"; thus, it is called Gandhadvārā.
"Unassailable" means difficult to overcome; the ellipsis implies "for those of little fortune. "Eternally nourished" means having the nature of eternal bliss.
"Karīṣiṇī" means that which attracts perfumes and so forth; or alternatively, it means that which is desired by *karins*, i.e., elephants.

I invoke here into this wheel Śrī, the Sovereign, the presiding deity of all beings, that Śrīvidyā who is surrounded [by her retinue]. By the mantra "Gandhadvārām," [are invoked] the fourfold Gandhākarṣiṇīs, the eight Vaśinī and others, and the twelve Yoginīs.

It is thus summarized. And so says the word of Śambhu: "One should meditate upon Tripurāmbikā, who is joined with Vaśinī and the Mātṛkās, accompanied by the Yoginīs, and endowed with the [powers] beginning with Gandhākarṣiṇī."

In this regard, the following should be considered: it has been stated that the powers (śaktis), beginning with Vaśinī, consist of the fifty phonemes. Among them, the power Vaśinī consists of the vowels. There are sixteen vowels, beginning with *a*. Their essential nature is described in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
As stated in the *Pañcaśatikā*, it is described in brief as follows: the power (*śakti*) whose nature is the letter *A* has eight arms,
holding in her hands the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the fear-dispelling gesture, the book, the rosary, the water-pot, and the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*).

Thus, the powers (*śakti*) whose nature consists of the letters *a*, *ā*, and so forth, are white in color. However, there is this distinction: the mandala of the power whose nature is the letter *a* is eighty lakhs of *yojanas* in extent; that of the letter *ā* is twice that; and that of the letter *i*—
It is ninety lakhs of yojanas in length; for the letter *ī*, it is twice that; for the letter *u*, the circumference of the mandala is measured at ten million yojanas.

The [mandala] of the vowel *ū* is twice that. The mandala of the vowel *ṛ* measures fifty million *yojanas*; that of *ṝ* is twice that; and that of both *ḷ* and *ḹ* is likewise twice that. Thus, the circumference of the mandala of the vowel *e* is one and a half crores.

The vowels *ai*, *o*, and *au* are equal to *e*. However, the mandala of the bindu and visarga is twice that of the letter *a*. The mandala of the powers of the consonants is half the size of the mandala of the letter *a*. These are the powers (*śakti*).
Those situated within the semivowels (*antastha*) hold a noose, a goad, a rosary, and a water-pot;
however, [the others] have hands displaying the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
Those of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) hold a noose, a goad, a rosary, and a boon-granting hand. [The deities of] the letters *la* and *kṣa* are as follows.
Their hands hold a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, and flower-arrows;
these fifty Śaktis consist of the nature of the phonemes.

Some, however, hold that the powers whose nature is the vowels are like crystal; those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are like coral; the nine beginning with *ya* are yellow in color; and the syllable *kṣa* is reddish-brown.
Others, however, hold that the letters beginning with *a* are smoke-colored; those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha* are vermilion-colored;
those from *ḍa* to *pha* are fair-complexioned; those from *ba* to *la* are reddish;
those from *va* to *sa* are golden-colored; and as for *ha* and *kṣa*, they are the feet.
[The reading "or their inclusion within the sibilants" is seen as an additional passage in manuscript Pa.
They say that *ha* and *kṣa* resemble lightning, while *la* is included within *la* itself;
this very view is also the opinion of the venerable teacher Bhagavatpādācārya. All of this—
This has been correctly explained by us in the *Candrakalā* commentary on the *Subhagodaya*. || 17 ||
He who remembers the entire sky and the earth submerged in crimson by the bodily radiance of her limbs— which follow the path of the splendor of the newly risen sun—
becomes the master of how many women, with eyes as shy as those of forest deer, along with Urvaśī herself?
The courtesans of the gods. || 17 ||
p. 58) By the shadows of your body— that is, by the splendors of your form—
which follow the path of the beauty of the youthful sun, [you surpass] that youthful sun, the morning sun.
By those whose path— the way— is like the splendor of Śrī, that is to say, their good fortune;
by them, the sky, the entire earth,
and the region between heaven and earth (rodaḥ-pradeśa)— in short, everything— was submerged in ruddiness, meaning it became exceedingly red.
...up to: or rather, [the state] deeply submerged, immersed in the luster of the dawn-red; as it was said by Śambhu:
"For one who contemplates heaven and earth as submerged in an ocean of liquid lac, for him all..."
The women of the three worlds quickly came under his control [the variant reading is "certainly"].

Thus, by the word *aruṇima* (redness), the ocean of lac (*yāvakābdhi*) is indicated; the meaning is "situated in the middle of the ocean of lac. That practitioner who remembers—that is, contemplates—[her].
For this practitioner, there arise women whose eyes possess the modesty of forest deer;

"forest deer" (*vana-hariṇa*) refers to those who are timid, and the word "forest" (*vana*) indicates extreme timidity due to their characteristic of wandering at will. Like those [deer], they are modest (*śālīna*), meaning bashful or exceedingly beautiful.

Those whose eyes [are like that] are so described; together with her, namely the celestial courtesan named Urvaśī, they were brought under control—that is, they fell under her sway. The repetition of "how many" (*katikati*) indicates frequency. "Not" (*naḥ*) is used in the sense of negation. "Gīrvāṇagaṇikāḥ" refers to the celestial courtesans, the beautiful women of the gods.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! He who remembers how the entire sky and the earth are submerged in ruddiness by the rays of the splendor of your youthful sun-like body—before him, the celestial courtesans, whose eyes possess the grace of startled forest deer, [bow down].
How many do not become submissive along with Urvaśī? The meaning is that all the Apsarases become submissive. || 18 ||

O Consort of Hara, he who meditates upon your form— the face as a single dot, the pair of breasts below it, and the half-moon of Shiva beneath them— which is but a digit of the God of Love, instantly agitates women; indeed, he swiftly whirls even the three worlds with extreme ease.
Her pair of breasts are like the sun and the moon.
p.

59) Having made the face—the mouth—into the form of a *bindu*, that is to say, having meditated on the face in the place of the *bindu*; [and] the pair of breasts, the two teats, below—that is, beneath it.

Of the face. Below that—that is, in the lower region of that pair of breasts—is the half of Hara (harārdha), meaning the power (śakti) of Hara, which is the triangle, the womb (yoni). The practitioner who should meditate—should contemplate—it there; the word "there" is to be supplied. [She is] the consort of Hara (haramahiṣī), of Hara.
O Queen, consort of Sadāśiva,

that practitioner immediately— right at that very moment— brings about, or causes, the arousal of the erotic art of your mind, the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, which effects the agitation of all the worlds and the transformation of the minds of women.
"Women"—the word "iti" here indicates an adverbial modifier. [It] very quickly and most trivially causes even the three worlds, even the triple universe, to whirl rapidly;
[a world] having the sun and moon as its pair of breasts—*ravīndū* refers to the sun and the moon, and those two are the breasts.
She whose [measure] is a yuga; her.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Queen of Hara! He who, having placed the *mukha* (the letter *ma*) as a *bindu*, having placed the pair of breasts (*kuca-yuga*) below it, and having placed half of Hara (*harārdha*) below that, meditates upon your digit of Love (*manmathakalā*) therein—he instantly causes the agitation of women.
That which leads is not at all light; rather, it swiftly causes even the three worlds—possessing the pair of breasts that are the sun and the moon—to revolve.
Here, by means of the qualification "possessing a pair of breasts" applied to the three worlds as being like the sun and the moon, there is the superimposition of femininity;
this is intended to indicate that this amorous practice should be employed only toward women.

In this regard, the following should be considered: the practitioner, having meditated upon the face of the beloved woman who is the object of his practice within the triangle at the location of the *bindu*, and having meditated upon her pair of breasts beneath that,
and having contemplated her vulva beneath those two breasts, [should focus] there.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of Māra in the primary limbs—the mouth, the two breasts, and the vulva—one should effect identity with that beloved. As it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
"Having visualized the bindu as the mouth, below that the two breasts, and below that..."
One should contemplate that half-moon as facing downwards; there, one should contemplate her who has the form of the Kāmakalā, ruddy in color.
Then, one should contemplate one's own form in that very same shape. Thus it is said.
p.
60) Thus, numerous applications of the *mādana* (enchanting) rite have been taught in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā* and the *Saptaśatī*. Herein, a few are described:
Having superimposed her face upon the *bindu*, one should contemplate the pair of arms below it, the pair of breasts below that,
and the *yoni* itself below those; one should meditate upon the five arrows within these five locations.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the seed-syllables of the five arrows— drāṃ, drīṃ, klīṃ, blūṃ, and saḥ— in sequence upon the face, the pair of arms, the space between the breasts, and the center of the womb.
This practice is to be performed specifically at the time of the Kāmarāja-prayoga.

In the triangular region at the seat of Bindu, one should contemplate [the face] facing downwards; the practitioner, having contemplated the face in the upper portion of the Bindu, the wise one should then remember the pair of breasts right above that,
and then the Yoni and Bhuvaneśvarī in succession right above those.
Having installed the Śrīvidyā and the Kāmarāja, one should quickly cause [the target] to be utterly deluded.
This application is extremely rapid due to the practice of "making the face into a drop" (*mukhaṃ binduṃ kṛtvā*).
Here too, the application of the five arrows is as before. Such applications for inciting passion (*madanaprayoga*) are described in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*.
These are to be understood; they are not stated here for fear of excessive prolixity. || 19 ||

He who holds you in his heart— resembling a statue carved from moonstone— as you radiate from every limb a flood of nectar-like rays, quells the pride of serpents like the king of birds and gladdens those scorched by fever with his very glance.
With a vein that is a stream of nectar. || 20 ||
Scattering— that is, raining down— from her limbs, which are the members [of her body],
the nectar-essence produced from that mass of rays, a multitude of beams consisting of the scattering of nectar-essence; [she who scatters] that [nectar-essence] into the heart.
In his heart he bears you— meaning, he remembers you— as a statue carved from moonstone; that is, as a form made of *himakara-śilā*, the moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*).
That practitioner who [creates] a puppet or a statue whose body is as if fashioned from moonstone gems— he, like Garuḍa, the lord of birds, subdues the pride of serpents.

The word "iva" (as if) is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*); it does not mean merely having the form of Garuḍa, but rather that he is considered capable of performing his functions. Thus, the meaning is that having become Garuḍa, he is manifest as if he were Garuḍa himself. "Jvarapluṣṭān" means those scorched by fever, i.e., those who are tormented by fever.

"By sight" means by looking; here, the employment of the word *dṛṣṭi* is stated. "Makes happy" means she makes [them] happy; by the rule *tatkaroti* (Pāṇini 3.1.25), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, and by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.155), there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the stem *sukhin*]. Thus, the form *sukhayati* is established. By the channel of the stream of nectar (*sudhādhārasirā*).

The vein that serves as the support for nectar is the channel that flows with ambrosia; or alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "the vein in which there is a stream of nectar. The masculine form is applied according to the rule beginning with *striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskāt*, resulting in the term *sudhādhārā*.
And it is that vein; or rather, there is the reading *sudhāsārasirayā*, meaning a vein consisting of the essence of nectar (*sudhāsāra*).
Herein is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Goddess!

That practitioner who places you within his heart—you who scatter from your limbs a mass of rays like the nectar-fluid of the moon, resembling a statue carved from moonstone—he, like the lord of birds, destroys the pride of serpents with his very glance.
He pacifies [them]; with a gaze that is a stream of nectar, he brings comfort to those scorched by fever.

By this verse, the practice of Garuḍa is described. As it is stated in the *Śataślokī*: "Through the yoga of meditation for six months, one becomes like Garuḍa; by his very glance he attracts the world, and by his very glance he brings it under his control; by his glance he agitates a woman."

By his mere glance, he removes poison; by his glance, he destroys quartan fevers and other fevers in an instant. By meditating upon his form as a moonstone (candrakānta-śilā), one may destroy all fevers of heat quickly, like another Tārkṣya.
"By means of the yoga of meditation on Garuḍa, one destroys poison through mere remembrance. (p.
62) And therefore, just as the lord of birds [destroys] snakes through a conventional connection (*prātītika-anvaya*), [so too does this yoga function].

It should be understood that just as the lord of birds [the Garuda] subdues the pride of serpents, so too the supreme practitioner, having cast aside those scorched by fever, pacifies their pride and brings comfort to those afflicted by fever. || 20 ||

The great ones, with minds that have crushed impure māyā, perceive Your digit seated upon six lotuses— slender as a streak of lightning and composed of fire, moon, and sun— and they maintain [that vision] within the forest of the Great Lotus.
A wave of supreme joy. || 21 ||

A streak of lightning (*taṭillekhā*) is a flash of lightning; likewise, she is slender, long and subtle, consisting of light, and possessing a momentary radiance. Her state of being a "momentary radiance" (*kṣaṇaprabhā*) is like that of a steady lightning bolt, due to her being perceived for only a moment at the *ājñā-cakra*. And this—
This was already explained previously on the occasion of defining the meaning of the word *ājñā*.

[She is] composed of the sun, moon, and fire—that is, consisting of the sun, moon, and fire—and this has been thoroughly established on the occasion of defining the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*). [She is] seated—meaning sitting.

The word "api" (also/even) serves as a conjunction that includes the triad of knots among the six—that is, the six in number. It also includes the triad of knots. Above [these] are the lotuses (*kamala*), which are the six wheels (*cakra*).

The lotus-nature of the centers consisting of the Ādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā has already been described. [I bow to] Your portion, the Sādākhya, the Bindu-portion, within the great forest of Mahāpadma— [portions that are] many and vast.

"Lotuses" refers to lotus petals numbering in the thousands; "in that forest" means within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of such a thousand-petaled lotus. Alternatively, "Mahāpadma" refers to a thousand-petaled lotus, and "in that forest" means within it. [He is] one by whom impure *māyā* has been crushed.

By that mind— that is, by that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— whose impurities, such as desire and the rest, as well as illusion, ignorance, egoism, and self-conceit, have been crushed and destroyed, the great lords of yogis behold [the Lord].

Experiencing the outpouring of the stream of nectar from the *kalā* known as Sādākhyā, they bear and attain a wave of supreme bliss—supreme meaning unsurpassed (*niratiśaya*), and bliss being joy (*āhlāda*).

The meaning is that they constantly bring about a specific excellence of bliss for him— the surge, the overflow, the state of supreme bliss produced by the experience of the nectar of the digit known as Sādākhya.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Bhagavatī! Your digit (kalā), which is slender as a streak of lightning and composed of the sun, moon, and fire, seated even above six lotuses in the great forest of lotuses (mahāpadmāṭavī).
Beholding [Him] with minds whose impurities and illusions have been crushed, the great ones experience a wave of supreme bliss.

"O Bhavānī, bestow upon me, your servant, a compassionate glance"— he who desires to offer such praise and utters "O Bhavānī, you," to him you immediately grant the state of union with yourself, whose feet are clearly honored by the crowns of Mukunda, Brahmā, and Indra.
O Bhavānī! O Consort of Bhava! Grant—bestow—your compassionate glance, endowed with mercy, upon me, your servant, who has become a slave and a messenger;
desiring to praise you or compose a hymn in this manner.

Desiring [this], he speaks, he says: "O Bhavānī, you; O Bhavānī, you—bestow upon me, your servant, a compassionate glance. This opening of the sentence, "O Bhavānī, you," is that very [utterance] by which the practitioner [attains his goal]. At that very moment, "O Bhavānī, you... [is realized].
At the very moment of uttering even a single portion of the sentence, you bestow— that is, you grant— to that speaker of the portion of the sentence, your own state of union (sāyujya),
which is identity with your own self.
Her feet are illuminated by the clearly visible crowns of Mukunda, Brahmā, and Indra— Mukunda being Viṣṇu,
Brahmā being Druhiṇa, and Indra being Ākhaṇḍala— their feet having been honored by the ritual of the waving of lights (nīrājana) performed with their crowns in a manner that is manifest and distinct.
[She] whose [feet are] those lotus-feet.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Bhavānī! Desiring to praise you by saying, "O Bhavānī, you, grant a compassionate glance upon me, your servant," to him who speaks thus, you [grant] those feet which are clearly honored by the crowns of Mukunda, Brahmā, and Indra.
You grant the state of union with your own self.
The meaning is this: in the phrase "O Bhavānī, you [are] toward me, your servant," and so forth, within the two words "Bhavānī" and "tvaṃ," regarding the word "Bhavānī"—

Having understood that [the verb] ends in the first person singular of the imperative mood (*loṭ*), and having realized that the word *tvam* is construed with it through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the Blessed Lady— considering that this practitioner has employed the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*)— bestows the fruit of the Great Sentence, which is identity (*tādātmya*).
Because meditation on identity yields its fruit immediately, unlike the rules for worship such as recitation and fire-offerings—
indeed, fire burns even that which it touches unintentionally.

Thus, according to this principle, even a great sentence uttered without the intention to convey a specific meaning is bestowing of fruit; this is the secret that the Goddess does not act without due reflection. || 22 ||

I suspect that after you had stolen his beautiful form with an insatiable mind, the other half of Śambhu’s body was also taken away; for this form of yours is entirely ruddy-hued, possesses three eyes, and is bent by your breasts.
[He] whose crown is adorned with the crooked moon—
having taken away or stolen your left half of the body, [Śiva],
with a mind that was not yet satisfied or contented, [seized] the other half of Śambhu’s body as well.

I suspect, indeed I believe, that the right side too has been taken away and seized; for this reason, this form of yours— which manifests within the lotus of my heart— is your entire body, consisting of both left and right parts, possessing the luster of Aruṇa.

That which has a luster like the sun at dawn; or rather, that which has an *aruṇā*—meaning red-colored—luster or radiance is *aruṇābha*. It has three eyes (*trinayana*), being endowed with three eyes, and is slightly bowed by its two breasts (*kucābhyām ānamram*).
"Kuṭilaśaśicūḍālamakuṭam" means that whose crown (makuṭa) possesses a crest (cūḍāla) consisting of the curved moon (kuṭilaśaśin), that is, the digit of the crescent moon.
p.65) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! Having taken the left body of Śambhu, with a mind that was not yet satiated, you took even the other half of his body.
I suspect that this form of yours— entirely crimson-hued, with three eyes, bowed by your breasts, and crowned with a diadem of the curved moon— is indeed that very one.

The meaning is this: it is imagined that when one half of Śambhu was carried away by the Bhagavatī, the other half was likewise carried away. Alternatively, this verse sets forth the doctrine of the Uttarakaula Siddhānta; for in the Uttarakaula Siddhānta...

There is no Śiva-principle (śivatattva) other than the Śakti-principle (śaktitattva). Therefore, since the Śiva-principle is included within the Śakti-principle, it is that very principle which is presented as the object of worship. And this was stated on the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "the state of mind" and "the state of space" [verse 35].
And we shall explain this more thoroughly on the occasion of commenting upon the verse beginning with "In your foundation, at the root" (śloka 49). || 23 ||
The Creator brings forth the world; Hari protects it; Rudra destroys it; and the Lord, setting this aside, conceals even his own form.
Yet Śiva, ever prior to all, bestows grace upon all this through the mere movement of his creeper-like eyebrows for a moment, relying upon your command.
The Creator (Dhātṛ), the progenitor, brings forth—that is, creates—the world consisting of the moving and the stationary;
Hari, Viṣṇu, protects—that is, preserves—it; and Rudra destroys—that is, withdraws—it.
Thus, Dhātṛ, Hari, and Rudra are the authorities over creation, preservation, and dissolution [respectively].
Disregarding and withdrawing this triad consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, the Lord— the principle of Maheśvara— conceals even his own body,
making it disappear; the Lord, having superposed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra upon himself.

The meaning is that he himself is also included within the principle of Sadāśiva. By this, the dissolution of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is described. Immediately thereafter, the desire to bring forth the cosmic egg arises in Sadāśiva. At that time, he says "preceded by 'sadā'. The word *sadā*—
That which has the word *śiva* as its preceding part is the word *sadāśiva*;
by that word *sadāśiva*. (p. 66)
Due to the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the signified and the signifier, the reality (*tattva*) whose nature is Sadāśiva is figuratively attributed [to the latter].
This aforementioned group of four realities—consisting of Dhātṛ, Hari, Rudra, and Īśāna—is entirely graced by Him. The word "ca" (and) serves to dispel doubt. Śiva.

Sadāśiva, in response to the doubt as to how he bestows grace, says: "Having taken recourse to your command. This means that by the movement of your creeper-like eyebrows—your eyebrows which have moved for even a moment—the [grace is bestowed].
The meaning is: "having relied upon the command that is to be known. By the mere movement of your eyebrows, the fourfold group of principles consisting of Dhātṛ, Hari, Rudra, and Īśāna arose;
by the mere knitting of your brows, they were destroyed.
The intended meaning is that the power consisting of the mere movement of your eyebrow performs the office of assisting Sadāśiva in the creation and dissolution of many millions of Brahmāṇḍas.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Blessed One! Dhātṛ creates the world; Hari protects the world;
Rudra destroys the world; Īśa, setting this aside, conceals even his own form;
Śiva, who is ever primordial, all this is yours.
Having taken up the command of her two creeper-like eyebrows that quiver for a moment, she bestows grace.
O Śivā, the worship performed at your two feet is itself the worship of the three gods born of the three qualities (guṇas). For it is thus: [24]
Indeed, these [gods] stand perpetually near the jeweled pedestal that supports your feet, with their hands folded as ornaments upon their crowns.

The meaning is: of the three gods—namely Dhātṛ, Hari, and Rudra—who are produced from the three qualities (guṇas), that is, originating from sattva, rajas, and tamas; O Śivā! O Consort of Śiva! [your worship] shall indeed be [the highest], for you are Bhavānī. The use of the potential mood (liṅ) indicates that the time has arrived; [this refers to] worship.
The meaning of the second word "pūjā" is that service (*saparyā*) itself is worship and nothing else. That worship which was performed—that is, fashioned—for your two feet—this is indeed appropriate;
he states this with the words beginning "for it is thus" (*tathāhi*), meaning that this is fitting.
Near that jeweled pedestal which has been fashioned for the purpose of supporting your feet— that jeweled seat for the bearing of your two feet—

They remained standing near the vicinity of the lion-throne; for these presiding deities— Dhātṛ, Hari, and Rudra— were constantly and incessantly holding their hands in the form of a crown with buds, that is, their hands were folded in the añjali gesture.
Those whose crowns are possessed of such [ornaments] are "uttasāmakuṭāḥ."
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Śivā! whatever worship may be performed for the three gods born of the three qualities, that alone is worship unto Your two feet;
for indeed, it is in the vicinity of the jeweled pedestal that bears Your feet.
