For these [deities] always remain with their crowns adorned by lotus buds held in their hands.
The meaning is this: service at the footstool of the Blessed Lady is not obtained by mere worship alone, but rather solely through the power of the Blessed Lady’s grace. || 25 ||
When this Great Dissolution is underway and sports forth, Viriñci goes to the state of the five elements, Hari attains cessation,
Kīnāśa meets his destruction, and Dhanada goes to his end; even the vast,
sleepless expanse of Indra’s power closes its eyes.
This is your husband. || 26 ||

Viriñci, that is Brahmā, goes to—meaning reaches—the state of the five elements (pañcatva), which is to say, death. Hari, that is Viṣṇu, attains—that is, reaches—cessation (virati), which is to say, death. Kīnāśa [reaches] destruction, that is, death.
Yama takes his portion; Kubera, the giver of wealth, goes to or attains death (nidhana);
she whose special lethargy (tandrī)—meaning exhaustion or dullness—is gone is "vitandrī," that is to say, she who is awake; and she belongs to Mahendra, thus she is "māhendrī."
She whose vision was closed by the collective gaze—the eyes being closed—of the multitude (saṅgha) of the fourteen Manus and Indras;

[the feminine suffix] *ṭāp* is applied here even after a word ending in a consonant (*hal*), according to the rule "it is desired [that *ṭāp* follows] even from a word ending in a consonant. Alternatively, it may be understood as "by means of the closed gaze" (*sammīlitadṛśā*).

The state of being free from drowsiness belongs to Mahendra. In this Great Dissolution at the end of the aeon, He dwells, existing in a state of unrestrained freedom. O virtuous one! O lady of steadfast vows!
Your husband Sadāśiva, Hara, is that very one who is perceived within the thousand-petaled lotus.
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: Viriñci goes to the state of the five elements; Hari attains cessation; Kīnāśa undergoes destruction; Dhanada goes to his end.
Even the expanse of the Mahendra mountain, its eyes closed and free from weariness, remains vigilant during this great dissolution;
for even now, your husband Hara sports there!

The meaning is this: at the time of the dissolution of all things, including all sovereign beings [the addition "sovereigns" (īśvarāṇām) is found in some versions], when the cosmic egg is destroyed, the wandering of your husband is dependent upon the greatness of your devotion to your husband (*pātivratya*). || 26 ||

May my muttering of prayers, my speech, all my crafts, the fashioning of mudrās, my movement, my circumambulation, the ritual of offering food and other oblations, my prostrations, and my rest— all my pleasure, through the vision of total self-surrender, become a succession of offerings unto You.
This is the playful manifestation. || 27 ||

Japa is the recitation of mantras, whether performed in a whisper or aloud, as prescribed by such rules; jalpa is spontaneous conversation; and śilpa is the entire collection of manual activities, such as the positioning of the hands and the formation of mudrās.

The construction consists of the [mantras] comprising the three sections: *saṃkṣobha* (agitation), *drāvaṇa* (melting), *ākarṣa* (attracting), *vaśya* (subjugation), *unmāda* (intoxication), *mahāṅkuśa* (the great goad), *khecarī* (the sky-farer), *bīja* (seed), and *yoni* (womb). Gait refers to movement at will and the act of circumambulation performed in a clockwise direction. Eating and so forth...

The "procedure of oblations" (āhutividhi) refers to the chewing of any substance whatsoever, such as boiled rice; it is the performance or ritual of oblations, which consist of the casting of sacrificial offerings (havis) intended for specific deities.
"Prostration" (praṇāma) is the act of salutation; "lying down" (saṃveśa) is rolling on the ground like a staff at will.
Apart from speech and manual arts, all pleasure— consisting of the bending of limbs, the opening and closing of the eyes, and every object that produces happiness,
such as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— is [to be viewed] through the vision of self-surrender.

With the intention of self-surrender, worship—which is a synonym for *saparyā*—is a synonym for worship; the meaning is that it is another form of worship itself. May that [worship] be yours, may it belong to you.
That which is well-known as my own playful manifestation (*vilasita*) or grace (*vilāsa*).
p.

69) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! Recitation (*japa*), speech (*jalpa*), every craft (*śilpa*), the formation of ritual gestures (*mudrā*), and movement (*gati*) consisting of circumambulation—all these are performed through the vision of self-surrender.
The ritual of offering food and so forth, lying down, prostration, and whatever brings me complete happiness— even my very manifestation— let all this become a succession of offerings unto you.

This is the meaning: the nature of recitation and so forth for speech and the like is conceived according to what is appropriate. In this way, the equivalence to the sequence of worship (saparyā) for the opening and closing of the eyes, the winking and unblinking, the flexing of limbs, yawning, and so forth, should be inferred as appropriate. [This applies] to sound and other things that produce pleasure.

The renunciation of an object through the thought of self-surrender, rather than by means of the sixteen types of ritual offerings, is indeed synonymous with worship; it does not refer to objects already accepted [as one's own]. Alternatively, when pleasure arises through the accidental occurrence of sound and other sense-objects, that pleasure is "my remnant" (maccheṣa).
However, the dedication "to Sadāśiva" is synonymous with worship (saparyā).
In this regard, the following should be considered according to the view of the *samayins*:
for them, the worship of the *samaya*—the principle known as *Sādākhya*—takes place solely within the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*) and not externally on a *pīṭha* or elsewhere.
Those who are *samayins*, lords of yoga, and liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), continue to follow the course of worldly existence.
Contemplating the principle called Sādākhyatattva, they remain solely intent upon the Self;

for them, the method of worship is described as consisting of mantra-recitation (japa), discourse (jalpa), artistic skill (śilpa), and so forth. As for those who are initiates (samayinaḥ) and masters of yoga, they sit in the lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) within a secluded cave or similar place.
Those who have restrained their senses and are solely devoted to meditation on the principle called Sādākhya abide;

for them, the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the fourfold and sixfold unities to be described hereafter constitutes the worship (*saparyā*) of the Blessed Lady—this is what is meant by implication. Therefore, in both positions:

The secret is that for those who observe the commitments (samayins), there is no affliction whatsoever regarding external worship, its ritual procedures, or the preparation thereof. As for what is stated in the *Candrajñānavidyā*:
"One should worship the Goddess Tripurasundarī, who stands in the center of the solar disc and holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows. Thus it is said.
The description of the types of external worship is, however, the view of a single school of the Samaya; this will be explained in detail later on. || 27 ||
70) He states with supplementary elaboration that which was said in the verse beginning "Viriñci [attains] the state of the five elements":
"Even after tasting the nectar that removes fear, old age, and death, all beings perish."

O Mother, that Śambhu—who has swallowed the terrible poison—does not experience the reckoning of time (death), even though he is a celestial being like Brahmā, Indra, and the others; the root cause of this is the power of your earring.
[The word] *api* implies a contradiction: having tasted—that is, drunk—even the nectar (*sudhā*).

She is the one who carries away the deer of fearful old age and death—that is, she who removes the two terrifying things, old age and death (*jarāmṛtyu*). All beings without exception, including Brahmā and Indra, perish and die; "Brahmā" refers to Vidhi.

The gods, those inhabitants of heaven whose first among them was Śatamakha, the lord of the gods, [could not endure] the reckoning by time— that is, death— of Him who had swallowed and consumed the terrible and most fierce poison,
the Kālakūṭa.
The "limiting time" (*avasānakāla*) refers to the calculation of time, its restriction, that is to say, death; it is not [death] for Śambhu.

That which is the root of that—namely, the cause of the absence of the calculation of time—is yours, O Mother! O Janani! It is the power of the ear-ornament (*tāṭaṅka*), the greatness of the ear-ornament.
The efficacy of the ear-ornament.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Mother! All the inhabitants of heaven, beginning with Brahmā and Indra, though they have tasted the nectar that removes the deer-like fear of old age and death, still perish; yet for Śambhu, who has swallowed the formidable poison, there is no reckoning of time.
That which is the root of [your thought] "it does not exist" is the power of your earrings.

The intended meaning is this: if even Śambhu were subject to misfortune, then there might be the falling off of his ear-ornament (*tāṭaṅka*). However, Time has no power to cause the falling off of that ornament, because the origination, maintenance, and dissolution of Time are strictly dependent upon that very ornament—so says the Goddess.
The greatness of devotion to one's husband surpasses all else. || 28 ||
Avoid the crown of Brahmā before the slayer of Kaiṭabha;
you will stumble against the formidable diadem of Viṣṇu— cast aside the tiara of Indra as you approach the residence of Śiva, who rises up with forceful haste when these [gods] bow down before him.
The speech of the attendants prevails. || 29 ||
p. 71) Cast far away— that is, keep at a distance— the crown, the diadem belonging to Viriñci (Viriñci-sambandhi),
in front— that is, in the space before you— of the slayer of Kaiṭabha (Kaiṭabha-bhid), who destroys the demon Kaiṭabha.

O you who are terrified of Kaiṭabha, you stumble upon the hard crest—the edge of the crown—of that Viṣṇu. Here, a change in intonation (kāku) is to be understood. Abandon, cast away, the crown of Jambhāri;
[cast away] the diadem of Jambhāri, that is, Indra. [This applies to those] among those bowing down, prostrating themselves like a staff.

When these— Viriñci, Kaiṭabha-jit, and Jambhāri— had bowed down, for you, who had arrived at the palace (mandira) of Bhava, the Supreme Lord, there was a rising to meet him (abhyutthāna), that is, a rising to face him with force, extreme haste, and agitation.
The speech of the attendants—the words of the servants—prevails; it exists with its own excellence.
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: "O Blessed One! First, avoid the crown of Brahmā;
you stumble upon the hard crest of Viṣṇu, the slayer of Kaiṭabha; cast off the diadem of Indra"—while these [gods] were thus bowing down, [she did so] as he was entering the palace.
In this instance, the speech of the attendants regarding your forceful emergence from existence prevails;
for here lies the figure of speech *udātta*, according to the definition: "The *udātta* is the description of a thing possessed of prosperity.
[This occurs] while you are being constantly attended on all sides by the compassionate powers beginning with *aṇimā*, which have arisen from your own body, in that eternal [state].

For one who constantly meditates with the thought "I am you," what wonder is there that the fire of the great dissolution performs the ritual of waving lights for him, as he regards the prosperity of the Three-Eyed Lord as a mere blade of grass? 30.
"Produced from her own body": *svadeha* means her own body (*svasyāḥ dehaḥ*); "produced from that.

Here, the word *deha* (body) indicates a limb of the body, namely the foot. It was stated previously that rays (*mayūkha*) arise from the feet. *Ghṛṇibhiḥ* means by rays; the fact that rays originate from the feet has been mentioned before.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "endowed with" the eight siddhis, beginning with *aṇimā* and *garimā*, which stand as surrounding enclosures on all sides; [according to the Pañcasāyaka and Śūnyasamādhitantra commentaries, these are the eternal goddesses Tripurasundarī and the others].
O you who are to be served! O you who are to be worshipped! O eternal one! O you who are devoid of beginning and end!
For that practitioner who always, at all times, meditates upon you as such through the sense of "I" (*aham-bhāvanā*), performing dhyāna—what wonder is there? There is no wonder for that practitioner.

The "three-eyed one" (trinayana) is so called because his vision consists of three eyes— the paths or modes consisting of the sun, moon, and fire— or else because the three paths known as *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* constitute his vision. His "prosperity" (*samṛddhi*) is the perfection of these three eyes.

The means for perceiving that [Reality] are the Three-Eyed One, Sadāśiva; or rather, he is "Three-Eyed" (trinayana) because he possesses three eyes (nayanāni = cakṣūṃṣi). Due to his inclusion in the *kṣubhna*-class of words, there is an absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. He regards his own abundant sovereignty (*samṛddhim aiśvaryam*) as a mere blade of grass (*tṛṇayataḥ*).
The fire of the great dissolution—the fire of the time of universal destruction—renders it as insignificant as a blade of grass;
that is, it performs the rite of *nirājana* (the waving of lights). The meaning is that even the fire of dissolution remains present during that very performance of the *nirājana* ritual.

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Eternal One! O Worthy of Service! that practitioner who always contemplates you—who are surrounded by the powers (*prakārāḥ*) such as *aṇimā* and others, which have arisen from your own body, are radiant, and are situated on all sides—as being "I."
What wonder is there in this: that for him who regards the prosperity of the Three-Eyed Lord as mere straw, the great fire of universal dissolution performs the rite of lustration (*nīrājanā*)?
This is the intended meaning: when identity with the Goddess is established through the contemplative realization (*bhāvanā*) of "I am [She]."
Thus, this rite of lustration (nīrājana) is not a cause for wonder. || 30 ||
Having bound the entire world with sixty-four tantras that are dependent on producing various supernatural powers (siddhis), Paśupati remains; yet,
due to your persistence, he has now made this [work] independent, as it accomplishes every human goal.
He brought this tantra down to the surface of the earth. || 31 ||
By sixty-four—that is, by the sixty-four tantras and established doctrines (siddhāntas), such as the Mahāmāyāśambara and others.

In this context, because the word "sixty-four" (*catuṣṣaṣṭi*) refers to the number of things to be counted, it takes the singular ending. Having entirely encompassed— that is, having led away and deceived— the entire world, the phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), he remains with his activity ceased, [surrounded] by those who are dependent upon the production of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

"And those various accomplishments" (*tāśca tāśca siddhayaḥ*) means the specific accomplishments (*tattatsiddhayaḥ*) that serve as the purposes within each individual tantra among the sixty-four tantras; that is to say, they are the individual accomplishments.
Their "production" (*prasavaḥ*) is their arising. In this regard, [it is achieved] by those dependent on other tantras (*paratantraiḥ*). Alternatively, [it refers to] theirs...

"Siddhis" refers to those various accomplishments which are the desired attainments of whichever practitioners there may be; "dependent on the production of those" means being restricted solely to their generation. "Paśupati" is the Lord of "paśus," that is, of living beings.
They are called *paśu* (beasts) because they see (*paśyanti*); alternatively, by the etymology that the senses themselves see, they are *paśu*.
He who protects (*pāti*) those *paśu* is *Paśupati*. Śiva himself is the individual soul (*jīva*), thus Śiva is *Paśupati*. Furthermore, due to your persistence, [he was addressed] by you...

Therefore, it is persistence; that is to say, you, O Goddess, have shown persistence by being intent on accepting the instructions of other tantras, which serve as the means for achieving all human goals in the form of all the established doctrines taught in the sixty-four tantras. Or else:

The word *tvad* is a separate term ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*). It means "independent" (*svatantra*) in the accomplishment (*ghaṭanā*) of all human goals (*akhilapuruṣārtha*) as their primary purpose; that is, it is independent by itself.
"The earth—the surface of the world—has descended into your dominion; *pradhānam* is the subject, and *tantram* is the object.

The form is that of the root *tṛ* (to cross) with the suffix *ṇic* followed by the reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*). Because it has the sense of motion, it takes two objects according to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...* and so forth. This refers to what is about to be said."

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Bhagavatī! Paśupati remains having deceived the entire world with sixty-four tantras that are dependent on the production of various supernatural powers (siddhis);
yet, due to your persistent entreaty...
This tantra of yours, which is the independent means for accomplishing every human goal,
has descended upon the surface of the earth.
Regarding the sixty-four tantras, the *Catuḥśatī* states:
"The sixty-four tantras are the most excellent among the Mother Tantras;
they are the Mahāmāyāśambara, the Yoginījālaśambara, and the Tattvaśambara."
And likewise the Bhairavāṣṭaka,
the Bahurūpāṣṭaka, the Yāmalāṣṭaka, and the Candrajñāna.

The Mālinī, the Mahāsaṃmohana, the Vāmajuṣṭa, the Mahādeva, the Vātula, and the Vātulottara; the Hṛdbheḍa, the Tantrabheḍa, the Guhyayantra, and the Kāmika; the Kalāvāda, the Kalāsāra, and likewise the other, the Kubjikāmata.

And the *Tantrottara*, the one called *Vīṇā*, the *Trotala*, and the *Trotalottara*; the *Pañcāmṛta*, the *Rūpabheda*, and the *Bhūtoḍḍāmara*; the *Kulasāra*, the *Kuloḍḍīśa*, and likewise the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*; the *Sarvajñānottara*, O God, and the *Mahākālīmata*.

Likewise: the Aruṇeśa, the Mahālakṣmīmata, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Kurūpikāmata, and the Devarūpikāmata; the Sarvavīramata and the supreme Vimalāmata; as well as the Pūrva, Paścima, Dakṣa, Uttara, and Niruttara.

The *Tantra*, the *Vaiśeṣikajñāna*, the *Vīrāvali*, and likewise the supreme *Aruṇeśa*, *Mohinīśa*, and *Viśuddheśvara*—this is the reading in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*. [In another version: *Modinīśa* and *Vikuṇṭheśvara*.
The Mahālakṣmīmata, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Kurūpikāmata, and the Devarūpikāmata; the Sarvavīramata and the supreme Vimalāmata;
the Pūrva, Paścima, Dakṣa, Uttara, and Niruttara Tantras.
The Vaiśeṣika-jñāna, the Vīrāvali, and likewise the Aruṇeśa, the Mohinīśa, and the Viśuddheśvara; [thus is the reading in the Vāmakeśvaratantra];
and the Pūrva, Paścima, Dakṣa, Uttara, and Niruttara; and the Vimala.
And thereafter, the Vimalottha and the Devīmata.
Thus, these sixty-four tantras were spoken to Pārvatī.

These tantras are the causes of the deception of the worlds and are the source of their destruction, because they stand far removed from the Vedic path. For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:
Having deceived the world through sixty-four tantras,
these sixty-four tantras— which delude the entire world of the learned— are as follows:
Thus, for example:

The *Mahāmāyāśambaratantra* is the fruit of the manifestation of the proliferation of illusion (*māyā-prapañca-nirmāṇa*). What is called the "manifestation of the proliferation of illusion" refers to [the manifestation] of all [faculties], such as the eyes and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be the apprehension of an object in a form other than its own, such as the appearance of a jar in the form of a cloth.

The *Yoginījālaśambara* is called *Śambara* because it is a tantra in which illusion (*māyā*) is predominant. In that tantra, there is the "vision of water" (*jala-darśana*) by means of yoginīs; and that is accomplished through unconventional paths such as cremation grounds and the like.

*Tattvaśambara* is the *śambara*—the art of Mahendra’s magic—of the principles (*tattvas*) such as earth and the rest. In the art of Mahendra’s magic, the principle of water and so forth appear within the principle of earth, and the principle of earth and so forth appear within the principle of water; thus they appear to one another.
They appear.

The *Bhairavāṣṭaka*, known as the eight tantras primarily consisting of Siddhabhairava, Vaṭukabhairava, Kaṅkālabhairava, Kālabhairava, Kālāgnibhairava, Yoginībhairava, Mahābhairava, and Śaktibhairava.
Even those practices that achieve worldly results through meditation and so forth are far removed from the Vedic path because they belong to the Kāpālika doctrine.

The Eightfold Bahurūpa: the forms manifested from Śakti are the eight forms—Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śivadūtī. It is by resorting to these that [the world] has proceeded.

The eight tantras constitute their group, the "octad. This too is to be rejected because it stands far from the path of the Vedas. Here, the mention of Śrīvidyā has been introduced incidentally in the context of the discussion on the "Octad of Many Forms" (Bahurūpāṣṭaka); thus, there is no fault.
There is no fault whatsoever.
Regarding the *Yamalāṣṭaka*: what is the *Yamala* known as the *Kāmasiddhānta*? The eight *Tantras* that expound it are the *Yāmalas*. The collection of these is the *Yamalāṣṭaka*.
That too is far removed from the Vedic path, even though [it is included among] the sixty-four *Tantras*.
The state of being twins is established by worldly convention; however, it should be understood that this [application] is figurative because of the commonality of being non-Vedic.
The *Candrajñāna* is the exposition of the sixteen *Nityās* within the *Candrajñānavidyā*.
Even though it expounds the *Nityās*, it is to be rejected because it falls within the scope of the Kāpālika doctrine.
The *Candrajñānavidyā* that is to be accepted transcends the sixty-four Tantras.
The Mālinī-vidyā is the cause for the means of sea-voyage; it, too,
stands far removed from the Vedic path.
The Great Delusion is the cause of sleep even for those who are awake;
it is prohibited because it is to be accomplished through improper paths such as cutting off the tongues of children.
In the *Vāmajuṣṭamahādevatantra*, it is stated that [the Vāmācāra] is to be abandoned because it promotes the practice of the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*).

The three tantras—the Vātula, the Vātulottara, and the Kāmika—expound the rituals beginning with the selection of the site (karṣaṇa) and ending with consecration (pratiṣṭhā). Within those three tantras, the rituals from the selection of the site up to consecration are taught in a single section. That...
And one part is indeed the Vedic path; the remainder, however, is non-Vedic.

The *Hṛdbhedatantra* is indeed Kāpālika. Although the piercing of the six lotuses and the entry into the *sahasrāra* are taught in the *Hṛdbhedatantra*, nevertheless, because that tantra is engaged solely in the left-hand practice (*vāmācāra*), it is indeed Kāpālika.

The distinction between the two types of Tantras— the *Guhyatantra* (Secret Tantra) and the *Prakāśatantra* (Revealed Tantra)— is that the latter consists of tantras composed by others; because the practice of their lore entails much violence, those two types of tantra are far removed from the Vedic path.

*Kalāvādam* refers to that tantra in which there is a discourse (*vāda*), that is, an exposition, of *kalās*, namely the digits of the moon; it is the system of Vātsyāyana and others. Although [this system] concerns the aim of human life consisting of desire (*kāma*),...

Because [practices] such as the grasping and releasing of digits (*kalā*), the calculation of the ten positions (*daśasthāna*), and the assignment of lunar digits (*candrakalā*) are of no use for the aim of human life consisting of desire (*kāma-puruṣārtha*), and because they teach prohibited conduct such as approaching the wives of others, [this system] is forbidden in one respect.

Although the prohibited portion does not constitute the Kāpālika-tantra itself, nevertheless, because a person engaging in it necessarily adopts the conduct of a Kāpālika, the tantra is classified as Kāpālika.
That in which the procedure for the excellence of phonemes proceeds is the Kalāsāra; it is primarily characterized by the left-hand practice (vāmācāra).
The Kubjikāmata is the cause for the attainment of the medicinal pill (guṭikāsiddhi); it too is primarily characterized by the left-hand practice (vāmācāra).
According to the view of the *Tantrottara*, there is the attainment of the alchemical elixir (*rasasiddhi*).
Regarding the one called Vīṇā: the yoginī named Vīṇā is accomplished [there], hence it is called "Vīṇā. Some say that this Vīṇā is the yakṣiṇī Saṃbhogā.
By means of this, one attains the accomplishment of the pill, the collyrium, and the sandals. The pill is a drinking vessel.
In the Trotalottara, there is the vision of sixty-four thousand yakṣiṇīs;
as for the *pañcāmṛta*, it is the tantra of the five nectars— the five elements beginning with earth— within which the absence of death is established in the cosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*).
That too is indeed Kāpālika.
The fivefold system of tantras beginning with the differentiation of forms is the cause of death; thus it is non-Vedic.
The five tantras beginning with the Sarvajñāna, as well as the Kāpālika Siddhānta and the Digambara doctrine, are to be rejected from afar.
The doctrine of the Digambara sub-sect of the Kṣapaṇakas, extending from the Pūrvācāryas to Devīmata,
is to be rejected as far removed from [true] reality.

Thus, even for those who have mastered the sixty-four Tantras, they are deceptive because they are intent solely upon worldly accomplishments and remain far removed from the Vedic path. Even among those who have mastered them, some who engaged with them out of a desire for worldly fruits were indeed deceived.
The secret.

If it is asked, "How can there be deceit toward certain individuals on the part of the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ishvara Paśupati, who is free from defects of intention such as the desire to deceive?"—
do not say so; for in the Supreme Ishvara, who is supremely compassionate, defects of intention such as the desire to deceive do not exist.

They certainly do exist; however, the Supreme Lord Paśupati composed the Tantras with reference to the classes of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as the mixed castes (jātis) such as the Mūrdhāvasikta, whether born in the natural or inverse order.

He created them. Among them, the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) have the authority (*adhikāra*) over the lunar arts (*candrakalā-vidyā*) to be described hereafter; whereas for the *śūdras* and others—including those of mixed caste—the authority lies in the sixty-four *tantras*.
Thus, those who are not thinkers (amīmāṃsakāḥ), not understanding the distinction between these scopes of authority, fall into confusion.
It should be understood that this fault belongs only to them, and not to Paśupati, the Supreme Lord.
The *Candrakalāvidyāṣṭaka*, the *Śrīvidyāpratipādaka-tantra*, *Candrakalā*, *Jyotsnāvatī*, *Kalānidhi*, *Kulārṇava*,
*Kuleśvarī*, *Bhuvaneśvarī*, the *Bārhaspatya*, and the *Dūrvāsamatam*— in this [collection].
In the *Tantrāṣṭaka*, there is eligibility for both the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*) and the Śūdras and others.

Among these, with reference to the Brāhmaṇas and the rest, the entire range of ritual practices is prescribed by way of the left (*savya-mārga*) and in a clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇya*). With reference to the Śūdras and others, however—
The practice of the left-hand path (vāmācāra) is defined by the counter-clockwise direction.

In the *Śubhāgamatantra-pañcaka*, the entire collection of ritual practices has been described according to the Vedic path. This path, as delineated in the *Śubhāgamapañcaka*, was taught by five sages: Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana, and Sanatkumāra.
This has been demonstrated; this very thing is designated as the "conduct of the covenant" (*samayācāra*).

In the same way, we too have composed this commentary by following the doctrine of the Covenant (*samayamata*), in accordance with the five auspicious scriptures (*śubhāgama-pañcaka*) and adhering to the thought of the venerable master (Bhagavatpāda).
The eightfold Vidyā of Candrakalā is called "mixed" (*miśraka*) by the wise because it follows the *Kula-samaya*. The sixty-four Tantras belong to the *Kula* path alone;
indeed, O Daughter of Śaṅkara, both the mixed and the *Kaula* paths are to be abandoned.
Thus, according to the word of the Lord, the Miśraka doctrine and the Kaula path are to be abandoned.

The Kaula path—that which is sought after and relied upon by the Kaulas—is the Kaula doctrine; [the suffix] *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). Therefore, only the fivefold Śubhāgama is to be honored by the followers of the Veda.
This is because its purpose is solely to demonstrate the path of the *samaya*.

However, we shall explain the essential nature of the path of the *samaya* more thoroughly during the commentary on the verse beginning with "In your foundation, at the root, together with the *samaya*" (verse 41).

In that regard, within the *Śubhāgamapañcaka*, the presentation of the sixteen *Nityās* is accepted as being included within the Root-Vidyā by way of being its limbs (*aṅga*). In the *Cakravidyā*, their inclusion is likewise stated to be solely by way of being limbs. For this very reason—
Within the Candrajñāna-vidyā, which is included among the sixty-four branches of knowledge (vidyāntara), the sixteen Nityās are presented as being preeminent.
Thus, the distinction is that the Tantra which expounds that [former] is the Kaula path, whereas this is the Samaya path.

In this regard, the following should be considered: the so-called *śubhāgamapañcaka* (the pentad of auspicious scriptures) consists of five compendia (*saṃhitās*), namely: the *Vāsiṣṭhasaṃhitā*, the *Sanakasaṃhitā*, the *Śukasaṃhitā*, the *Sanandanasaṃhitā*, and the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*. Among these—
In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā, within the words of Īśvara addressed to the Goddess, Śakti was enlightened by Vasiṣṭha as follows:

Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim to you the *Nityāṣoḍaśaka* [in another reading: "the ninth *Ṣoḍaśikārṇava*, O Viśveśvarī"]. It has not been told by me to anyone; it is concealed within all the Tantras. Therein, first, is the first [Nityā].
The eternal Mahātripurasundarī; then the eternal Kāmeśvarī, the eternal Bhagamālinī, the eternal Klinnā, as well as Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Mahāvidyeśvarī,
Raudrī, Tvaritā, and Kulasundarī— the eternal ones.
Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī, and Citrūpā—

these sixteen are the eternal goddesses. One should worship these goddesses from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the full moon (paurṇamāsī), and from one until the new moon (darśa), O Goddess, by increasing and decreasing [the offerings] respectively.
The body.
And this fact— that the sixteen Nityās consist of the essence of the sixteen lunar days— is established in the following verse.
Now, the inclusion of the sixteen Nityās as constituent parts within the Śrīcakra is described:
the sixteen Nityās, being of the nature of eight groups,
reside respectively upon the eight petals of the eight-petaled lotus and within the eight-cornered wheel.
Beginning from the eastern direction and the corners, two by two are contained within each corner;
thus, eight pairs are contained within the eight corners. These very Nityās, consisting of the sixteen vowels, abide in the sixteen-petaled lotus.
They are included within the twelve-spoked [wheel]. Among these Nityās (p.
80), the first pair of Nityās exists in the form of the triangle and the bindu.
The remaining fourteen Nityās are included within the Mantras;
they are contained within the three girdles and the three fortresses, and within the Bindu and the Triangle. Thus is the inclusion of the Nityās within the Cakra. This very inclusion—
They call this the Meru-prastāra. For this very reason, the status of being a *saṅga* (conjunction) for the *candrakalā-vidyā* and the *cakravidyā* of the *Nityās* is established.
In the *Sanandana-saṃhitā*, Sanandana’s words to the sages are as follows: "These, however—"

The sixteen Nityās are constituent parts of the Cakra-vidyā of the lunar digit (candrakalā). These sixteen Nityās, whose nature consists of the vowels, are subsumed within the letter *sa*— which comprises the vowel *a* and the visarga— and the letters beginning with *e* found in the fifteen-syllable mantra.
Those whose form consists of the *jīvakalās* (vital energies) are established in the *baindava* station and are contained therein.

The letters from *ka* to *ma*, being joined with the seed-syllables of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), are contained within the eight-spoked wheel and the two ten-cornered wheels. The remaining nine, beginning with *ya*, however—

By repeating the sequence of letters twice, fourteen letters are contained within the fourteen corners of the *manvaśra* (the fourteen-cornered figure); the remaining four letters are contained within the four wheels of Śiva (*śivacakra*). This very arrangement they call the *kailāsaprastāra*.
Thus, it has been established that the eternal [mantras] constitute the constituent parts of the Cakra-vidyā.
In the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā* as well, the status of the sixteen *Nityās* as limbs (*aṅga*) of the *Cakravidyā* is established. As stated in the words of Sanatkumāra:
"The *Nityās* are the limbs of the Śrīcakra, [grouped] two by two with Vaśinī and the others."
Having merged [the letters] into the bindu and excluding the triangle, they are to be internalized within the eight corners. Tripurasundarī is to be internalized in the center.
As for the eight groups, they consist of the eight [deities] beginning with Vaśinī, the sixteen Nityās, and the twelve [others].
The four Yoginīs, beginning with Gandhākarṣiṇī, likewise make forty-four.
Here, excluding one Śakti, forty-three deities— forty-three being included within the corners— are to be placed, along with one Tripurasundarī.
Below the Baindava-sthāna, [the deities] beginning with Gandhākarṣiṇī are located at the four gates;

thus, their status as ancillaries (aṅga) to the Nityās is established. This very arrangement on the ground is what they call the "ground-extension" (bhū-prastāra) for the eight [deities] beginning with Vaśinī and for the twelve Yoginīs.
The names of Gandhākarṣiṇī and the others have been stated during the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "by those who are the mothers of speech" (verse 17). || 31 ||

81) Now, it was stated in the preceding verse that Lord Paśupati brought down to the surface of the earth the Tantra of the Blessed Lady, which is independent in accomplishing all human goals; that very [Tantra]—
He introduces the Tantra:
Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Earth, then the Sun, the Moon, Smara, Haṃsa, Śakra, and thereafter Parā, Māra, and Hari; these...
O Mother, at their conclusion, those letters joined with the three *hṛllekhā* mantras become constituent parts of Your name.

Śiva is the letter *ka*; Śakti is the letter *e*; Kāma is the letter *ī*; Kṣiti is the letter *la*. The word *atha* indicates the end [of the preceding section]. Ravi is the letter *ha*; Śītakiraṇa is the letter *sa*; Smara is the letter *ka*; Haṃsa is the letter *ha*.

Śakra is the letter *la*. And thereafter, the word *ca* indicates the pause (*avasāna*). Parā is the letter *sa*. Māra is the letter *ka*. Hari is the letter *la*. These are the twelve syllables. [They are joined] with the three *hṛllekhās*, that is, the three *hrīṃ*s.

The syllables— the aforementioned *ka* and so forth— joined and placed above groups of four, five, and three at the ends, that is, at the points of pause, attain [their respective positions] for you, O Lady.
O Mother! O Mother! "Nāmāvayavatām" means the state of being a constituent part, that is, the state of being a symbolic representation, of the name—the Tripurasundarī mantra.

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Mother! Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Kṣiti, then Ravi, Śītakiraṇa, Svara, Haṃsa, Śakra, and thereafter Parā, Māra, and Hari—these are the syllables [formed] with the three Hṛllekhās.
Those syllables joined at the ends become constituent parts of your name.

In this regard, the following should be considered: the four syllables Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, and Kṣiti constitute the fiery (āgneya) section. The five syllables Ravi, Śītakiraṇa, Smara, Haṃsa, and Śakra constitute the solar (saura) section.
Between the two segments is the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā*, which occupies the position of the *rudragranthi*.
The gentle (*saumya*) segment is defined by the three syllables *parāmāraharayaḥ*.

Between the *saumya* and *saura* segments is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, which occupies the position of the Viṣṇu-knot. The fourth is the single-syllabled segment of the lunar digit (*candrakalā*).
Between the *saumya* and *candrakalā* segments is that which occupies the position of the Brahmā-knot.

The seed-syllable *hṛllekhā*. As for the fragment of the digit of the moon (*candrakalākhaṇḍa*), it is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru; therefore, it has not been disclosed here. For this very reason, it is said: "The *mātṛkā* mantra consists of three parts and is composed of the Moon, Sun, and Fire."

The phrase "in the order of descent" is to be understood as the ellipsis. While it would have been sufficient to say "consisting of the nature of Moon, Sun, and Fire," the expression "three sections" (trikhaṇḍa) is used to indicate that the three sections consist of the powers of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), will (icchā-śakti), and action (kriyā-śakti).
It consists of the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
it consists of the three functions of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña; and it consists of the qualities of Tamas, Rajas, and Sattva—thus is it supreme. We shall elaborate upon this further ahead.

In this context, words such as "Śiva" and "Śakti" refer to the phonemes beginning with 'ka' either through indirect indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) or through direct indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For instance, the mantra of Tripurasundarī consists of sixteen syllables; and these sixteen syllables are, by virtue of being the essence of the sixteen Nityās—

They are established here. In this context, the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) is designated as "eternal" (*nityā*) due to its similarity with the nature of the lunar digit. And that supreme digit (*parā kalā*) consists solely of the essence of consciousness (*cidekarasā*).
Its shadow revolves within the sixteen-spoked Viśuddhi-cakra in the form of a digit.
[The word "bhrājati" appears in the manuscript. This is the secret. She is the Pradhāna and the Prakṛti.
Although fifteen syllables beginning with the letter *ka* are heard, it was established in the preceding verse that the fifteen Nityās are her constituent limbs (*aṅga*).

These must be understood through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*). Although it is said that "the one phoneme consists of sixteen parts and is the primary [or fundamental] nature" (*pradhāna*/*prakṛti*), and that the sixteenth part is to be understood only from the mouth of the Guru, nevertheless, the explanation would be incomplete if that were not set forth.
It is indeed dependent; therefore, it would necessarily be non-adoptable—thus that *kalā* is defined.
And it is said:
"That art (kalā) should be taught to a good disciple who is devoted to the guru."
It should be said that this must be taught only to disciples and not to others; however, those who,
having seen my book, come to know that art, they alone are my disciples— this is our favor.

If it is asked: "But how can there be the status of a disciple in those cases, given the absence of that collection of constituent parts— such as prostrating at the feet, clasping the feet, and joining the hands and head— which brings about the status of being a disciple?"

Let there be no discipleship for those who, having seen our book, claim to know the nature of the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) solely from the mouth of another teacher; however, for those who do not know it even from the mouth of a teacher,
instruction is simply not possible at that time.

When the inquiry arises among those seekers— both those currently existing and those yet to come— as to "who are our gurus in this mantra that is entirely dependent on the Guru alone," [the Lord] bestows grace upon them by [revealing] that "we ourselves are their gurus."
It has been done by us.
The mantra known as the Sixteenth Kalā consists of the letters *śa*, *ra*, *i*, and the nasal bindu (*m*).

Of this very seed-syllable, the name is Śrīvidyā; the secret meaning is that Śrīvidyā is the knowledge whose essence is the seed-syllable Śrī. Thus, these are the primordial forms of the sixteen Nityās.

These begin with the letter *ka* and so forth. These sixteen *Nityās* take the form of the lunar days (*tithis*) starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) up to the full moon, and starting from the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*) up to the new moon; these alone are designated as the "digits of the moon" (*candrakalā*).

It is well known that the lunar phases (*kalā*) themselves constitute the lunar days (*tithi*), beginning with the first (*pratipad*). As it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "The first phase of the moon should be understood as having the name *pratipad*; the second and so forth..."
"The second and subsequent [days] of both the bright and dark fortnights. Thus [it is said].
The meaning is this: the first digit of the moon is named "the first lunar day" (*pratipad*).
That very digit, consisting of a single digit, has emerged from the solar orb during the bright fortnight;
however, during the dark fortnight, it has entered the solar orb. Thus it is in the bright fortnight.
The second digit (kalā) emerging from the solar orb is the second lunar day (tithi);
in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), the second digit entering the solar orb is the second lunar day. In this manner, it should be inferred everywhere.
And for this reason, that [day] on which there is a separation of fifteen digits between the sun and the moon is the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
occurring on the fifteenth digit.

The absolute conjunction of the sun and the moon should be known as Amāvāsyā. Therefore, according to the Kaula system, there is the performance of only one of the sixteen Nityās, who consist of the digits of the moon, every day; whereas, according to the Samaya system, it is [the performance] of all of them, specifically that of the sixteenth.
The performance of Kalā is established for all fifteen lunar days (tithis),
because the fifteen Nityās are included within these very [days].
Although this sequence of oral tradition has been correctly explained, because the range of objects of knowledge is difficult to comprehend, it is stated once more for the sake of clarity:
on the first lunar day (pratipad), the digit of Tripurasundarī is to be meditated upon; on the second, the digit of Kāmeśvarī.
On the third [day], the digit Bhagamālinī is to be worshipped; on the fourth, the digit Nityaklinnā;
on the fifth, the digit known as Bheruṇḍā; on the sixth, the digit Vahnivāsinī; and on the seventh, the digit Mahāvidyeśvarī.
[The Kalās of Viśveśvarī]: On the eighth day is the Raudrī-kalā; on the ninth day, the Tvaritā-kalā; on the tenth day, the Kulasundarī-kalā;
on the eleventh day, the kalā named Nīlapatākā; and on the twelfth day, the kalā named Vijayā.
On the thirteenth day is the digit named Sarvamaṅgalā; on the fourteenth day is the digit named Jvālā;
on the fifteenth day is the digit named Mālinī. On all lunar days, the sixteenth digit named Cidrūpā is to be worshipped. She who is Tripurasundarī is present on the first day (pratipad).

That which has been described does not possess the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because it is practiced as something distinct from the root-ignorance (*mūlavidyā*) which possesses the nature of consciousness. Furthermore, regarding the division of mantras,
that specific mantra is to be practiced only in relation to the first [deity] and not in relation to the second.
It should be understood that there is a correspondence of names between [the goddess] Tripurasundarī and the Nityā.
The seat of the Viśuddhi-cakra is a sixteen-spoked wheel, which is the locus of these sixteen Nityās who consist of the digits of the moon.
Therein, the sixteen Nityās revolve in the corners [of the spokes] in the sequence beginning with the east. Below that, in the twelve-spoked Saṃvit-lotus, [they likewise revolve].
Twelve solar discs revolve in a clockwise direction;
these twelve suns hold authority over the twelve months.
And this has been described in seven hundred verses in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*—

which is now stated in brief: [it is described in brief] regarding the movement of the sun and moon through the paths of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels, which constitute the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*), during day and night respectively.
Movement:
85) The moon, however, moves by way of the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*).
It sprinkles the path of the seventy-two thousand channels with nectar; the sun, moving through the path of the right channel, brings forth the droplets of nectar ejected by that [moon].
When there is the simultaneous entry of both the moon and the sun into the foundation-cakra (ādhāra-cakra), [this occurs].

Then the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā) arises; from that, the lunar days of the dark fortnight arise. For this very reason, the Kuṇḍalinī power [awakens] in the Ādhāra-pit due to contact with the rays of the sun.
He sleeps in that which is filled with nectar dripping from the center of the melted lunar orb;

this state of sleep itself is called the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). When the yogi, with a concentrated mind, seeks to restrain the moon in the place of the moon and the sun in the place of the sun by means of the vital wind (vāyu), [he enters this state].

When that [nectar] is exhausted, the moon and sun— incapable of either pouring forth or bringing back the nectar— are obstructed. Then, as the pool of nectar has been dried up by the fire of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* ignited by the wind, the *kuṇḍalinī*, having been without food, awakens from her sleep.
Hissing like a serpent, she pierces the three knots and bites the lunar disc situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus; from that,
streams of nectar flow down to the lunar disc located above the *ājñācakra*.

They cause [the body] to overflow. Therefore, they cause the entire body to overflow with streams of nectar that have trickled down. And from that, there are the fifteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon situated above the *ājñā-cakra*, which are the fifteen *nityās*. These are the fifteen...
They revolve by relying on the wheel of purity (viśuddhicakra) situated below that.
The lunar orb situated within the thousand-petaled lotus is the station of the bindu (baindavasthāna).
Its digit (kalā), consisting of consciousness and having the nature of bliss, is sung as the Self; she alone is Tripurasundarī.

Thus, it is a secret that the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī can be accomplished by the lords of yogins only during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) and not during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). All the lunar dates of the bright fortnight are designated as full moons (paurṇamāsī). All...
The lunar days of the dark fortnight are included within the new moon day;

indeed, the single new moon day alone is designated as the "dark fortnight. For this very reason, the *ādhāra* is *andhatāmisra*, whereas the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is so called because of its contact with the rays of the sun.

The mixed world (*miśraloka*). Although Maṇipūra is the locus of fire, because water is present there, it is indeed a mixed world due to the reflection of the sun's rays. Anāhata is the world of light (*jyotirloka*).
Thus, up to the end of the Anāhata-cakra, the world is a mixture of light and darkness.

The Viśuddhi-cakra is the lunar world (*candraloka*). The Ājñā-cakra, however, because it is the abode of the moon, is the world of nectar (*sudhāloka*). In these two worlds, there is no moonlight due to contact with the rays of the sun.
The thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*), however, is a world consisting entirely of moonlight; the moon resides therein.
Endowed with the eternal *kalā*. (p.
86) The lunar disc is the *Śrīcakra*; the *kalā* is that which is called *Sādākhya*. Therefore, it is the triangle.

The foundation is the eight-spoked [lotus]; Svādhiṣṭhāna is the ten-spoked; Maṇipūra is the second ten-spoked; Anāhata is the fourteen-spoked; Viśuddhicakra is the fourfold Śiva-cakra; Ājñācakra is the station of the Bindu, which is square.

Thus, it is established that [it is] the "thousand-petaled lotus. Within the moon situated in the *ājñācakra*, there are fifteen digits (*kalā*) and the reflection of the sixteenth digit. In the lunar orb which is the form of the *śrīcakra*, there is only one digit; that is the supreme digit. Taken together, these constitute the sixteen digits. As follows:
"There are sixteen digits of the moon and twelve of the sun; in the fire, they are twice ten.
That energy, consisting of fifty digits, should be known as having the form of the Mātṛkā-cakra. Thus it is said.
These fifty *kalās*, consisting of fifty phonemes,
are included within the fifteen-syllable mantra; just as the final letter *la* is implied by the initial letter *ka*, so too are the letters situated between them.
The grasper: this very letter *la* is drawn back by the vowel *a* situated before the letter *e*, thereby becoming the grasper of all fifty phonemes.
Now, by this very inclusion of the *pratyāhāra*,
since the *mātṛkā* consisting of fifty phonemes would already be grasped, what is the purpose of the effort to include the *kakāra* and *lakāra* as *pratyāhāra*s?

It is said that the designation of the letters from *ka* to *la* as "parts" (*kalā*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), because the consonants are subordinate to the vowels; thus, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the relationship of subordinate and principal between the parts and the vowels that the vowels are considered primary.
It should be understood that Sanaka and the others have relied upon two types of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).

The four *anusvāras* are the indicators of the *bindu*. By that *bindu*, the *nāda* perceived above it is included. Thus, the *śrīcakra*, consisting of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, is said to be threefold (*trikhaṇḍa*). [This is] the *kalā* called Sādākhyā.
She is Śrīvidyā, whose other synonym is that which transcends nāda, bindu, and kalā.

These are included within the sixteen *nityās*. For instance, there are sixteen vowels; sixteen consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*; sixteen beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*; and sixteen beginning with *ṣa* and ending with *ha*.
Thus, the group of three sets of sixteen is included within the sixteen *nityās*.
The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*), merged within the space of the bindu. The letter *la*,
although included among the semivowels (*antasthā*), is [also] [included] by means of the letter *ka* for the purpose of the *pratyāhāra*.
It is taken up again; however, the letter *kṣa* consists of the aggregate form of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*.
The sixteen letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*, when accompanied by the vowels, are included within the Nityās.
The letter *kṣa* is withdrawn by means of the letter *a*; thus it is called the "garland of letters" (*akṣamālā*).

Therefore, by means of the letter *kṣa*—[according to the Pa-kośa manuscript: "by means of the withdrawal [of all letters] starting from 'a'"]—all the *mātṛkās* (mother-letters) are subsumed. For this very reason, [or rather, according to the Pa-kośa].

In the final section, by the combination of the letters *ka* and *la* in the phrase *sakalahrīm*, the word *kalā* is produced; likewise, by the combination of *ka* and *ṣa*, the letter *kṣa* is produced. Thus, the intended meaning is that all the *mātṛkā* letters are encompassed within the mantra.

And therefore, the sixteen Nityās consist of sixteen phonemes found within their mantras; these sixteen phonemes consist of the fifty phonemes; and these fifty phonemes consist of the digits (kalās) of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire.
The state of being threefold by way of the forms of the Sun, Moon, and Fire—
this is the fourfold unity that should be contemplated [the manuscript *ta* reads "the fourfold Vidyā"].

The same applies to the wheel (*cakra*) and the mantra. Just as the three *hrīṃ* syllables and the seed-syllable of Śrī are included within the form of the bindu in the triangle consisting of the four wheels of Śiva; and just as the Mātṛkā, whose nature is the rosary of phonemes, is comprised by the three letters beginning with *sa*.
The *mātṛkā* consists of both [the vowels and consonants], which are included within the wheel (*cakra*) as appropriate. To explain:

the four semivowels (*antasthā*) and the four sibilants (*ūṣman*)—these eight phonemes consist of the eight corners. This excludes the fifth letter of each group from among the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.

The [consonants] contained within the two sets of ten spokes are included within the bindu; the fifth letters of the groups (varga-pañcama), however, are included within the bindu in the form of the anusvāra. The fourteen vowels are included within the fourteen-spoked [wheel].
The anusvāra and visarga are included within the bindu. Thus is the identity of the wheel and the mantra.
This has been told according to the Subhagodayamata.
According to the Pūrṇodayamata, however, the wheel (cakra) consists of three segments by virtue of its nature as moon, sun, and fire. Likewise, the three-segmented nature of the mantra is well known.
The sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon, which belong to the point (bindu), are included within the lunar segment.

And that lunar segment (indukhaṇḍa), which consists of two parts, is included within the segment of the instrument (yantrakhaṇḍa) consisting of the moon. In this manner, there are twenty-four digits (kalā) of the sun.

They are included within the Bhānu-khaṇḍa (Sun-section), and that section is included within the Yantra-khaṇḍa (Instrument-section). Likewise, the ten Agni-kalās (Fire-energies) are included within the Āgneya-khaṇḍa (Fire-section),
and that section is included within the Āgneya-khaṇḍa of the Yantra.
The unity of the arts, mechanical devices, and mantras should be investigated.
In the *Subhagodaya*, the essential nature of the Nityās is stated as follows:

"The fifteen digits (kalās), beginning with Darśā and ending with Pūrṇimā, are indeed [the first fifteen]; however, the sixteenth digit should be known as having the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: the lunar days (*tithi*) beginning with *darśa* and ending with *pūrṇimā*. *Darśa* refers to the first digit (*kalā*) occurring immediately after the new moon (*amāvāsyā*); it is called *darśa* because [the moon] is slightly visible therein.
Those for which *darśa* is the first are "those beginning with *darśa*. Those for which *pūrṇimā* is the end are "those ending with *pūrṇimā*."
Darśā, Dṛṣṭā, Darśatā, Viśvarūpā, Sudarśanā, Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyā, Sūnṛtā, Irā, Āpūryamāṇā, Āpūryamāṇā,
Pūrayantī, Pūrṇā, and Paurṇamāsī— these are the names revealed by the Śruti.
By the phrase "comprising those beginning with Darśa and ending with Pūrṇimā," their essential nature will be explained further on. Corresponding to the fifteen digits (kalās) beginning with Darśa,
there are fifteen [deities] beginning with Tripurasundarī in their respective order.

The presiding deities (adhidevatās) are eternal. Since the sixteenth digit (kalā), whose nature is consciousness, is of the essence of the principle called Sādākhya, there is no other presiding deity for it; it should be understood that she herself is the presiding deity of all. She is the one who presides over these eternal Nityās.
The presiding deity (devatā) is Kāmadeva alone; the presiding deity of the locus (adhiṣṭhānadevatā) is Kāmeśvarī alone.

Therefore, it should be understood that the fifteen syllables contained within the root-mantra (mūlavidyā)—namely the lunar phases (darśa) and so forth—are the Nityās and their limbs (kalās), which constitute another form of the body. For this very reason:

The threefold division of the digits (kalās) beginning with Darśā is clear: Darśā, Dṛṣṭā, Darśatā, Viśvarūpā, and Sudarśanā—this is the Āgneya (Fire-related) section. Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyā, Sūnṛtā, and Irā—this is the Saura (Solar) section.
Fragment. (p.
89) "The waxing, the filling, the full, the full-moon"—this is the lunar [fortnight].

The third section has been described. Having established the unity of these digits (*kalā*) through their eternal nature, the method of worship on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth has already been illustrated by way of a mere indication. The digit of the new moon (*darśā*) is of the nature of the Śiva-principle; it is perceived.
The *kalā* named *Kalā* consists of the *śakti-tattva*; the *kalā* named *Darśatā* consists of the *māyā-tattva*;

the *kalā* named *Viśvarūpā* consists of the *śuddhavidyā-tattva*; the *kalā* named *Sudarśanā* consists of the *jala-tattva*. Thus, this section (*khaṇḍa*) consisting of five *tattvas* belongs to Agni.

It has been stated that Agni is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) here, while Kāmadeva is the presiding deity everywhere; Kāmeśvarī is the governing power (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) everywhere. The nourishing digit (*kalā*) consists of the principle of fire (*tejas-tattva*); the nourishing digit consists of the principle of air (*vāyu-tattva*). [The digit] being nourished...

The *kalā* Manas is of the nature of the principle of mind (*manastattva*). The *kalā* Sūnṛtā is of the nature of the principle of earth (*pṛthivītattva*). The *kalā* Irā is of the nature of the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*). The *kalā* Āpūryamāṇā is of the nature of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
This is the second solar section (*saura-khaṇḍa*). In that [section], the Sun is the deity; however, Kāmadeva is...

The presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) is everywhere. It has been stated that Kāmeśvarī is the presiding power (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) everywhere. Even though the *kalā* called Āpūryamāṇā resides within the lunar segment (*candrakhaṇḍa*), it is included within the solar segment (*saurakhaṇḍa*), because it is a specific division of the *irākalā*.
The unity of the two states of being filled with *irā* (the nectar of immortality) is to be contemplated.

The *kalā* that is being filled consists of the principle of Maheśvara; the *kalā* that is filling consists of the Supreme Principle (*paratattva*); the full *kalā* consists of the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*); and the *kalā* of the full moon consists of the principle of Sadāśiva.
This is the Saumya-khaṇḍa. Soma is the presiding deity (adhidevatā) here; Kāmadeva is the presiding deity everywhere; and it is said that Kāmeśvarī is the presiding power (adhiṣṭhātrī) everywhere.
The eternal digit (nityā-kalā), whose essence is the principle called Sādākhya, resides in these [deities] within the Viśuddhi-cakra.
In the sixteen-spoked [wheel], they revolve in the sixteen directions according to the sequence beginning with the east.

As for what has been explained in the *Subhagodaya*— that those [energies] are the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon-maṇḍala situated above the *ājñācakra*— that refers to the circulation of only fifteen digits within the sixteen-petaled lotus,
while the sixteenth digit resides in the thousand-petaled lotus.

It should be understood that the intended meaning is simply this: the mass of light of the eternal *kalā* which abides there, as it remains established therein, radiates forth within the sixteen-spoked [cakra].
The meaning is as follows: Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, and Kṣiti; by the word "Śiva," the digit (kalā) called Darśa, whose essence is the Śiva-tattva and who bears the name Tripurasundarī, is indicated.
It is explained as follows: by that [letter], its corresponding radical *ka* is indicated.

Likewise, by the word "power" (*śakti*), the letter *e* is indicated by that visible digit which consists of the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*). By the word "desire" (*kāma*), the letter *ai* is indicated by that visible digit which has the deity Kāma as its presiding divinity.

The letter *ī* is indicated [by the word *māyā*]. By the word "earth" (*kṣiti*), the letter *la* is indicated, as it is well-known in other scriptures that the earth-principle (*kṣititattva*) corresponds to the letter *la*. By the word "sun" (*ravi*), the letter *ha* is indicated, because the sun consists of the solar portion (*sūryakhaṇḍa*). [The moon] is the cool-rayed one.

Candra is the letter *sa*, which, according to the well-known convention of other scriptures, refers to the seed-syllable of the Moon; thus, by the term "cool-rayed one" (*śītakiraṇa*), the letter *sa* is indicated. By the term "Smara," the letter *ka*, which constitutes the nature of Kāmarāja, is indicated. Haṃsa is the Sun.

It was stated previously that [the letter] *ha* is the presiding deity (*adhipati*). *Śakra* is Indra. Since it is well-known in other treatises that the letter *la* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Indra, the letter *la* is indicated by the word *śakra*. "The supreme digit of the moon" (*parā candrakalā*) indicates the letter *sa*, which is the seed-syllable of the Moon. *Māra*...

The term "kāmarājabīja" indicates the letter *ka*, which is its constituent element; the term "hari" (Indra) indicates the letter *la*. Thus, in certain instances, words such as "Śiva" serve as indicators (*lakṣaka*) for the letters *ka* and so forth that occur within a mantra.
It should be understood that these are terms that indicate by means of what they themselves have been indicated.

Thus, the performance of the mantra consisting of the aggregate of the fifteen Nityās is prescribed for the fifteen lunar days (tithis). However, the daily performance of each individual Nityā is fixed separately for each day. And this is an extreme secret [to be learned] only from the mouth of the Guru.
This has been stated out of a desire to favor the disciples, even though it was already understood. And for this very reason, the Śruti also declares this same meaning:
"The digits (kalās) beginning with the new moon and ending with the full moon are indeed fifteen."

Regarding this matter, whatever much remains to be said, we shall explain it on the occasion of commenting upon the Śruti. Thus, in the Taittirīya recension, it is heard in the Kaṭhaka in the section beginning, "This indeed is the honey-bee" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10).

In this regard, the fruit of fully knowing the day consisting of the sixteen *nityās* has been set forth, because it establishes the fruit of mere knowledge (*jñānamātra*). This is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) following the section on the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha-kāṇḍa*): "Consciousness, discernment" (*saṃjñānaṃ vijñānam*; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa).
[3-10-1] Thus, there is indeed a difference in context between the passages that set forth the lunar days (*tithi*).
The Brāhmaṇa for that Anuvāka is: "This, verily, is the honey-bee" (Tai.
Thus, this collection of sentences consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, studied as unattached (anārabhyādhīta), has knowledge alone as its fruit.
This indeed is the *saraghā*;

its meaning is as follows: this digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), known as Sādākhya, is the *saraghā*—like a honeybee, it is a "flowing with honey," a "flowing with nectar"—belonging to the moon that is the essence of the Śrīcakra.
An investigation into the nature of the soul.
Of that [Vāk], fire itself is the honey of the bee.
Of that bee, fire itself— that is, the locus of fire, the triangular bindu—
is the honey of the bee (*sāragham*), produced by the bee, because it is of the nature of an ocean of nectar.
He describes the manner of the accumulation and depletion of the honey of the bees (*sāragha*):
"The nights of the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10).
These [nights] are mentioned in the *Saṃjñāna-anuvāka*. [The phrase "of which bee" (*yasyāḥ saraghāyāḥ*) is an addition.]
The Kathīs [say]: the nights of the two fortnights, the bright and the dark, [are the days].
Those are the honey-makers (*madhukṛtaḥ*).

Those nights are called honey-makers because they produce honey; it is a worldly convention that the collection of honey occurs specifically during the nights. For it is during the night alone that [the moon] exists in the form of its digits...

The instruction is that the practice of Śrīvidyā should not be performed during the day. The nights of the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa), beginning from the new moon (darśa) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī), have been described previously. However, the names of the nights of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) are as follows:
Sutā—pressed, well-pressed, pressed forth, being pressed; Pītī—a drinking-place, a gathering, satisfaction, satisfying;
Kāntā—lovely, desirable, born of desire, long-lived, the fulfiller of desires.
p.

92) These are the nights of the dark fortnight. Because these nights of the dark fortnight abide within the *ādhāra-cakra* itself in the form of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), for those who observe the sacred observance (*samayin*) there...

Because of the absence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and because the digits of the moon (*candrakalā*) circulate only during the nights of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), it is precisely therein that the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs; thus, only the indication of her essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) has been made.
Only the nights of the bright fortnight possess the status of being "digits" (*kalā*). That essential nature has already been [described] previously.
It has been explained.

For this very reason, the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs only at night and not by day, because days cause the flow of honey; thus he says: "Those which are the days" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10); "they are the showers of honey."

They are called *madhuvṛṣāḥ* because they rain down honey (*madhu*). For this very reason, yogis do not awaken the *kuṇḍalinī* during the day; thus, the names of the days of the bright and dark fortnights have not been mentioned here, as they are irrelevant to the present context. Nevertheless, [they are mentioned] because their fruit is heard in the Veda.
They are stated merely by way of enumeration. The names of the days of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) are:
Saṃjñāna [Tai. Brā. 3.10.9], Vijñāna, Prajñāna, Jānat, Abhijānat, and Saṅkalpamāna.
That which is being fashioned, that which is being prepared, that which has been prepared, that which has been fashioned; the better, the more excellent, the future, the arisen, and the become.
Thus are the names of the days of the bright fortnight. As for the names of the days of the dark fortnight—[as stated in Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9]:
Prastuta, Viṣṭuta, Saṃstuta, Kalyāṇa, and Viśvarūpa.
It is pure, immortal, and radiant; it is kindled energy, ruddy, luminous, possessed of rays, intensely heating, and full of fervor.
He states the fruit for one who knows the names of both these sets—the white and black fortnights and the days and nights: (p.
He who indeed knows these honey-makers and honey-bees— for them he makes honey in the fire, and they do not consume his merit from sacrifices and charitable works—
he who [knows] these honey-makers as the nights and the honey-bees as the aforementioned days.
Whoever knows this, let them know these [rays]: they turn the ocean of honey and nectar into the fire situated at the *bindu*.
They do not consume, nor do they empty, his merit from sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*) or the fulfillment of his desired objects.
He states the undesirable consequence in the case of the opposite:
"Now, as for him who does not know this— [Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10] 'verily, they do not produce honey for him in the fire.'"
They consume his merit from sacrifices and charitable works.
This has been almost entirely explained.

This is the meaning: the practice known as the *candrakalā-vidyā* consists of the identity of the *mātṛkā* and the mantra, the identity of the mantra and the *cakra*, the identity of the *cakra* and the *nityā*, and the identity of the *nityā* and the *kalās* beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*). This is the essential truth of the *Samaya* system. In this practice:
The distinction between the bright and dark fortnights, as well as the distinction between day and night, is employed.
The contemplation of the fourfold unity occurs only during the lunar digits from the new moon (darśa) up to the full moon (paurṇamāsī), and not on the day of the new moon itself.

It has already been stated previously that the term "dark fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa) refers to the new moon day (amāvāsyā). Therefore, it should be understood that there is no performance [of the rites] on the days of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), just as there is none on the new moon day.
Thus, by the method of elimination (pariśeṣavṛtti), the prohibition of meditative worship (upāsanā) applies to the new moon day, but not—
This applies to the entire dark fortnight; therefore,
by virtue of the guru’s instruction, it should be understood as a secret that worship is performed on all nights— excluding the new moon day— but not on all days.
To this, the following reply is given: "He who indeed knows the names of the days and nights" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9).

One does not meet with distress during the days and nights. "Consciousness, discernment, the new moon, the sight"—these two *anuvākas* are the names of the days and nights of the first fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"The one being offered, the one praised, the daughter, the pressing one"—[these are the names of the days and nights of the second fortnight].
These two sections contain the names of the days and nights of the dark fortnight.
He who knows this does not meet with misfortune regarding the days and nights.

Thus, this collection of statements has already been explained by the preceding commentary. Hereafter, the collection of names for the divisions of time—such as moments (muhūrta), half-months, ghaṭikās, and so forth—which will be mentioned, is included within that very [preceding] context; therefore, it is explained by that same commentary.

The phrase "it has been explained" is to be understood as a reference to what precedes. For this very reason, it should be understood that both the *saṃjñāna* section and the section beginning with "This indeed is the honeybee" (*iyaṃ vāva saraghā*) have already been explained.
As for the section concerning the Sāvitra [mantras] which begins with "Prajāpati created the gods" (*prajāpatir devānasṛjata*) in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*...

[3-10-9] Beginning with "When he says... and ending with "Janaka, indeed, of Videha," the lunar nature of the Sun is established; that, however, pertains to the lunar digit of knowledge (*vidyā*), which consists of the principle known as *sādākhya*.

The Śruti speaks by way of metaphorical usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) in order to demonstrate that the power of the Sun is obtained solely through the grace of the *Vidyā*— which is another name for *Śrīvidyā*, consisting of fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), and whose nature is *Vidyā*— and not otherwise. Therefore:

"This indeed is that" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9); thus, the recourse to figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*) has been made manifest. Therefore, the sentence immediately following this collection of texts is:
"Janaka of Videha arrived after [the passing of] days and nights" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9).

Thus it is traditionally taught. Janaka is the progenitor and the *ṛṣi* of the Śrīvidyā. Vaideha refers to Manmatha, who is indeed bodiless (*videha*). By means of the fifteen syllables of the mantra, which consist of days and nights (*ahorātra*) and embody the lunar digits (*kalā*) from the new moon (*darśa*) to the full moon (*pūrṇimā*).
"He came together" means that he has brought forth that mantra. He who brings forth a mantra is called a seer (*ṛṣi*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Aruṇopaniṣad*:
The son of Nirṛti is Vaideha; [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11.1]. Of Nirṛti means of Lakṣmī; or rather, of Anirṛti (the opposite of destruction) means of Lakṣmī. The son is Vaideha, Manmatha.
"He who is both non-conscious and conscious" (Tai. Ā.
1.11.1): he is devoid of mind precisely because he lacks limbs; yet he is conscious because he is the inner ruler of all beings.
He found that jewel.
That Anaṅga found—that is, obtained and beheld—that well-known jewel consisting of knowledge. This Anaṅga, though blind, saw; thus he is called "the blind one" (Andha).

This is obtained by the force of the supplementary statement: "He found the jewel" (Tai. Ā. 11.1). For this very reason, Manmatha became the seer (ṛṣi) of the supreme consciousness-power, Vidyā Tripurasundarī;
he, being without fingers, caused it to be woven (Tai. Ā. 11.1).
That Manmatha, being bodiless (anaṅga) precisely because he lacked a body, was without fingers (anaṅguli) and thus sewed (āvayat), that is, he stitched.
He describes the action immediately following the sewing:
"He, being neckless, fastened it on" (Tai.
Ā. 1.11.1). He, Manmatha, was indeed neckless because he is bodiless; thus, he [obtained] the fruit of the production of the jewel.
"He performed the releasing" means that he held [the reins].
He states that the fruit of bestowing the status of a jewel upon the Jewel of Knowledge is not merely its retention: "He was tongueless and without deceit" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11).
He, being bodiless (anaṅga), was for that very reason tongueless (ajihva), i.e., devoid of a tongue; yet he sucked (asaścata), meaning he tasted.
This is what is meant: previously, Anaṅga [revealed] the Vidyā-ratna,
which consists of fifty syllables, comprises the sixteen Nityās, and consists of sixteen kalās, appearing in various Vedas, various Smṛtis, various Purāṇas, and various types of Āgamas.

He saw it scattered. Immediately thereafter, having seen this mantra scattered, he performed the stitching. Having divided the fifty phonemes into three parts and formed three sections, [he assigned them to] the sixteen Nityās beginning with Tripurasundarī.
Therein, having included the sixteen lunar days beginning with Pratipad, and having likewise included them there,
one should form three sections consisting of fifteen syllables; therein, by way of being composed of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and by way of being composed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—

Having ascertained that [the fourth state] consists of the Śrīvidyā, by virtue of its establishment in the principles of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; its possession of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and its being the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Having determined the inclusion of the fifteen digits within the [five] sections (khaṇḍa),
and having accepted the inclusion of the nine Yoginī-mantras beginning with Bhuvaneśvarī— grouped into three triads— within each single syllable *hrīṃ*.
It is the self of all beings, the self of all mantras, the self of all principles, the self of all states, the self of all deities, the self of the meaning of all Vedas,
the self of all sounds, the self of all powers, the self of the three qualities, and the three sections.

Having determined that the Mūlavidyā consists of twenty-five syllables and is composed of the union of the twenty-sixth Śiva and Śakti— transcending the three guṇas and synonymous with Sādākhya (or Sādākhya-kalā)— he sewed together the King of Mantras. Immediately thereafter, he [revealed] the sewn-together King of Mantras.

Having grasped [her] by the neck, he held her for a long time and worshipped her through the yoga of meditation; thereafter, he tasted the nectar of the crescent moon. Thus, that sage Manmatha is the one who [knows] this mantra—this is the meaning.
"One should not enter the city without knowing this seer" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11).
Having known this seer, who is Manmatha, one should not enter the city consisting of the Śrīcakra;
that is, one should not worship the city consisting of the Śrīcakra without prior knowledge of the seer.
"One should not perform external worship" is a prohibitive injunction (p.
it is precisely in the case of external worship that there must be prior knowledge of the seer, the meter, and so forth.

In internal worship, which consists of the contemplation of identity (*tādātmyānusandhāna*), there is no knowledge of the *ṛṣi* and so forth at all; its utility is far removed. Therefore, external worship of the Śrīcakra is performed by way of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and other such factors as established in reality.
It is prescribed that this [inner worship] must not be performed by those of the three [upper] castes (*traivarṇika*). This has been stated in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
"External worship must not be performed; it is to be performed by those of the external castes (*bāhyajāti*). That...
They yield meager fruits for men, because they serve solely as a means to achieve worldly ends.
The Kaulas, Kṣapaṇas, Kapālikas,

Digambaras, and Itihāsas [sometimes seen as Vītāvāsas], as well as the proponents of the Vāma Tantras, are devoted to external worship; whereas the followers of the Vedas are intent upon internal adoration.
The exponents of Brahman say: "These liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta) wander constantly throughout the three worlds.

Thus say the Kaulas, who are devoted to the worship of the *ādhāra-cakra*; the Kṣapaṇakas, who are devoted to the worship of the triangle of women; and the Kāpālikas and Digambaras, who are devoted to both.
The Niratas; the Itihāsas, who maintain the authority of the Bhairavayāmala [sometimes "Vītāvāsas" is also seen];
the Vāmakas, whom some say are proponents of Tantra, while others say they are proponents of the authority of the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
The grammatical connection is that those who worship only the external wheel are outside the Vedic fold (*vedabāhya*).
