Those who delight in internal worship are exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) and knowers of the reality of the auspicious scriptures (*śubhāgama*). The fivefold auspicious scriptures have already been mentioned; furthermore, the method of internal worship will be explained below.
"If he should enter" (Tai. Ā.
1.11)—this expression of doubt where there is no doubt is like saying "if the Vedas are authoritative"; the meaning is that he would certainly enter.
Having practiced in secret (*mithau*), one should enter.
*Mithau* means "in secret" (*mithas*). Having practiced—that is, having understood—in solitude and seclusion;
for the root *car* signifies both "to move" and "to consume. "One should enter" means that one should perform the internal worship (*antarapūjā*).
Alternatively, having understood the union of both Śivas who have become a couple with one another, one should enter— that is, one should contemplate it.

Even in the previous explanation, no other assistance should be sought in the contemplation of the unity of the Self; the instruction is that knowledge bears fruit only in solitude. Anticipating the question "How is that so?", he confirms it by means of an illustration:
The vow of *sambhava* (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11).
*Sambhava* is the god of love (*manmatha*), because he is born from the mind (*citta*). His vow is his majesty, which, setting aside all other companions, exists in solitude and secrecy.
It consists of the union of woman and man.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that for those who perform the mantra rites taught by Manmatha, the practice is exactly like that; thus, this knowledge is to be kept secret. In the second explanation, *manmatha* refers to the couple (*mithuna*).

Having understood this, he enters that couple; the meaning of the scripture is that the practitioner must enter after having understood this "encasement" (*saṃpuṭa*) of Śiva and Śakti. And for this reason, Janaka Vaideha is mentioned in the passage: "The son of Nirṛti, Vaideha" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 1.11) and "Janaka indeed, Vaideha" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*).

And because these two scriptural passages [Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9] refer to both Vaidehīs as the object of a single recognition, the collection of sentences beginning with "sa yadāha" [Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9] refers to her who consists of the digits of the moon in the form of the lunar days (tithis), starting from the first day (pratipad).

Thus, everything is faultless, as its purpose is to show that the greatness of the Sun—which arises from the grace of Śrīvidyā—is not possible otherwise, by means of the exposition of Śrīvidyā. || 32 ||

Having first placed this triad— Smara, Yoni, and Lakṣmī— within your mind, O Eternal One, certain seekers who delight in the flavor of boundless great enjoyment worship you in the fire of Śiva, their rosaries strung with the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem.
They offered oblations with hundreds of streams of fragrant clarified butter.

O Nityā! O Thou who art devoid of beginning and end! Having placed this triad at the beginning of Thy mantra—namely Smara (the letter *ka*), Kāmarāja (the letter *ha*), Yoni (the letter *sa*), Bhuvaneśvarī (the letter *ha*), and Lakṣmī (the letter *śrī*, the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*)—and having joined them together, only a few rare *samayins* [know this].
This means that they are supreme lords of yoga who take delight in boundless great enjoyment and who know the taste of the unconditioned, eternal experience.

They worship and serve you, having brought you down from the thousand-petaled lotus and established you within the heart-lotus; they possess rosaries strung with the threads of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*). The "thread" (*guṇa*) refers to the string of those wish-fulfilling gems.

Those whose rosaries (akṣavalaya) or garlands of beads (akṣamālikā) are composed of— or fashioned from— *guṇana*, meaning repetition (*āmreḍana*) or, in short, a collection (*samūha*). Alternatively, [the phrase refers to] wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) themselves as the beads strung upon a thread (*sūtra*), namely lotus seeds.
Those who possess bracelets and garlands are so described. "Śivāgni" refers to the fire of Śiva;

that is to say, the fire consecrated within the "Śivā," which is the triangle (trikoṇa). Having separated the fire of the Svādhiṣṭhāna from its location in the Bindu within the triangle and having cast it therein—

Having restrained [the deity] with the noose and goad and having enveloped [her] with Bhuvaneśvarī, that fire in which the sixteen sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) are performed is the *Śivāgni*; this is the secret. This is the intended meaning: in the triangle, in the station of the Bindu.

Regarding the phrase "having cast the fire of *svādhiṣṭhāna*": although the station of *bindu* (*baindavasthāna*) is quadrangular, nevertheless, during the ritual of *puraścaraṇa*, one superimposes a triangle upon the lotus of consciousness (*saṃvitkamala*).
Then, from the thousand-petaled lotus, [one brings forth] Kāmeśvarī, who resides in the station of *bindu*.

"Having performed the planting [of the seed-syllable], the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) must be carried out; this is the secret of the Samayin tradition and the intention of the Ācāryas. Thus they offer oblations and satisfy [the deities] with hundreds of offerings of streams of fragrant ghee—the ghee belonging to Surabhi, the wish-fulfilling cow.
Clarified butter (ājya) is its streams; by means of those [streams] there are oblations (āhutayaḥ), which are the castings of the sacrificial offerings (haviḥ);
by means of hundreds of those, [there are] thousands.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Eternal One! having first placed this triad—Smara, Yoni, and Lakṣmī—within Thy mind, certain [ascetics], who delight in the flavor of boundless great enjoyment, bind rosaries with the threads of wish-fulfilling gems and offer Thee into the fire of Śiva.
They become those who offer hundreds of oblations of fragrant streams of clarified butter.

In this regard, the truth is as follows: for those who possess the *samaya*, there is no preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) for the mantra; there is no recitation (*japa*); there is also no external fire-offering (*bāhyahoma*); indeed, there are no external rules for worship.
Everything is to be performed within the heart-lotus alone. And this [is what is meant by]: "recitation is speech, and artifice is [the heart]."
Some [points] were stated during the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with [27 ślokaḥ].

We shall establish the remainder in its entirety, including the six verses beginning with [36 ślokaḥ], "That which resides in your wheel of power" (*ājñācakra*), with greater precision during the occasion of their explanation.

100) Intending to define the Sāmayika doctrine with the six verses beginning with "tavājñācakrastham" (verse 36), he first explains the Kaula doctrine along with its subdivisions for the sake of its utility.
He explains: the Kaula doctrine is twofold, namely Pūrvakaula and Uttarakaula.
He states this pair in succession with two verses:
"You are the body of Śambhu; the moon and sun are the pair of your breasts; you are the Self."
I consider you, O Blessed One, to be the faultless Navātman;

therefore, this relationship between you two—who are devoted to the supreme bliss of *samarasa*—exists as one shared by both, such that Śeṣa is the dependent (*śeṣa*) and [you] are the supporter (*śeṣin*). [Your] body is the physical form; you are she.

O Mahābhairavī, I consider the pair of breasts of Śambhu, the Blissful Bhairava— the moon being *śaśin* and the sun being *mihira*, those two themselves being his breasts, that pair— to be your own self, O you who are Mahābhairavī.
I know. O Blessed One! "Bhagavatī" is a vocative form derived from the fact that she possesses *bhaga*;
she knows the origin and destruction of beings, as well as their coming and going.
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance is to be called the Blessed One.

According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), "bhaga" is the knowledge of [the goddess's] arising and so forth; she who possesses that is *Bhagavatī*. Alternatively, because the *vidyā* consisting of the digit of the moon (*indukalā*) consists of nine wombs (*navayoni*), she who possesses the nine wombs is *Bhagavatī*. The suffix *-matup* is used here in the sense of excellence; the meaning is that she is excellent by virtue of the nine wombs. [She is] the ninefold self (*navātmāna*).
Ānandabhairava is proclaimed as being of the nature of the ninefold manifestation (navavyūha).

[Ānanda] is that which consists of the ninefold manifestation. The fact that Ānandabhairava consists of the ninefold manifestation will be explained further below. It is "anagham," meaning faultless; therefore, for this reason, because...
The meaning is that because of this cause, there is unity between Parā and Ānanda;
"the rest" refers to that which is subordinate (guṇabhūta) and secondary (apradhāna), while "the principal" (śeṣī) is primary (pradhāna)— this very manner [of relationship] is common to both.

The relationship between both Bhairavī and Bhairava, which exists and persists as a commonality— that is, by virtue of being shared— is of the nature of the relation between the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva), and it belongs to you two.

Of you two who are intent upon the supreme bliss (*parānanda*) within the *samarasa*—the *samarasa* being that which is endowed with *sāmarasya* (perfect union)—there is the supreme bliss (*parānanda*), which is Ānandabhairava;
and *Parā*, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) in the form of Ānandabhairavī, is the *kalā*. And those two are both within the *samarasa* and intent upon the supreme bliss (*parānandapara*).
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Bhagavatī! You are the body of Śambhu, consisting of the pair of breasts which are the moon and the sun; this is the ellipsis.
This is because Ānandabhairava is included within the *kālavyūha* (the array of time), [and thus] of the sun and the moon.

The attribution of the status of a pair of breasts to the moon and the sun is appropriate. Alternatively, the construction is as follows: O Blessed One! You alone are the body of Śambhu, whose pair of breasts are the moon and the sun;
those two [the sun and moon] are traditionally considered the eyes of the Goddess. Both...
"This pair of earrings"—such is the Vedic revelation.
By this, the state of being a subordinate (śeṣatva) of the Blessed Lady toward Śambhu has been stated: "O Blessed Lady!

I consider Your self to be the sinless Navātman; therefore, this relationship of the subordinate and the sovereign (śeṣa-śeṣī) exists between You two, who are intent upon the supreme bliss of the state of equal flavor (samarasa)."
It exists as common to both.
In this regard, the following should be considered: Mahābhairava is designated as "Navātman" (the Ninefold Self) because he consists of nine manifestations (*vyūha*). These nine manifestations are:

the manifestation of Time (*kālavyūha*), the manifestation of the Kula (*kulavyūha*), the manifestation of Name (*nāmavyūha*), and likewise the manifestation of Knowledge (*jñānavyūha*). And so forth.

Immediately after that, there should be the array of consciousness (cittavyūha); likewise, the array of sound (nādavyūha), and immediately after that, the array of the point (binduvyūha); then the array of the digits (kalāvyūha) and the array of the individual soul (jīvavyūha)—these are the nine.
The meaning of this is as follows:

"Kālavyūha" (the array of time) refers to the collection of time delimited by the range from a *nimeṣa* (a blink of an eye) up to a *kalpa*. Since the sun and the moon also serve as delimiters of time, they too are included within the *kālavyūha*.
Inclusion has been stated.
The array of lineage (*kulavyūha*) refers to the array of forms such as blue and so forth. The array of names (*nāmavyūha*) refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is called the "array of knowledge" (*jñānavyūha*); it also has another name, the "array of experience" (*bhogavyūha*). It is of two kinds, distinguished by the division into homogeneous and heterogeneous.
[Due to the distinction between sharing and not sharing: "Sharing" is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), while "not sharing" is non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*). "Sharing" is conceptualization;
"not sharing" is non-conceptualization.

The aggregate of the fivefold egoity is called the "array of mind" (*cittavyūha*). The fivefold egoity consists of egoity, mind, intellect, the great principle (*mahat*), and the mind-organ (*manas*).

The aggregate of passion, desire, form, and effort is called the *nādavyūha*. By means of this, the *mātṛkā* has four forms: *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. *Parā* is that which has the nature of internal reflection (*ūha*); "internal" (*antara*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and by means of reflection (*ūhena*) therein—

She whose form is accompanied by reasoning (tarka) is "one whose form is with an interval" (sāntaroharūpā). The intention is that she is to be known only in the state of yoga. As it has been stated in the *Kāmakalāvidyā*:
That supreme Maheśī who possesses an internal form and is meditated upon in three ways is indeed that very one named Parā;
this same one, when clearly manifest, is called Paśyantī. As it is said in that very same place:
The clear Trimātṛkā, known as Paśyantī, has attained the state of the Cakra.

The *mātṛkā* consisting of fifteen syllables is endowed with three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) and has the three mothers (*trimātṛkā*) as its essence. She has attained the state of being a wheel (*cakratā*), that is, the nature of a wheel (*cakratva*). The secret [teaching] is this: the identity of the wheel consisting of three sections with the *mātṛkā* consisting of three sections. And this has been explained extensively before.

This has been explained. The intention is that they are clearly perceived as extremely subtle during the state of *yukti*. That which is called *madhyamā* consists of the states of high and low between *parā* and *paśyantī*; it is of two kinds, in the form of the individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*) such as *vāmā* and so forth.

And she is the form of the aggregate of Vāmā and the others. She is subtle as the aggregate of Vāmā and the others, and gross as the individual manifestations of Vāmā and the others. The powers beginning with Vāmā are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā; these are the four powers.
Within the wheel, they consist of four downward-facing yonis;
these are the five powers (śaktis): Will, Knowledge, Action, Peaceful, and Supreme.

These [powers] consist of the upward-facing power-yonis situated within the Śrīcakra. By means of these powers, which constitute the ninefold manifestation (navavyūha), the ninefold nature of the Goddess is expressed.
As it is said in that very same [text]:

One is supreme, while the other is the nature of the emanation of the individual matrices (mātṛs) such as Vāmā and the rest; by that, the Mother Navātmā is born through the two designations [of the supreme and the individual]. For that Madhyamā is indeed twofold: subtle and gross in form, the latter being stable and the former subtle.
The gross [form] consists of the nine sounds and is composed of the nine classes [of consonants], known as the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script).
Of these two, the former is the cause and the latter is the effect; for this reason, they are indeed one and the same, for there is no difference between them.
This identity of essence (*tādātmya*) is what is intended by the relationship of cause and effect.

The meaning of this is as follows: "One" (ekā) refers to that which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇa*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. "The other" (*parā*) means the *paśyantī* [speech], which consists of the disequilibrium of one or another of the qualities. *Madhyamā* is the gross form consisting of the individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*) such as Vāmā and the others; these are the powers (*śakti*).

They abide as an enclosure on both sides of the Baindava station; for this very reason, these realities, being denoted by the term "array" (vyūha), are designated by the word "ninefold self" (navātman).
However, in their collective form, they are included within the Supreme (Parā). For that reason, she is the Mother (Mātā).
The Mātṛkā has arisen as Navātmā. She is indeed twofold by way of her designations, because that Madhyamā is twofold: subtle (sūkṣmā) and gross in form (sthūlākṛti).
He states the nature of the subtle [form] with the word "stable" (sthirā): in the state of stability...
It is to be manifested only in the state of yoga. "Consisting of nine sounds" means there are nine sounds:

*a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *kṣa*. These are mutually distinct classes, being the vowels and the *ka*-group, *ca*-group, *ṭa*-group, *ta*-group, *pa*-group, *ya*-group, *śa*-group, and *kṣa*-group.

Because they are perceived as being mutually distinct. Regarding this, he states the proof: "called the earth-script" (*bhūtalipī*). The capacity of the script—which is false and has a false nature—to denote [its object] is not like the capacity of a reflection in a mirror to indicate a face.
It is contradicted; the first is the cause of the other, while the first is the subtle form and the middle is the cause. (p. 104)
Because this very [power] which is gross— consisting of the nine groups and belonging to the intermediate state—
is also this same subtle one, due to that very cause of the relationship between effect and cause,
there is no difference whatsoever even in the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding the identity and non-duality of the gross and the subtle.

It was stated with the intended meaning that "the cause exists," because [it arises] from that cause; he demonstrates this very point by saying "for there is no difference. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the identity (*tādātmya*) between cause and effect is what is intended. In all cases, identity exists apart from the distinction between cause and effect.

The meaning is that it does not exist. Consequently, the ninefold nature of the consciousness-power (cicchakti), which is essentially the Middle Way (madhyamā), is established. Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva are well-known in the scriptures as the causes of attachment (rāga), desire (icchā), formative activity (kṛti), and effort (prayatna). Regarding these [factors] such as attachment...
The principles (tattvas) are included;
by them, Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, which serve as their substrata, are to be understood as being included.

The "Array of Bindus" (binduvyūha) is the collection of the six cakras. The "Array of Kalās" (kalāvyūha) is the collection of the fifty kalās consisting of the phonemes. The "Array of the Living Being" (jīvavyūha) is the aggregate of the enjoyer.
Thus, the nine manifestations (vyūha) possess a threefold nature in the form of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the enjoyment.

Although the manifestation of the Self (ātmavyūha) is the enjoyer, its threefold nature is not contradictory because it is identical with the enjoyed and the enjoyment. The same should be inferred for the manifestation of the enjoyed (bhogyavyūha) and the manifestation of the enjoyment (bhogavyūha). Thus...

The same should be inferred for the *bhogavyūha* as well. This is the intended meaning: the teachers intend a threefold classification, wherein the *ātmavyūha* is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the *jñānavyūha* is the act of enjoyment (*bhoga*), and the *kālavyūha* and others are solely the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Of all these manifestations (*vyūha*s)...

The unity of the *jīvavyūha* arises from its pervasion everywhere; the unity of the *kālavyūha* arises from its being the delimiting factor; the unity of the *kulavyūha* and *nāmavyūha* arises from their being the defining characteristics;
and the unity of the *jñānavyūha* arises from its identity with the *binduvyūha*, due to the unity of *nāda* and *kalā*.

The fact that the Supreme Lord consists of nine manifestations is already established; therefore, the secret of the Kaula doctrine is that the ninefold unity of Bhairava and Bhairavī must be known. For this very reason, the Kaulas refer to the Supreme Lord as the "ninefold self" (*navātman*).
They speak thus: as the Kaulas say—(p.
105)—"The Lord consists of the ninefold array; the Lord Bhairava is the self of the nine, whose supreme nature is supreme bliss."
The bestower of enjoyment and liberation; the Supreme Bliss and the Supreme Power,
the Blissful Bhairavī whose form is consciousness— when there is the state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) between those two, then the universe arises.
Thus, only a mere indication has been given; the remainder will be explained in the section beginning with "In your foundation, at the root" (verse 41).

The underlying meaning is this: once the identity of Ānandabhairava and Mahābhairavī—known as Parānanda and Parā—is established, the state of the two being the ninefold self (*navātmatā*) is realized.
They are equal. Therefore, the relationship of subordinate and principal is always relative;

when an effort arises on the part of Ānandabhairava—known as Parānanda—and of Mahābharavyā, whose nature is supreme consciousness, during the processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, then [this relationship occurs].

Because Bhairavī is predominant, she who is denoted by the word *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is Mahābhairavī; her predominance is her status as the principal (*śeṣitva*), while Ānandabhairava’s non-predominance is his status as a subordinate quality (*guṇabhāva*) or as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*). This is when there is a withdrawal of all [attributes].
When Prakṛti abides as the subtle elements (tanmātra), because Bhairavī is absorbed within her own self, Bhairava is then the remnant (śeṣin) and Bhairavī is the remnant (śeṣa). || 34 ||

You are the mind, you are the sky, you are the wind, you are the charioteer of the wind, you are the waters, and you are the earth; when you have thus transformed yourself, there is indeed nothing else beyond you. You alone, O Consort of Śiva, transform your own self through the form of the universe, which is the very nature of consciousness and bliss.
You uphold [it]. || 35 ||
You alone are the mind, the principle of *manas*, situated in the *ājñācakra*.

You alone are space, the principle of *ākāśa*, situated within the *viśuddhicakra*. You are the wind, the principle of *vāyu*, which resides within the *saṃviccakra* known as the *anāhata*. Thus it is.

*Tvam* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "you. *Marutsārathiḥ* (the charioteer of the Maruts) means the friend of Vāyu; this is the fire-principle (*agnitattva*) located in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. *Asi* is an indeclinable as before, meaning "you are. *Tvam āpaḥ* (you are the waters) refers to the water-principle (*aptattva*) situated within the *maṇipūra*. *Tvaṃ bhūmiḥ* (you are the earth) refers to the earth-principle (*bhūmitattva*).
Located within the *mūlādhāra*, when you have thus been transformed— having reached a state of transformation that is identity (*tādātmya*) with [the deity]— there is indeed nothing beyond this.

The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever beyond this. You alone, in order to transform— meaning to effect the transformation of— your own self, your own essential nature, into the form of the universe (*viśvavapuṣā*),
which is the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [assume] the form of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandākāra*) consisting of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and Ānandabhairava.

O Śivayuvati! [The term] "Śivayuvati" refers to the wife of Śiva; the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the word *yuvati* according to the rule "sarvato 'ktinnarthāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.45). This is her vocative case. You adorn yourself with *bhāva*, that is, with the mind. Or else, you are the form of bliss-consciousness (*cidānanda*), which is the very nature of Brahman.
The Śiva-principle [is realized] through the state of being the consort of Śiva; "consort" (yuvati) means the wife of Śiva, and the "state" (bhāva) refers to her essence—that is, by means of that.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Blessed Lady! You are the mind; you are the ether; you are the wind;

you are the charioteer of the wind; you are the waters; you are the earth. When you have undergone transformation, there is indeed nothing else. O Consort of Śiva, you alone transform your own self into the universal form.
By your very nature, you bear the form of consciousness and bliss.

The meaning is this: by the passage beginning with "the state of mind" (*manastvam*) and ending with "the ground" (*bhūmiḥ*), the transformation (*pariṇāma*) consisting of the five elements in the form of an effect has been described. By the phrase "when you have transformed," there is indicated a specific state of abiding in the form of the cause, which is characterized by being free from modification (*nirvikārātman*).

The transformation of *prakṛti* has been stated. By the words "not beyond" (*na hi param*), it is meant that there is no further transformation of that which is unchanging, for that would lead to an infinite regress; such is the meaning of the word "hi. Thus it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:

Listen, O Goddess, to this great knowledge, the supreme among all knowledges, my dear; by the mere realization of which one does not sink into the ocean of worldly existence. O Maheśvarī, the supreme power Tripurā was born as the primordial one, through the division of the gross and the subtle.
The Mother of the Arising of the Three Worlds.
She is the embodiment of the entire collection of principles swallowed up without remainder;
when she has reached her full development, nothing further is desired beyond her.
This is the meaning:
[the meaning of "having the nature of the entire multitude of principles swallowed up" is as follows]— it has been swallowed up (kabali-ikṛta),
that is, superimposed upon the Self and existing as its causal essence, just as...

Just as a jar [is produced] from clay, so too, in its entirety— that is, in such a way that nothing remains— the group, which is the collection, of the principles (tattva), namely the five principles.
She whose very nature consists of the entire collection of principles (tattva-grāma) swallowed up [within herself]— the meaning is that she,

having withdrawn her effects into their cause, abides as the cause itself; for in the view of those who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavādins), the effect also exists within the cause.

"Because it exists in the form of power (śakti). This is what is meant: in the Uttarakaula doctrine, Pradhāna alone is the creator of the world. Precisely because it is Pradhāna, there is no state of being subordinate, as Śiva is absent. Its transformation consists of the five principles (pañcatattva).

The power whose essence is *pradhāna* has evolved in the form of the principle of *manas* and so forth; therefore, the evolution of the principles such as *manas* is the evolution of their own nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*) from that power. Thus, having superposed the phenomenal world, which is of the nature of an effect, upon itself—

She exists in the form of the cause, and she is designated as the *ādhārakuṇḍalinī* (the Kuṇḍalinī in the foundational casket). Whatever remains to be said hereafter will also be addressed on the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "In your foundation, at the root" (*mūle*) [verse 41].
We shall establish this more thoroughly. || 35 ||

I bow to the Supreme Śambhu, who resides in your *ājñācakra*, who bears the brilliance of ten million suns and moons, and whose sides are embraced by the Supreme Consciousness; for by worshipping Him with devotion, one dwells in the world of light, beyond the reach of the sun, moon, and fire, in that realm where there is no darkness.

In you—meaning in your own *ājñācakra* (the wheel of command)—resides [the deity] situated in the *ājñācakra*, bearing the luster of ten million suns and moons; "tapanas" is the sun and "śaśi" is the moon, and "koṭis" means their countless millions in number; such is the meaning of their radiance (*śruti*).

I bow to that supreme Śambhu, the "Bearer" (dhara), because he bears that splendor (kānti). "Supreme" (para) is a designation for Śambhu. He is one whose two sides—the right and left—are closely joined; and she is both supreme (parā) and consciousness (cit).

*Paracit*: The word *para* is well-known in the sense of *cit* (consciousness). By propitiating—that is, pleasing through devotion—the Supreme Śiva who is permeated by that *paracit*, and by means of the love for worship...
He dwells in union with you in a place beyond the reach of the sun, moon, and fire— therefore devoid of light, free from illumination, in a worldless, solitary, and secluded retreat.

The word "having attained" (prāpya) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The particle "hi" indicates well-known fact. In the world of light, in the realm consisting of moonlight, that is, in the thousand-petaled lotus.
Herein is the word-arrangement: O Bhagavatī!

I bow to the supreme Śambhu, who resides in your Ājñācakra, who bears the luster of ten million suns and moons, and whose sides are embraced by the Supreme Consciousness (Paracit), whom one worships with devotion.
Indeed, he dwells in that world beyond light, which is devoid of illumination and outside the range of the sun, the moon, and fire.

In this regard, the following should be considered: by the word "cakra" in the phrase "situated in your *ājñā*-cakra," the four *śiva*-cakras located within the *śrī-cakra* inside the space between the eyebrows of the practitioner are meant;
it does not refer to the two-petaled lotus, as that would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the word "your."

The same should be inferred for what follows hereafter. In this regard, it has already been established that there is a fire-maṇḍala at the tip of the Svādhiṣṭhāna, a sun-maṇḍala at the tip of the Anāhata-cakra, and a moon-maṇḍala at the tip of the Ājñā-cakra. Consequently, these are the rays of fire, sun, and moon.

[Including the *kiraṇa*] there are three hundred and sixty rays that circulate precisely from the *ādhāra-cakra* up to the *ājñā-cakra*. This too has already been correctly explained previously. [The moon situated in the *ājñā-cakra*] is indeed distinct [from the others].
It has already been correctly established that the moon situated upon the thousand-petaled lotus, which is the very essence of the Śrīcakra, is eternally full. || 36 ||
For the sake of purification, I worship Śiva— the progenitor of the sky— who is as clear as pure crystal, and also the Goddess,
whose resolve is equal to that of Śiva; by the radiance of these two,
who follow the path of similarity to the moonbeams, the inner darkness is dispelled and shines forth.
The world is like a female cakora bird. || 37 ||
In the wheel of purity (*viśuddhicakra*), that [nature] of yours is as clear as pure crystal,

resembling a flawless crystal stone— [where "fear" (*trāsa*) refers to a defect residing in gems and the like, according to the *Medinī* lexicon]— extremely stainless, and the progenitor of space, [that is,] of the principle of space (*vyoman*).
It is the progenitor and the producer; for from this very Self (ātman), space was produced, according to such scriptural passages as *Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1. [End of page 109] in the Ājñācakra.

The meaning is that the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*) has arisen from the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*). Here, the word "self" (*ātman*) is a synonym for the mind (*manas*). I serve—that is, I worship—Śiva, the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). The goddess, the Blessed One (*bhagavatī*), is also included by the word "also" (*api*) in the sense of conjunction; she whose resolve is equal to that of Śiva.

The meaning is that she whose resolve is identical— her exertion (*vyavasāya*) being effort— is herself also denoted by the word "Śiva" [the Śiva-principle]. Of those two Śivas, by the splendor of their radiance— which flows forth, moving along a path possessing the same nature as the rays of the moon— ...
Having shaken off the inner darkness— she whose internal ignorance has been dispelled— she shines forth and manifests from the path resembling the rays of the moon,
like a female cakora bird illuminating the world, the three realms.

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Blessed Lady! I worship Your two pure states—Śiva, who is as clear as pure crystal and the progenitor of the ether, and also the Goddess whose resolve is equal to Śiva’s, from whom [the world] proceeds as You go forth.
By means of her splendor, which follows the likeness of the moon’s rays, the world shines like a female cakora bird whose inner darkness has been dispelled.
The meaning is this: just as the female cakora bird has its inner heart satisfied by drinking the moonlight,
so too the world of practitioners, having dispelled the darkness within by means of the radiance of Śiva and Śivā which resembles moonlight, has its inner heart satisfied.

In this regard, the following should be considered: during the worship of the Viśuddhi-cakra, due to the cessation of the sun and moon, there occurs the drying up of the moonlight of the sixteen digits (kalās), beginning with Śrī Tripurasundarī, which reside within the sixteen spokes; consequently, it is only the Śiva and Śivā situated in that cakra who [remain].
By her radiance, the function of moonlight was performed. || 37 ||
I worship that indescribable pair of swans dwelling in the Mānasa lake of the great ones, who take singular delight in the nectar of the blossoming lotus of consciousness;
from whose conversation arises the mastery of the eighteen branches of learning, and upon whom [the world] depends.
One should extract every virtue from a fault, just as one extracts milk from water. || 38 ||

p. 110) "Samunmīlatsaṃvitkamalamakarandaikarasikaṃ" means: *samunmīlat* (blooming), *saṃvit* (consciousness), *jñānam* (knowledge)—that itself is the *kamalam* (lotus); therein, *makarandaḥ* is the nectar of the flower (*puṣparasaḥ*), and that very [nectar]... [is the one whose sole delight is therein].

And although it is "one" (*eka*), the word "one" does not take the prior position because of the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṙyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), which allows for the subsequent placement [of the qualifier]. Alternatively, it is a compound formed later as *ekarasikaḥ*, meaning "one who is a connoisseur (*rasika*) of that," specifically a connoisseur of the nectar (*makaranda*). Thus he is so described.

The attribution of the nature of a swan to the Śivas, who are the very embodiment of the supreme swan (paramahaṃsa), serves as the basis for attributing the nature of a lotus to consciousness (saṃvit). Thus, once consciousness is established as a lotus, the aesthetic flavor (rasa)— of which the sole proof is its being relished as nectar (makaranda) in its partial form— is superimposed.

For this very reason, the word *makarandaika* is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). I worship— that is, I serve— the pair of swans (*haṃsa-dvandvam*), which is indescribable (*kimapi*), impossible to point out as "this," the twenty-sixth principle (*ṣaḍviṃśa-tattvam*) consisting of Śiva and Śakti joined together, belonging to the great ones.
It is frequented in mind by the lords of yogis. Here, by the word "mānasa," the nature of Lake Mānasa is superimposed upon the mind, because of the constant residence of swans in Lake Mānasa.
"From whose conversation" means from the conversation of that pair of swans.
The transformation of the eighteenfold sciences means that the eighteen sciences have transformed into the form of speech; that pair of swans which takes up—
that is, grasps— the quality, having separated it from the defect (the ablative case here being used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*, meaning "having extracted the quality from the defect").

The word "guṇa" (quality) is also indicative of the absence of defects, because the absence of defects is to be grasped just like the presence of qualities. "Akhilam" means the whole; [he extracted it] from the waters, like milk from water.
Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Blessed One!
I worship that certain pair of swans moving within the minds of the great ones—which, as it were, relishes the singular nectar of the blossoming lotus of consciousness—from whose conversation...
Through the transformation of the eighteenfold sciences, he extracts every virtue from defects,
just as one takes milk from water.

In this regard, the following should be considered: it has already been stated previously that the lotus of consciousness (saṃvitkamala) is named the Anāhata-cakra. It is the view of a certain school of the Samaya tradition that practitioners worship the "pair of Paramahaṃsas" (paramahaṃsamithuna)—that is, the pair of Haṃsas—within the lotus of consciousness. For this very reason:
It has been stated that [the deity] moves within the minds of the great ones. However, according to the view of Bhagavatpāda,
the Supreme Lord, whose form is a flame of fire, united with his own power Śikhinī,
appears in the Anāhata-cakra like the bud of a lamp-flame.
As it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in his commentary on the *Subhagodaya*:
"In this context, the convention (*samaya*) consists of the form of the flame of fire; that very [flame] is the *samayā* here. May there be the union of these two for me."
May he who has his sole abode in the lotus of the heart grant [this].
Thus; this very point is also our own accepted view. || 38 ||

O Mother, I praise that great Samayā, who, presiding over the fire within your own Svādhiṣṭhāna, is ever intent upon it as Saṃvarta; for when the world is being consumed by that great fire ignited by her wrath,
she casts a glance moist with compassion— a cooling remedy.
He composes [it]. || 39 ||

O Mother! I praise that well-known fire named Saṃvarta, who, having presided over—that is, taken recourse to—the fire-element within your own Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra, remains there incessantly and unceasingly. O Janani! I laud him.

O Mother! [I bow] to that Great One, denoted by the word "Mahat," who is in the form of the fire of universal dissolution (saṃvartāgni); when, while burning the worlds—Bhūr and the others—at the sight of which [the world] is consumed, she is filled with great wrath yet remains moist with compassion, permeated by mercy.
That vision which provides light and cool, refreshing treatment.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Mother! I praise that Fire, who is intent upon presiding over the Saṃvarta fire in your Svādhiṣṭhāna; I also praise that great Samayā. When she, filled with great wrath, looks upon the worlds and burns them, she who remains moist with compassion—her I praise.
The glance— meaning "that glance of yours"— creates a cooling remedy.

In this regard, the following should be considered: the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is established upon the origin of the fire-principle (*agnitattva*). Having superimposed the fire produced there as the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvartāgni*), the power (*śakti*) remains right there in the form of the flame of the great fire of universal destruction.
It is possible. Then, by the light of those two, the worlds were consumed;
yet those worlds were once again filled with the essence of compassion by the gracious Bhagavatī herself.

The view presented by Maṇipūra—that it performs a cooling treatment—is mere praise and not a reality. [It is] like one possessing lightning, through its power that flashes against the darkness. || 39 ||
I worship your dark cloud-like form, which is the sole refuge for Maṇipūra, adorned with a rainbow formed by shimmering ornaments of various gems,
raining down upon the three worlds scorched by the sun of Hara. 40.
"Taṭittvantam": *taṭit* is *saudāminī* (lightning); that which possesses it is *taṭittvān*.
[He is addressed] with his power (*śakti*), which is of the nature of lightning and whose flashing is the adversary of darkness—that is, the adversary of the darkness located in Maṇipūra;
for it was stated previously that the *maṇipūra-cakra* is the world of *tāmisra*.

She whose manifestation is obstructive and adverse; by this, the Lord’s state as a steady lightning flash is indicated. This too is an epithet indicating the cloud's nature as belonging to the rainy season:
[she who possesses] a rainbow formed from shimmering ornaments of various jewels.

And those various kinds of jewels were shimmering; by them were fashioned ornaments and decorations, and by them was woven and fashioned a rainbow—referring to that [which possesses such a rainbow]. The suffix *naṅ* is not applied here because it is used in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*).

Furthermore, another reason for its being characteristic of the rainy season is that it produces the illusion of a rainbow, appearing like a steady flash of lightning blended with the luster of various kinds of jewels. As it is said in the *Siddhaghuṭikā*:
"Sadāśiva, whose sole abode is Maṇipūra, shines forth as the monsoon cloud; the auspicious Śivā appears as the steady lightning within that cloud. Thus it is said.
O Lady, [I behold] Your Śyāma— the dark-hued Paśupati who exists in the form of a cloud— whom it is impossible to define by any measure,
whose sole refuge and abode is Maṇipūra.
Regarding that: by the word "maṇi," the jeweled bow (maṇidhanus) is meant, because the Blessed Lady has the nature of the jeweled bow; she fills the sanctuary, and thus the secret name is Maṇipūra.
"I serve" means I serve intensely. "Varṣantam" means raining down.

Hara himself is the sun (mihira); that is to say, the great fire of universal destruction (mahāsaṃvartāgni). By him, the three worlds were scorched—that is, consumed by heat. The three worlds were heated by Hara, who was like the sun.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Bhagavatī! [I meditate upon] You, whose sole refuge is Maṇipūra, who are dark-complexioned, who possess a flashing rainbow formed by the array of various glittering jewel-ornaments, and who are made radiant by Your power that flashes as the adversary of darkness.
I take refuge in some ineffable cloud that rains upon the three worlds scorched by the heat of the sun.

In this regard, the following should be considered: it was previously established that the water element (*jalatattva*) arises in the location of Maṇipūra. The manner of its arising is as follows: the very rays of the sun, when permeated by fire and having attained the state of clouds, take on the form of water; such is the case for Maṇipūra.
The placement is between the *ādhāra* and the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
The rays of the sun situated above the *anāhata*, having merged with the fire of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, enter the *maṇipūra* and attain the state of water; by means of that water...
The secret of the scriptures is that [the rays] bathe the world which has been consumed by the fire of one's own self-projection (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

In this context, those who know the scriptures say that by the phrase "encircled by Indra’s bow consisting of various shimmering jewel-ornaments," they mean a rainbow devoid of the *mairva* (the primary spectrum). And that is heard [in scripture]:

In the *Aruṇopaniṣad*: "That which is called the bow of Indra is not to be discarded; they speak of it among the colors of the clouds. This very thing belongs to Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya; this is the bow of Rudra. [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.5]

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is: the bow of Rudra, who is of the nature of the cloud, is *ajyam*, meaning it is devoid of a *jyā* (bowstring), that is, a *maurvī* (made of sinew). The remaining words found in the scripture have been explained in the commentary on the *Subhagodaya*. All of this is contained in the *Aruṇopaniṣad*: "He who is the flower of the waters" (*yo'pāṃ puṣpam*). [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.23.1]
In the section [Āraṇyaka 1–22], beginning with "yo'pām" and ending with "ime vai lokā apsu pratiṣṭhitāḥ," it is established that from water arises the moon,
the sun, and fire, as well as the days consisting of the lunar digits.
The origin of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), which are portions thereof, has been explained; immediately following that, a Rigvedic verse is cited as corroborative evidence:

Regarding this, the following verse is recited: "The essence of the waters, gathered by the sun like bright gold—that which is the essence of the essence of the waters, that supreme [essence] I take from you.
The meaning of this *ṛc* is as follows: the lords of yogis, while causing the moon—the essence of the waters—to rise...
The meaning is "attaining. In the sun—that is, in the solar orb—the nectar (*śukram*) is perfectly and completely filled;
for it is by the streams of ambrosia (*pīyūṣa*) flowing from the lunar orb alone that the sustenance of the sun is maintained.

This is the meaning. Of the essence of the waters, which takes the form of flowers—that essence of the Moon situated in the *baindava* station (as stated above, by way of being of the nature of the *kalā*s)—I take that supreme one, which consists of the eternal *kalā*s; that which consists of the eternal *kalā*s.

"Rasaṃ vaḥ" means from you; since water is the subject under discussion, "vaḥ" refers to the waters, indicating that water has arisen at Maṇipūra. Those waters are the producers of the fire of Svādhiṣṭhāna [from] the moon situated in the Ājñācakra.
They are the producers [of light], and they are also the producers of the sun situated above the *anāhata* wheel;
therefore it is said, "I accept that supreme one from you. The meaning is: I recognize that supreme moon, which resides upon the thousand-petaled lotus, as being from your presence.

In this very section it is heard in the Śruti: "He who knows the boat established upon the waters stands firm indeed" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka). [This refers to] the boat established upon Maṇipūra, which consists of the reality of water.
[One] knows her as being of the nature of the Śrīcakra.
And so says another Vedic text:
"May we ascend the divine ship, well-oared, faultless, providing good shelter, easy to guide, the earth, the heaven, Aditi, and the well-leader, which is sinless and flows unceasingly."
For well-being. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.11)
The meaning of this verse is as follows: the root *su* means "to press. He who presses is *Sutrāmā*, which is Agni;
the meaning is that the reality (*tattva*) of Agni resides in its own locus, namely the Earth.

To Dyaus situated at the *mūlādhāra*, to Gaganam situated at the *viśuddhi*, to Anehas (Time) as the principle of mind (*manastattva*) situated at the *ājñācakra*, to Suśarman as the principle of air (*vāyutattva*),
to Aditi who is of the nature of Aditi as the principle of water (*jalatattva*), and to Supraṇīti on the excellent path of liberation.
The meaning is: this divine (daivī) boat— meaning this science of the discus (cakravidyā) belonging to the Goddess— which leads [one] forward with excellence, is well-oared,
and possesses very firm [rudders], serving as the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.

We shall board— that is, we shall become inclined toward, devoted solely to— that which possesses oars and plows, which is immovable (meaning unshaken) by the gale-winds of evil karma, which is faultless, which does not flow out (meaning it is without leaks),
and which is itself firm.

The meaning is: "May we be intent upon His worship. "For our well-being" means for liberation, that is, for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. The remainder of the collection of scriptural passages has been thoroughly explained by us on the occasion of the commentary on the *Subhagodaya*. || 40 ||

I consider you, at your base in the foundation, together with your consort devoted to the *lāsya* dance, to be the Great Soul (*Navātmā*), the dancer of the great *tāṇḍava* of the nine aesthetic sentiments (*navarasa*).
From these two, who have become the protectors out of compassion for the purpose of bringing about the manifestation [of the world], this entire universe was born as Father and Mother. (41)

In your foundation (*ādhāra*), meaning at the root, in the *mūlādhāra-cakra*; together with her who is known as *samaya*, she whose supreme intent is *lāsya*, that is, dance; [this refers to] the action performed by a woman.

Dance is called *lāsya*. I consider and know the ninefold self as Ānandabhairava—the great dancer of the *tāṇḍava* through the nine sentiments (*rasas*), beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). The *tāṇḍava* is a great and wondrous dance performed by a male.
In that context, the dancer—the performer—is said to be *tāṇḍava*.
By means of both of these, namely Ānandabhairavī and Mahābhairava, (p. 116) [the dance is performed].

[By Ānandabhairava and Mahābhairavī. (Pā. With reference to the procedure of arising—that is, the origin of the world—he asks "from what? and answers: "out of compassion. It was born from the union of those two who were presided over by compassion for the sake of generating again the world that had been consumed by fire.

The world has arisen; this aforementioned phenomenal universe possesses progenitors, that is, it has a mother and father. Through the exposition of the arrangement of *lāsya* and *nāṭya*, it is shown that the origin of the world occurs upon the vision of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, while the dissolution of the world occurs precisely at the conclusion of the *lāsya* dance.
The Kaula doctrine.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Bhagavatī! I consider the Ninefold Self (Navātmā) to be a dancer of the great *tāṇḍava* of the nine sentiments (*navarasa*) at Your base, the foundation, together with Your consort who is intent on the dance (*lāsya*).
With respect to the process of arising, [I consider Him so] by means of these two, who are graced by compassion.
This world was born from Janaka and Jananī.

The meaning is this: because the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna* are worlds of darkness (*tāmisraloka*), the Kaulas have authority there; however, even in the absence of the propitiation of the Samayins, the Goddess is to be worshipped in the *sahasrāra* lotus according to one's own tradition.
She who is to be served in the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna* is called Mahābhairavī by means of the term *samaya* (an alternative reading is *upadeśena*). Thus it is said. Thus it is said.

In this regard, the following should be considered: it is well known that the *ādhāra-cakra* is triangular and that the *bindu* resides within the *ādhāra*. Here, according to the Kaula system, the triangle itself is the locus of the *bindu*;
that very *bindu* is the object of worship there. For this very reason, they are called Kaulas.
They constantly worship the *bindu* within the triangle. That triangle is of two kinds:

the *yoni* situated in the center of the nine *yonis* within the *Śrīcakra*, and the manifest *yoni* of a beautiful young woman. [One should worship] the *yoni* located in the center of the nine *yonis* situated within the *Śrīcakra*.
The Pūrvakaulas worship [the deity] as depicted on birch bark, golden plates, cloth, thrones, and so forth;

the Uttarakaulas worship the manifest vulva (*pratyakṣayoni*) of a young woman. Both of these two types of "vulvas" are merely external and not internal. Therefore, for them, it is the *ādhāracakra* alone [that is the true object of worship].
It is to be worshipped. The Kuṇḍalinī energy residing therein is called Kaulinī;
she alone is the object of worship for those who venerate the Triangle—this is the secret. This is the Kuṇḍalinī energy.
The Sleep in the form of the Bindu is to be worshipped while still asleep, because its inherent nature is always that of sleep; that worship is *tāmisrā*. [Next is] the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī.

When that occurs, at that very moment liberation comes for the Kaulas; for this very reason, there is the conventional usage that "the Kaulas are liberated in an instant. Therefore, within the triangle of the Kaulas, Ānandabhairavī and Mahābhairava are to be worshipped. By means of these two, [liberation is attained] for the practitioners.

Abiding in identity with that. For this very reason, it is stated in certain manuscripts as an additional reading: "At the time of the worship of the *bindu*, both men and women of the Kaulas worship by assuming the form of Bhairava and nakedness. In that regard:
They worship by means of substances such as wine, meat, honey, fish, and so forth,

through engagement in the Vāmācāra practice; having fashioned the triangle of Manmatha as a parasol over the Bindu-sthāna within the manifest triangle, they perform the worship with the triangle facing downwards.
They worship the parasol with its face turned downwards. However, the Digambara Jains and others, having placed the woman face upwards, worship a triangle pointing upwards; this is the secret.
There is much more that could be said on this matter, but because it belongs to non-Vedic paths, it is not even worth remembering.
Nevertheless, a mere indication has been stated for the purpose of demonstrating the path of the system's doctrine as that which is to be negated; enough of this elaboration.

Here, the view of the Samayins is examined. It has already been established that the six wheels, beginning with the triangle, which constitute the *cakra*, are transformed into the nature of the six wheels beginning with the *ādhāra*.
Among those, it is well known that within the *śrīcakra*, the triangle is the location of the *bindu*.

In that regard, regarding the construction of the eight-petaled lotus from three triangles, the location of the *bindu* arises from the triangle itself; and that is indeed a square. That, moreover, is the lunar mandala situated within the thousand-petaled lotus, as has already been explained in many ways previously.
This has been elaborated upon. This center of the four corners is the station of *bindu*, the ocean of nectar (*sudhāsindhu*), and the bee (*saraghā*);

this has already been explained in many ways previously. This center of the four corners is the station of *bindu*; thus there is the external worship, as well as the worship of the triangle of the young woman (*taruṇī*) and the worship of the young woman (*taruṇīpūjā*).

It should be understood that [the former] has been rejected from afar. For this very reason, there is the worship of Samayā and of Śambhu—the Samaya—in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*) of those who possess the *samaya*. She is called *Samayā* because she attains a fivefold equality (*sāmya*) with Śambhu; such is the nature of the *samaya* [of the female messenger].

Even for Śambhu, a fivefold equality with the Goddess occurs; therefore, their equality should be understood as being through the equal primacy of both. As for the fivefold equality, it consists of equality of substratum and equality of location.
(118) There are five kinds of similarity— similarity of performance, similarity of form, and similarity of name—
pertaining only to two [pledges (samaya) or primary elements (pradhāna), according to the variant reading].

Regarding the two Śivas: as in the phrase "in your support" (*tavādhāre*), the equality of their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is stated, because for both, the *ādhāra-cakra* (foundation wheel) is of the nature of a substratum. The equality of their performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is established by the verse beginning "this world, born from the Father and Mother," with respect to the act of production.

Because both are actively engaged, the equality of their state is established by the terms *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*. It was stated previously that *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava* are identical in their nature as dance (*nṛtya*). Their equality of form (*rūpa*), however, is [likened to] redness (*āruṇya*).
For both [deities], it is established in another tantra:
"I bow to the parents of the world, whose nature is Bhairava and Bhairavī, who resemble hibiscus flowers and whose eyes are rolling with intoxication."

Alternatively, it should be understood that in the phrase "the ninefold self" (*navātmānam*), both similarity of form and similarity of name are established. The same principle should be inferred for other instances as well; for example, in "the one possessing lightning" (*taṭittvantam*) and so forth, there is similarity of both name and form, as in *taṭittvān* and *taṭittvatī*. Even though...
Although the state of possessing lightning does not exist [in her] because she is of the nature of steady lightning— being identical with lightning itself—

it should nevertheless be understood that the expression "possessing lightning" (*taṭittvatī*) is appropriate, since the very steadiness of the lightning constitutes her being perpetually endowed with it. [The location is] the Maṇipūra center.
By the phrase "the abode, the sole refuge of Maṇipūra," the similarity to the [rain] abode is stated;
by the phrase "possessing a rainbow formed by various shimmering jewel-ornaments," [it is stated that he is] raining.
By this, the similarity of the state of being situated during the rainy season (*prāvṛṣeṇya*) has been established.
In the verse beginning with "In your own *svādhiṣṭhāna*," the similarity of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is stated by the term "in your own *svādhiṣṭhāna*. By the term "great" (*mahatīṃ*),...

When the identity of names and forms consisting of the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃvarta*) has been established, the similarity of their abiding is shown by the reliance upon the fire located within one's own empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). The similarity of their function is established by the statement "it burns the worlds. Within the *anāhata* wheel, there is the *anāhata*.

Regarding the term "foundation" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it refers to the equality of foundation. Through the form of a spark of fire, there is equality of form and equality of name. By the mention of being like a lamp in a windless place, there is equality of station.
The production of the principle of air (*vāyutattva*) constitutes the equality of practice; such is the secret.
(119) By the phrase "the wheel of purity is the locus," the similarity of the locus is stated.
By the phrase "clear as pure crystal," the similarity of form is stated. [It is] the progenitor of space.
By this, the equality of practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) is stated; by "I serve Śiva," the equality of name (*nāma*);
by "following the path of the likeness of the moon's rays," the equality of state (*avasthāna*);
and by "residing in your wheel of command (*ājñācakra*)," the equality of locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is stated.
By the phrase "bearing the luster of ten million suns and moons," similarity in form is expressed;

by the phrase "the supreme Śambhu," similarity in name is expressed; by the phrase "worshipping whom with devotion," similarity in state is expressed; and [by the phrase] "bestowing liberation," similarity in practice is expressed.
The fivefold equality should be understood; this, being an extreme secret, has been revealed out of a desire to favor the disciple.
Therefore, those who worship the *samaya* are the *samayins*. For them, worship of the six chakras is not mandatory;

rather, their worship is performed solely at the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*). Worship of the thousand-petaled lotus refers to the moon-maṇḍala situated in the center of that thousand-petaled lotus, by virtue of the latter being the station of *bindu*.

One should perform a contemplative realization (*anusandhāna*) of that [mandala] as a square in its essence, and from the central point, as the Self known as *Sādākhyā*, which consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti— the twenty-sixth principle that transcends the twenty-five categories (*tattvas*). For this very reason, in the Samaya system, there is external worship.
It is rejected from afar; and the entire collection of ritual limbs consisting of the sixteen-fold utterance is even further removed than that.

For instance, there is identity between the six cakras beginning with the *ādhāra* and the six cakras beginning with the triangle; there is identity between the location of the *bindu* and the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*) which is square-shaped;
likewise, there is identity between the *bindu* and Śiva, and similarly, identity between the Goddess and Śiva—thus also [regarding] "the body."

[The reading: there are three types of identity (*tādātmya*). Since the oneness of the wheel and the mantra has already been stated, their oneness with that [the teacher] makes fourfold; this is the oneness of those who observe the commitments (*samayin*), which is the fulfillment of the commitment (*samayārādhana*)—this is a great secret.

Regarding this, something is said: it is universally agreed that for those who observe the pledges (*samayins*), the very contemplation of the fourfold unity is the propitiation of the Blessed Lady. However, some speak of a sixfold unity, as in the statement: "The reality of the Lord (*bhāgavata-tattva*) transcends sound (*nāda*), the point (*bindu*), and the digit (*kalā*)."
The secret of all the scriptures: it has already been stated that *nāda* is fourfold, consisting of the forms of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. Parā is of the nature of the triangle (p.
The Paśyantī is in the form of the eight-cornered wheel, the Madhyamā is in the form of the twenty-cornered [wheel—
there is also a reading "miśrāra"], and the Vaikharī is in the form of the fourteen-cornered [wheel];
thus, the inclusion of the Śiva-cakras within these very [cakras] is established.
The Śrīcakra, consisting of four wheels (cakras), is denoted by the term *nāda*. As for *bindu*, it consists of the six cakras:
Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā.

The things denoted by the term *bindu* have already been explained. The *kalās* are fifty, or three hundred and sixty in number. Thus, the Blessed Lady transcends *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. The thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*) is beyond *bindu* and constitutes the abode of *baindava*.
That which is another synonym for the ocean of nectar (*sudhāsindhu*) is denoted by the word *saraghā*; however, the reality beyond sound (*nādātītatattva*),
which is designated by such terms as *Tripurasundarī*, has alternative synonyms such as *darśa*, *dṛṣṭā*, and *darśatā*,
and is known by the names of mantra-syllables such as *ka e ī la hrīm*.
Consisting of fifty phonemes,
comprising the nature of Mahākāla as enumerated by the number three hundred and sixty,
and transcending the fifteen kalās, she is Sādākhyā, whose synonym is Śrīvidyā.

The secret of those who know reality is this: the divine Bhagavatī, denoted by the term *citkalā* and synonymous with *brahmavidyā*, is the Bhagavata-tattva which transcends *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
In this regard, the contemplation of the mutual identity of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā* occurs in six ways.

They speak of a sixfold unity. Having thus contemplated and worshipped the Blessed Lady through this sixfold unity, one becomes dissolved into the state called Sādākhya. Thereafter, by the power of that contemplation of the sixfold unity—

And by the power of the great piercing (*mahāvedha*) produced by the glance of the Guru, the Blessed Lady instantly pierces the two wheels consisting of the *mūlādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and becomes manifest in the *maṇipūra*. The method of the great piercing has been explained previously.

In the stage of practice, being solely dependent upon the guru, one should receive the Great Vidyā from the mouth of the guru alone and perform the dry recitation (*śuṣkajapa*) of the root mantra according to the method taught by the guru, preceded by the [recitation of] the seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity,
during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.

On the eighth day, which is designated by the term Mahānavamī, one should perform the clasping of the Guru’s feet at the time of midnight. By virtue of that greatness, there shall then be the joining of the hands and the head with the Guru’s [hands], followed by the instruction of the mantra once again.

Regarding the instruction on the method of worshipping the six cakras: by virtue of the instruction on the contemplation of the sixfold unity, the Śaiva Great Piercing (mahāvedha) arises as the light-form of Sādākhya; such is the secret of the Guru. When this Great Piercing has thus occurred, the Goddess becomes manifest in the Maṇipūra.
She is to be propitiated.

[One should perform] the entire cycle of worship, beginning with the offering of water for the guest (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), and ending with the presentation of ornaments. (p. 121)
Having completed [the rites] in Maṇipūra and led the Blessed Lady to the temple of Anāhata,

and having finished there the entire cycle of ritual acts ending with the offering of incense and the washing of her hands, [he beholds] the Blessed Lady seated upon a lion-throne in Viśuddha along with her female companions.

One should worship her as she converses through dialogue with jewels resembling pure crystal; the "jewels resembling pure crystal" are not pearls and the like, but rather the sixteen digits of the moon situated upon its sixteen petals—this is the secret. Thus...

Having worshipped [the deity] and brought her to the Ājñā-cakra, one should fully gratify the goddess Kāmeśvarī with numerous rites of *nīrājana*. For this very reason, it has been stated in my own *Karṇāvataṃsa-stuti*:

"O lotus-eyed one, with earrings like flower-buds reflecting the clusters of lamp-rays from your cheeks, you then stand upon a two-petaled lotus of the nature of supreme knowledge, resembling lightning and intensely radiant with the union of sun and moon. Thus it is said.

Having thus performed the rite of lustration (*nīrājana*) at the *ājñācakra*, one should satisfy [the deity]. Immediately thereafter, like a flash of lightning, she enters the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*),
into the ocean of nectar, within the shade of the five wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) on the jewel-island (*maṇidvīpa*), in the midst of the honey-bees.

She remains sporting together with Sadāśiva. Then, having spread out the *tiraskariṇī* (the veil), she herself should settle nearby in the temple. One must remain there until the Goddess has emerged and re-entered the primary source (*mūlādhāra-kuṇḍa*).
The secret reality of the essence of the samaya.
Here, following the contemplation of the fourfold unity by Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda,

the form of the Goddess who is directly perceived in Maṇipūra is described as having four arms, as established in the meditation beginning with the words "kvaṇatkāñcīdāmā" (with tinkling girdles and necklaces).
The secret [teaching] concerning the bow, arrow, noose, and goad appears in exactly the same way even to those who follow that doctrine;
so too does the Blessed Lady appear.

But for us, following the contemplation of the sixfold unity, the gracious Goddess— ten-armed, holding in her hands a bow, arrows, a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a book, a rosary, and a lute— pierces the two centers at the *mūlādhāra* and appears in the *maṇipūra*.
According to those who hold a particular view of our own school,

[the deity] has hands holding a noose, a goad, a *puṇḍra* mark, a sugarcane bow, flower-arrows, a rosary, a parrot, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*),
with a lute placed upon the chest between the two hands. Both [of these views] are ours.
This is indeed agreed upon. In my own *Karṇasastuti*:
"O Bhavānī, you carry in your noble hands the serpent-noose and the goad below, and the bow. (p. 122)

He holds a Pauṇḍra bow, a flower-arrow, a rosary of *japa* beads, and a pair of excellent parrots; furthermore, with two hands he displays the gestures (*mudrā*) of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and with two other hands upon his chest he holds a sounding lute.
The Blessed Lady remains visible, being perceived directly by those who observe the commitments (samayins). An internal worship must be performed by the samayins as far as the thousand-petaled lotus;
however, within that thousand-petaled lotus, there is only the vision [of her] up until the spreading of the veil (tiraskariṇī).
The propitiation: As it is said in the *Subhagodaya*:

"The excellent practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess Tripurasundarī, who resides in the center of the solar disc, holding in her hands a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows; [she who pervades] the three worlds."
"May he quickly cause delusion through a multitude of excellent women—[or rather, through hundreds of groups of men and women]. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Carcastotra* composed by Kālidāsa:
"O Mother, those who contemplate Your form situated within the orb of the rising sun..."
"Delightful with the fresh mud of lac-dye [some read 'red'], the deer-eyed women, their chests forever pierced by the arrows of the flower-weaponed god, remain ever under their control.
Thus it is said.

Regarding this, some say that because external worship is prohibited for those who have taken the pledges (samayins), worship within the solar disc is also prohibited; however, that is not so, because of the identity between the sun and the moon residing in the microcosmic body (piṇḍāṇḍa) and those residing in the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa). Of the sun...

Because of the power of the flowing nectar of the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), there is a restoration of life; for this has been previously established by the scriptural passage beginning with "extracting the essence of the waters" (*apām rasaṃ samudvayan*) [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.22]. Therefore, through the contact of the digit of the moon’s knowledge (*vidyā*) with the sun...

Some maintain that there would be a concealment of its radiance; however, that too should be understood as refuted. For this very reason, because of the identity of the microcosmic body (piṇḍāṇḍa) and the macrocosmic universe (brahmāṇḍa), it is appropriate to worship the Vidyā of the lunar digit as being situated within the lunar orb.

As for the previously mentioned statement (p. 123) regarding the prohibition of worshipping the Goddess as being located within the lunar orb, that refers instead to the internal moon situated above the Ājñā-cakra.

"Revivification" occurs through the outpourings of the nectar from the digit of the moon situated within the thousand-petaled lotus; thus, there is no insistence on worshipping her in that [external] location,
precisely because of the identity between the moon of the microcosmic body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) and the macrocosmic universe (*brahmāṇḍa*).
This is intended to show that there is no insistence on performing worship even regarding the lunar orb situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

Thus, when the Blessed Lady is propitiated within the heart-lotus itself, she bestows all worldly fruits. When meditated upon as joined with Vaśinī and the others, she grants the eloquence of Sarasvatī. When meditated upon as drenched in the juice of *yāvaka*, she grants the power of subjugation. [The] face...

By the verse beginning with "having made the *bindu*," [verse 19], it is taught that the meditator bestows such a fruit. One should remember that the performance of fire-offerings (*homa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*), which are means for attaining worldly fruits, must be carried out within the heart-lotus itself; thus, one should contemplate the womb as Lakṣmī.
This has been explained more thoroughly during the commentary on verse 33 and so forth.
Therefore, the reality of the Samaya doctrine is that the internal worship (*āntarapūjā*) is the means for practitioners (*samayins*) to achieve results pertaining to both this world and the next.

In this context, the venerable Bhagavatpāda has described a mode of worship by means of the descending sequence, starting from the *ājñācakra* and so forth, while omitting the sequence beginning with the foundational lotus (*ādhārakamala*). The underlying intention is as follows: from the Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced; from space, air (*vāyu*).
"From air comes fire; from fire, water; from water, earth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Relying on this Vedic sequence, the order of descent has been stated. For this very reason, the Maṇipūra, which occurs immediately after the Svādhiṣṭhāna, is located in the region below it.
This definition is appropriate. That the location of Maṇipūraka follows immediately after the foundation (ādhāra) and svādhiṣṭhāna is established in all yoga scriptures.
Furthermore, that [location] is the arising [of the world] immediately after the resurrection of the universe that had been consumed by the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartāgni).

It should be understood that this means "to speak. Furthermore, in the *Śuka-saṃhitā*, beginning with the words "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim," ninety-one verses are devoted to introducing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) of the Śrīcakra; then, beginning with the words "Now I shall fully proclaim... [the text continues].
It has been explained in detail through one hundred and fifty verses;
therefore, it should be understood from that very source.

Furthermore, according to the Vedic scripture, "He who knows the tree whose roots are above and branches below" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11), the head alone is the root of the tree that takes the form of the body.

The hands, feet, and other limbs are the branches; therefore, the lotuses of the six centers, which are compared to the flowers of a plantain tree and are downward-facing, are described according to the order of descent (avaroha-krama). Thus, worship is easily performed there in accordance with that [descending sequence].
It should be stated that this was said by the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda), because worship is impossible apart from meditation on identity (tādātmya-dhyāna); or, even if it were possible,
it would contradict the fact that the six cakras, such as the triangle and others within the Śrīcakra, are not downward-facing.
"One should awaken the Goddess who resides in the *mūlādhāra* while she is still asleep.

Since awakening occurs precisely there, it is understood from the mouth of the Supreme Guru that the worship of the *samayins* and the *kaulas*, and so forth, must be performed according to the sequence beginning with the *mūlādhāra*. This is known as the "bodily" (*kāyika*) method.
The Secret: A specific detail regarding self-worship is stated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"His noose and goad are considered to consist of passion and hatred;
sound, touch, and the other [objects of the senses] are his arrows, and the mind became his bow."
"One who possesses all perfections should worship the Goddess, whose nature is pure consciousness, residing in the wheel of the organs of action, with the flower of universal egoity.
This is the method of worship (*upāsanā*). "Method" (*vidhi*) consists of ritual action.
It is not to be respected. || 41 ||
Having thus correctly expounded the doctrine of the Samaya, he describes the Blessed Lady of the Samaya from her crown down to her feet:
"Your crown, densely set with sky-jewels that have attained the state of rubies..."
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, he who praises this golden [bow]—
does he not fix his mind upon the bow of Śunaḥśepa’s father, variegated by the shimmering shadow of its notch, which is like a fragment of the moon? 42.

By the "sky-jewels"— the twelve suns— who have attained (*gataiḥ*) or reached the state of being rubies (*māṇikyatvam*), [this is done] for the sake of performing service in the closest proximity to them.

The quality of being gems belonging to ornaments is appropriate [for you]. O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain! O Pārvatī! Your crown—your diadem—is fashioned densely, meaning it is constructed so as to be thick and without gaps, set with jewels, and made of gold, a product of gold.
He who proclaims and describes [this] is the lord of poets (*kavīndra*).
"Nīḍeya" refers to the *nīḍa* or sphere; it is variegated by the scattering of its shadow. "Khacita" means inlaid therein;
"nīḍeya" refers to the collection of jewels, and by their "chāyā"—that is, by the scattering (*churaṇa*) or pervasion (*vyāpana*) of that shadow—[it is so described].
Why does his intellect not fix its thought upon the variegated, multi-colored crescent moon as a bow— the weapon of Śunāsīra, that is, Indra?
Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain!

He who praises your golden crown, which is densely fashioned from sky-jewels that have attained the state of rubies—he [beholds] the crescent moon on the plow-wielder’s (*Śaunāsīra*) head, variegated by the scattering of its own shadow within the nest [of the crown].
Does it not bind the intellect to the notion that "this is a bow"?

The sense is this: how could this lord of poets, while striving to compose a description of the crown, not suspect that the crescent moon situated upon it—suffused with the luster of various jewels—is actually Indra’s bow? It must certainly be so for him.
Thus, that doubt certainly arises.
Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the crescent moon is fancied as being the bow of Indra;

or else, there is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), because of the appearance of a denial that "this is not a crescent moon, but rather the bow of Indra"; or else, there is the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt).
This is either a doubt (*saṃśaya*) arising from the uncertainty as to whether this is Indra’s bow or a fragment of the moon;

or else, it is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because of the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the moon’s fragment with Indra’s bow, and because of the general statement: "Why does she not fix her own intellect upon Indra’s bow?"

Among these, because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka-pramāṇa*) to establish that one is primary and the other subordinate, there is a confusion of doubt (*sandeha-saṅkara*). (Hyperbole and Poetic Fancy are clear; as for Concealment (*apahnuti*), why does the intellect not [recognize it] even due to the absence of its characteristic marks?)

Since it is possible to formulate a negation by saying "it binds," whereas doubt— because the rainbow has ascended to the level of memory upon seeing a fragment of the moon— is indeed capable of being formulated, the combination with doubt (sandehasaṅkara) alone is superior. || 42 ||
O Śivā, may that mass of your hair— dense, glossy, and smooth, which has surpassed and crushed a forest of blue lotuses— dispel our darkness. That [mass] whose...
I believe that the flowers of the trees in Indra’s garden dwell here in order to obtain their innate fragrance.
May he dispel—that is, remove—the darkness, the inner gloom, of us;
[he] whose [face] resembles a grove of blue lotuses (*indīvara*) that have been crushed—that is, made similar to, split open, or blossomed. That [face].
