"Densely smooth and soft" (*ghanasnigdhaślakṣṇam*): "dense" (*ghana*) means thick and without gaps; "smooth" (*snigdha*) means as if possessed of oiliness; "soft" (*ślakṣṇa*) means tender. This is the compound of these adjectives. "The mass of curls" (*cikuranikurumbam*) refers to the hair.
A "keśapāśa" is a mass or collection of hair, meaning a braided coil (*dhammilla*). O Śivā! O Blessed Lady! [I wish] to perceive that innate, natural fragrance belonging to this *dhammilla* of yours.
To attract the *sumanas* flowers, they remain here with their mouths open;
I believe that in this braid of hair resides the *valamathana*—
the subduer of Bala (namely Indra)— for whom the substitution of *ba* for *va* is permissible.
For the sake of alliteration, he accepted [the gift]; its garden (vāṭī) is a park (udyāna), and therein are the trees (viṭapinaḥ), which are wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣāḥ). Of those...

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Śivā! May your mass of hair, which resembles a forest of crushed blue lotuses and is thick, glossy, and smooth, dispel our darkness. To perceive its innate fragrance, [one must look] in this...
I believe that the flowers of the trees in the garden of Valamathana dwell there.

Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the flowers of the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree), which were actually worn for the sake of adorning her mass of hair, are fancied as something else. Its definition is:
"Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the imagining of the subject at hand as being another thing."
In the phrase "tulitadalitendīvaravanam" (a forest of blue lotuses weighed and crushed), there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile).
There is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) between these two [the simile and the other figure], because they are combined like sesame seeds and rice grains.
The relation [between the two] is like that of milk and water; this is commingling (saṅkara). || 43 ||
May the parting of your hair grant us security, appearing like a flowing stream from the overflow of the beauty of your face; it bears vermilion as if it were a host of captive suns,
the enemies of the dense darkness of your thick tresses.
The rays of the newly risen sun. || 44 ||
"May it spread"—that is to say, may it extend and grant—peace (*kṣema*), which consists of both acquisition and preservation, to us;
[this peace] is like the flow of the stream from the overflowing surge of the beauty of Your face, as if through this single word (*padam*). The word "like" (*iva*) is used here.

This is due to the rule: "A compound with *saha* is obligatory (*nityasamāsa*), there is no elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktyalopa*), and the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is retained]. *Vadanam* means the face; the surge (*laharī*) of its beauty—that is, the state of being beautiful—is its overflow (*parīvāha*), meaning its current. [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied after a prefix (*upasarga*) when it does not refer to a human being.

The word *bahulam* indicates that there is lengthening of the vowel *e* in the prefix *pari*. In this context, "the path of the parting" (*sīmantasaraṇi*) refers to a line formed in the shape of a path upon the parting (*sīmanta*), that is, in the region between the braided hair (*dhamilla*), resembling the flow of a stream; it is like a path for a stream, that is, like the course of a river's current.

Carrying and bearing vermilion—the dust of vermilion—which, by virtue of having taken birth as her own mass of hair, is powerful against the darkness of the thick tresses; for those tresses themselves are powerful. And they are the masses of her braided hair. They alone...
The mass of her tresses of hair is itself the darkness; those very [darknesses] are the enemies, the foes.

By their multitudes—that is, by their throngs—she has been made a captive, held in confinement. The word "iva" (as if) is used here in the sense of poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*). In the context of a poet's bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*), the word "iva" [is employed].

The meaning is simply "conception" (saṃbhāvanā); the distinction is that in other instances it means "similarity" (sādṛśya). "Navīnārkakiraṇam" refers to the rays of the new sun—the sun belonging to the early morning—and its rays.
p.
128) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! [Your face] stands like a channel for the flow of the overflowing stream of the wave of beauty of Your countenance.
May she, who bears vermilion upon her parting line as if it were the newly risen sun’s rays captured by the hosts of enemies of the darkness of her thick tresses, grant us well-being.

Here, the figure of speech is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the parting of the hair is fancied as being a stream of water; nor is this the figure of *upamā* (simile), because it arises by depending solely on the poet’s bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) rather than upon something established in its own right. Nor...
It should be stated that this is indeed a simile (*upamā*), because there is no rule for compounding the word *iva* when it is used in the sense of "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*).

However, it should be understood that a compound exists in both cases as well, because the word *iva* is included in the general rule "with *iva*" (*ivena saha*), which applies to its meaning in both senses.

In the latter half [of the verse] as well, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because of the imaginative attribution (*saṃbhāvanā*) of the vermilion to the nature of the sun’s rays; furthermore, there exists the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor), due to the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) of darkness upon the mass of the braid of hair. Thus, there is a *saṅkara* (commixture) of these two through their relationship of primary and subordinate elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
Because the metaphor (rūpaka) serves as the cause for the attribution of identity (saṃbhāvanā). || 44 ||
Your face, surrounded by curling locks that naturally possess the beauty of young bees, mocks the splendor of the lotus; for upon it— sweetly smiling,
radiant with the filaments of the luster of your teeth, and fragrant— the [bees] become intoxicated.
The bees are the eyes of the fire of passion. || 45 ||
With curls that are arālaiḥ—crooked by their very nature (svābhāvyāt)—and possessing a splendor equal to young bees (alikalabha-saśrībhiḥ), that is, similar in luster to young bees (bhramara-potaiḥ);
the absence of the suffix *ka* is due to the non-universality of the rule for forming compounds with suffixes (*samāsānta-vidher-anityatvāt*). [Thus, it is] with *alakaiḥ*—curls.

Your face, surrounded on all sides by curly locks of hair—meaning it is encompassed and pervaded—ridicules the beauty of the lotus; that is to say, nothing is equal to it. [It surpasses] the splendor of the lotus (paṅkeruha), the beauty of the water-lily, while you yourself are slightly smiling (darasmere).

In that [face] which is thus blossomed, beautiful with the filaments of the luster of the teeth— the very radiance of the ten teeth being the filaments— [the bees] delight and rejoice in its fragrance, which possesses the sweet scent of a fine lotus.

(129) The bees of the eye of the fire of love: the bees are the very eyes of the fire of love, that is, of the Lord Śiva, the enemy of Smara; for even though he has conquered Manmatha, [the bees still hover there].
The point is: if even the mere sight of the beauty of a face is a cause of passion, what need is there to mention the actual nature of the beauty of your own face?
Here is the word-connection (*padayojanā*): O Blessed Lady! Your face, surrounded by locks of hair that are naturally curly and possess the beauty of young bees, mocks the splendor of a lotus;
for it is slightly smiling, beautiful with the filaments of the luster of its teeth, and fragrant.
The bees, whose eyes are the fire of passion, become intoxicated.

Here, there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) in the phrase "mocking the luster of the lotus," because this evokes the resemblance of the face to a lotus. There is also the figure of speech *upamā* in the phrase "possessing the beauty of young black bees. These two are combined through the relationship of *saṅkara* (blending), wherein one serves as the subordinate member (*aṅga*) to the other, which is the principal member (*aṅgin*).

In the phrase "beautiful with the filaments of the luster of her teeth" (*daśanarucikiñjalkarucire*), there is the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor), because the luster of the teeth is superposed as being filaments. In the phrase "the bees that are the eyes of the fire of love" (*smaradahanacakṣurmadhulihaḥ*), there is the figure of speech *rūpaka*, because the eyes are superposed as being bees.
There is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of these two through the relationship of subordinate and principal, and a coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the two types of commingling.

That forehead of yours, which shines with a purity born of loveliness, I consider to be a second fragment of the moon set within your crown; through their inverted placement and by joining together, both become the full-orbed moon,
appearing as if plastered with nectar.

Your forehead—known as the *niṭila*—shines brilliantly all around, pure with the radiance of loveliness; for "loveliness" (*lāvaṇya*) is indeed fluidity, and "radiance" (*dyuti*) is moonlight, by which it is stainless and glossy.
I think, I suspect, that what constitutes its second part is fashioned into a crown.
The crescent moon (*candraśakala*) set upon the crown is a fragment of the half-moon; through its inverted placement,
the forehead is positioned at the downward angle, while the crescent moon above the forehead exists as an upward-pointing horn—
thus there is an inverted arrangement of both.
Therefore, the union of the four horns—both [the eyebrows and the eyes] having come together and met upon the crescent moon of the forehead—the particle *ca* expresses an intensification (*atiśaya*).
*Mithaḥ* means mutually or reciprocally. *Sudhālepa-syūtiḥ*: *sudhā* is nectar; *lepa* is an ointment or coating;

*syūtiḥ* is its stitching or weaving—that which has this is "sewn with an ointment of nectar," meaning it is thick with the essence of nectar. *Pariṇamati*: it attains that state, assuming that form, being fashioned into that very shape.
This is the meaning: "the moon of the Rākā" refers to the moon (himakara) on the Rākā, which is the full moon day (pūrṇimā).

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! I consider that forehead of yours, which shines, pure with the radiance of loveliness, to be a second crescent of the moon fashioned upon your crown; for this reason, both [the natural face and the ornament]—
Through the mutual application of inversion and the joining together of the plastering of nectar, the moon of the full-moon night undergoes transformation.

"How could there be fullness of the moon on the full-moon day? Since the moon is seen as occupying only half of his body upon his crown, the forehead is poetically imagined by taking the full-moon moon as the point of reference."
Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the forehead is fancied as being the half-moon;

or else, in the second half [of the verse], the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), since there is no actual connection between the full moon (*rākā-himakara*) and the creation of the pair of crescent moons formed by the two halves of the crown upon the forehead.
Because of the statement regarding their connection:
here, there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) between the beauty of the poetic fancy (*kavikalpita-vastu*) and the actual event (*vṛtta*), based on their non-difference.
Furthermore, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) through the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

When the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the act of identification (*adhyavasāya*) is predominant, it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy); when the object identified (*adhyavasita*) is predominant, however, it is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). This is the meaning of the two aphorisms: where there is predominance of the operation consisting of the act of identification with respect to the object of that identification.

In that case, there is the emergence of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). When, within the object of identification (*adhyavasāya-viṣaya*), the predominance of the thing identified (*adhyavasita*) itself is perceived, then there is the emergence of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
Identification (*adhyavasāya*) is a cognition of certainty; and that [certainty] is established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, not...

In reality, however, poetic conceits (*utprekṣā*) serve to indicate the predominance of the act of identification (*adhyavasāna*). Words such as *manye*, *śaṅke*, and *dhruvam* indicate conceits based on essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*).
In a conceit based on cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), the cause itself is the indicator; in a conceit based on effect (*phalotprekṣā*), the effect itself is the indicator.

For this very reason, since cause and effect are impossible in the absence of words such as *iva* in a *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential nature), there is no distinction between *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and *utprekṣā*; thus, that very *utprekṣā* is included within *atiśayokti*. This has been stated merely by way of illustration. || 46 || (p. 131)

When your eyebrows, ever intent on shattering the fears of the world, are slightly arched, I imagine that the bow of the Lord of Rati— held by his right hand at the grip and its string drawn back— is concealed within his forearm and fist by your two eyes, which possess the luster of bees.
O Umā, whose inner nature is profound! || 47 ||
Your two eyebrows are like two curved creepers, bent and coiled in the form of downward-pointing horns;
O You who are somewhat—not excessively—addicted to the task of destroying the fear and calamity of the worlds! "Worlds" refers to the universes (*jagat*);
"fear" refers to affliction (*upadrava*); "destruction" means causing its end; and "addiction" refers to being solely intent upon that task.

The vocative address "O she who is intent on destroying the fear of the world" refers to her. "Belonging to you" (*tvadīye*) means related to you; "by the two eyes" (*netrābhyām*) means by the two organs of sight;
"having the luster of bees" (*madhukararucibhyām*) means possessing a splendor like that of *madhukaras*, or bees.

The meaning is: "by those two" which have been fashioned in the form of bees. I consider—that is, I suspect—that the bow, whose string (guṇa) has been taken up—that is, secured—is held by his right and its other (left) hand; "savya" means right, and "itaras" means the opposite, namely the left.

And that [arrow] was held by his hand; by the word *savyetara* (the other than the left), it is indicated that it was always held with one hand alone, and not for the purpose of discharging an arrow. It was at the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*), the wrist (*maṇibandha*), the fist (*muṣṭi*), and the knuckles of the fingers (*aṅgulīnāṃ granthau*) of the Lord of Rati, Manmatha.

This word *muṣṭi* is feminine by virtue of grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), yet due to its frequent usage it has acquired a masculine gender, just like the word *gaṇḍūṣa*. For example, there is the usage in the *Naiṣadha*: "He measures his belly with his fist" (*udaraṃ parimāti muṣṭinā*). [It] covers.
O Umā! O Pārvatī! when there is concealment—that is, covering—of the interior, that [bow] has its inner space hidden between the two bamboo shafts.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Umā, you who are devoted to the destruction of the world's fears! Your two slightly curved eyebrows conceal, with your eyes possessing the luster of bees, the bowstring held by the right hand of the Lord of Rati—[the string] which was grasped by his left forearm and fist.
I consider the bow to have its interior concealed when it exists.
Here, "the two eyebrows are a bow" is a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), because the eyebrows are described in the form of a bow;
for this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the dual and the singular in the expression "the two eyebrows are a bow.

The meaning is this: a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is of four kinds—namely, the distinguishing qualifier (*vyāvartaka-viśeṣaṇa*), the coloring qualifier (*uparañjaka-viśeṣaṇa*), the indicating qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa-viśeṣaṇa*), and the supporting qualifier (*upadhāna-viśeṣaṇa*). Among these, the distinguishing qualifier...
In cases such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), the blueness serves to exclude [the lotus] from being white or other colors.

There are two types of coloring qualifiers (*uparañjaka-viśeṣaṇa*): that which functions by way of the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*) and that which functions by way of the object being superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*). Among these:

The state of having the superimposed object as its domain occurs in such cases as "the face is the moon. Therein, the face is colored by [the quality of] being the moon. For this very reason, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is established even when there is a difference in gender, as in: "that [face], becoming those high breasts..."

In the *Naiṣadha*: "There, he [is one], the jar is one, and the two breasts are [the other]; thus there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two. However, the qualifying attribute of that which is being superimposed is "clouds are the curtains"; here, the state of being a curtain is what is being superimposed.
It exists as the very nature of the object of superimposition; this has already been established previously.

Regarding the distinction between an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*): "Devadatta’s house has a crow" is an example of an indicator. For those who know indicators, an indicator is that which exists separately from the substratum (*dharmin*).

Because that which is already permeated by a genus such as "cuckoo-ness" (*kākatva*) serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is a distinction [of the former] from a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

In the case of "the red crystal," the redness is a qualifier because it is the substrate of the imposition. There is a distinction [of the latter] from a secondary indicator because it functions as an indicator through its nature as a property (*dharma*), since it acts as a differentiator.
The exclusion [of the term] from blue lotuses and so forth.

In this regard, the essential point is as follows: in instances involving qualifying adjuncts that serve as coloring attributes (uparañjaka-viśeṣaṇa)— such as "the face is the moon," "the breasts are jars," or "the eyebrows are a bow"—
the qualifying adjuncts like "moon" or "jar" indeed adopt the gender and number inherent [in the substantive they qualify].
Since they qualify [objects] such as the face and the breasts, they do not take on the gender or number of the breast or the face; for, by virtue of having a fixed gender,
they lack the property of conforming to the gender of the substantive (viśeṣya), thereby distinguishing them from other qualifiers.
Because of the use of the word "manye" (I think) and the arising of a probability, there is also the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).

The coexistence (*anusṛṣṭi*) of these two occurs because the two figures, which do not exist separately, stand in a relationship of mutual subserviency (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). [This applies to] those that do not exist separately.

The secret of the science of poetics (*alaṅkāra*) is this: when two figures of speech stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), it is called *anusarjana*; however, when they exist separately, it is *saṅkara*. Furthermore, there is also *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) here, because of the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the space between the eyebrows and the space between the nostrils as being covered by a fist and a forearm, respectively. In this case, [the figure pertains] to the nose...
Because the act of placing [the nose] is perceived through the state of being the "other hand" (i.e., the right hand), the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) is suggested (*dhvanyate*).

Alternatively, because the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the nose with the "other hand" is perceived, there is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). The commingling (*saṅkara*) of these two is a case of doubt (*sandeha*). || 47 ||
(133) Your right eye produces the day by virtue of being the nature of the sun; your left eye creates the night by virtue of being the lord of the night. Your third...
Her gaze, possessing the luster of a slightly blossomed golden lotus, assumes the twilight that moves between day and night. || 48 ||
Your right eye,

being of the nature of the sun (*arkātmaka*), produces— that is, generates— the day; and your left eye, being of the nature of the moon (*candrātmaka*) as the lord of the night, creates— that is, produces— the three-watch night.
[Consisting of the lord of the night, having the nature of the moon: Your third eye, situated on your forehead, possesses the luster of a slightly opened golden lotus;
"slightly opened" (daradalita) means somewhat blossomed, and "golden lotus" (hemāmbuja) refers to a red lotus [or a golden lotus]; it is that which has the luster of such a lotus.

He applies himself, he correctly applies himself; he performs [the rite] during the transition between day and night— that is, between the two parts of the day and night— the intermediate period consisting of the two junctions (saṃdhyā) of evening and morning,
because the Agnihotra is to be accomplished at those two times of saṃdhyā.
The state of being.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Blessed Lady! Your right eye, being of the nature of the sun, produces the day; your left eye, being the leader of the night, creates the three-watch night. Your third eye is that which... [is the moon].
Possessing the luster of a slightly opened golden lotus, it assumes the form of twilight, moving between day and night.

Here, by means of the three eyes consisting of the sun, moon, and fire, there is the manifestation of the Blessed Lady’s specific limbs as the various divisions of time— such as day, night, and twilight— as well as fortnights, months, seasons, yugas, kalpas, and so forth.
By stating that the Blessed Lady arises at a specific time, it is suggested that her being limited by time is cast far away. This is excellent poetry;
even the perception of it as mediocre poetry [arises] because, while it is solar in nature, it is also composed of the lord of night.
Because it is being stated [explicitly].
134) By the phrase "having the luster of a slightly opened golden lotus," his having three eyes (*agninetra*) is suggested through poetic suggestion (*dhvani*).

This [example] consists of *anuprāṇana* (life-giving resonance) and is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the middle and supreme types of *dhvani*. The two suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) being combined are merged with the predominant *dhvani* through the relationship of subordinate and principal; such is the general direction [of the analysis]. || 48 ||
The vast and auspicious Ayodhyā, radiant with blossoming lotuses, the source of the earth’s splendor, exceedingly sweet and expansive; Avantī,
whose vision triumphs over the expanse of many cities— surely these are your [eyes].
She who is fit for being designated by those various names reigns supreme. || 49 ||

Viśālā (the vast), Vipulā (the expansive), Kalyāṇī (the auspicious), Maṅgalātmikā (whose nature is auspiciousness), Sphuṭaruciḥ (of radiant splendor), Prasphuṭakāntiḥ (of manifest beauty), Ayodhyā (unconquerable), [and] Kuvalayaiḥ Kṛtā (adorned with blue water-lilies)— Ayodhyā is the receptacle for streams of compassion, the support for those who possess the flow of mercy.

It is the substratum (*ādhārabhūtā*). Since the word *ādhāra* ends in the suffix *ghañ* with the sense of the object (*karman*), it functions as a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by conforming to the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*). It is somehow sweet—that is, indistinctly sweet—and possessed of expansion (*ābhogavatikā*); "expansion" (*ābhoga*) refers to internal breadth or, in other words, length.

The Avantī is your protective gaze; your eye, which triumphs over the expanse of many cities—triumphant through the total extent of numerous cities—is surely certain [of victory]. It is fit for the designation of those various names.

The names—namely, Viśālā, Kalyāṇī, Ayodhyā, Dhārā, Madhurā, Bhogavatī, Avantī, and Vijayā—are the eight names of cities; by means of these, there is their designation, which is their conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). That [city] which is worthy therein prevails with supreme excellence.
It proceeds.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! Your vision is vast, auspicious, and of manifest luster; it is superior to blue lotuses, a receptacle for the support of compassion, indescribably sweet, expansive, protective, and victorious over the extensive array of many cities.
She who is certainly fit for being designated by those various names reigns supreme.

135) Here, this should be kept in mind: there are eight cities beginning with Viśālā and ending with Vijayā, as well as eight views (*dṛṣṭi*). The view named Viśālā consists of internal expansion (*antarvikāsa*).
The Kalyāṇī glance is astonished; the Ayodhyā glance has smiling pupils; the Dhārā glance is languid; the Madhurā glance is turned [or playful];
the Bhogavatī glance is affectionate; the Avantī glance is innocent.

The *vijayā* glance, the *prāntakanīnikā* glance, and the glance called *ākekarā*—these eight glances are common to all women; however, in the case of the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*), there is this distinction:
these glances [are applied] in their respective order.
They are combined for the rites of agitation, attraction, liquefaction, intoxication, subjugation, expulsion, causing enmity, and killing.

This is what is meant: that region where the Blessed Lady, staying in a certain place, caused an agitation among the people by means of her gaze known as "the wide-open" (*viśālā*), which is characterized by an internal expansion—that region is the city of Viśālā. In that region...
Having stationed herself there with a squinting glance, she named Vijayā brought about the destruction of the enemy;
that region is indeed Vijayanagarī. In this manner, the names of the six intermediate cities are to be inferred. As it was stated by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya: "Viśālā and the others."

The specific glances of the Bhagavatī, which serve as the means for accomplishing rites such as *saṃkṣobha* and so forth, consist of internal expansions (*antarvikāsa*) and other such forms; thus, everything is beyond reproach. This very point has been clarified by the commentators on that [text], and it should be understood from that source alone. || 49 ||
Seeing Your pair of ears— which, like young elephants, are never without the bees of Your sidelong glances, and which delight solely in the nectar of the poetic compositions of the wise—
and seeing Your forehead-eye, which is restless in tasting the nine aesthetic flavors, become envious due to that very association; [the latter] gazes upon the former.
Slightly reddish. || 50 ||

Of poets, that is, of the lords of poets; "sandarbha" refers to a literary composition (*kāvyasandarbha*), which is itself a cluster (*stabaka*) of flowers; within that cluster, it is the "makaranda," the nectar, which is the "ekarasika," the singular or primary connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*).
The meaning is: "one whose sole aesthetic flavor (*rasika*) is the tasting of the nectar of poetry.
The two young elephants that are the bees [attracted] by the casting of side-glances (*kaṭākṣa*) are the side-glances themselves.
The compound is: "those two who possess distraction and deceit, and who are also a bee and a young elephant.

"Bhramara-kalabhau" refers to a bee and a young elephant. Here, although the word *kalabha* primarily denotes the young of an elephant, it [is used here] by virtue of its frequent employment by great poets.
Having seen that your pair of ears—
the two auditory organs— did not let go [of the bees], being greedy for the taste of their nectar, they were like bees and young elephants; [this was so] because your third eye is situated above.
"Moving with the savoring of the nine rasas"— the nine rasas are those beginning with *śṛṅgāra* (erotic),

which are nine in number; the term "nine rasas" (*navarasāḥ*) is formed by the elision of the middle member according to the *śākapārthiva*-type compounds, otherwise, by the rule *dvigoḥ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applied.
In the Kṛta age, it would be called Navarasī. Because of its attachment (*tarala*) and greed (*lampaṭa*) for the tasting and enjoyment of the nine rasas,
and due to contact with envy— that is, the association or connection with *asūyā*, which is jealousy—
the eye in the forehead (*alika-nayana*) became somewhat reddened.
As if slightly angry, he turned his face toward the west.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Blessed One! Your pair of ears, which alone relishes the nectar of the clusters of compositions of poets—[ears] that do not release the two young bees of Your sidelong glances, which are restless in tasting the nine aesthetic flavors (navarasa).
Having seen [him] with slightly reddened, false eyes due to contact with indignation.

The meaning is this: since two out of the three eyes have already accomplished the drinking of nectar, it is only fitting for one eye to feel envy. This is a *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on the description: "the Goddess whose eyes extend to her ears."

In this instance, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because it describes a connection between the ears [or eyes; "śravaṇagata" is the reading found in the Kalyāṇapura edition of the manuscript] and the tasting of the nectar of poetry, even though no such connection exists.

In the phrase "the bee and the young elephant," there is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment). Alternatively, it may be explained as *rūpaka* (metaphor), wherein the casting of a sidelong glance exists in the form of a sidelong glance itself.
Furthermore, there is another instance of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) regarding the bee and the young elephant.
Because a relationship is described even when no actual relationship exists with the tasting of the nectar (makaranda),

there is a relationship between the two types of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)— that created by the poet and that inherent in the object— consisting in the state of the vitalized and the vitalizer, based on the identification of their respective beauties. As for the concealment (*apahnava*), however...
It is intermingled by way of being a constituent factor. || 50 ||
Toward Śiva she is moist with passion; toward others she is intent on reviling; she is full of wrath at the Gaṅgā;
she is filled with wonder at the deeds of Giriśa; and she is terrified of Hara’s serpents.
O Mother, your glance toward me is compassionate, smiling among your friends, and the source of the lotus’s good fortune. 51.

O Śivā! Toward Sadāśiva, you are moistened by *śṛṅgāra*—that is, drenched with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). Toward other people—that is, toward persons other than that Sadāśiva—you are intent on reviling them; thus, regarding that [other] object, you are possessed by the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsarasa*). Here, "reviling" refers to...

The contraction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) produced by the tasting of the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsarasa*) is metaphorically designated as "sentiment" (*rasa*) through the non-differentiation of cause and effect. Similarly, the description of anger—
characterized by being possessed by the *raudrarasa*— as a "sentiment" refers to the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of anger, which is spoken of as a "sentiment" only figuratively.
"In the Gaṅgā" means "in the co-wife," as is the understood sense. Regarding the conduct of Giriśa (Śiva) in the conquest of Tripura and other such deeds, [the eyes] were filled with wonder;
however, in the reading "Giriśanayane," it refers to the eyes being permeated by the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta-rasa*).
In that case, the burning of Manmatha occurred by means of the third eye alone, and now it is in that very same eye... [that this occurs].

One should contemplate this as a marvel: "a glance full of significance. Those who are terrified—overcome by the sentiment of fear—of the serpents of Hara (the Supreme Lord Śiva), [take refuge in her];
she is the mother of the beauty of the lotuses, for she generates the auspiciousness—the crimson hue—of the lotuses.
His mother, the one who gave him birth, possesses the luster of a red lotus;

she is red in color, meaning she is permeated by the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). Here, the heroic sentiment is suggested (*dhvanita*) by the emotional consequence (*anubhāva*) of the redness of her eyes.
Among her female companions (*sakhīṣu*), that is, her friends, she is smiling, yet her pupils are fixed and motionless.

Here too, the sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*) is suggested by the power [of the words]. O Mother! O Janani! Your glance toward me is compassionate, permeated with the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*).

Here is the word-connection (*padayojanā*): O Mother! Your gaze is moist with passion for Śiva, intent on reviling other people, wrathful toward the Gaṅgā, filled with wonder at the deeds of Giriśa [and wonder-struck at the eyes of Giriśa], and terrified of Hara’s serpents.
She who brings forth the beauty of the lotus smiles among her companions, yet is full of compassion toward me.

(138) Here, because it is stated that there is a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of mutually contradictory aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) brought together in a single place, this constitutes the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction), since the contradiction is resolved through a difference in their respective states.
That contradiction is merely apparent; its definition is that "apparent contradiction" (virodhābhāsa) is a contradiction.
According to Bharata’s doctrine, there are eight rasas, for it is held that only those [rasas] produce transformation (vikriyā).
Because the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa is devoid of modification (*nirvikāratva*), they did not consider *śānta* to be a rasa.
Thus, because tranquility lacks the nature of a rasa, only eight rasas are included.

Having reached the vicinity of your ears like wings, these eyes of yours— acting as buds upon the crest-ornament of the lineage of the Mountain’s daughter— bear lashes that result in the melting away of the savor of tranquility in the mind of the Destroyer of Cities,
manifesting the grace of Cupid’s arrow drawn back to the ear.
Of the two who reckon. || 52 ||
Having reached the vicinity of the ears— that is, being near the ears—

it bears lashes like feathers, such as those of a heron; it has as its fruit the draining away of the essence of mental tranquility from the mind— the internal organ— of the Destroyer of the Ancient Cities.

The "essence of tranquility" (*praśamarasa*)—meaning freedom from desire (*naiṣpṛhya*)—is that which is "melted away," that is, destroyed; this amounts to the production of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). These two [the *cittapraśama* and the *rasa*] have that very thing as their fruit or purpose; thus, they are the "two whose fruit is the melting away of the essence of tranquility of the mind. In this regard:

By the word "fruit" (phala), referring to that which is determined [by the context], the iron needle at the tip of an arrow is meant. These two eyes, visible within the lotus of the heart, are like two flower-buds upon the crest-ornament of the lineage of the Lord of the Earth. "Gotrā" means the earth; he who supports it is "dhara."

The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *dhr* according to the rule *pacādyac*; thus, from *gotrā* and *dhara*, we have *gotrādharaḥ*. Otherwise, if the analysis were *gotrāṃ dhārayati* ("he holds the mountain"), the suffix *aṇ* would be required by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, resulting in the form *gotrādhāraḥ*. With this very intention, in the case of *śaktidharaḥ*, [the analysis is] *śakteḥ dharaḥ* = *śaktidharaḥ*.

Thus it was stated by Kṣīrasvāmin: "Gotrādharapati" refers to Himavat; "kulottaṃsakalikā" means a bud that is the crest-ornament of his lineage; this is its vocative form: "O you [who are] such, O lady. (p. 139)

They possess, that is, they display, the grace—the beauty—of the arrows of Love drawn as far as the ear; that is, they display the splendor of the two arrows of Manmatha drawn up to the edge of the ears. [This is the dual form of the present indicative, parasmaipada.]

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Kalikā, crest-jewel of the lineage of the Lord of Adhara! These two eyes of yours have reached the vicinity of your ears, possessing lashes like feathers, and they bear the fruit of causing the melting away of the essence of mental tranquility in the Destroyer of the Cities (Śiva).
He displays the graceful charm of Cupid’s arrow drawn back to the ear.
The meaning is this: for the five-arrowed one (the god of love), the side-long glance of women is the sixth arrow.
He is renowned as "five-arrowed" with the intention of emphasizing the majority [of his arrows].
A glance-constituted arrow is equal to the other five arrows; therefore, he is not called "six-arrowed."

This is figurative usage (*vyavahāra*). Here, the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is *nidarśanā* (illustration), because there is an implication of a reflection (*pratibimbākṣepa*) due to the manifestation of a playful charm resembling the playful charm of the arrows of Love.

O beloved of Īśāna, this triad of your eyes shines with its three distinct colors, appearing as if they were mixed with playful collyrium; it seems as though the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* have assumed these forms to create once again the gods Brahmā, Hari, and Rudra, who had ceased their work.
It is like a triad. || 53 ||

"Vibhaktatraivarṇyam" is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has the three colors (varṇas)—white, black, and red—distinctly divided and unmixed with one another. The suffix *ṣyañ* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*).
There are red lines in the eyes of persons of great fortune (*mahābhāgya*).

Although both eyeballs are white and the pupils are blue, he says "by means of the mingled playful collyrium" because there is an absence of blueness in the pupil of the third eye; *vyatikarita* means blended or intermingled.
By means of that state of having applied collyrium for the sake of sport and for the sake of grace— that is, by accepting the whiteness of the sphere of the third eye—
your triad of eyes shines forth, it is resplendent.
p.
140) O beloved of Īśāna— this is an address to her who is the most cherished wife of Īśāna, the Great God— these three eyes of yours that are now visible.
In order to create once again within this universe— after the previous universe had passed—
the gods endowed with divine dharma, namely Druhiṇa, Hari, and Rudra [Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara], who were withdrawn into his own self; he, the Lord, became manifest.

Bearing the dissolved *rajas* (the quality of passion), *sattva* (the quality of goodness), and *tamas* (the quality of darkness)— that is, bearing these three qualities known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— he appeared like a triad of those very qualities.

Here is the construction of the words: O beloved of Īśāna! This triad of your eyes, possessing a threefold coloration through the blending of playful collyrium, consists of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* in order to create again the gods—Brahmā, Hari, and Rudra—who have ceased [their functions].
It shines, bearing as it were the triad of qualities.

In this context, it is a well-known convention among poets that the quality of *sattva* is white in color, the quality of *rajas* is red in color, and the quality of *tamas* is blue in color. Furthermore, even when the object (*karman*) is expressed by the indeclinable particle *tama*, the case-ending for the object is not employed, because such enumerations are generally indicative rather than exhaustive.
Because they are designated by the term "nipāteti" (as particles), the words *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* may be in the nominative case;
alternatively, they may be in the accusative case, since the designation as particles is generally conventional. As it has been stated by Vāgbhaṭa:

"One should abandon through body, speech, and mind the tenfold sinful action: violence, theft, sexual misconduct, slander, lying about persons, frivolous chatter, malice, covetousness, and perversion of view. Thus it is said.

Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the triad of white, red, and blue lines present in the eyes is fancied as being the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Here, it is implied that through the mere sight of the Blessed Lady’s eye-ointment, creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe] occur.
A great excellence is suggested; thus, this is a suggestion of a fact (vastudhvani) by means of a poetic figure (alaṅkāra). || 53 ||
O Goddess whose heart is devoted to Paśupati, may you purify us with your eyes—
like friends full of compassion— which possess the luster of red, white, and dark blue, and which are like the rivers Śoṇa, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā.
O daughter of the Sun, you certainly bring this faultless confluence of the three sacred fords to this place.
This very same triad of castes is again envisioned for the sake of purification—to make those who are impure pure.

Here the suffix *cvi* is used in the sense of "becoming that which one was not," with the agent being the act of becoming (*sampadyakartari*). O you whose heart is entirely dependent on Paśupati! O you whose mind is devoted to Hara! (O you who make us so! To us, [who are thus purified].
With eyes moist with compassion and possessing reddish, white, and dark-blue lusters respectively—
this is the ellipsis for each— the river is the male stream [the flow of merit],
the Śoṇa is the Hiraṇyavāha (which is red in color), and the Gaṅgā is the Bhāgīrathī.
It is a well-known convention among poets that the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) is white in color, while the Kālindī is blue;
thus, it is certainly true that you lead us to this visible confluence, the meeting of the waters of the three sacred fords.
You accomplish that which is sinless and which removes all evil.

Here is the construction of the words: O you whose heart is subject to the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati)! By means of these three eyes—possessing the hues of dawn-red, white, and dark-blue—which are friends of compassion, [behold] this sinless confluence of the three sacred waters: the river Śoṇa, the Gaṅgā, and the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā).
"You are surely bringing us here to purify us; such is the thought, that it is due to the Goddess's affection for her devotees."

Here, the poetic figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is employed, as the three lines on the eye— naturally established and consisting of white, black, and red colors— are fancied as being the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Śoṇa rivers. || 54 ||
(142) "O daughter of the King of Mountains, the virtuous say that by your closing and opening of your eyes, the world undergoes dissolution and emergence;
this entire universe is born from the opening of your eyes."
I suspect that your eyes, which have abandoned blinking, remain so in order to protect [the world] from dissolution (*pralaya*);

for "blinking" (*nimeṣa*) is the closing of the eyelashes, while here "unblinking" (*unmeṣa*) is the opening of the eyes by the eyelashes— by these two, respectively, [the world undergoes] dissolution (*pralaya*, i.e., *saṃhāra*) and emergence (*udaya*).

"It goes forth," that is, it attains [existence]. "The world (*jagatī*) is yours," thus say, that is, they speak; the substitution of *āha* for *brū* occurs according to the rule beginning with "for the five roots, the first [is substituted]. "The virtuous" refers to holy men such as Vyāsa and others, according to the doctrine of the creation of perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*).
It should be understood that because there is no object of knowledge apart from knowledge, the statement "by means of closing and opening [the eyes]" is straightforward.
O daughter of the mountain-king, O daughter of Himācala! From your unfolding...

I suspect that this entire visible world— the whole universe— was born from the twinkling of an eyelash, and that it was created to protect and preserve itself from dissolution, that is, from the great cataclysm; for its inhabitants have abandoned blinking, having suppressed the movement of their eyes.
Your eyes are your visions.
Herein is the construction of the words: O daughter of the king who supports the earth!
The wise say that by your closing and opening of the eyes, the world undergoes dissolution and emergence.
Therefore, this entire world born from the opening of your eyes [is withdrawn] through dissolution.
I suspect that your eyes have become free of blinking in order to protect [me].
Here, the figure of speech is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). The fact that deities do not blink is established by their very nature;
however, because this is fancied as having the purpose of protecting the world—viewed as a result—it is a case of *phalotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the result).
In that regard, it is the Goddess’s [power] such that during the states of closing and opening the eyes, there occur the creation and dissolution of the world.

The fact that his greatness is beyond the reach of speech and mind is suggested as the underlying matter (vastu). Therefore, this is a case of suggestion of matter (vastudhvani) by means of a figure of speech (alaṅkāra). || 55 ||
O Aparṇā, the minnows, terrified by the backbiting malice of your ear-whisperers, surely hide within the water with unblinking eyes; and this—
The goddess Śrī abandons the blue water-lily at dawn, its petals closed like a door, and enters it at night, having opened them wide.

O Aparṇā! O Pārvatī! We are terrified by the backbiting of your eyes—that backbiting which, being ever-present near your ears (*karṇejapa*), consists of the malicious intent (*paiśunya*) or the revealing of secrets (*marmodghāṭana*) that those two eyes will perform.

Therefore, they remain hidden, trembling, meaning they stay concealed by the suppression of their outward appearance. In the water—that is, in the liquid—they are certainly (niyatam) and resolutely (niścayaḥ) without blinking (animeṣāḥ), namely the female fish (śapharikāḥ). And this visible beauty (śrīḥ) residing in the eyes is Lakṣmī herself.

"With its leaf-covers fastened as doors" means that its leaf-covers themselves are joined together like a door; the sense is that it exists like a house with its doors shut. It abandons—that is, leaves—the *kuvalaya*, the blue water-lily, at dawn (*pratyūṣe*) and during the night (*niśi*).
And at night, having opened [the door], he enters and lies down.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Aparṇā!

Terrified by the treachery of your ears and eyes acting as informers, the little fish surely hide themselves in the water without blinking; moreover, this Goddess Lakṣmī has her door-panels closed with folded lotus-buds.
The water-lily abandons it at dawn, and having parted from it at night, it enters within.

The meaning is this: in the world, it is well known that there are two things equal to the eye—namely, the *śapharikā* fish and the blue lotuses—and that the eye is equal to this pair. Here, the poet [establishes] the similarity between the two by attributing the beauty of the eye to both the *śapharikās* and the blue lotuses.
Taking this as his basis, he employs poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the two eyes, which, desiring to seize that good fortune, practice backbiting (*paiśunya*) there.

In the first half of this verse, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the fish's dwelling in the water and their state of being unblinking— which are established by their very nature— are here fancied as being otherwise. In the second half, there is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) regarding the beauty of the eyes.
Having left his eye [the sun], out of excessive devotion to the blue lotuses (*indīvara*), he dwells within their interior at night for the sake of protecting them, and by day he leaves them.
The state of being turned by the eyes is impossible because it is based on a connection where no connection exists.
For the night-blooming of the blue lotus (*indīvara*) and its closing during the day are established by its very nature;
yet, despite the lack of a connection between these two qualities and the act of being made beautiful by Lakṣmī, they are described as being so connected.

This is another instance of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). It is a combination (*anusṛṣṭi*) of both [figures]. The definition of *anusṛṣṭi* has already been stated [in the commentary on verse 47]. Here, the blooming of the blue lotus occurs at night, while the blooming of the two eyes occurs during the day; consequently, Lakṣmī [resides] in the eyes during the day.

The night-lotus dwells at night; thus, Lakṣmī moves about both day and night, and nowhere else. Among the objects in the world used as comparisons for eyes, such as the *śapharī* fish and others, none possess equality with the eyes of the Blessed Lady.
Since it is only logical that the sapharikās should be dissolved within the water, this is a case of *kāvyaliṅga-dhvani*, which constitutes an *alaṃkāra-dhvani*. || 56 ||

O Śivā, bathe even me, who am far away and miserable, with your exceedingly long glance that has the luster of a slightly opened blue lotus; by this he becomes blessed, yet there is no loss for you on your part,
for the moon sheds its rays equally whether in the forest or in a palace.

With a gaze— a sidelong glance— that was exceedingly long and possessed the luster of a slightly blossomed blue lotus (indīvara), meaning it had the beauty and radiance of a slightly opened blue water-lily; [she looked] at one who was very far away.
"Dūravartinam": by the rule *sthūladūra* etc., there is the elision of the *yaṇ* [vowel] of the word *dūra*;

when the *guṇa* substitution has been made for the preceding vowel and the *av-ādeśa* has been applied, the form *davīyān*—ending in the suffix *īyasun*—is established. "Dīnam" means poor; "snapaya" means to bathe.
Act! Out of compassion and pity—even me, as the sense of "also" (*api*) implies one who is no different from any other person.
O Śivā, whose nature is auspiciousness! By this alone—by even such a mere bathing—this person, that is, I myself, [shall be purified].
(145) One becomes fortunate and one has accomplished one's purpose; there is no loss for you, nor any destruction of wealth,
merely by this much common sight, whether in the woods, in the forest, or in a palace.
In the palace, there was an equal descent of rays; that is to say, he is so described because of the simultaneous and uniform falling—that is, the spreading—of rays (karāṇām) or beams.
The "moon" (himakaraḥ) is the one with cool rays.

Here is the word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*): O Śivā! With a gaze that is exceedingly long and possesses the luster of a slightly blossomed blue lotus, bathe even me, who am distant and wretched, with Your compassion; by this, he [who is so bathed] becomes blessed, and there is no loss for You thereby.

For indeed, whether in the forest or in a palace, the falling of moonlight is equal for all; the point is that for those whose inner hearts are pure, such universal accessibility is established by their very nature.
The figure of speech here is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), because a particular instance is supported by a general principle.

The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that since the observation of universal commonality is itself the reason for its being supreme among all things, there is no need to demonstrate its uniqueness as one's own. || 57 ||
O daughter of the king of serpents, for whom does your pair of curved locks not evoke the curiosity of the flower-arrowed god’s bow? For there,
the playful extension of your side-glances, stretching obliquely and surpassing the path of the ears, imparts its own charm.
The concentration upon the aiming of the arrow. || 58 ||

O daughter of the mountain king! O daughter of the lord of mountains! To whom does this pair of your curling, curved locks—not situated between the pair of ears and the pair of eyes—not impart the charm of the flower-arrowed god’s bow? It certainly bestows upon everyone the splendor of the God of Love’s bow.
Transverse means extended obliquely; where, in the pair of locks of hair,
having transcended the path of hearing and reaching the vicinity of the ears, the playful, quivering extension of the outer corners—
the extension (*vyāsaṅga*) meaning the length of the outer corner (*apāṅga*), that is, the sidelong glance— shines forth.
"He directs" means he performs the mental application of aiming the arrow;
"the mental application of aiming the arrow" refers to the intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) involved in joining the shaft,
that is to say, the mental state of having fixed the arrow.
p.

146) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O daughter of the king of the Aṅgas! To whom does that pair of your cheeks, resembling a pair of swans, not provide the pleasure of being the bow of the flower-arrowed god? For, since—where...
Glancing askance with a playful sidelong glance, it transcends the path of the ears and imparts the intent of fixing an arrow.
Here, there is the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (error), because it arises from the delusion that the [two] outer corners of the eyes are joined arrows.

Furthermore, the perception of the pair of ear-lobes as the bow of the Flower-Arrowed God (*kusumaśara*) is a determinate cognition preceded by doubt; thus, it is indeed the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt). These two [figures] exist in a relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
Confusion. || 58 ||
I consider this face of yours, with its pair of earrings reflected in the expanse of its quivering cheeks, to be the four-wheeled chariot of the God of Love;
mounted upon which the great hero Māra assails the Lord of the Pramathas, whose chariot is the earth and whose wheels are the sun and the moon.
In the prepared forest. || 59 ||
"Whose pair of earrings is reflected in the expanse of his quivering cheeks"—
the meaning is that those two quivering cheeks are as spotless as mirrors;
he is one in whom that pair of earrings is reflected, that is, mirrored, therein.
I consider, I suspect, this face of yours— the mouth visible within the lotus of my heart— to be a four-wheeled chariot, one possessing four wheels or rims,
the vehicle of Manmatha, the god of love.

Having mounted and occupied that chariot, he who deceives, offends, or—so to speak—pierces [his enemies]; the "earth-chariot" is a chariot whose vehicle is the earth; the "one whose feet are the sun and moon" is the Great Hero (Mahāvīra), for the sun and moon are his very feet.

By virtue of mounting his chariot with its four wheels, Māra, the god of love whose prowess is unimpeded, [prepared himself] for Tripurāntaka, the destroyer of the three cities and lord of the Pramathas, who was "sajjitavate"— that is to say, making himself ready, putting on armor, and becoming fully equipped.

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! I consider this face of yours, with its pair of earrings reflected upon the expanse of your quivering cheeks, to be the four-wheeled chariot of Manmatha; having mounted which, Māra, being a great hero, [conquers the world].
He offends the Lord of the Pramathas, who has prepared his chariot—the earth—with the sun and moon as its wheels;

[here] the fourth case is used according to the rule: "The fourth case is used for those expressing anger toward someone, in the sense of *krudh* (to be angry), *druh* (to injure), *īrṣyā* (envy), and *asūyā* (malice)."

In the first half of this verse, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the face of the Blessed Lady is fancied as being a chariot. In the second half, by stating that ascending [the chariot] brings about the state of a great hero (*mahāvīratva*), there is the figure of speech *hetu* (cause) based on the meaning of the words (*padārthahetuka*).

The poetic figure is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause). There is also *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because a connection is described between the Supreme Lord and Manmatha regarding their preparation for battle, even though no such connection exists.
There is a *saṅkara* (commixture) of *kāvyaliṅga* and *atiśayokti* through the relationship of principal and subordinate.

It should be understood that in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) serves merely as its vitalizing factor (*anuprāṇaka*), and thus there is neither *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) nor *saṅkara* (blending). That which assists by existing separately is the vitalizing factor (*anuprāṇaka*); that which acts as the motivator by not existing separately is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*). By existing separately...

The *prayojaka* (the instigator) is the subordinate element (*aṅga*). That which is distinct from this is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture); such is the secret doctrine of the Alaṅkārikas. Although this has been stated previously, it is set forth again for the sake of clarity. || 59 ||

As Śarvāṇī incessantly drinks with the ladles of her ears the streams of nectar— the skillful waves of Sarasvatī’s eloquent verses— her head sways in admiration of their wonder, and the multitude of her earrings produce sharp, resonant jingling sounds.
It is as if they are delivering a reply.

The *sūktis* (well-spoken verses) of Sarasvatī, the Goddess of Speech, are sweet words that steal away the skill and beauty of the "waves of nectar"— that is, they take away the excellence and fortune of the splashing forth of a stream of ambrosia. The word *hari* here is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* should be stated [after a word] ending in a *kṛt* suffix containing the vowel *ī*, provided it does not end in *ktin*.
Thus, [the form is] *pibantī*. O Śarvāṇī! O Consort of Śarva, the Supreme Lord!
With your ears—where *culuka* means a handful or half a *prasṛti*—and with your two ears (*śravaṇe* = *śrotre*).

"In the hollow of the palms" (*culuke*) means with those two hands in such a way as to be without any gap; that is to say, with great attentiveness. "With heads moved by the praise of the marvel" (*camatkāraślāghācalitaśirasaḥ*):
*camat* is an indeclinable used to imitate the sound of wonder.

The word *kāra* refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Alternatively, it is the wonder (*camatkāra*) consisting of the transformation of the mind arising through force (*haṭha*), produced by the blisses born from pleasure and pain.

Her mass of earrings— the collection of ear-ornaments belonging to her whose head was moving amidst a multitude of imitations of wonders and praises of marvels— [resounded] with tinkling sounds (*jhaṇatkāra*), as she produced whistling sounds and caused her body to thrill.

The word *jhaṇat* is an indeclinable imitating the sound of ornaments; the word *kāra* denotes the essential nature [of the sound]. With those *jhaṇatkāras*—shrill, exceedingly abundant, and very loud—they seemed to announce an assent, a responsive echo, or words of approval.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Śarvāṇī! This is the cluster of earrings belonging to Sarasvatī, whose head is shaken by the wonder and praise [of you], as she incessantly drinks with the two hollows of her ears your well-spoken words, which possess the skillful grace of waves of nectar.
With loud jingling sounds, it seemed as if it were giving an answer.

In this second half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the clanging sounds (*jhaṇatkāra*) are imagined as being the responses [to Sarasvatī’s words]. In the first half, there is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole),
because there is an absence of any actual connection between Sarasvatī and the shaking of her head.

Because a relation is expressed where there is no [actual] relation, based on the imposition of a relation, there is a commixture (*saṅkara*) of both through the relationship of subordinate and principal. (60)
May this bridge of your nose— the silken banner atop the lineage of the Snowy Mountain—
grant us our fitting reward,
for it bears within pearls fallen from the breath of the Moon, and by their abundance, they are visible even on the outside.
Wearing pearls and gems. || 61 ||

This visible object is not merely the bridge of the nose; "nāsā" means the nose, and "vaṃśa" refers to the bridge-bone—this is a metaphorical expression. O banner-cloth of the lineage of the Snowy Mountain!
O flag of the family of Himācala!

"May that which belongs to you—your own—bear fruit, that is, bring to completion its result, which is our desired object; this includes those related to me and myself. This is an appropriate adverbial modifier meaning 'in accordance with what is desired'."
He wears within,
inside, pearls— pearl gems— and the moon, whose rays are cool, sheds cool droplets like breath.
The moon is his exhalation, the air moving through the path of the left channel (vāmanāḍī); because of that, it has flowed forth—
that is, it has issued out— in abundance, meaning with great intensity, from those pearls even externally, that is, even in the external region on the left side of the tip of the nose.
The bamboo staff, fashioned from a nose [of an elephant], bore a pearl; it held a pearl. "muktāmaṇim adhāt" is the correct reading.

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O you who are the banner-cloth for the lineage of the Snowy Mountain! May this nasal bridge of yours, which belongs to you, bear fruit for us—a fruit that is appropriate and very near.
It bears pearls within; for by reason of their abundance [it is so].
And he wears pearl gems outside as well, which have fallen from his breath like the rays of the cool-rayed moon.
Here, because the nose is superimposed upon the quality of being a bamboo flute (*vaṃśa*), there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

The second half of the verse establishes and explains this quality of being a bamboo flute. It is the established convention of worldly science that pearls arise from within a bamboo flute; therefore—
Pearls are produced even within the bridge of the nose;
for otherwise, how could the possession of pearl-jewels on the exterior of the nasal bridge be accounted for?
Thus, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the shape of the nose is established as being like that of a bamboo stalk.
The metaphorical representation alone is correct. || 61 ||

O lady with beautiful teeth, I shall describe the resemblance of the natural redness of your lip; let the coral creeper bear fruit [of this comparison]. But how could that *bimba* fruit, reddened only by the reflection of its own image, ever ascend to the scales of equality?
One should be ashamed even by a fraction [of a fault]. || 62 ||
O lady with beautiful teeth, [I shall speak] to you, whose teeth are naturally and inherently slightly reddish-copper;
I shall describe in detail the excellence of the luster— the beauty— of your lips, which are the covers for your teeth.
Let him speak. Let similarity—the state of being similar—be produced, that is, let it be generated.

The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of expectation (*āśaṃsā*). If there were a fruit of coral, then there would be the existence of a truly similar object; however, coral alone is not what is similar. "Fruit" refers to a ripe fruit—a fruit produced from yellow-colored creepers—which is something superior.
The intended meaning is that it is precisely similar to this: what need is there to mention the redness of one produced from a red creeper?
"Vidrumalatā" means a coral creeper. It is not the *bimba* fruit itself, but rather due to the redness of its reflection, that [redness] belongs to those two lips (*dantacchada*) of the *bimba*.

Reflection is the act of mirroring; from that comes redness (*raktimā*), and because of that, it is conventionally designated as a "reflected fruit" (*bimbaphala*). This designation is obtained through the grace of the reflection of the lower lip as a reflected image;
otherwise, its conventional status as a "reflected fruit" would not exist, just as in the case of a crystal and similar objects.

Just as the redness of crystals and other substances arises solely through the power of the reflection of a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) and so forth, so too is it with the reflected fruit. Because of the coloring from the reflection of that [fruit],
how could it possibly ascend onto the scale to remain in a state of equilibrium within the discourse on equality?
The word *iti* is used as a rhetorical ornament; *vilañjeta* means one would feel shame, even by a mere fraction or trace.

Herein is the construction of the words: O lady with beautiful teeth! I shall describe the resemblance to the luster of your naturally reddish lips. Let the coral creeper produce its fruit; but as for the *bimba* fruit, it is only reddened by the reflection of the glow from that [lip].
How could one not feel ashamed to ascend even a fraction of the scales?
For the verbal root *lajj* (to be ashamed) is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is a conceptualization based on the expression of the word "if" (*yadyartha*). In the second half [of the verse],
there is *atiśayokti* based on the relation of what is not related (*asaṃbandhe saṃbandhanibandhana*),
because it expresses non-difference by describing a relation even where there is no relation between the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbanāsaṃbandhe*).
The combination of both. || 62 ||

As the cakora birds drink the mass of moonlight from the moon of your smiling face, their beaks become numbed by its excessive sweetness; therefore, at night, they drink the nectar-waves of the cool-rayed moon according to their own will, as their desire for sourness has been satisfied.
At night, [he ate] excessively with the thought that it was sour gruel. || 63 ||
p.
151) A mass of moonlight from your smile: the smile itself is the moonlight, and its mass is its canopy;
of your moon-like face—the face itself being the moon—for those who drink [from it].
As the *cakora* birds— a particular species of bird— tasted [the moonlight], their beaks became numbed and their tongues dulled due to its extreme essence and excessive sweetness; for this reason,
those *cakoras* [could not perceive] the wave of nectar from the cool-rayed moon, the *amṛta*.
"Sprinkling" (utseka) means the nectar of moonlight. "Those with a craving for sourness" (āmlarucayaḥ) refers to those who have a desire or longing for the sour taste;
they drink—that is, consume—according to their own will, as they please, night after night, during the moonlit nights (the word "jyotsnāsu" being understood).
Exceedingly, that is, to a great degree, with the notion of *kāñjika*, that is, through the delusion of it being *āranāla*.

Here is the word-connection (*padayojanā*): O Blessed Lady! For the *cakora* birds drinking the mass of moonlight from the smile upon your moon-like face, their beaks became numbed by its excessive sweetness;
therefore, having a craving for sourness, they mistook the wave of nectar from the cool-rayed moon for fermented gruel (*kāñjika*).
They drink deeply at will night after night.
Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole),
because there is a statement of a connection— namely, the drinking of moonlight— where no such connection exists,

based on the numbness of the tongue caused by the drinking of exceedingly sweet mother’s milk; [the moonbeams are described] as being thirsty for sourness due to that numbness of the tongue resulting from the habit of drinking very sweet breast-milk.

Because children perceive [the two] as non-different. O Mother, victorious is that tongue of yours, which is like the hue of a hibiscus flower, incessantly chanting the repetitive recitation of the multitude of your Lord’s qualities; for when it sits upon its tip, it possesses the clear luster of a crystal stone.
The form of Sarasvatī transforms into a body of ruby. || 64 ||

Without rest and without ceasing, the multitude— that is, the collection— of the rosary-strings of the recitations (*japa*) concerning the repeated accounts of the Lord Sadāśiva’s qualities, such as his victory over Tripura and other deeds; the *kathā* is the narrative, and its *āmreḍana* is the repetition thereof.
The repetition twice or thrice of that very [mantra] constitutes her *japa*; the meaning is that she is one whose mind is not directed elsewhere.
"Japā-puṣpa-chāyā" means like the luster of the *japā* flower—that is, the *raktapuṣpī* flower.
She whose luster is her radiance—O Mother! O Janani! Your tongue, the organ of taste, triumphs; it shines forth. That pronoun "she" (sā) refers to the renown that is about to be described.
[It is the tongue] at the tip of which, while seated,
Of her who was seated—that is, sitting—the body was abundant with a luster as clear as that of a crystal stone;
[the suffix] *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). The meaning is that it was white like crystal.
The form— that is, the essential nature— of Sarasvatī, the goddess of eloquence, undergoes transformation,
meaning it attains a modification or reaches another state; [this occurs] by means of a body of ruby, that is, a body of *padmarāga* gemstone.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Mother! Victorious is that tongue of yours, which, having the luster of a *japā* flower, incessantly performs the recitation (*japa*) of the repeated narration of the multitude of virtues of your husband;
for it is made of the very same translucent brilliance as the crystal stone upon which Sarasvatī sits.

The form transforms into the nature of ruby; it is not merely redness on the tongue, but possesses the power of redness even in coloring those who stand as bystanders. For this very reason, the word "conquers" (jayati) is employed.
This is the figure of speech known as *tadguṇa*, according to its definition:

"The taking on of another's superior quality through the abandonment of one's own quality. It is a secret of the scriptures that the goddess Sarasvatī always dwells within the lotus-face of the Queen in her own form.
In battle, having conquered the Daityas, the warriors— wearing helmets and armor,
returning from the fray, and turning away from the discarded floral offerings of the Sun, Śiva, and Viṣṇu— cause fragments of camphor as white as the moon to melt away.
O Mother, [these are] the morsels of betel from your mouth.
Having conquered them in battle— that is, having defeated the Daityas in war— with those by whom the head-wraps (śiroveṣṭana) had been stripped away.
It is the established custom that after completing their master’s business, when it is time for servants to bow before the king,
they must remove their turbans, head-covers, and so forth, and then perform the prostration. This is the traditional rule.

Relying on the sequence [of the text], he says: "by those whose helmets had been snatched away. By those wearing armor (*kavacin*), that is, those equipped with mail; by those who had turned back, that is, those who had desisted from battle;
and by those averse to the *nirmālya* (wreaths) of the fierce-rayed one (*caṇḍāṃśu*), the fierce-rayed one being the fierce sun.
The *pramatha* named Caṇḍa is his portion; that very thing is the *nirmālya* of the Destroyer of Tripura—the perfumes, betel, and so forth remaining after [the Lord] has accepted them.
Regarding this, there are Smṛti texts such as: "The *nirmālya* of Hara must be discarded," and others, [which apply] to those who have turned away from that [practice].
It should be understood that they are intent on prohibiting the use of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of the Sun, Śiva, and Viṣṇu; this is what they teach. They teach:
by Viśākha, Indra, and Upendra—Viśākha being the commander-in-chief, for whom alone there is preeminence in battles, he is thus reckoned as foremost.

Indra, Mahendra, Upendra, and Viṣṇu—by them [are meant those whose] pieces of camphor are as white as the moon; that is, they possess fragments of *ghanasāra* (camphor) as bright as the moon. They dissolve; that is, they are caused to melt away.
O Mother! O Janani! These morsels of betel from your mouth—those morsels of betel issued from your mouth.

Here the construction of the words is as follows: O Mother! by Viśākha, Indra, and Upendra—who, having conquered the Daityas in battle, returned with their helmets removed and their armor on, yet turned away from the discarded floral offerings of Caṇḍāṃśu and Tripurāntaka—[you were worshipped].
The fragments of camphor, pure as the moon, from the betel-chewings of Your mouth dissolve away;
this is the meaning: Viśākha, Indra, and Upendra, having slain the Daityas and placing Kumāra at their head, have arrived to worship Your feet and removed their helmets.
They did not perform the ritual salutation by grasping his feet. Immediately thereafter, the gracious Goddess offered them morsels of betel that she had already tasted slightly.
They ate them until the pieces of camphor within them had completely dissolved, as she said:
Such grace belongs only to the Blessed Lady Kumārasvāminī; the intention is that even among Indra and the other gods, it is only occasional. (65) p.
154) While you were beginning to sing with the lute the various heroic deeds of Paśupati—
When he moves his head to speak words of praise,
the Goddess Vāṇī silently covers her own lute with her garment (cola),
its sweet tones having eclipsed the melodious sound of its strings. (66) [With the lute.]
Singing— that is, performing songs— of various kinds,

she recounted the heroic deeds (*apadāna*) of Paśupati, the Lord, such as his victory over Tripura, the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the swallowing of Hālāhala poison, the slaying of Jalandhara, and the killing of Gajasura.
When you, Madam, had begun— that is, commenced— to speak or utter [the words],
with your head moving due to the influence of inner joy, you yourself nodded your head while [uttering] words of praise and sweet speech related to his [words].

With her sweetness—that is, the quality of sweetness—she [Bhāratī] causes her own lute, the *vipañcī*, to drown out its own sweet-toned strings; that is, she causes it to be eclipsed or mocked by the sweetness of her voice.
Her own sweet-toned strings are eclipsed or ridiculed by that [sweetness]. She thus mutes her own lute, the *vipañcī*. It is Bhāratī who does so.
He makes it *niculavatī*. *Nicula* is a bodice (*kūrpāsa*).

A *cola* is a specific type of bodice, a *vīṇākūrpāsa*. There is no tautology in the statement "he makes it *niculavatī* by means of a *cola*," because of the relationship between the general and the particular. However, some who follow the doctrine of Bhoja...
They say that the root *cul* signifies concealment; it means to cover or hide thoroughly. [The word *nibhṛtam*] means in a manner that is quiet and secret.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Blessed One! while you were beginning to speak words of praise with your head moved as you sang forth, unfolding the various heroic deeds (*apadāna*) of Paśupati, your own sweet voice surpassed the melodious sound of the lute strings.
The lute is covered by the garment of the Goddess of Speech.
Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because it describes a connection between the lute and its case despite the absence of such a connection.
For when a defeated lute-player covers his own lute with his upper garment, it is because of the perception of an identification [of the two] with that garment. || 66 ||

Touched by the tip of the hand of the Snow-Mountain out of affection, and repeatedly raised by the Lord of Mountains out of eagerness to drink from your lower lip— O Daughter of the Mountain, how can we describe your chin, which is within reach of Śambhu’s hand, circular as a mirror for his face, and utterly peerless?

Touched and rubbed by the tip of the hand—that is, by the foremost hand—with the Snowy Mountain, the Himādri, his father; for *vātsalya* refers to the affection that fathers and others feel toward their children and so forth. As it has been said:

By Sarvajña Someśvara, there is affection (*vātsalya*) toward sons and the like, love (*prema*) toward wives and the like, favor (*anugraha*) toward disciples and the like, and devotion (*bhakti*) toward elder brothers and the like. Here, by the word "and the like" (*ādi*),
secondary sons, secondary wives, secondary disciples, and secondary elder brothers are included.

A secondary son (*gauṇaputra*) is one for whom a relationship of sonship has been conceptually established, but not one who is purchased or otherwise acquired, because such a person lacks the status of a true son. A secondary wife (*gauṇapatnī*) is a female servant (*bhujiṣyā*). A secondary disciple (*gauṇaśiṣya*) is precisely one for whom a relationship of discipleship has been conceptually established, and not merely one who has accepted the [Vedic] mantras after being formally initiated.

The "elder brother by adoption" (gauṇāgraja) is one whose relationship is merely nominal, not one such as a *kṣetraja* son. He was repeatedly raised up (*udastam*) by Girīśa Śambhu; that is, lifted up excessively due to the agitation of drinking from his lower lip, meaning out of intense love. [He was] graspable by the hand (*karagrāhyam*), [held] by the hand.

O Daughter of the Mountain, O Himādritanayā! How could Śambhu possibly grasp that very face—which, being preoccupied with looking at and kissing [your] face, serves as the handle for the mirror of his own countenance? (For the face itself is the mirror, and its "handle" is the staff upon which it rests.)

How do we say it? We describe it thus: by the rule *vibhāṣā katham i liṅ ca*, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of deliberation (*saṃpradhāraṇā*). Your chin, O Lady, is below the lower lip; it is without comparison (*aupamyarahitam*), meaning devoid of any likeness. This is the absence of comparison.

However, due to the lack of the extraordinary beauty produced by Śambhu’s caressing with his hand— the snow-mountain rock— of such things as the lotus pericarp, a mirror, a stalk, or the summit of Mount Udaya, there is no comparison for the Blessed Lady’s chin.
p.

156) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain! [Your hand] was touched by the Lord of the Mountains with the tip of his hand out of affection; it was repeatedly raised by Giriśa out of agitation caused by his desire to drink from your lower lip.
