How can we describe your chin, which is fit to be grasped by the hand of Śambhu, which is beyond all comparison, and which serves as the handle for the mirror of your face?

Here, the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison) is suggested; for by the negation of all other comparisons, the realization of the *ananvaya* figure arises from the fact that "itself is the likeness of itself. || 67 ||
From the constant embrace of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), your neck, bristling with horripilation,
bears the beauty of a lotus-stalk for his lotus-face; naturally white yet darkened by the thick mud of black aloe-ointment, it beneath it possesses the grace of a lotus-fiber.
Hāralatikā || 68 ||
From the constant embrace of the arms— that is, from being perpetually embraced by the arms—
of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), your neck, bristling with horripilation like thorns,
bears the beauty of the stalk of his lotus-face; for his face itself is indeed a lotus.
The beauty of the stalk and the splendor of the stem—this neck is naturally white and inherently translucent; yet it is soiled by the thick mud of black aloe-wood (*kālāguru*).
"Kāla" means dark blue in color, and "agaru" refers to light wood; thus, the meaning is *kṛṣṇāguru* (black aloe-wood). Of that...
It bears— that is, it attains— the loveliness of a lotus stalk (*mṛṇālī*), which is soiled and darkened by the abundant and thick mud;
for this reason, there is a pearl necklace (*hāralatikā*) below, in the lower region.

Here is the construction of the words: O Blessed Lady! This neck of yours, from its constant embrace by the arms of the Subduer of Cities (Śiva), bears the beauty of the stalk of your lotus-face as if it were thorny;
for beneath it, the pearl necklace—which is naturally white—has become darkened by the thick mud of black aloe-wood paste.
It possesses the graceful charm of a lotus stalk.

In the first half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), because in the phrase "the beauty of the lotus-stalk of the face," a beauty similar to [the original] beauty is suggested through the projection of a reflection. There is also the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor), because in the phrase "the lotus-face," the face is metaphorically represented as having the nature of a lotus.
p.

157) There is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of these two through the relationship of subordinate and principal; furthermore, in the second half-verse, there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* in the phrase "the grace of the lotus-stalk."
"The grace is like the grace [of the beloved]"—this is due to the implication of a reflection;
there is a commingling (saṅkara) of both through the relationship of subordinate and principal. || 68 ||

Upon her neck, which is uniquely skilled in the melodies of the *gatīs* and *gamakas*, shine three lines that serve as guarantors for the number of excellent qualities bound together in marriage; they belong to the three *grāmas*, which are the source-lands of various kinds of sweet musical scales (*rāgas*).
They were like the very boundaries that define the limits of stability.
In the throat, at the region of the neck, there are three lines in the form of folds known as the lines of fortune;
both for women and men, this triad of folds on the forehead, the neck, and the middle [of the chest] should be known as indicative of great good fortune.

Thus ends the section on *sāmudrika* (physiognomy). O you who are uniquely skilled in *gati*, *gamaka*, and *gīta*! *Gati* refers to the movement of music; there are two types of *gati* in music: *mārga* (classical) and *deśī* (regional). *Gamaka* is the modulation of a note; it is the trembling of a note, and that is remembered as being of five kinds.

Thus it is stated in the *Bharata*. Furthermore, those [elements] are to be understood as being of five kinds in that very same work: "Song (*gīta*) is of two types, consisting of *dhātu* and *mātrā*.
That which consists of speech alone is called *geya*, while that which consists of *dhātu* is designated as *dhātu*. Thus [it is said].

In that context, "ekā" means she who is both preeminent and skillful; this is her address. Regarding the phrase "guarantors for the enumeration of the straight and excellent qualities bound at the wedding": at the time of the wedding (*udvāha-samaya*), they were specifically bound (*vyānaddhāḥ*) following the tying of the auspicious thread (*maṅgala-sūtra*).
In its vicinity, all around the neck,
excellent cords— threads composed of many strands— are bound and fastened. There are exactly three of them,
as stated by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras:
"Having tied this auspicious thread as a *maṅgalasūtra*, one should tie a single-strand thread on the left hand and likewise a triple-strand thread around the neck.

Furthermore, this practice is established according to region; for this very reason, in some regions there is the binding of the auspicious thread (*maṅgalasūtra*), in some regions the binding of the triple cord (*saratraya*), and in some regions neither exists. His opinion, however, is that it exists everywhere. Or else:
It should be understood that both of these practices indeed exist in the country of the author of this work.
The number of excellent qualities is three;
its guarantor is likewise the guarantor who informs the creditor of the debtor [and thus of the number].

It has been stated that they "make known" (jñāpayati) because they are pledges (pratibhuvaḥ). They make known to the observers that "at this spot, Śambhu previously bound the triple-strand [of the river] upon our necks at the time of the Blessed Lady’s wedding," thereby making known their number.
The meaning is "the three folds. They shine forth most brilliantly;
they are the source-lands of various kinds of sweet passions—that is, the mines or origins of various (aneka-prakāra) and manifold (madhura) and charming (manorama) passions.
The locations of the vowels are their support.
The meaning is as follows: there are five *gītayas* (or *gatayas*); thirty *grāmarāgas* arising from them; eight *uparāgas*; twenty *rāgas* which are *janakarāgas*;
fifteen *bhāṣārāgas*; and ninety-six *vibhāṣārāgas*.

The twenty intermediate languages (*antarabhāṣā*) and the three [principal ones], and so forth, which are expounded in the *Rāgādhyāya*, should be understood here. And those *rāgas* are well-known, such as Madhyamāvatī, Mālavī, Śrībhairavī, Vaṅgālī, Vasantā, Dhanyāsī, Deśyā, and others.
The *rāgāṅga* consists of one [type].
The *bhāṣāṅga* includes the *velāvatī*, *śuddhavarālī*, *puṇnāgavarālī*, *nāṭya*, and so forth.
The *kriyāṅga* includes the *rāmakriyā* and so forth. [Also] the *pravīdhī* [or *draviḍī*].

It has been stated that the *upāṅgas* (subsidiary forms), such as *ghūrjarī*, *varālī*, and *malaharī*, as well as the *uparāgas*, are included under the term "rāga" in the phrase "the source-land of various kinds of sweet rāgas. This refers to the three *grāmas*.
The word *grāma* denotes a collection. All notes (*svaras*) are grouped into three:
the *ṣaḍjagrāma*, the *madhyamagrāma*, and the *gāndhāragrāma*; thus, the collection of notes is threefold. Among these, only two *grāmas* prevail in the world of mortals (*bhūloka*).

The seven notes (*svara*) possess the quality of being the basis for melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) through the sequence of ascent and descent; and that [quality] occurs in three ways, according to the states of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*). Because the *gāndhāra* scale (*grāma*) has its locus in the *śara* [note], it is impossible for it to begin with the low register; therefore, the *gāndhāra* scale...
It has spread throughout the world of the gods. As stated by Śārṅgadeva (p.
"A *grāma* is a collection of notes (*svara*); it is the common substratum for the *mūrchanās* and so forth. These two [types of *grāma*]..."
On this earth, there are two: the Ṣaḍja-grāma and likewise the Ādima (or Tadādima).

The second is the Madhyama-grāma; their characteristics are now stated: "The ascent and descent of the seven notes in sequence is called a mūrcchanā; there are seven such [mūrcchanās] in each of the two grāmas. Thus it is said.

These *mūrchanās* are called *śuddhatānas*. Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of the three *grāmas* in the description of the three folds on the neck of the Blessed Lady is appropriate because of its connection with the conventions of the divine realm (*devaloka*). Of those *grāmas*:

The boundaries for the regulation of stability— the limits established at the edges of those villages to ensure that their fixed positions do not become intermingled with one another— are like embankments for you.

Here is the word-by-word construction: O Blessed One! O Thou uniquely skilled in singing the paths and the means of progression! On Thy neck, the three lines are the guarantors for the number of the straight strings bound during the marriage ceremony;
they are the witnesses to the three scales (*grāmas*), which are the source-lands of various kinds of sweet melodies (*rāgas*).
They shine forth like the very boundaries that define the limits of stability.

In the first half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference), because the presence of the three lines serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of the three auspicious arrows. The fact that *anumāna* possesses the nature of a poetic charm (*vicchitti*) arises precisely from its distinction from worldly (non-poetic) inference. And this distinction is as follows:

The secret is this: if there were only the property of being a subject (pakṣadharmatā) without the absence of pervasion (vyāptyabhāva), even when both are present, it would be merely worldly. "Vicchitti" refers to extraordinary beauty. In the second half [of the verse], there is the poetic figure of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the Blessed Lady.
This is because the three folds [of the neck] are conceived as the marks that serve as the cause for the three scales (*svaragrāma*) situated within the throat. || 69 ||
The lotus-born Brahmā praises with his four faces the beauty of your four creeper-like arms, which are as soft as lotus stalks; he does so while trembling at your nails,
fearing them to be the first churning-sticks used by the enemy of Andhaka against his four heads.

With the intention of extending the hand of fearlessness equally [to all], [there is] the lotus-fiber (mṛṇālī), a stalk of lotus-root; likewise, for the lotus-fibers that are soft (*mṛdvīnām*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *vā* or *ṅīp* follows words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanāt*). Of your, O Lady, creeper-like arms (*bhujalatānām*).
The lotus-born Brahmā praises and extols their fourfold beauty and good fortune with his four faces; yet, trembling and fearing from their nails— that is, from their fingernails—
he becomes a cause of fear for those who seek safety.
Thus, the fifth case (pañcamī) is used in the sense of the ablative (apādāna). [The word *mathitavat*] refers to one who has previously crushed [the substance] before its first churning;
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). As the author of the Vṛtti stated regarding the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*:
"that which has expressed a quality (*guṇa*) is 'quality-expressive' (*guṇavacana*)."

"Hara severed the fifth head of Brahmā with the tip of his fingernail"— so it is said in the Purāṇas. Therefore, from that first churning, the four heads of Sadāśiva, the enemy of Andhaka, [were severed] simultaneously and all at once.
"With the intent of offering the hand of fearlessness" means desiring to take hold of hands that grant fearlessness.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed One! the beauty of your four creeper-like arms, soft as lotus stalks, was first fashioned by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] from the nails of Andhakaripu [Śiva], who had been churned by his four faces.
Trembling, he praises [the deity] with the thought of offering his hands in fearlessness to all four heads simultaneously.

The poetic figure is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), because the praise restricted solely to Brahmā is supported by such statements as "trembling from [her] nails" and so forth. It should be understood that this is a *kāvyaliṅga* based on the meaning of the entire sentence (*vākyārthahetuka*). Furthermore, regarding the description of the vine-like arms, Brahmā alone possesses the authority [to offer such praise].
By the poetic figure (kāvyaliṅga) "not others," a fact (vastu) is suggested; thus, this is a case of suggestion of a fact by means of a poetic figure (alaṅkāreṇa vastudhvaniḥ). || 70 ||

O Umā, tell me, how can we describe the beauty of your hands, which mock the hue of a fresh lotus with the radiance of their nails? Alas, perhaps the lotus may attain some slight resemblance to them if it were stained with the red lac-dye from the soles of the feet of Lakṣmī as she sports.
Of the hands, which, by the splendors— the masses of radiance— of their nails and claws, mock and surpass the hue of a fresh lotus, that is, the beauty of a morning-blown water-lily.

Describe, tell us—how, in what manner, O Umā! O Pārvatī! or by what means? The word *vā* here expresses uncertainty, yet it is used in a statement of certainty. By some [means]... we shall compose a poetic work. Tell us, speak of the splendor and beauty of your hands.
How [shall we describe it]? By what method? O Umā! O Pārvatī! Or by some other way? The particle *vā* indicates doubt where there is no doubt; that is, by some [unfathomable] means.

The meaning is that it does not exist in any manner whatsoever. Let it possess—that is, accept—similarity, which is likeness, even by a "kalā," meaning even by a slight fraction; alas! (the word *hanta* is used here at the beginning of a sentence—in the sense of joy, compassion, the commencement of a speech, or dejection).
Thus says Amara. "Kamalam" means a lotus; even if there is doubt, the meaning remains "doubt" (sandeha).

It is "crimsoned by the lac-dye from the soles of the feet of Lakṣmī while she plays," meaning it is stained by the lac-dye on the soles of the feet of Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, as she sports.
The word *vitta* is appropriate; by that [rule], namely *vittaścuñcupcaṇapau*, the suffix *caṇap* is applied.

Herein is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Umā! How shall we describe the splendor of your hands, which mock the hue of the fresh lotus with the radiance of their nails? Tell us, let the lotus attain even a fraction of similarity with some [other object]. Alas, the lotus—
If it is [already] stained by the lac-dye from the soles of the feet of Lakṣmī as she sports, then let it indeed attain equality;
or else, according to the reading "vidhayā," let the lotus attain equality with something by some means. Alas! Let it then attain—reach—equality with something by some means.

This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). He explains that very same mode [of connection]: "If [it is] stained by the lac-dye from the soles of the feet of Lakṣmī while she plays, then it is not otherwise"—thus the syntactical connection is established as a single sentence.
Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because an exaggeration is conceived through the expression of the word "if" (*yady*).

In the first half-verse, the figure is *tadguṇa* (the quality of one thing being transferred to another), because the hands are exceedingly red due to the luster of the [jeweled] nails. In the phrase "mocking the color of the fresh lotuses," the figure is *upamā* (simile).
The conjunction of both occurs because they function as motivators by not existing separately; thus, there is a conjunction of both. || 71 ||
O Goddess, may this pair of breasts of yours, which are symmetrical, drunk from by the elephant-faced Skanda, and with nipples constantly streaming, remove our distress.
Upon seeing this, Heramba, his heart agitated by apprehension and causing laughter, suddenly feels his own two jars with his hand.
O Goddess! O Blessed One! Simultaneously, at the same time, the pair of breasts—the two nipples—of yours, the venerable lady, were drunk by Skanda, the youth, and Dvipavadana, Vināyaka;
this [act] of ours causes us distress and affliction.
May she remove [my fear]. Constantly, at all times, having looked again and again upon that pair of breasts whose faces were streaming with milk, my heart was agitated by apprehension—
an apprehension that she had stolen my two jars.

The meaning is that their hearts and minds were agitated, overwhelmed, and extremely distracted; such was the state of the parents (and the prince) that they laughed out of affection, thinking, "This one is a fool.
[He struck] his own two frontal globes at the temples.
Heramba, Vināyaka, touches—that is, he feels with his hand to see whether it exists or not; "jhaḍati" means quickly.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Goddess! May this pair of breasts of yours, drunk by the elephant-faced Skanda, with its surface streaming with milk, constantly remove our distress—that which, upon seeing, Heramba, his heart agitated by apprehension, became a source of laughter for us with his hand.
Suddenly, he touches his two jars.

From the fact that her two sons were Vināyaka and Kumārasvāmin, whose feet are worshipped by the world, the supreme majesty of the Goddess is clearly perceived. Furthermore, there is even a hyperbolic figure of speech (*atiśayokti*) suggesting that if there were any comparison between the Goddess’s jar-like breasts and anything else, it would be only with the jars used for Vināyaka.

It is understood that by the phrase "the leader (Vināyaka) touches with his hand," the breasts of the goddess—which are equal to the frontal globes (kumbha) of Vināyaka—are also suggested through the figure of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison).

Thus, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of the various types of suggestion (*dhvani*)—namely, those of fact (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and so forth—through their entry into a single suggester (*ekavyañjaka*). || 72 ||
O banner of the Lord of Mountains, these two breasts of yours are undoubtedly two ruby jars filled with the essence of nectar; there is not even a flicker of doubt in our minds.

For even now those two youths, who drink [the nectar] while remaining unaware of the pleasures of union with their wives, continue to crush the elephants of the quarters and the peaks of Mount Kauñca.
These two breasts of yours that are visible here are ruby jars of nectar-essence—
the meaning being that they are ruby jars filled with the essence of nectar. Although the word *kutupa*— [the remainder of the sentence would follow].
The word "pātrī" denotes a vessel resembling a pot that serves as a receptacle for oil and other liquids made from leather;
nevertheless, because such a vessel lacks the capacity to convey the likeness of the Blessed Lady’s breasts, the two "kutupa" vessels are accepted as being fashioned from rubies for that purpose. No.

The "tremor of doubt" (sandehaspanda) means the mere flickering of doubt; O Banner of the Lord of Mountains! because those two princes, while still children, drank from those two jeweled jars in our minds—jars which remained unaware of the pleasure of union with a bride.

Even now, even at this present time, even at the time of composing these verses, [there remain] the Elephant-faced One and the Splitter of Krauñca— the Elephant-faced One being Vināyaka, and the Splitter of Krauñca being Kumārasvāmin, who pierced the Krauñca mountain.
Here the construction of the words is as follows: O banner of the Lord of Mountains!

These two breasts of yours are caskets of ruby filled with the essence of nectar; in this matter, there is no flicker of doubt in our minds, because they drink [from them] without having known the pleasure of union with a wife.
Even today, you two remain as Kumāras, the crushers of the elephant-faced [Gajāsura] and the crane [Krauñca].

Here, the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), based on the meaning of the sentence, is indeed evident. In the preceding quarter-verse, there is the figure *rūpaka* (metaphor), because of the superimposition of the two breasts upon the nature of *kutupa* (leather water-bags). Alternatively, there is *niścayāntasandeha* (doubt ending in certainty), as there is a doubt: "Are these two breasts, or are they *kutupa*s?"
The certainty is that they are indeed water-jars, because the childhood of the two boys resulted from drinking nectar;
there is no rule that the state of childhood lasts merely from drinking breast milk,
since after childhood, youth and so forth are experienced [or rather, are to be experienced].
Since Vināyaka and Kumāra remain eternally in a state of childhood solely due to the power of drinking the nectar of immortality,

the second half of the subject matter— which serves as the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for dispelling doubts regarding the jar of nectar-essence— is well-stated as "doubt ending in certainty."
Maṅkhuka [holds that] there is no inexpressibility regarding the two alternatives imagined by the poet. (73)
O Mother, the expanse of your breasts bears a pure necklace of pearls fashioned from the frontal globes of elephants and demons,
variegated within by the luster of your bimba-like lips— like a garland intermingled with the heat of your majesty.
Like the fame of the subduer of cities (Indra). || 74 ||

It carries and bears [the pearls]. O Mother! O Mother! By those whose very nature (prakṛti) is the frontal globes (kumbha-sthala) of the demon Stamberama—that is, Gajāsura—pearls arise from the frontal globes of elephants. (For the frontal globes of elephants are their source of origin.)

As stated by Sarvajña Someśvara: "The production of pearls occurs in six ways: in the frontal globes of elephants, in bamboo, on hoods [of serpents], in clouds, in oyster shells, and in sugarcane stalks. [In the case of] the elephant's frontal globes...

Those in the bamboo lineage are known to have a variegated luster, red and white; those on the hoods of Vāsuki are proclaimed to be blue in color. Those with the luster of light are found in clouds, while those in oyster shells are known to be white;
pearls from sugarcane stalks are yellow in color.
Thus it is said.

The meaning is that pearl-ornaments having the shape of an elephant’s frontal globe (*gajakumbha*) are variegated in color, whereas those having the shape of the frontal globe of the elephant-demon (*gajāsurakumbha*) are especially so. [The story] has begun...
The expanse of her breasts— the region between them— [bears] a pure necklace of pearls, inlaid with gems and free from defects such as flaws,
yet not white [in the sense of being colorless], for those originating from elephant frontal globes are variegated;
[this necklace] is a string of pearls possessing the luster of her bimba-like lips.
"Bimbādhara" means a lower lip having the form of a *bimba* fruit; it is grammatically correct according to the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva*.
[The phrase "having the interior variegated"] means variegated—that is, possessing diverse colors—by the lusters of the *bimbādhara*, like the luster of a *bimba* fruit.
(165) *Citraka*, *kimmīra*, *kalmāṣa*, *śabala*, and *etā* denote variegated colors;
thus says Amara. It was like a string of pearl necklaces mingled with the luster of lower lips.
That which shines is a "bhāva" (an entity or state). It is as if it were the fame of the subduer of cities, the destroyer of Tripura, intermingled with his majesty;
for it is a well-known convention among great poets that majesty is red in color, while fame is white. Precisely for this reason, of this poet—
The gems produced from the frontal globes of elephants are pale-red (pāṭala) in color, not variegated; therefore,
it should be understood that even the statement "internally variegated" is intended to refer to the pale-red color.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Mother! Your expansive breasts possess a stainless necklace composed of pearls whose nature is like the frontal globes of elephants and demons, which is variegated within by the luster of your bimba-red lips.
It bears a fame, as it were, of the subduer of cities (Śiva), mingled with his majesty.
Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there is an imaginative attribution (*saṃbhāvanā*) of the pearl necklace to being fame mingled with majesty. Furthermore,
in the phrase "by the luster of the bimba-fruit lips," there is *utprekṣā*, as it suggests that [the necklace] is as if mingled with the luster of bimba-fruit lips, which are naturally red in color.

Because of the imaginative conception of the cause (*hetu*). The relationship between the two is one of the sustained and the sustainer (*anuprāṇyānuprāṇaka-bhāva*), since they function as mutual supports by virtue of not existing separately. || 74 ||

O Daughter of the Mountain, I believe that from your heart flows an ocean of milk like the Sarasvatī; for the Draviḷa child, having tasted what was given by you, the compassionate one, became a lovely poet among mature poets. (75)
I consider, I know, your breast-born milk, O daughter of the Mountain-Bearer! [O daughter of the Snowy Mountain! From your heart, it is an ocean of milk;
or rather, a torrential downpour of nectar.
The text reads: A downpour of streams of nectar, a flow of ambrosia, carries forth that which is like the Sarasvatī itself—consisting of Sarasvatī. (p.

Because of the white color of the milk, it is poetically imagined as being composed of Sarasvatī; and because of its sweetness, it is imagined as having the nature of nectar. The Dravida infant—the child born of the Dravida caste—was given this milk by the compassionate one, who is endowed with praiseworthy mercy.

The composer of this hymn, having tasted and drunk [it], for that reason was born—meaning he became—desirable and exceedingly beautiful among the poets, that is, among the lords of poets who are mature and bold;
the genitive case here is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). He was born as one who is lovely and most charming.
The poet is the one who composes poetry.

Herein is the construction of the words: O Daughter of the Mountain! I believe that the ocean of milk, which has arisen from your heart as a downpour of streams of nectar, flows forth like the Sarasvatī;
for it was given by you, who are full of compassion. Your...

Having tasted mother’s milk as a child from Draviḷa, he became a beloved poet among mature poets. Two poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*) regarding this have been explained during the commentary on the verse; both of them—
Commixture. || 75 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, the Mind-born (Cupid) took refuge in the deep lake of your navel, his body licked by the rows of flames from Śiva’s wrath; from that [lake] there arose a streak of smoke,
which people, O Mother, know as the line of hair upon your body.
By your body, which was licked— that is, pervaded— by the rows of flames from the fire of Hara’s wrath,
the Mind-born One, Manmatha, became attached to your deep and low navel-lake (the lake that is your very navel) and thus sank therein. This is the meaning.
It arose; it emerged from that navel-lake, O Daughter of the Mountain, Pārvatī!
A streak of smoke—a column of smoke—produced at the time of extinguishing the embers. People, the world, know and describe that streak of smoke as yours, O Mother, O Janani!
"Romāvali" means "romarājī."
p.

167) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Daughter of the Mountain! the Mind-born [God of Love], with his body consumed by the rows of flames from Hara’s wrath, [is cast] into your deep...
Having taken its seat upon the lake of your navel, a creeper of smoke rose up from it;
O Mother! People perceive that as the line of hair upon your body.
Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the line of hair is fancied as being a streak of smoke.
Alternatively, by the phrase "people perceive her [thus]," the figure *bhrāntimān* (illusion) is suggested, since the sight of the line of hair produces the illusion of a streak of smoke. Or else...

This is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is the cognition that "the person perceives that as a line of hair"; or else, it is *niścayāntasaṃdeha* (conclusive doubt), because one determines "that is a line of hair.
Thus, these four figures of speech arise from the word "knows" (*jānīte*).
*Saṅkara* (commingling) occurs through the entry [of figures] into a single expressive word. || 76 ||
O Auspicious Mother, that which appears to the wise as something like the form of a very slender wave of the Yamunā in your thin waist—
[it is] the sky, thinned by being caught between your two jar-like breasts as they press against one another, as if entering your navel.
The one with caves. || 77 ||

"That which shines here before us"—the word *yat* (which), being accompanied by the word *etad* (this), does not possess the sense of referring to something already well-known; for this very reason, the word *yat* is employed once again. [The phrase] "having the form of the extremely slender ripples of the Kālindī" refers to the Yamunā.

O Śivā! O Blessed One! O Mother! That which appears—shimmering—in your slender, delicate waist, which has a form like that of an exceedingly subtle wave, [manifests] through the friction or intense contemplation of the wise and learned.
The space (*vyoma*) situated between—that is, in the middle of—the two jar-like breasts, having become attenuated or subtle, seems as if it were entering or making entry;
for it is well known even among children and cowherds that the sky is blue. [This refers to] the sky.
The blueness and the corporeality are well-known through poetic convention. The navel is "cavity-possessing," meaning it has a hollow.
p.

168) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Śivā! O Mother! that which exists in your slender waist—this certain object in the form of a line of hair, having the appearance of the extremely thin ripples of the Kālindī river.
To the wise, that which appears between her jar-like breasts is the sky thinned out;
it seems to enter the hollow of her navel as if due to their mutual pressure.
The dark, embodied sky, by virtue of being pressed against her jar-like breasts, appears to have slipped down to the lower part.
The meaning is that it remains reaching down to the navel in the manner of a creeper made of lac, and this they call the "line of hair" (romāvalī).
Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the creeper-like line of hair is imagined as a celestial vine (*gaganalatikā*).

In the first quarter-verse, there is the figure *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile), because the form of the waves suggests a relationship between the original object and its reflection. There is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of these two figures. || 77 ||

O Daughter of the Mountain, your navel is a steady whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, a basin for the creeper-like line of hair upon the bud-like breasts, a sacrificial pit for the fire of the Flower-Arrowed God’s splendor, a certain pleasure-chamber of Rati,
and the entrance to the cave of Siddhi for the eyes of Śiva.
He is victorious. || 78 ||
"Stable" means devoid of destruction; a "whirlpool of the Gaṅgā" is the swirling of the waters of the Gaṅgā, and because a whirlpool is momentary, its opposite is "stable.

"The creeper-like line of hair on the bud-like breasts" refers to the two breasts themselves as the buds. The "basin" (*kulāvālam*) is the enclosure for that creeper. (Note: *kalāvālam* is a variant reading for *kulāvālam*. The breasts are the buds, and the line of hair is the creeping vine. The "basin" is the surrounding area.
The two *puṣpa* flowers are their buds; the line of body hair (*romāvali*) itself is the supporting creeper, the progenitor [the Mother of the World];
its family is the youth; its art is the curved line;
its basin is the *āvāla*; the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is fashioned as a circle for the sake of the oblation.
It is the abode of fire, the brilliance of the flower-arrowed consumer of oblations, Manmatha; it is the very radiance of that fire, the pleasure-chamber of Rati, the wife of Madana,
for it is there that the presence of the God of Love is ever constant.

Her beloved remains right there; the meaning is that she is indescribable and exceedingly beautiful. O Girijā! O Pārvatī! Your navel is the entrance to a cave, the gateway to the mountain, the portal to the cave of attainment—that is, the attainment of ascetic power—for the eyes of Giriśa.
It triumphs and shines with supreme excellence for those who possess the eye of Sadāśiva.
p.
169) Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Daughter of the Mountain! Your navel is the steady whirlpool of the Gaṅgā;
the circle of hair on your bud-like breasts is the irrigation trench for the fire of the brilliance of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma].
The pool of Rati, the pleasure-chamber of the eyes of Śiva, and the entrance to the cave of spiritual perfection—
something truly victorious!
This is the figure of speech *ullekhālaṅkāra* (the ornament of delineation), because a single navel is delineated in multiple ways.

This is not *atiśayokti* (poetic exaggeration), precisely because it consists of the delineation of one thing as many. Nor is it a series of *atiśayoktis*, because it is impossible to determine [any specific identity] through the term "something" (*kimapīti*), and because of its association with that very term.
The secret is that the state of being a garland is inappropriate [for the individual flowers]. || 78 ||

O ornament of women, may it be well with your waist— which is naturally slender, weary from the burden of your swelling breasts, and bending as if slowly breaking under the weight of its own form— may it possess a stability equal to that of a tree on the bank of a river whose shores have long since crumbled away.
O Daughter of the Mountain! || 79 ||

O ornament of women! O jewel among womankind! [Look at her] who is naturally emaciated, wasted by her very nature, and exceedingly thin; who is overcome with fatigue from the weight of her swelling breasts, and whose form is bent low. Gently...
For a long time, as if breaking or being split slightly, your waist—
the middle part of your body— was pressed against a tree on the bank of a river that had been broken and shattered by the current of the flowing stream.

May there be well-being— the absence of fracture— for you who possess steadfastness (sthemā) in an equal state (samāvasthā), that is, stability in an even condition; O Daughter of the Mountain, Pārvatī!
Here the construction of the words is as follows: O daughter of the mountain! O ornament of women!

[the river]—whose banks are naturally diminished, which suffers fatigue from the weight of its sloping breasts, whose form bends, and which seems to break apart slowly like the trees on the banks of a stream that has been severed—is [described].
May there be long-lasting well-being for you, who abide in the stability of equanimity, remaining in the middle way.

Expressions such as "of the middle one" (*madhyasya*) and so forth, which delight the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), are acquired through the practice of the instructions of great poets. One who is proficient in such usage—
He is called a great poet.

Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), wherein the similarity between the breasts and the roots of trees growing on the crumbling banks of a river is established through their middle portions.
79. The breasts, which immediately cause the bodice fastened to their slopes to burst asunder, rub against the base of the arms.

O Goddess, as if fearing that your waist might break, the Creator has bound it threefold with the creeper-like folds of your triple-fold, which resemble golden jars, as if to protect it from fracture.

The breasts (*kucau*) were such that at that very moment, the seams of the bodice (*kūrpāsa*) fitted against their slopes were bursting; "bursting" means sweating, possessing perspiration, on those two slopes or sides, and thus bursting—that is, breaking—through the bodice fitted there. The suffix *kurac* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), even though it is technically a reflexive passive (*karmakartari*).
Regarding the suffix *kurac*: he explains that *kurac* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).

In the reading "sadyastanaghaṭitakūrpāsabhidurau," [the meaning is] "those two which tear through the bodice (*kūrpāsaka*)—that is, the bodice fashioned at that very moment (*sadyastana*), being newly made."

The sense is that by constantly contemplating the form of Sadāśiva, the lord of her life, at every moment, her bodice is torn at the joints by her swelling limbs. Scratching— that is, rubbing— their armpits, which are the regions near the sides of the chest, they resemble golden jars.

By him who fashions, creates, or produces a splendor or beauty like that of two golden jars (*kanakakalaśa*), that is, two gold pitchers— [the purpose being] to protect or preserve your waist (*valagna*)— or rather,
[this refers to] the word *valagna* here as a nominative form.

The connection is with "karmatvena" (as the object). Regarding "alam" in the phrase "bhaṅgāt... alam," the word *alaṃ* here has the sense of prohibition; the meaning is "let there be no breaking (*bhaṅgaḥ*) [caused] by the weight of the breasts. The waist (*valagnam*), that is, the middle region, [is addressed] by the God of Love (*tanubhuvā*).
O Goddess! O Radiant One! O Blessed Lady! Your waist is bound in three ways—that is, in three manners—by Manmatha;
it is that which possesses three folds, three transverse creases.

"By the creepers of *lavalī*, as if by [other] *lavalī* creepers; that is, by those *lavalī* vines. The *lavalī* vine is yellow, while its flowers are white. In the *Akārādinighaṇṭu*, having mentioned *tulavalī*, it is stated that its creeper is the *vanakulattha* creeper; this should likewise be accepted here."
The word *iva* signifies probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), meaning "certainly" (*dhruvam*). It has already been stated previously that the word *iva* also possesses the function of indicating probability.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Goddess!

As the God of Love, whose two breasts resemble golden jars, rubs his arms against your shoulders—arms that tear through the bodice fastened to your sides because they are suddenly perspiring—he makes your waist appear exceedingly slender with every movement.
To protect your waist with its three folds, it is as if bound in three places by the lavalī creepers.

Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the three folds of the waist are imagined as being the *lavalī* creeper. In the first half-verse, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), in that the agency in the creation of the Goddess’s breasts belongs solely to the God of Love (*Manmatha*) and not to the aged Brahmā.

Even though there is a connection with the creation of an old Brahmin, the assertion of non-connection results in an identification (adhyavasāya) between the beauty produced by the poet and the beauty produced by nature alone. There is a commingling (saṅkara) of both through the relationship of subordinate and principal. Now, while thus fashioning the breasts...

If it is argued that, by the power of the qualifying attribute of the subject (*anuvādya*) in the phrase "by Manmatha," the agency of Manmatha is established as a matter of fact through inference, and thus— since there is no actual connection between him and the act of creating the breasts—
the statement of a connection where none exists is indeed straightforward, we say: not so, [regarding] the breasts.

One should not argue that the expression of a connection where no connection exists is straightforward because the present tense— conveyed by the suffix *śatṛ* in the word *kalayataḥ* (which resembles "golden jars")— indicates that the act of touching the breasts is connected to the present time; for [the same logic applies] even when there is a connection with the past time.
In the employment of a verbal root ending in a finite verb (ākhyāta) that expresses an action in the past tense,

it is appropriate to state a connection even when no such connection exists; however, this does not apply in the case of a restatement where the action is presented as already established by virtue of being part of what is to be restated (anuvādya).
O Pārvatī, the Lord of Mountains, having severed his own weight and breadth from his hips, deposited them upon you in the form of a gift.
Therefore, this broad and heavy mass of your hips covers the entire earth and yet brings it to a state of lightness.

O Pārvatī! O daughter of the mountain! The Lord of Mountains, Himavat, having severed—having detached—from his own, his very own slopes (nitamba), that which possesses weight, dignity, vastness, length, and circumference, has bestowed it upon you in the form of an adornment.

"By taking" (haraṇātmanā) means he deposited or offered it. "Taking" (haraṇa) refers to a woman's property consisting of what was received at the fire (*adhyagni*) and what was received upon her arrival (*adhyāvāhanika*). As stated by Hārīta:
"What is received at the fire and what is received upon her arrival is recorded as 'taking,' which is a woman's property."
The meaning of this is as follows: "Adhyagni" refers to that which was given with reference to the fire at the time of marriage— namely,
what was given by the father and others near the fire—
and that which was given by the father and others on the occasion of the desire to return to one's own home after taking the bride, following the conclusion of the marriage ceremony.

Some say that this is *adhyāvāhanika*; others say it is *adhyāhavanīyaka*, referring to what was given by the father and others at sacrifices and the like near the *āhavanīya* fire—this is an additional reading.
Both of these are recorded by Manu and others as being denoted by the term "taking" (*haraṇa*). Therefore:
For that reason, this vast, heavy, and broad expanse of your hips that is now visible completely covers the entire earth.
This "nitamba-prāgbhāraḥ" refers to the excessive massiveness of the hips.
It covers; it brings about and causes one to attain lightness (*laghutvam lāghavam*). The syllable *śa* means that in this matter of cutting away doubt, one should not have any suspicion.
Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Pārvatī! The Lord of Mountains, having severed his own weight and breadth from his own hips, deposited them upon you in the form of a gift.
Therefore, this mass of your hips, being heavy and expansive, [supports] the entire...
It covers the earth and brings about lightness.

The meaning is: concealment by means of expansion, and the production of lightness by means of heaviness. Within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), specifically upon the earth (*vasumatī*), both heaviness and expansion reside in one place;
the concealment of these two occurs precisely by means of heaviness and expansion residing in another single location.

(173) It is to be understood as follows: having apprehended the weight and extent residing in the Himālaya mountain as being greater than the weight and extent residing in the earth— on the grounds that the Himālaya is a *bhūdhara* (earth-bearer)— with this intention.

The intention of the Lord of Mountains, who employs the words "the concealment of that" and "the entire earth," is as follows: [he intends to say] "the concealment of that [mountain] and the entire earth."

Here, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is an identification (*adhyavasāna*) between the heaviness and breadth residing in the Himālaya mountains and the heaviness and breadth residing on Pārvatī’s hips, despite their difference.
This is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* based on the non-difference of things that are different. [81] Her thighs...
And he describes her knees in a single stroke:
"By means of both her well-rounded thighs, she has surpassed both the trunks of lordly elephants and the cluster of golden plantain stalks."
O Daughter of the Mountain, you who know the ritual, with your knees hardened by bowing to your husband, you have become the pair of frontal lobes of the elephant of the gods.
The trunks—the staff-like proboscises—of the lordly elephants;
for according to the opinion of Rakṣita, the word *śuṇḍā* can also be masculine.
[He saw] a multitude of golden plantain-stalks—a collection of golden *rambhā* pillars.

Having conquered and utterly surpassed both types of thighs— those consisting of the trunks of elephants and the stalks of plantain trees— you have become, O lady of virtuous conduct, one whose thighs are beautiful and perfectly rounded, yet hardened by the prostrations of your husband, the Supreme Lord.

"By prostrations"—meaning by the two knees touching the ground during the state of bowing. "O Girijasute!"—O daughter of Himavat! "O Vidhijnē!"—one who knows the *vidhi* (the meaning of the Vedas) is *vidhijnā*, meaning omniscient. Or else:

She is the performer of the Vedic rites; therefore, the daily salutation to the husband is performed as a matter of scriptural injunction (*vaidha*), and not out of deference to his superiority—this is a humorous remark. This is her address.
[The feet] with their knees [touching] the pair of frontal globes of the elephant of the gods...
O sword, you become the two temples of the tusks of the world-elephant.
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O Knower of Rituals! O Daughter of the Mountain!
O Bhavānī! [of] the lordly elephants...
Having surpassed with both your thighs the cluster of golden plantain trunks,
and having surpassed even the pair of frontal globes of the celestial elephant with your well-rounded knees, which are hardened by prostrating before your husband— you exist, you shine forth!
Up to... [or] as far as... [or] until...

In this context, even when joined with the word *bhavat*, the second person singular ending *-asi* occurs precisely because it is intended solely for the purpose of addressing [the person]. Herein lies the essential point: the word *bhavat* is of two kinds—that which refers to the person being addressed (*saṃbodhya*) and that which refers merely to the act of addressing (*saṃbodhana-mātra*). When it refers to the person being addressed...

Since the word *bhavat* does not have the sense of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*), the rule "when *yuṣmad* is an upapada," etc., does not apply; therefore, in its conjunction, the third person alone occurs by the rule "in the remaining cases. As in: "O Goddess, you give birth to the worlds, you sustain them, and you remain awake for them" (from *Carccāstava*, verse 4).
"O Bhavānī, you are the one who brings about the destruction of that [suffering]," and so forth.

When the word *bhavat* functions solely as a form of address (*saṃbodhana*), then because it refers to the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*), the second person verbal ending (*madhyama-puruṣa*) must indeed occur, as in "O sir, give alms" (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*). In that case:

Even when the word is intended solely as a vocative, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is established because the stem *bhavat* is listed in the *gaurādi* group of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, Rakṣita stated: "Let it be that, by virtue of the power of the nominal stem itself, the word *bhavat* possesses only the feminine gender."

"Being intended merely as a form of address. This is the underlying intention: since the word *bhavat* is included among the pronouns (*sarvanāman*), the suffix *ṅīp* is already established by the rule *ugitaśca*; therefore, the inclusion of the word *bhavat* in the *gaurādi* group [of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*] would otherwise be redundant.
This indicates that the feminine gender itself is intended solely for the purpose of address.

Now, if it is thus protected [by the rule], then *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would indeed have identical genders in the feminine, masculine, and neuter, because they refer solely to the vocative; however, their reference to the singular, dual, and plural numbers is due to their characterizing the person being addressed. And this is not so...

It has been stated that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) lacks the characteristic of an indicator (*liṅga*). By that same logic, it follows that your word (*bhavat-śabda*) would also lack the status of an indicator. Do not say so, for an answer has already been given; enough with excessive prolixity. As for [the verse]: "I speak to you, who are among the learned..."
Thus, on the occasion of explaining this verse, what was stated by Bhāskara, the author of the commentary *Kāvyaprakāśikā*, has not been cited here as it is baseless, but has been refuted.
Here, the ornament of simile (upamālaṅkāra) is as if evident. || 82 ||
To defeat Rudra, the God of the Uneven Arrows (Kāma) firmly fashioned two quivers for the Daughter of the Mountain, filled with double the number of shafts; for at their tips,
ten arrow-heads are seen.
The tips of the nails on his pair of feet, disguised as such, were sharpened exclusively on the whetstone of the crowns of the gods.
O Girijā! O Pārvatī! Your two quivers—those two quivers whose interior contains double the number of arrows, namely ten shafts—are upon your two shanks, in order to conquer and humiliate Rudra, Hara.
The five-arrowed god of love, Viṣama-viśikha, certainly and surely performed this:
that at the tips of those two quivers which are seen before one’s eyes, there appear the ten arrow-heads— meaning the ten-fold (doubled) five arrows.

The fruits were iron-tipped arrows disguised as the tips of her ten toenails; those [arrows], which bore the guise and pretext of the ten nail-tips of her two feet and two foreparts, were sharpened solely on the whetstone of the crowns of the gods.
They are primarily sharpened— that is, whetted— upon the whetstones that are the very crowns of Indra and the other gods.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Daughter of the Mountain! It is indeed true that the God of the Uneven Arrows (Kāma) made your two shanks into quivers containing double the number of arrows in order to defeat Rudra;
for, under the guise of the tips of the nails of your pair of feet, [the arrows remain hidden].
The ten arrowheads are seen sharpened on the whetstone of the excellent crown.
Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because of the imaginative attribution of the nature of quivers to the two shanks;
and there is also the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), because of the concealment of the tips of the nails by treating them as fruits.
There is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of these two, since they do not exist separately and their relationship as the instigator and the instigated is understood.
In the phrase "the god with uneven arrows did not truly create this," the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole),
because it is perceived as being distinct from the common creation of Brahmā. This has already been clarified previously in the verse beginning, "the breasts immediately perspiring" [verse 80].

On the occasion of commenting on these two verses [beginning with "ityādi"], there is also the suggestion of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāradhvani*) through the use of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāreṇa*), namely: "those who have within them two arrows of double-shafted reeds" (p.

By means of the two words "ten" (daśa) and "arrow-fruits" (śaraphalā), there is the apprehension of an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the toes of the feet and the arrows; enough said. || 83 ||

O Mother, place with compassion upon my head those two feet which the crests of the Vedas bear as their crowning ornament; for the water from whose lotus-feet is the river that flows from the matted locks of Paśupati.
The beauty of lac-dye and the luster of the crest-jewel of Aruṇa [the Dawn] belong to those two.

The meaning is that the "summits" (mūrdhānaḥ)—that is, the heads or the Upanishads (vedāntāḥ) of the Śrutis and Nigamas—bear or uphold [you]. This means they establish [you] as the object of their teaching. Your two feet (caraṇau), O Blessed One, are worn as crests (śekharatayā) or as ear-ornaments (uttaṃsatayā). Or alternatively, of the Śrutis...
The Vedas, which are the heads of the brides that are the Śrutis, adorn the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady. As was stated by Vasiṣṭha to Śakti in the words of the Śruti:
"Salutations to the Goddess Mahālakṣmī, to Śrī, to Siddhi; salutations, salutations."
To him whose feet are worshipped by the knowers of the Vedas—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna.
Regarding the phrase "by the knowers," it means "by which heads of the Vedas"? [The answer is: "Salutations to Tripurasundarī, to Śivā, whose form is the universe," and so forth.
Thus praised by the Vedic hymns, the Great Goddess, the Sovereign of the Immortals, with a delighted mind, spoke to them in words of a corresponding nature.

Thus it is said in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā. O Mother! O Janani! Place these two feet of mine upon your head—upon the crown—with compassion, with mercy; that is to say, with a heart filled with grace. Place them, set them down. [I offer] the water for the feet (pādya) belonging to those two feet.

*Pāthaḥ* refers to the water used for washing the feet. Although the connection with the feet is understood when the word *pādya* is uttered, nevertheless, when *pādya* is said, it conveys merely that [the water] is worthy of being used for washing the feet.
(177) There is no tautology, because the phrase "of which two" is construed with [the specific forms].
The river on the crest of Paśupati’s matted locks refers to the river on the *kaparda* (matted hair-tuft) of Paśupati Śiva.

The river Gaṅgā is the splendor of lac— the hue of liquid lac— upon the feet of those two; it is also the radiance of the crest-jewel of Hari, that is, the Kaustubha gem, which is both reddish and the crest-jewel of Hari, and its brilliance is its crimson luster.

The meaning is this: for the sake of pacifying the anger born of love, as Paśupati bowed down, the Gaṅgā residing in his mass of matted hair came to rest at the tips of his feet; thus, it is described that the Gaṅgā serves as the water for washing the feet (*pādya*). [This occurs] every day, morning and evening, for the purpose of service.
It should be meditated upon that the redness of Viṣṇu— who is white-complexioned, whose crown is set with the Kaustubha gem, and who is offering salutation— is produced by the application of lac-dye.

Here is the word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*): O Mother! Those two feet of yours which the crests of the Vedas bear as their crowning ornament—O Mother! place these two feet upon my head also out of compassion. [The water for] washing those feet—*pādyaṃ pāthaḥ*—is... [as follows].
The river from the matted locks of Paśupati [the Gaṅgā] and the splendor of lac [the Yamunā],
which possess the radiance of the reddish crest-jewel of Hari.

This is what is meant: the two lotus feet of the Bhagavatī always move upon the crest of the Vedas, upon the crest of Sadāśiva, and indeed upon the crest of Viṣṇu; thus, they possess the inherent nature of moving upon crests. Therefore, may she also move upon my crest.

The poet’s intention is that the expression “the lotus-feet” (pādāmbuja) ensures the propriety of the prayer. Alternatively, Hari, Viriñci, Paśupati, and Vedānta— being within the phenomenal world— bear upon their heads the lotus-feet of Sādākhyā, the mother of the universe.
It is indeed logical that those whose bodies have been purified by the water used for washing it [the Linga] partake in their respective offices through its majesty.
Here, the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) is evident. || 84 ||
We offer our salutation to this pair of your feet, which are delightful to the eye and possess a clear,
radiant luster from the red lac-dye.
The Lord of beasts feels extreme resentment toward the mango tree in the pleasure grove, longing to strike it down.
*Namovākam* means the word *namaḥ*. The term *namovāka* is grammatically correct due to its irregular formation (*nipātana*).
We say, or we speak; the meaning is "we pay homage. To that which is delightful to the eyes—that which is pleasing to the two eyes—and to those feet, your visible [feet].

[He] envies—that is, feels jealous of—the pair, the couple, which possesses bright and beautiful red lac, which is of brilliant luster, which has shimmering radiance, which is endowed with liquid lac, and which is moist with lac; this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). He envies it excessively, that is, intensely.

The meaning is that he does not tolerate the striking—that is, the beating—by whichever pair of feet is used for the purpose of striking. [This refers to] the *Aśoka* tree, which is said in the *Dohalakauteuka* to manifest its flowers when struck by feet. To him who desires—that is, who feels longing—the Lord of Beasts (*Paśunāmīśāna*) [offers his protection].

Paśupati is envious— that is, he feels jealousy— toward the *kaṅkelitaru* (the *aśoka* tree) in the pleasure grove (*pramadavana*). In both cases, the dative case is used for the object of envy according to the rules beginning with *krudhadruh-* and ending with *spṛher īpsitaḥ*.

Herein is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Blessed Lady! To this pair of your feet, which are beautiful to behold and possess a clear, lovely luster from the red lac-dye, we utter words of salutation;
for the Lord of Creatures (*paśūnām īśānaḥ*) longs to strike them down.
She is extremely envious of the *kaṅkeli* tree in the pleasure grove.

"At the time of a lovers' quarrel, a foot-strike intended as a favor is not conceivable for anyone"—thus it is said. Therefore, how could such a thing happen even to that *kaṅkeli* tree, which is an insentient object? It is precisely regarding this that there is indignation (*asūyā*).

The sense is that it is not found elsewhere. By this, Pārvatī’s absolute devotion to her husband is established. It is suggested that such devotion to her husband does not exist even in Lakṣmī or Sarasvatī.

Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is the perception of an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) through the description of a relationship between Śiva and jealousy, even though no such relationship exists. || 85 ||

Having falsely committed a slip of the tongue regarding your lineage, she now strikes her husband on the soles of his feet with her forehead, bowed in embarrassment; thus, after a long time, she extracts the thorn from within.
The enemy of Īśāna, having uprooted the fire that had been produced, let out a triumphant shout with the tinkling of his anklets.
"Falsehood" (*mṛṣā*) refers to the accidental lapse of a name (*gotraskhalana*).

A "lapse of a name" is the utterance of another woman's name by one who, while manifesting passion for the heroine, has—due to negligence in her very presence—had his mind possessed by that other woman. Now, [the definition of]...
"Following the slip of the tongue, he was bowed down by embarrassment" means he was bowed down by embarrassment—

that is, by the confusion regarding what ought to be done. Here, because of the primacy of embarrassment, it is said that "he was bowed down by embarrassment," rather than that he bowed down of his own accord due to embarrassment.
The intention of the one employing the word "namita" (bowed) is that there was an exceedingly great embarrassment.
While striking— that is, hitting— the husband Paśupati with her lotus-foot upon his forehead, the region of the brow.
The meaning is: "when you have struck your husband's forehead.
Since striking the forehead reaches as far as the person to whom it belongs, the expression "she strikes her husband" is a direct and appropriate usage; such constructions are [grammatically] valid.
These [words], which have come forth by the power of the great poet Śakṣāva and which gladden the hearts of the connoisseurs (sahṛdaya), shall burn— that is, consume—
the "dart within," meaning the dart of the heart, namely the enmity that has been sewn into you for a long time,
produced by burning, that is, caused by the scorching of the fire of his eye.
By the tinkling sounds (*kvāṇaiḥ*) of the tips (*koṭayaḥ*) of the anklets (*tulānūpuram*)— the tips being their ends— which had uprooted [the enemy],
the gems and small bells contained within them were perceived;
by their *śiñjita* (jingling) sounds, there was a *kilikilitam*, an imitation of the sound "kilikili."

The victory of the one who is well-known [Manmatha] is celebrated; the meaning is that a cry of "kili-kili" was raised. The sense is that the status of Manmatha as an enemy toward Īśāna was thereby established.

Herein, the construction of the words is as follows: O Blessed Lady! when [Śiva], having falsely committed a slip of the tongue regarding your lineage, struck his own husband—who was bowed with embarrassment—upon the forehead with his lotus-feet;
then, by that enemy of Īśāna (Kāma), who had long since uprooted the internal thorn caused by the fire [of Śiva's wrath].
They shrieked with loud cries like the clanging of the tips of a balance scale.

180) Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the tinkling of the tips of the balance-beams is identified with the sound of joyful shouting (*kilikilita*); this is an *atiśayokti* based on the non-difference [of one thing] from another when there is actually a difference.

O Mother, your two lotus feet are superior to the lotus: they are capable of destroying the great mass of snow, uniquely skilled in dwelling upon the snowy mountain, and are radiant while sleeping at night during the final watch; they are worthy recipients of Fortune, bestowing prosperity upon those who observe the sacred times.
What wonder is there here for one who is victorious? || 87 ||

"To be destroyed by the mass of snow" means to be slain or annihilated by the accumulation of frost; "exclusively skilled in dwelling on the Snowy Mountain" means that they always reside only upon the Himālaya. "Sleeping at night" means being closed like buds during the night, and also during the final portion of the night.
The sense is that they are clear and serene because the power of consciousness arises right there.
By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that they are serene even during the day. "Varam" means desired;
"lakṣmīpātram" means presided over by Lakṣmī. "Śriyam" refers to Lakṣmī.

O Mother! O Janani! Your two feet, which bring forth and generate the very nature of the *samaya* for those devoted to You who observe the *samaya*, as described in the verse beginning with "In Your foundation, the root" (verse 47), conquer—that is, they are ever-victorious—over the lotus (*saroja*), which is the object of their action.
"Citra" means wonderful; "iha asminnarthe" means in this matter; "kiṃ na" means nothing at all.

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Mother! Your two feet—dwelling solely on the Himālaya mountain, pure during the final part of the night, and bestowing abundant glory upon those who observe the sacred time (*samayin*)—are like a supreme vessel of Lakṣmī who, having been asleep during the night, is now to be awakened from her slumber by the snowfall.
The meaning is: what wonder is there that the lotus is victorious here, since its superiority is so manifest?
Here, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is manifest. || 87 ||
O Goddess, how has your foot— the source of fame and the refuge for those without support— been brought by the virtuous to a likeness with the hard shell of a tortoise? Or how [could it be so]?
That which was taken by the Destroyer of Cities with his two arms at the time of the marriage ceremony and placed upon the sacrificial stone with a compassionate mind; || 88 ||

O Goddess! O Radiant One! O Blessed One! How, indeed, has that place—the very footstep of your glories and fame, yet the non-place (apada) beyond the reach of feet—been brought to, or reached by, the virtuous through their misfortunes and calamities?
How indeed, or in what manner, did the lords of poets [describe] the comparison of that hardness to the shell of a female tortoise— the shell of a female tortoise being the carapace of a turtle—
at the time of taking her hand, namely at the moment of marriage, by means of their two arms?
That foot which was taken—that is, grasped—by Purabhid, by Sadāśiva, and then placed or cast upon the *dṛṣad*;
for *dṛṣad* means a stone serving as a base, a grinding-stone (*upala*) used for pounding substances such as turmeric;
that stone which serves as its support is the *dṛṣad*. It is that [stone].
At the time of the wedding, it was used as the vessel for the ritual of placing the stone;
how could Your lotus feet, which are exceedingly tender, have been placed upon that grinding stone by one with a compassionate heart— how could You have cast aside compassion?

By Śambhu, through his poetic expositions that flow with nectar, how could the lords of poets be compared to the back of a tortoise? The meaning is that both of these [the comparison and the poetic excellence] have been stated.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Goddess! How was your forefoot—which is the abode of fame and the non-abode of calamities—compared by the virtuous to the hard shell of a tortoise?
For it was grasped with both arms by the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), whose mind was moved with compassion, at the time of your marriage.
Or how could it be placed upon a grinding stone?

Here, the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison) is suggested (*dhvani*) because, by the negation of any other similar object, there arises the realization that the object—the lotus-foot—is itself its own equal. || 88 ||

O fierce goddess, your feet seem to laugh at the celestial trees with their nails— which are like moons causing the lotus-hands of the women of heaven to close— and at the fruits [of those trees] which remain on their own branches.
May those two, who swiftly bestow auspicious prosperity upon the poor with the tips of their sprout-like hands, grant [it] incessantly. 89.

With his nails— those moons which cause the closing of the lotus-hands of the celestial women (surāṅganā), such as Śacī and others; for at the moment of seeing his feet, their hands, which are like lotuses, close up in the form of buds.
The splendors of his nails are indeed the rays of the moon;

from his hand, they cause the buds to close, making him perform the gesture of joined palms (*añjali*). He laughs at the trees—those celestial beings existing in heaven. The genitive case in "tarūṇāṃ hasataḥ" (laughing at the trees) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

O fierce one! O Blessed One! Your two feet are indeed laughing; for it is understood from the force of the qualification that you grant fruits only to those established in their own well-being and those residing in heaven, and not to the poor.
With the tips of your sprout-like hands, [you hold] only sprouts.
Among those who give and bestow, he is the foremost; to the poor and the wretched,
he grants auspicious and abundant prosperity and fortune incessantly, at all times, and swiftly.

This is the meaning: the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) gradually grant fruit according to one's desires only to those who are already well-off, using their sprout-like hands; but Your lotus feet, however, swiftly bestow auspicious prosperity upon both those who are well-off and the poor alike.
The negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Herein is the word-connection (*padayojanā*): O Caṇḍī! Your two feet—which incessantly and swiftly bestow auspicious prosperity upon the poor from those divine trees that grant fruits even to those who stand by them with the tips of their sprout-like hands—[are worshipped] by the women of heaven.
With their moon-like nails that cause the lotuses of hands to close, they seem as if they are laughing.

Here, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast) is quite evident; furthermore, it should be understood that this is enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the phrase "to those who remain in their own state" (*svasthebhyaḥ*). || 89 ||

While you incessantly bestow upon the wretched prosperity that accords with their hopes, you scatter an abundant nectar of exquisite beauty upon this [hand] of yours, which is as lovely as a cluster of mandāra blossoms.
May my life, having submerged itself at his feet, attain the state of a six-legged bee.
While he bestows upon the wretched and the poor a fortune— splendor that is incessant, conforming to their hopes, and in accordance with their desires— abundantly and exceedingly.

It scatters— that is, it pours forth— the nectar of a profusion of beauty; for this visible [form] of yours, which is as lovely as a cluster of mandāra stalks, is indeed a heap, a collection, of beauty and grace.

May my life—my very soul (majjīva)—attain the supreme immersion by plunging into her lotus-feet; for "my life" consists of myself and this life-force, and "limbs" refers to the five sense organs. May she, who possesses the auspicious beauty of a cluster of wish-fulfilling trees, grant this.
He whose feet are those very [senses] with the mind as the sixth has attained the state of a six-legged being, that is,
the condition of a bee.

Herein is the word-arrangement: O Blessed Lady! in this foot of Yours—which is as beautiful as a cluster of mandāra flowers, which scatters an abundant nectar of loveliness, and which incessantly bestows upon the wretched a fortune that accords with their hopes—my life, whose very movement consists of its senses, is immersed.
May it sink down and attain the state of a six-legged bee.

In this [verse], the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the foot is determined as being a lotus through the process of concealment (*nigīryādhyavasāna*). In the phrase "beautiful as a cluster of *mandāra* flowers," the figure of speech is *upamā* (simile). There is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) of these two. In the phrase "karaṇacaraṇa" (the hand and the foot)...
It is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) because of the imposition (*āropaṇa*) and the transformation (*rūpaṇa*) of the senses into the state of being feet.

In the phrase "may my life attain the state of having six feet," the ornament of *pariṇāma* (transformation) is evident. There is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of these two through their relationship as subordinate and principal elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

In the phrase "scattering the nectar of the blossoms of beauty," the basis for the identification [of the face] through the suppression of its own nature (*nigīryādhyavasāna*) is the *rūpaka* (metaphor). For this very reason, it is not a "partial metaphor" (*ekadeśarūpaka*), because the individual parts [of the face] are explicitly stated. [The intended meaning is: "Let the hand become a bee."

Because it is designated as the fruit, it possesses the status of being a constituent part (*avayava*). Therefore, in the phrase "in this foot" (*caraṇe*), having taken "foot" (*caraṇa*) as the locus of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*), [the superimposition occurs].
It is correctly understood that [the lotus] was swallowed by the cognition of it being placed upon the [head].
Thus, it should be noted that this is indeed a *saṅkara* (commingling) of *pariṇāma* (transformation) and *atiśaya* (hyperbole), and not a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coexistence).
[The rays of the moon], stumbling as if intending to begin the practice of the sport of placing their steps, move playfully...

The swans of your mind do not abandon their dwelling; therefore, O lady of beautiful conduct, your lotus-feet proclaim their instruction under the guise of the tinkling of your auspicious jeweled anklets. 91.

"Padanyāsakrīḍāparicayam" means: the placing of the feet (*padanyāsa*), the play (*krīḍā*) therein, and the practice (*paricaya*) or training (*abhyāsa*) thereof. The word "iva" (as if) expresses a supposition (*saṃbhāvanā*), meaning "certainly. "Skhalantaḥ" means those who, desiring to accomplish it, are of a mind to begin it, yet are stumbling.
The domestic swans— the specific types of *kalahaṃsa* birds raised in your palace— do not abandon following you; they do not forsake your playful, graceful movements and your stately gait.
The meaning is that they never abandon [their gait] even for a moment.

For this reason, the instruction of those swans—the training in their graceful movement—is imparted by means of the pretext of the tinkling of beautiful jeweled anklets (*maṇimañjīra*). The jeweled anklet...

That anklet, preeminent with jewels and most fortunate—that is, exceedingly beautiful—or else endowed with auspicious gems such as rubies and the like; by way of, or under the pretext of, the tinkling and jingling sounds of that anklet, it was as if speaking: "ācakṣāṇam" (proclaiming).
O lady of beautiful conduct! O lady of graceful gait! Teach [me] the lotus-feet, the water-lily feet.

Here, the construction of the words is as follows: O lady of beautiful conduct! the domestic swans, whose minds were intent on beginning the practice of the sport of placing their feet, though stumbling, do not abandon your playful movement.
Therefore, her lotus-feet, under the guise of the tinkling of their auspicious jeweled anklets,
seem as if they are imparting instruction to them.

Here, the figure of speech is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there is a conceiving of the sounds of the anklets as being of the nature of instructional words. In the first half-verse, there is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the natural following of the keepers by the palace swans is [exaggeratedly] described as such.
Because it is determined as being for the purpose of practicing the sport of placing the feet, there is an *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) based on a connection where no connection exists;
this occurs through the relationship of part and whole between the two.
[This concludes] the *saṅkara* [section]. || 91 || Having thus described [the Lord] from the crown down to the feet, he praises His true nature once more:
"Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, Īśvara, and Bhṛgu have attained the state of being couches for Śiva."
With a deceptive coverlet fashioned from his own clear reflection,
and rendered crimson by the glow of the reflections of your rays, he— like the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) personified— yields delight to the eyes.

Those who are supported by Druhiṇa, Hari, Rudra, and Īśvara—namely Druhiṇa (Brahmā), Hari (Viṣṇu), Rudra, and Īśvara—these presiding deities are included within the principle of Maheśvara; they have attained, that is, reached, the state of being your couch, the form of your bedstead. And they are those very ones.
And "bhṛtaḥ" (hired). This word ends in the *kvip* suffix and is plural.

"Bhṛtāḥ" becomes "bhṛtakāḥ" [in the compound] through a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). For the purpose of extremely close service by those who can assume any form at will (*kāmarūpa*), the couch takes on the form of four legs.
This is indeed appropriate. The word *śiva* has been explained as the qualified person (*adhikāripuruṣa*) whose very nature is the *śiva-tattva*, or else as the *sadāśiva-tattva*.
It is like a deceptive covering-cloth fashioned from clear shadow; for it is both "clear" (*svaccha*) and "shadow" (*chāyā*).

The meaning is that her very clear shadow—her radiance—is itself fashioned into a deceptive covering-cloth; it is her own bright luster existing in the form of a garment. [This refers to] the splendors—the radiances—belonging to you, that is, related to you.

By virtue of being reddened by the passion transferred through reflection—that is, the redness (raktimā) that has been transmitted through the process of reflection—[the moon] is crimson, meaning it is of a red color; the state of being so is "that-ness" (tattā), and by that [state].
It is like the embodied, personified erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the aesthetic flavor known as the erotic.

It is the established convention among great poets that the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) is red in color. The word "iva" is used here in the sense of possibility. It yields—that is, it milks, produces, or brings about—curiosity, which is to say, joy, for the eyes, meaning for your glances.
Herein is the construction of the verse: O Bhagavatī!

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara have attained the state of being your couches; while Śiva, possessing a deceptive coverlet fashioned from your own pure radiance, remains [as the bed]. Of those belonging to you...
Through the crimson glow of the reflection of his radiance, the embodied Śṛṅgāra (the Erotic sentiment) yields wonder to the eyes, as if he were the Rasa itself.
186) Here, the following should be kept in mind:
[the body] consists of the cakras known as Ādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā.

The abode of the six cakras consists of the presiding principles (tattvas) of earth, fire, water, air, ether, and mind, as well as the seat of the eleven sense organs. Thus, up to the end of the Ājñācakra, twenty-one principles are presided over and established in their own essence. Above that—
The fourfold group of principles consisting of Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara,

and Sadāśiva resides within the four gates of the Śrīcakra, which consists of three sets of four-gated enclosure squares appearing immediately after the Brahma-knot; specifically, it is situated at the locations of the gates starting from the east.
The four principles beginning with *māyā* are the four legs of the couch.

Due to the absorption of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) into the principle of Sadāśiva, Śiva— residing within the thousand-petaled lotus and consisting of the nature of Sadāśiva— [arises] through the casting of that shadow by the power of passion.
Through the integration with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), identity is perceived;
[this refers to] the Śrīcakra, which resides within the thousand-petaled lotus, consists of four gates, and has the form of a pericarp (karṇikā).

The union of Śiva and Śakti occurs within the ocean of nectar, which is characterized by a central square, is synonymous with the term *bindu*, and is designated by the word *saraghā*. All that remains [is contained] "within the ocean of nectar," as will be explained during the commentary on the eighth verse.
It has been told.
Here, the figure of speech is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), vitalized by the figures of *tadguṇa* (assimilation of qualities) and *alaṃkāra* (ornament).

This is because there is the poetic fancy that Śiva—who is exceedingly white—appears as if he were the embodied *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, due to his attaining the same quality (*tādguṇya*) through the luster of Kāmeśvarī’s body. [92] *Arālā* (curly) in the hair...

Naturally simple in her gentle smile, possessing the hue of the *śirīṣa* flower in her heart, yet as hard as a stone in her breast; exceedingly slender at the waist, yet broad across the expanse of her swelling breasts— may the compassion of Śambhu triumph for the protection of the world!
A certain [woman] was ruddy. || 93 ||

"Arālā" means curved in the hair, and not elsewhere; "prakṛtisārā" means naturally straight by her very nature; "mandahasite" means in a gentle smile; "śirīṣābhā" means having the luster of a *śirīṣa* flower, that is, extremely soft; [and] "citte" means in the mind or internal organ.
