The beauty of a grinding stone; that which is like a stone upon a stone—that is, like a hard grinding stone (*peṣaṇikā*)—upon the breast-slope (*kucataṭa*), which is like a stone.
It has already been stated that she possesses the very splendor of a stone slab;

she is exceedingly slender (*tanvī*) at the slope of her breasts (*kucataṭe*), meaning at the surface of her bosom, yet broad (*pṛthuḥ*) at the waist (*madhye*); and she is likewise broad in the region of her breasts (*urasijārohaviṣaye*) and in the region of her hips (*nitambaviṣaye*).

The word *viṣaya* signifies "place. It means that which shines forth as "I alone am," triumphing over the world—the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*)—in order to protect or preserve it for Śambhu, the eternal Śiva. *Karuṇā* is a certain power (*śakti*) consisting of compassion, ineffable and red-hued, known by the name Aruṇā. Or else:

The meaning of the sentence is that a certain compassion, red in color—compassion appearing as if embodied through the superimposition of redness upon itself—shines forth. By implication, the Śakti named Aruṇā is understood here;
the construction of the words is as follows: "Of Śambhu, a certain [Śakti], curly in her hair, with a gentle smile..."
Naturally straight in her mind, with the hue of a *śirīṣa* flower upon the slope of her breasts, possessing the brilliance of a stone on her waist,
exceedingly slender at the middle yet broad in the expanse of her bosom, and ruddy in compassion—
may she who triumphs protect the world.

Here, through the poetic identification (*adhyavasāna*) of Kāmeśvarī with the words "ruddy" (*aruṇa*) and "compassion" (*karuṇā*), there is the figure of speech known as Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). [The moon] is a spot of musk; its orb is composed of water; its digits are camphor; and it is a beryl casket.

It has become dense. Therefore, for your sake, the Creator surely makes this hollow interior, which becomes empty day by day through your enjoyment, increasingly dense again and again. (94) *Kalaṅka* means a mark;
*kastūrī* means musk from the musk deer; *rajanikarabimba* means the orb of the moon.

"Consisting of water": the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (svārthe), meaning "consisting of water. "Together with *kalās*": together with camphor, which consists of *kalās*. "An emerald casket" (*marakatakaraṇḍa*): fashioned from emerald gems (*marakatamaṇi*). The word *marakata* is derived from the word *makara* through a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*).

"From Makara" means from the Makara; Bhojarāja says that "Makarata" refers to what is born from the mouth of the Makara. "Karaṇḍa" means tightly closed or filled within. Therefore, by "your enjoyment," meaning by the experience of your consort's pleasure.
p.
188) Through the daily experience of musk, camphor, and saffron,
the Creator has made this visible orb of the moon hollow within and empty in its interior day after day.
Brahmā thickens and fills [it] again and again every day; "certainly for your sake" means "for you.
Regarding the sense of purpose, two particles (*arthe* and *kṛte*) are said to be used.
Thus, the word *kṛte* is prescribed as a particle (*nipāta*) in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*); when used in conjunction with it, only the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed.
Here is the word-by-word construction: O Blessed One! The spot [on the moon] is musk;
the lunar orb is composed of water; it is packed with digits that are camphor—a casket of emeralds. Therefore, this [casket], its interior hollowed out by your daily enjoyment, [is seen as empty].
Fate surely binds you more and more tightly for your sake;
here, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the lunar orb is identified as an emerald casket. Alternatively, it is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment).

This is not a stain, but rather musk; this is not the orb of the moon, but rather water reflected from outside that has entered within; these are not digits, but rather camphor powder—this is the lunar disc.

Because of the reflection of objects situated within it, it is perceived as yellow in color, whereas in reality it is white; such is the perception of the *Avasthāpahnava-mālā* (the series of negations of states).
Furthermore, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding [the moon] which possesses increase and decrease on the first lunar day and subsequent days.

Because it is possible for the moon to be slightly diminished or full due to the expenditure or influx of substances such as musk, there is a blending of these two through their relationship as subordinate and principal, owing to their remaining in separate states. || 94 ||

Therefore, you are the inner sanctum of the Enemy of Tripura; consequently, the boundaries of service to your feet are difficult for those of restless senses to attain. For indeed, these gods, headed by Indra, have been led to incomparable perfection by the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, which abide at the very threshold of your door.
The inner apartments of the Enemy of Tripura, the Destroyer of Cities—that is, the harem—consist of the principal queen;
you are that [queen]. Therefore, for that reason, the boundaries of worship for your two feet—your two lotus-feet—are established.
The manner of worship is difficult to obtain— that is, hard to attain— for those of unsteady senses and flickering minds;
for those with restless hearts, there is no entry into the inner apartments.
This is well known. Therefore, it is stated in the *Nītivākyāmṛta*: "The attendants must enter with steady minds.

The meaning is that service to the lotus feet of her who dwells in the midst of the ocean of nectar is known only by those of pure mind, and not by others. Indeed, [the word] *tathā hi* indicates a well-known fact.
These gods, headed by Indra— the foremost among the deities beginning with Śatakratu— have been led to incomparable and peerless perfection and complete success by you,
O Bhavati, through those who stand at the threshold, that is, those whose positions are near the door.
Together with the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*— that is, those headed by *aṇimā*— the immortals are free from decay.
Herein is the construction of the words: O Blessed One! You are the inner sanctum of the Enemy of Tripura.
Therefore, the limit of service to Your feet is difficult for those of restless senses to attain.
For indeed, these immortals, headed by Indra, [remain] standing at the threshold of Your door.

They have been led to incomparable perfection along with the powers such as *aṇimā*. Just as these powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, attend upon you even at the very threshold of your door, so too do Indra and the others; however, this is the distinction regarding the eight perfections beginning with *aṇimā*: [that they attend upon you alone].
Their constant residence there as gatekeepers is established by their very nature.

However, because Indra and the others possess restless faculties and are thus unfit to enter the inner apartments, their stationing at the gateway with the permission of the doorkeeper is the meaning of the word "attainment" (siddhi).
The Essential Meaning (Tātparya) || 95 || How many poets do not resort to the wives of Brahmā?

Or who does not become a husband to the Goddess Śrī through whatever riches? O virtuous lady, you who are the foremost among chaste women, having abandoned Mahādeva, your breasts have found their attachment [only] in you.
It is difficult to find even on the *kuravaka* tree. || 96 ||

A wife (*kalatra*) is so called because she protects (*trāyate*) from distress (*kaśmala*); *kaśmala* here means hell, and the elision of the middle vowel is justified by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Thus, Rakṣita explains: "She protects from distress. *Vaidhātram* means relating to the Creator (*vidhātṛ*).
When the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *vidhātṛ* according to the rule *tasyedam*, it denotes a mere relationship;
then, when there is a desire to know the specific nature of that relationship, the word *kalatra* is construed [with it].

The point is this: when it is said that "the wife is the element" (*dhātuḥ kalatram*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) placed in mere relation ultimately resolves upon the related entity itself; thus, there is a direct syntactic connection (*sākṣād-anvaya*). Therefore, this usage is not faulty. [How many] Sarasvatīs are there who are the wives of Brahmā? (*vaidhātraṃ kalatraṃ sarasvatīṃ katikati*)?
They worship; they serve. Who indeed are not poets? No one; the meaning is that all indeed worship.
Who indeed does not become the husband of the goddess Śrī, Lakṣmī? By whomsoever through riches. [The reading *adhipatiḥ* (lord) is an addition. [He worships] Mahādeva.

O Satī! O devoted wife! O foremost among the chaste and faithful! Having abandoned Sadāśiva, even the embrace of the Kuravaka tree—once difficult to obtain—is no longer easily accessible to you by means of your breasts.
The meaning is that even for an insentient kuravaka tree, an embrace of the breasts cannot occur even as a mere longing (dohada);
what then need be said of another man? Thus, her devotion to her husband (pātivratya) is beyond the reach of words.

Here is the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*): O Satī! How many poets do not resort to the wife of Vidhātṛ? By which riches does one not become the husband of the goddess Śrī? O you who are not the last among virtuous women! Having abandoned Mahādeva, [who is there for you? Your...
Even attachment to the *kuravaka* tree by means of one's breasts is difficult to obtain.

This is the meaning: those who have attained mastery over eloquence (*sārasvata*) through the recitation of mantras and other such practices are celebrated as "Beloveds of Sarasvatī" (*Sarasvatīvallabha*);
those who possess abundance of wealth, grain, horses, elephants, and so forth are [celebrated] as "Lords of Lakṣmī" (*Lakṣmīpati*).
Thus they are sung: that the Lord of Pārvatī is indeed Mahādeva himself, and so the greatness of devotion to one's husband is beyond the reach of speech and mind. || 96 ||
Those who know the scriptures speak of the Goddess of Speech as the consort of Brahmā, of Padmā as the wife of Hari,
and of the Daughter of the Mountain as the companion of Hara; but you are some ineffable fourth power,
whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend— you, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who causes the universe to wander.
The great queen of the Supreme Brahman. || 97 ||
Those who know the scriptures say that she is the goddess, the presiding deity, the wife of Duhin, and the consort of Brahmā; they speak thus with their words.

You are the wife, the consort, Padmā, whose abode is the lotus, of Hari Viṣṇu, who knows the secrets of the Āgamas; you are the companion of Hara, the wife of Śambhu, the daughter of the mountain, Pārvatī;
and you are some fourth, indescribable being, whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend.
The meaning is that she is one whose greatness is boundless— incapable of being attained through suffering and immeasurable in terms of space, time, and substance. O Mahāmāyā,
you cause the entire phenomenal world (*viśva-prapañca*), which is the *māyā-tattva* contained within *śuddha-vidyā*, to wander in delusion.
By saying "you cause to revolve," he extends the attribute of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation), which is a property of Brahman, to Māyā.
O Queen of the Supreme Brahman, O Consort of Sadāśiva, the Supreme Brahman! Thus it is heard in scripture: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13).

In the *Puruṣasūkta*: "Hrīḥ, Bhuvaneśvarī, Lakṣmī, and Śrīvidyā—these two are the wives of Brahmā. Here, between the two, Śrīvidyā holds primacy because Bhuvaneśvarī is included within Śrīvidyā, whereas [Śrīvidyā] is not included within Bhuvaneśvarī.
Regarding the inclusion within Śrīvidyā, it should be understood that she alone is the Queen (mahiṣī) by virtue of the predominance of the digit of the moon (candrakalā).

Herein is the construction of the words: O Great Queen of the Supreme Brahman! Those who know the scriptures call you alone the consort of Druhiṇa, the Goddess of Speech; they call you alone Padmā, the wife of Hari; they call you alone the daughter of the Mountain, the companion of Hara; you are the Fourth.
A certain Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend, deludes the universe while remaining ever-true;

this is the meaning. Those who know the scriptures praise that one Blessed Lady alone by various names, for she is the Consort of the Supreme Brahman, known by the alternative name Śrīvidyā, and is indeed the single digit of the Moon. || 97 ||
O Mother, at what time shall I, seeking knowledge, drink the water used for washing your feet, which has been colored with the dye of alaktaka?
When will she, by being the cause of poetry even for those who are naturally mute, take on the state of betel-juice within the lotus-face of eloquence? 98.

"At what time?"—the remainder of the sentence being "from birth until the end. "O Mother! O Janani! "Tell me"—that is, instruct me correctly. "Smeared with lac-dye" means smeared or anointed with *alaktakarasa*, which is lac-juice or red dye (*yāvaka*). [This refers to] women's...

The *sairandhrīs* apply liquid lac for the purpose of coloring the feet and lower lips. "I would drink" (*pibeyam*) is used in the sense of a wish (*prārthanāyām*), employing the *liṅ* (optative) mood. A "student of knowledge" (*vidyārthī*) is one who seeks knowledge (*vidyāḥ arthayate*). Alternatively, an "arther" (*arthī*) is one for whom wealth (*arthaḥ*) is the purpose (*prayojanam*).

Regarding the phrase "one who desires [knowledge] through sciences" (*vidyābhir arthī*), Rakṣita states here that the suffix *ini* is applied after the word *artha* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). For this very reason, Kālidāsa employed the suffix *matup* itself in the verse: "by him, who was possessed of purpose (*arthavān*) and turned away from greed. (Māgha).

In the phrase "nitāntamarthinaḥ," only the suffix *ṇini* is used. Likewise, in expressions such as "arthī," "samarthī," and "vidvān," only the suffix *ṇini* is employed. For this very reason, the previous explanation alone is correct. [The word] "caraṇanirṇejanajalam" means the water for washing the feet—that is, the water for cleansing the two feet—of yours, O Lady.

The state of being that which is the essence of betel-juice from the lotus-like mouth of Sarasvatī—[that state].
The meaning is this: the water used for washing the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lady, still bearing the red lac, becomes the cause of poetry;
residing in the mouth of the lord of poets, it shines as if visibly present like the essence of the betel-leaf of Sarasvatī. That lord of poets has attained the state of a male being.
She shines like the Sarasvatī river.

Here is the word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*): O Mother! Tell me, at what time shall I, a seeker of knowledge, drink that water used for washing Your feet, which has been touched by Your hands?
And that [water], by its very nature, is for those who are mute—meaning those who are not deaf-mute—to speak and to hear.
And when will it take on the state of betel-juice for the lotus-face of speech, acting as the cause of poetry even for those who have not studied?
193) Here, this should be kept in mind: the two *Laghucarcā* hymns were recited by the venerable Bhagavatpāda for those who were deaf and mute through the power of joining his hand with their heads.
By her majesty, the Blessed Lady gave the water used for washing her lotus feet into his mouth;
the Teacher now requests that same water of purification once more. By this, liberation through proximity (sāmīpya-mukti) is indicated. We shall explain its specific details in the following verse.
By saying "the water for washing the feet," the view of the Samaya school alone is expressed; for in the Kaula school,
because the Goddess resides in the form of a serpent within the thousand-petaled lotus itself, there is no such thing as water for washing the feet.
That this water is for washing the feet has already been explained extensively on many occasions. Therefore:

"Sprinkling the phenomenal world once again with showers of nectar-streams trickling from between her pair of feet, she [is the embodiment] of the splendor of the tradition of aesthetic essence. (The Tenth Verse)
Thus, this half-verse establishes the doctrine of the *samaya*.
Having reached your own ground, having made yourself like a serpent coiled in a middle loop, you sleep within the hollow *kulakuṇḍa*. [The Tenth Verse]
Thus, this half [of the verse] establishes the Kaula doctrine; such is the distinction.
Here, the poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the red lac-juice from the washing of the feet is identified with the essence of Sarasvatī’s betel-chewing,
and because the initiate (*samayin*) is identified as being directly the very form of Sarasvatī herself; thus, there is a combination of *utprekṣā* and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

Concluding the praise thus far commenced, he indicates the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the piercing of the six lotuses (*ṣaṭkamalabheda*), which is the division of the scripture (*śāstrabheda*):
"The rival of Brahmā and Hari sports with Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, while the chastity of Rati..."
With his beautiful form, he loosens [the bonds]; even while living for a long time,
having destroyed the entanglement of the fetters of the individual soul (paśupāśa), he relishes through the wind of your worship that essence known as supreme bliss.
p.
194) [He is] the rival of Brahmā, Hari, and Lakṣmī—the latter being Padmālayā—respectively;
the word "respectively" (yathākramam) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By virtue of being the husband of Sarasvatī, he is Brahmā.
A rival means an object of envy; the meaning is that Hari is an object of envy because he is the Lord of Fortune (Lakṣmī).
While sporting—that is, while enjoying himself—he loosens the chastity, the duty of a devoted wife consisting of non-association with other men, of Rati, the chief queen of Kāma.

The sense is that, by appearing in the form of Manmatha (the God of Love), he produces the delusion of being Manmatha in Rati, thereby generating a desire for sexual union; this occurs through the identification [of her] with his body, which is most beautiful—meaning, through the cognition of identity with such a form. Thus, of the kalā known as Sādākhyā...

Having stated the worldly fruit for the lay follower (*upāsaka*), he also speaks of the otherworldly fruit: "Living long indeed," that is, living eternally. The eternity of a substance possessing parts is caused by the destruction of the connection between the bound soul (*paśu*) and the fetters (*pāśa*). In this regard, there is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki anumāna*).

That which is composed of parts and must be employed as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and which has not yet exhausted the entanglement of the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu-pāśa*), is not eternal—just like a sacrificial animal and so forth; thus is established the liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Kapila and others, as well as Mārkaṇḍeya and others, are likewise composed of parts.

Therefore, whether it be by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), let there be a proof for the eternity of that which possesses parts. Thus, being one whose life is eternal, he has destroyed the entanglement of the fetters of the bound soul (*paśu*); "destroyed" means rendered non-existent.
The term *vyatikara* [is explained as follows]: the "beast" (*paśu*) is the living soul (*jīva*), who perceives the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) through the senses.

Alternatively, from the verbal root *paśa* (meaning "to bind"), the "beast" is the living soul bound by ignorance (*avidyā*), and the "rope" (*pāśa*) is that ignorance. And this is heard in scripture:
May Aditi release this bond; I offer this salutation to the cattle and to Paśupati.
The meaning of this [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.1.4] is as follows: Aditi is the Bindu-Śakti residing within the solar orb (ādityamaṇḍala).
May she completely and utterly release the bond—the fetter created by ignorance (avidyā).

May he liberate! I offer this salutation, *namaḥ*, to Paśupati. The dative case in *paśubhyaḥ* is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). Its purpose is cessation; that is, for the sake of the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*).
This is the meaning: Aditi, joined with Sadāśiva, the Lord of Beasts, effects the release from bonds.

"Let him do so. Regarding the word *paśu* (animal/sacrificial victim), its denotation of the individual soul (*jīva*) is found in the *Saumya-kāṇḍa* of the *Taittirīyaka*, in the passage concerning those Asuras: [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.3].

This is established in the Anuvāka [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.3], beginning with "Of those Asuras... and ending with "...therefore Rudra is the lord of cattle. Therefore, the two—*paśu* (the bound soul) and *pāśa* (the bond)—are respectively the individual soul (*jīva*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); their *vyatikara*, or connection, has been destroyed.
Having severed the connection with the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), he abides as the essence of the Sadāśiva-tattva;
he relishes— that is, tastes— the flavor which is bliss, that light whose radiance is known as supreme bliss (parānanda) and whose nature is supreme bliss.
"One who possesses devotion to you" means a devotee of yours; "bhajana" refers to service to you.

Herein is the word-connection (*padayojanā*): O Blessed Lady! One who worships you sports as one whose rival to Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī has been surpassed; with a beautiful body, he causes the conjugal fidelity of Rati to slacken; and he has destroyed the entanglement of the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu*).
Living for a long time, he indeed savors the essence known as supreme bliss.

In this regard, the following should be kept in mind: even when ignorance (*avidyā*) has been sublated for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), their connection with the body persists according to the analogy of the spinning of a potter’s wheel. As it is stated in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra-saptati*:

"Upon the attainment of right knowledge, when dharma and the other factors no longer function as causes, he continues to maintain his body through the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the whirling of a potter's wheel. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the phrase "one who possesses devotion to you" (*tvadbhajanavān*), there are two types of devotion: that consisting of service to the six chakras and that consisting of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*). The first is now described:
because the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna* are worlds of darkness (*tāmisra*), they are not to be worshipped. [Devotion extends] from the *maṇipūra* up to the *sahasrāra* lotus.

"The five wheels (cakras) are to be worshipped. In that regard, for those intent on the worship of the *maṇipūra*, liberation takes the form of *sārṣṭi*. *Sārṣṭi* is defined as the state of one who, having constructed another city near the city of the Goddess, remains there performing service.

For those devoted to the worship of the *saṃvit*-lotus, there is liberation as *sālokya*; *sālokya* means residing in the city of the Goddess. For those who worship the *viśuddhi*-cakra, there is liberation as *sāmīpya*;
*sāmīpya* means being an attendant (*aṅgasevaka*) [of the Goddess]. For those who worship the *ājñā*-cakra...
Liberation through similarity (*sārūpya-mukti*).
"Similarity" (*sārūpya*) means having an identical form; that is, by virtue of possessing a separate body.
There is a distinction from *sāyujya* (union). These four types are secondary;

they are designated as "liberation" merely because one has transcended external suffering. However, the supreme, eternal liberation consists solely of *sāyujya*, and it belongs only to those who worship the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrārakamala*).
Therefore, one who engages in your worship experiences, as is appropriate, that aesthetic flavor known as supreme bliss.
In this regard, the essence of the doctrine is as follows: according to the system of the *Ṣaṭkarmalabheda*, liberation is of the very nature of bliss (*sukha*).
And that bliss, by way of a worldly analogy, consists precisely in sexual union with a woman;
for even in the world, there is no happiness greater than the company of a woman.

Thus, immediately after the absolute cessation of suffering, liberation consists precisely in that [cessation] itself, because through the attainment of union (*sāyujya-saṃsiddhi*), one is contained within the embrace of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus, the essential point here is this: first, the identity of the six wheels (*cakra*s), beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, with the nature of the triangle, the eight-spoked wheel, the two ten-spoked wheels, the pentagon, and the *śivacakra* has been established. This very [identity] is the unity of *nāda* and *bindu*. For it is thus:
That which is called *nāda* is the Śrīcakra; that which is called *bindu* will be described as the dense cluster of six lotuses.
Their unification is the four-petaled *ādhāra-cakra*, whose pericarp consists of a triangle; [then] the six-petaled *svādhiṣṭhāna*, whose pericarp...

Maṇipūra consists of eight triangles and is a ten-petalled lotus; its pericarp consists of ten triangles. Anāhata is a twelve-petalled lotus; its pericarp likewise consists of a second set of ten triangles. Viśuddhicakra is a sixteen-petalled lotus.
Its pericarp consists of fourteen corners; up to this point, there is the unity of the wheel of power (*śakticakra*).

The *ājñācakra* has a two-petaled pericarp, which is divided into two parts: one with eight corners and the other with sixteen corners. The meaning is that it is twofold [distinct from the two-petaled form].

It has been explained that [the region] is divided, consisting of four square natures (*caturaśra-prakṛti*) which are the essence of the four wheels of Śiva (*śivacakra*), namely the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*. There are three circles at the end of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and one circle at the end of the *anāhata*, which consists of the *rudragranthi*.

One consists of the Viṣṇu-knot at the end of the Ājñā-cakra, and one consists of the Brahma-knot. Above that is a triple enclosure of cities (tripura) provided with four gates, and at the four gates it is equipped with stairways. And that—
The pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus: that lotus has a thousand petals.
The station of the *bindu* (the *baindava-sthāna*), endowed with four gates, is located in the center of the pericarp.
In this way, according to the principle of the temple, the unity of the Śrīcakra and the lotuses should be contemplated.
And this unity of Nāda and Bindu, the most secret of secrets, has been taught out of favor toward the disciple.
The inclusion of the fifty *kalās* within these six *cakras* has been described:

the vowels are in the lunar portion (*candrakhaṇḍa*), the consonants (the *sparśas*) are in the solar portion (*sūryakhaṇḍa*), the semi-vowels (*antasthā*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)— excluding the letter *ha*— are in the fiery portion (*agnikhaṇḍa*), while the letters *ha* and *la* reside in the *bindu*.

That the letter *kṣa* is present everywhere has already been established by the verse beginning with "savitrībhiḥ" (verse 17). Furthermore, the inclusion of the *kalās* within the petals starting from the *mūlādhāra* has already been explained. As for the nature of the *tithis* belonging to the *kalās* of the *Nityās*:
The nature of the *kalās* consists in their being composed of the fifteen syllables contained within the root mantra;

the fifteen syllables consist of three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*); the three sections consist of the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; and the Moon, Sun, and Fire consist of the nature of the three knots (*granthi*).

The three knots consist of the three *hrīṃ* syllables contained within the mantra; the *hrīṃ* syllable is the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī; the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī is included within the root mantra (*mūlamantra*); and the root mantra is one with the *cakra*.

There is identity between that group of nine wheels (*cakranavaka*) and the six wheels beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, as well as the triad beginning with the *brahmagranthi*, and the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrakamala*).
This very thing is what is called the unity of *kalā* and *nāda*.

This is the essential point here: the unification of the *bindu* with the *nāda*, the unification of the *kalā* with the *bindu*, and the unification of the *kalā* with the *nāda*; thus, this triad constitutes the unification of the *bindu* with the *kalā*, the unification of the *nāda* with the *kalā*, and the unification of the fivefold group of Śrīvidyā.
That the oneness [of the Goddess] is sixfold is a supreme secret to be known through the instruction of the Guru.
Thus, the worship of the Blessed Lady as the sixfold oneness has been correctly described.
Following the contemplation of the sixfold oneness, the ten-armed Blessed Lady Śrīvidyā [appears].

It should be understood that my intention in saying that "the very contemplation of unity is the worship"—insofar as [the deity] is directly perceived in Maṇipūra and is to be brought into presence through ritual service—is as follows.
Now, the nature of the Bindu is elaborated; it is called "Bindu."

The six cakras beginning with the mūlādhāra; the bindu, which is the cause of the creation and dissolution of the universe and a particular power (śakti) of Śiva; and that [bindu], being one alone, resides within the center of the pericarp consisting of a four-cornered figure at the end of the thousand-petalled lotus, which itself consists of four gates.
The principle of Śakti (śaktitattva). The principle of Śiva situated within that is called Nāda.
It has already been stated that this is of four kinds. Of both [principles], p.

Since Śakti and Śiva consist of word and meaning, their nature as *kalā* (limited power) is common to both. Therefore, their union transcends *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*; this is the secret of the Samaya doctrine. Furthermore, that *bindu* is divided tenfold, as it has been said:
The single drop, which is of the nature of the Supreme (Parā), is divided tenfold:
fourfold in the lotus of the Foundation (Ādhāra) and sixfold in the lotus of the Empowerment (Adhiṣṭhāna).
"Because it possesses the nature of both forms, the others have that as their essence.

This is the meaning: the single *bindu* itself is divided tenfold—fourfold within the four petals of the lotus at the *mūlādhāra*, and sixfold within the six petals of the lotus at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
The meaning is this: the Mūlādhāra is a four-petalled lotus,
the Svādhiṣṭhāna is six-petalled, the Maṇipūra is ten-petalled, the Anāhata lotus is twelve-petalled,
the Viśuddhi lotus is sixteen-petalled, and the Ājñā-cakra is [two-petalled].
That it has two petals is established in all the Yoga scriptures. Here, the four petals of the *ādhāra*-lotus consist of four points (*bindu*);
these points are known as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*), and they are of the nature of *prakṛti*.
That these are the causes of the creation of the universe is established in all Yoga scriptures.

The six petals situated upon the lotus of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* consist of six drops (*bindu*) whose nature is desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy; for this very reason, they are [so called].
They say these are the "dissolution drops" (*saṃhṛtibindu*). This was stated by the venerable Patañjali:
"In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, dissolution is formed by six drops. Thus, there are ten drops consisting of the petals of the two lotuses. [The next center is] *maṇipūra*.
Considering it to consist of the *mūlādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*, there is a ten-petalled [lotus];
in the *anāhata* wheel, there is a ten-petalled [lotus] whose nature is the *maṇipūra*,
and two petals whose nature is the two preceding lotuses, making the *anāhata* lotus twelve-petalled.
The Viśuddhi lotus, which is of the nature of the Anāhata-cakra, has twelve petals;
that of the nature of the Ādhāra has four petals, thus making sixteen petals in total. Likewise, that of the nature of the Maṇipūra has ten petals, and that of the nature of the Svādhiṣṭhāna...

"Six-petalled" means sixteen-petalled. The *ājñā-cakra*, however, consists of the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and is thus two-petalled. In this way, there are four lotuses beginning from the *maṇipūra* up to the *ājñā*.

The [lotuses] of Mūlādhāra and Svādhiṣṭhāna are of the nature of Prakṛti. For this very reason, the four subsequent lotuses are included within the pair of Mūlādhāra; thus it is established that the single Bindu possesses ten states, and not otherwise.
(199) Although for the Kaulas the fruit of contemplating the six lotuses will be accomplished through the contemplation of the dyad,
nevertheless, because of the absence of the contemplation of the sixfold unity, it remains merely the path of Kula.

In the Kaula doctrine, it is impossible for the Goddess to have a fivefold presence in Maṇipūra due to the absence of the method for the fivefold liberation, and even the state of transcending *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā* is inconceivable; however, for those who observe the *samaya*,
[liberation occurs] precisely through the contemplation of the four elements that constitute the effect.

The fruit of contemplating the two lotuses that constitute the cause will be accomplished. Therefore, when the fivefold equality is established, the relationship between the convention (samaya) and the one who possesses the convention (samayin) is directly perceived among the convention, the possessors of the convention, and the attendants of those possessors; such is the essential truth of the doctrine of the venerable Bhagavatpāda.
Having thus established the meaning of the word *bhajana*, the meaning of the word *bhajana* is now defined in another manner:
"When [the Lord] says,
'Liberation comes from the thorough knowledge of the *dhāraṇās*,' its meaning is the *dhāraṇās*."

They number three hundred and sixty. What is called *dhāraṇā* is the restraint of the vital wind (*vāyu*) within the lotuses by means of the *nāda* and *kalā*. That [restraint] is sixfold in the six lotuses, and becomes sevenfold when combined with that which is designated by the term *samaya* in the seventh lotus.
There are fifty [dhāraṇās] in each lotus, thus making three hundred and sixty dhāraṇās.
Furthermore, those infinite dhāraṇās, which arise from various methods of union with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā* individually, are to be understood through the instruction of the Guru.

The fruit of the *dhāraṇās* within the six wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the *ādhāra*, in their respective order— consisting of the nature of intellect (*mati*), memory (*smṛti*), understanding (*buddhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), retentive power (*medhā*), intuition (*pratibhā*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*)—
has been shown here merely by way of direction. A more detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Subhagodaya* and the *Caraṇāgama*.
This has been established in many ways; therefore, it should be understood from those very sources, as it is not described here for fear of excessive length.
For this very reason, Kālidāsa-Bhagavatpāda [stated] in a verse that establishes the distinctions between the *kula-samaya* and other systems:
It is stated in the *Sakalajananīstotra* as follows:

"O You whose creeper-like luster possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning-flashes, fire, and suns, and who resides within the womb of the six-petaled lotus at the end of the four-petaled one;
having first pierced the hexagon, [enter] the ten-petaled [lotus]."
Salutations to you, O Daughter of the Mountain, who have entered into the twelve-petalled, sixteen-sided, and double-triangular [lotuses].
The meaning of this is: that [lotus] within which the four-petalled foundational lotus is situated—that is, internalized—exists.

The term *svādhiṣṭhāna* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and not a *tatpuruṣa*, because the latter [member] cannot be subsumed within the former; furthermore, it must be a *bahuvrīhi* because it would otherwise fail to connect with the subsequent sentence, "having first split the hexagon. And that [lotus] ends with four petals.

The Svādhiṣṭhāna has six petals, and the [Anāhata] has four petals ending with six petals. Its "vulvas" (bhagas) consist of cavities, being of the nature of hollows—that is, they are of that same essential nature—and those vulvas are triangles. This refers to the four cakras beginning with Maṇipūra.

Since their nature as being rooted in the *mūlādhāra* has been stated, they consist of triangles (*trikoṇa*). This has been properly determined in the passage: "The *baindava* [point] is joined within the triangle; the eight-petaled lotus is within the eight-spoked [circle]. "Within the *puṭabhagas*" means in the middle. "The triple circle" (*trivalaya*)...

The meaning is that the three knots (*granthitraya*)—situated at the ends of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *anāhata*, and *ājñā* [cakras]—exist as synonyms for the Rudra-knot (consisting of fire), the Viṣṇu-knot, and the Brahma-knot. Therein, "throbbing" (*sphurat*) means throbbing intensely; [this refers to] the woman.

The masculine form is applied by the rule *puṃvadbhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ samānādhikaraṇe* and so forth. [This refers to] the lightning (*vidyut*), the *saudāminī*, the fire (*vahni*), the flame (*agni*), and the sun (*dyumaṇi*). The word *niyuta* indicates a specific number of horses.

She whose luster is like that [of lightning], she who is the eternal creeper of light—that is to say, the steady flash of lightning; this is her vocative address. At the end of the *ājñācakra*, at the moment of piercing the *brahmagranthi*, she possesses the luster of ten million flashes of lightning; [and] at the end of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*...

The distinction is as follows: at the time of piercing the Rudra-knot, it has the brilliance of ten million fires; at the end of the Anāhata-cakra, at the time of piercing the Viṣṇu-knot, it has the brilliance of ten million suns.
Having first pierced the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which contains the six-cornered Mūlādhāra;
Then, immediately after that, having pierced the ten-petaled Maṇipūra, having pierced the twelve-petaled Anāhata-cakra, having pierced the sixteen-cornered Viśuddhi-cakra,
and having pierced the two-cornered Ājñā-cakra, it has gone— this is the ellipsis— to the thousand-petaled lotus.
O Daughter of the Mountain! O Daughter of Himācala! Salutations to you!
It has already been established that here the Kaulas worship the four-petalled *mūlādhāra* as being included within the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. However, for the Samayins,
[the goddess] has entered the *maṇipūra* after piercing through the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
Thus it is taught that they perform worship and that this is the reality of the Samaya doctrine.
Herein, this secret [truth] is that within the six lotuses, the five elements together with the mind as the sixth abide in a state of identity. And that—
By the power of contemplating the identity of the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa),
by the power of contemplating the six lotuses, by the power of contemplating the fivefold equality,
and by the power of contemplating the sixfold unity, [one realizes] the microcosm...
"It manifests as if it were the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)"—this is the secret of all Yoga scriptures.
201) For this very reason, the yogi must indeed practice the contemplation of the fourfold unity. And thus:
It is heard [in scripture]:
"The identity of the microcosm (piṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa), as well as that of the subtle body (liṅga) and the thread-soul (sūtrātman);
the identity of deep sleep (svāpa) and the undifferentiated state (avyākṛta), and that of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme Self (paramātman)."
The meaning is this: one must realize the identity between the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa).

Following that, the identity between the subtle body (liṅgātman) and the thread-self (sūtrātman) is to be understood. The subtle body (liṅgātman) is the subtle form (liṅgaśarīra), consisting of the group of eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātra).

The subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) consists of sixteen components. The *sūtrātman* is the air delimited by the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which leads the subtle body along the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*).
The identity of these two should be understood. Between sleep (*svāpa*) and the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), [the former is] sleep.

The witness (sākṣī) who has entered the state of deep sleep is the Prājña; he is the unmanifest Brahman as conditioned by ignorance (avidyā). There is identity between these two. The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the individual soul (jīva), is the Supreme Self (paramātman), whose true nature is Brahman; their identity is that which must be known. Thus...

This is a summary of the secret oral tradition (*saṃpradāya-rahasya-saṃkṣepa*). The detailed exposition, however, is to be understood from the *Subhagodaya* and the *Śārīraka*. In this verse of the *Saundaryalaharī*, the entire range of objects of knowledge is presented as the secret doctrine of the *Samaya* school and the secret doctrine of the *Kaula* school.
We have set forth all this in brief; it should be investigated with subtle vision by those of great soul. Thus, everything is beyond reproach. || 99 ||

O Mother, the rite of waving lights for the Moon, the source of nectar, is performed by the flames of your lamps; the offering of water is made with droplets from moonstones; and the ocean is satiated by its own waters—yet all this is surpassed by your words, O Mother of Speech.
This is a hymn of praise. || 100 ||
The rite of *nīrājana*—the act of waving lights—for the lamp was performed by the flames of the small lamps; for the sun, by its rays;
and for the moon, the progenitor of nectar, by the droplets of water from moonstones (*candrakānta*).
The arrangement of the *arghya* offering is performed with outpourings (*niṣyanda*). The word "own" (*svakīya*),
meaning "belonging to oneself," connects with this term [outpourings] by way of transposition as "with their own [outpourings]," as in the case of "with the flames of lamps" and so forth.

(202) By "ambhas" (waters), it is meant the waters; "salilanidhisauhityakaraṇam" refers to the cause of the ocean's satisfaction, a specific kind of gratification. "Tvadīyābhiḥ" means those produced from you, having your very nature.
"By words"—that is, by compositions of speech—"of you, O Mother!"; "mataḥ" means "O Progenitress. This is a praise of the expansion of words.
Here, the construction of the words is as follows: "O Mother of words! just as by your own... [The sentence continues: ...by your own [words].
Just as the rite of waving lamps before the sun is performed with the flames of a lamp,
just as the preparation of an offering for the nectar-born moon occurs through its own droplets of water from the moonstone, and just as the ocean is satiated by its own waters, so too [is it].
This praise of yours is indeed by means of your own words.

In this context, when there is a reflection upon the similarity between the meaning presented here as this praise and the meanings set forth in the previously mentioned sentences concerning the flame of a lamp and so forth, then the figure of speech is *prativastūpamā* (parallelism).

Because of the correspondence between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison through the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (thing-to-thing correspondence), when this is merely referred to as "this praise" (*stuti*), then, by virtue of being distinct sentences that imply a reflection and its counterpart (*bimba-pratibimba*), it constitutes the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). Thus...

It should be understood that because the *prativastūpamā* and *dṛṣṭānta* ornaments are perceived through a difference in their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and rely upon two distinct sentences, they constitute a case of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) alone.

In this *Śataślokī* of the *Saundaryalaharī*, the verse beginning with "padbhyām" (which follows "ayaṃ arālā keśeṣu") is placed after the verse beginning with "samudbhūtasthūlastanabharam" (which follows "ayaṃ girimāhuḥ").

[The following] is recited: "O Treasure, ever-smiling one" (nidhe nityasmere). [These verses are indicated as being recited immediately after "This [is the work] of Sarasvatī" at the end of the first appendix.
Thus, there exist three verses; however, they were not composed by the venerable Bhagavatpāda.
It has not been explained that [the work] was composed by someone else; rather, only the hundred verses have been commented upon.
Thus ends the [work] which shines forth through the grace of the boon of Bhramarāmbikā, the founder of the venerable Lolla-kula tradition...

[This work was composed] by Lakṣmīdhara Ārya, the sixth [in descent] from Śrī Mahopādhyāya Mahādevācārya— the seventh [in descent] from the author of the commentary on the *Sārasvata-bhaṭṭa-lolla-ṭīkā*, and the author of the treatises *Sāhityapārijāta* and *Smṛtikalpataru*.
By the fifth son of Viriñci Miśra, the author of the two treatises on literary criticism known as *Bharatārṇava* and *Potā*.

By the great preceptor (Mahopādhyāya) Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, the supreme person who brought to life the two Mīmāṃsās, [this work consists of] a collection of numerous treatises, such as the *Prābhākaramṛtavāhinī*, the *Prabhāvalī*, and the *Khaṇḍana*.

By the son of the venerable Viśvanātha Bhaṭṭāraka— who was marked by numerous titles such as Mahopādhyāya Ha-Pravartaka, Mahopādhyāya Vidvat-Sārvabhauma, and Nūtana-Vyāsa— and who was the grandson of Lakṣmaṇārya, the Mahopādhyāya who composed the treatise *Nayavivekadīpikā*.

By him who has studied the ten hundred [verses] of the *Naya* (the *Mīmāṃsā*), who is a pearl-jewel released from the oyster-shell of Pārvatī’s womb, who has produced many jewels of wisdom, who is the moon to the ocean of the *Lolla* lineage, who is tall with fame, who is a wish-fulfilling tree for the Harita clan, and who is a follower of the *Āpastamba* school;
By him who has reached the further shore of the six philosophical systems; by him who is a gale-force wind to the trees of opposing doctrines;
by him who has attained a preeminent power of intuition through the grace of Bhramarāmbikā; by him who is like the serpent Śeṣa upon this earth;
and by him who is a Rudra for plunging into the entire ocean of the Yāmala Tantras.
By Vīrarudra, who has made the Lord of Elephants his refuge,
who is a bee at the beautiful lotus-feet of Nīlagiri, who is the companion of Vāṇī,
and [the author] of numerous works on the Smṛtis such as the *Sarasvatīvilāsa* and numerous treatises on Sāhitya such as the *Lakṣmīdhara*.
The author of the *Yogadīpikā* and numerous other treatises on the Pātañjala system— such as the *Bandhana*, *Nayaviveka*, and *Bhūṣaṇa*—
and the commentator on the *Mānavadharmaśāstra* known as the *Mahānibandha*, whose ear-ornament was the *Savarhā*.

This commentary on the *Saundaryalaharī* hymn, titled *Lakṣmīdhara*, was composed by the venerable Mahopādhyāya Lakṣmīdhara Śiṣya, who is like a creator of many poetic works such as the *Vataṃsa*, who is like a sustainer of those who seek refuge, and who possesses skill in both restraint and favor.
May the Blessed Lady Bhavānī be satisfied with this.
A verse by our own teacher Lakṣmīdhara Ācārya:
"Whether we here pursue the science of words (grammar), the Tantras, or the science of logic (Ānvīkṣikī) on the right path or a wrong one—
that alone is the path which the sun follows in whichever direction it moves."
For the eastern quarter does not rise as a boat dependent on another direction.

In the evening, the one named Lolla Śrīlakṣmaṇa— whose speech is made resonant by the waves of the celestial river shimmering in continuous succession, and who possesses a delightful longing for the sweetness of nectar fragrant with the scent of fully blossomed jasmine flowers— shines as an ocean of jewels of virtue.
This foremost among the learned was like a hundred-rayed sun for the row of lotuses that were the assembly of Brahmins.
p. 204) He for whom the seventh [is as follows]:
he who was made like gold in the great court of the sovereign of the land of Karṇāṭa; he who...
O learned one, he who was tested in the royal palace of the lord of the earth named Vema,
who is heard of by the name Lolla as a disciple of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mollaṭa, and who is the crest-jewel of the Śeṣa lineage— he is indeed the great and wise Mahādeva.
His statement is:
"I desire either to test it or to turn it into gold; I desire only to turn it into gold, for testing itself is no ornament."
Let my status as a debater remain, having humbled the multitude of arrogant disputants through logic;
likewise, let my role as an expounder endure, praised by a host of noble disciples.
Let there be the exultation of words that converse with the surging waves of the river of the Siddhas as they descend from the heavenly realm.
Whose mind has not been struck with wonder by me?
This Śaṅkarācārya has departed; Vīramāheśvara has departed. Who else knows my exertion in piercing the six cakras?
This work is completed. Appendix 1: Index of Verses in the Saundaryalaharī.
The seed-syllable, the yantra with its associated worship, the preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), the food offerings (naivedya), and the fruits [of these practices]— p. 206)— Note:

Furthermore, it is indeed observed that the worship of yantras accompanied by seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and the fruits of the offerings (*naivedya*) for all the verses contained in the *Saundaryalaharī* have been published, having been printed in both the Kerala and Bengali languages.
These very [mantras] have been translated into Sanskrit for the convenience of practitioners who desire results in this life and incorporated here; thus it should be understood.
Salutations to the illustrious Tripurasundarī.
Of this *Śrī Saundaryalaharī* hymn, Govinda is the seer (*ṛṣi*).

The meter is *anuṣṭubh*. The deity is Śrī Mahātripurasundarī. "Śiva joined with Śakti" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). "In the midst of the ocean of nectar" is the power (*śakti*). "Recitation, speech, and art" is the pin (*kīlaka*). This is for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī during the recitation.
The application (viniyoga): Hrāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs; hrīṃ, salutation to the two index fingers; hrūṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers;
hraiṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers; hrauṃ hraṃ.
Vauṣaṭ with the two little fingers; phaṭ with the palms and backs of the hands. Hrāṃ, salutation to the heart; hrīṃ, svāhā to the head; hraṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor; hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; hraḥ.
Phaṭ to the weapon!
In meditation, she possesses a crimson hue that surpasses the redness of the hibiscus flower; she holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows;
her eyes are copper-red, and she is adorned with ornaments of scarlet garlands.
I bow to Tripurā, whose mouth is filled with betel.

Laṃ, I offer fragrance to the self of earth; Haṃ, I bow to Tripurā, whose mouth is filled with betel and camphor. Yaṃ, I offer flowers to the self of space; Raṃ, I offer incense to the self of fire. Vāyavyātmane... [I offer] perfume to the self of air. (Note: The text provided for the air element was truncated, but the standard mantra is typically *vaṃ vāyavyātmane dhūpaṃ kalpayāmi*). Raṃ, [I offer] light to the self of fire.
I offer a lamp to Vaṃ, the self of water; I offer food offerings. Oṃ.

1) (i) Having drawn this diagram on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice flour (*taṇḍulapiṣṭa*),...

(i) Having inscribed this yantra on a golden plate and having worshipped it for ten days, [one should proceed].

Following the indication, three verses not commented upon by Lakṣmīdharācārya are presented here for the readers' perusal, along with the *Saubhāgyavardhinī* commentary composed by Kaivalyāśrama: — ) [The verses follow] — )
(Verse 94) (Page 186) He extols the majesty of the reflection of the face of the Blessed Goddess:
"The lotus has been brought to the state of a jeweled mirror by the sun..."
Out of fear, the moon’s interior, smooth with its steady rows of rays,
bears the reflection of your face— unfading and free from distress—
as if it were the lotus of its own heart.

"Bringing together" means that the sun, the jewel of the sky, has attained the state of a jeweled mirror— the beauty of Lakṣmī, who is like a lotus made of jewels— having become smooth with rows of rays stilled within due to fear of her face, through contact with its own rays.

Out of fear that the Mother of the World’s face might become weary, [the moon], becoming smooth and glossy through its rays drawn inward within, bears the reflection of your face; like what? Like a flower that blooms incessantly.

The meaning is that your face—uninterruptedly blooming, free from fear like the moon, and unfading—is reflected in the sun, which has become a mirror, as if it were the lotus of your own heart; thus, it has entered the expanse of that [sun’s] heart-lotus. It has been brought together.

In some versions, the reading is "padbhyām. [The meaning is: "He has been brought to the state of a mirror by your two feet. The dative case is used here in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). The sense is: "He has attained the state of a mirror for the sake of your feet; he is fit to be the reflection of your feet."
What power does it have to hold the reflection of your face? Nevertheless, the sense is that it holds the reflection of your face through the compassion of your feet.
(Verse 98) (P.

190) Now, he describes the fruit of the worship of the Śrīdevī, which consists of attaining a form identical to her own: "The chest [of the devotees] bears the weight of full, swelling breasts; their smiles are beautiful; and in their side-glances, there are Cupids."
O Goddess, those few pure rays of yours which possess the luster of the Kadamba flower have produced the illusion that they are Śiva within the minds of men.
O Umā, this is the ultimate fruition of these devotees.

Regarding the word *samudbhūtā*: O Umā! this is the fruition of the worship of those devotees of yours who are pure through their actions of mind, speech, and body, who are intent on the service of your feet, and who are free from defects such as hypocrisy. It is the fruition of their worship.
What is that transformation? It is a chest bearing the weight of fully developed, full breasts; a beautiful smile;

and in her side-glances, many Cupids are brought to life by the casting of those glances—this is the sense. Her body possesses the luster of a *kadamba* flower, and her form is enveloped in a cloak of horripilation.

The secret is this: it is a state of *sāttvika* emotion (*bhāva*) arising from the gaze of Mahādeva. Such a transformation occurs, producing an illusion of you within the mind; having attained a resemblance to you, they remain in your very presence like friends, [beholding] Mahādeva just as you do.
They appear in the mind. By this, the greatness of the fruit of the aforementioned meditation has been established. Here, the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is Bhrāntimān (the appearance of error).
(Śloka 100) (P.
193) He concludes his self-composed praise: O Treasure, eternally smiling, possessed of boundless virtues, skilled in policy, and whose knowledge is unimpeded!

O You who are the sole abode of self-restraint and the minds of others, who are liberated from destiny, whose state is praised by all the Upanishads, and who are free from affliction and eternal— cause this hymn of mine also to reach You.

"O Nidhi!"—He is called *nidhi* because the universe (*jagat*) is deposited (*nidhīyate*) within Him; O Nidhi! O You who are the substratum of the universe. Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "You alone are the substratum of the universe. O Nityasmere! O You whose face is radiant with the unfolding of an ever-present abundance of bliss!

But was it not previously established that [the powers] are the support of the universe? Now, however, it is said that they are "ever-smiling. Smiling is an attribute of the body, whereas the power that is the support of the universe is bodiless. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction between the preceding and subsequent vocatives.
Therefore, he says: "O You of boundless qualities. O Niravadhiguṇe!
You whose qualities—consisting of the manifestation of countless powers—are boundless, and whose smiling countenance has as its very body the grace bestowed upon devotees.
There is no contradiction in [the Lord] being bodiless despite possessing the power to sustain inconceivable forms, provided that [He assumes them] for the sake of favoring His devotees.
If that is so, then from where does the gradation among devotees arise—such as one being a king, another a lord, another poor, and another detached? To this he says:
"O you who are skilled in policy (*nītinipuṇe*)!"—that is, one who is proficient in policy (*nītau nipuṇā*). [She knows] what kind of grace is appropriate for whom.

Such grace is bound to that karma which is conjoined with beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). If it is argued that, in that case, the Blessed Lady would lack independence and be subject to the power of karma—thus becoming like ourselves and others—the author replies: "possessing unimpeded knowledge" (*nirāghāṭajñāna*). *Āghāṭa* means... [text fragment ends]

The meaning is that within the form of the unimpeded, indivisible radiance of such consciousness, which is devoid of any connection with limited measurements, there occurs the favoring of various actions through the conjunction of their respective powers by virtue of its proximity.
How can such a one be worshipped?
Since She is unfit to be grasped through meditation (*dhyāna*) and other such means, he says:

"O Thou whose sole abode is the disciplined mind of others!"—those who worship [Thee] through the disciplines (*niyama*) of recitation (*japa*), ritual service (*pūjā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth.

The meaning is that [the Goddess] manifests and shines forth within the minds of those whose sole abode is the mind. If it is then argued that the Blessed Lady’s manifestation occurs only in the minds of those devoted to discipline and nowhere else, thereby resulting in a state of dependence on necessity (niyati), he says:

Regarding the term *niyatya*: O You who are liberated from necessity (*niyati*)! You shine within the minds of those devoted to discipline through Your divine play (*līlā*), and not by being subject to necessity. Just as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), though common to all, grants fruit only to those intent on service and not to others; or as the sun [shines] upon water and so forth.

The meaning is that a reflection appears only in a pure object and nowhere else; therefore, it is not the case that the sun is subject to such necessity. To the question, "What is the proof for the existence of this deity? he says: "O Thou whose feet are praised by all the Upaniṣads! (nikhilanigamāntastutapade).

The *nigamas* are the Vedāntas, the Upaniṣads; the meaning is that the Upaniṣads are the authority regarding the state characterized by them. In what manner is that state praised? He states that very manner [by saying]: "O Nirātaṅke" (O Fearless One)! That is to say, O Eternal One! And thus says the Śruti:

"Brahman is fearless, imperishable, immeasurable, minute, not gross, changeless, absolute, and consisting solely of pure consciousness. Having been praised in this manner, [the Lord says: "Conclude this praise of mine as well;
bring it to its conclusion, make it complete. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of "to cause that to be done," as in the case of [completing] the Veda.

Make it accepted by all. The meaning is: just as the words of Vālmīki, Vyāsa, and others—namely the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth—have been made into scripture (nigama) and accepted by all, so too let this hymn of mine be made into scripture. Likewise...
And in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, there is a statement of the Blessed One to Himavat (p.
"The supreme Śakti, whose form is the Veda, operates within my world; by her [I] am presided over."

The best of the gods perform their respective duties; likewise do the celestial sages (*devarṣis*), the royal sages (*rājarṣis*), and sages such as Vyāsa. By them were indeed composed all the Kalpa-sūtras and other works, as well as the Dharma-śāstras, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Smṛtis.
And these should be known as equal to the Vedas; no deliberation is required in this matter.
Thus, because multiple causes are here connected to a single action, there is the poetic figure *mālādīpaka* (the lamp-in-a-garland).
The Śrīcakra.

accompanied by the commentary composed by Bhāskararāja,
[is that] whose intellect is free from passion through the singular eclipse caused by the dust of the feet of Śrīnātha.

In this context, the ritual actions constituting the worship of the illustrious Tripurasundarī—who indeed possesses a threefold nature through the divisions of her gross, subtle, and supreme forms—are likewise threefold: physical, vocal, and mental. These consist of the forms of the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga), recitation (japa), and the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).

Although each one involves the integration of the other two, they are designated as "bodily" (*kāyika*) and so forth due to their predominance and abundance. Among these, the first two are taught in the *Tripuratāpinī* and other Upaniṣads; beyond those, [the following] is of a more secret nature.
The Vedic Puruṣa named Atharvaṇa, desiring to favor practitioners of yoga, reveals the third form of worship called the "Meditation on the Śrīcakra within Kālacakra.
First, he describes the nature of the true Guru as the supreme form: "The Śrī Guru..."
By the two statements beginning with "śakti is the cause of all," and here at the end of the Upaniṣad, the statement heard— "one becomes liberated while living through meditation" (bhāvanā)—
is like the injunction regarding the Āgneya sacrifice; it means that one should bring about liberation while living through such meditation.

The rule is unprecedented in that it concerns something already transformed. Furthermore, because the *parabhāvanā* (the cultivation of another form), which serves as the instrument for the *arthabhāvanā* (objective cultivation) and consists of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), is non-worldly— just like heaven—
and because [the *bhāvanā*] is not restricted to its own specific form (*avyūḍhāvadatāsvikatvena*).

The entire passage beginning with "The Śrī Guru for the purpose of defining its true nature" is supplementary to that injunction. Therefore, its authority regarding its own meaning should be understood as being through syntactic unity with the injunction, like the statement "That which is not [accompanied] by suffering," and so forth. And although those meditations (bhāvanās) are...
[The teaching] has two characteristics due to the division of the Kādimata and Kaulamata (p. 270); [due to the division of the matas, it is mutually distinct—kha].
Although these are found in various tantras,

they are nevertheless described here in this very Upaniṣad according to the Kādimata system alone; for the conclusion states, "He who knows thus," thereby indicating that the internal meditations on the cakras are established by the Kādimata within this very Upaniṣad.
Although differences in recension are observed due to the division of branches (*śākhā*),
we shall here provide an exposition following the reading that accords with the supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) such as the *Kādimatatantra* and its *sūtras*. For this very reason:
At the time of writing the manual for ritual practice (*prayogavidhi*),

although certain elements are not heard of in this particular recension (*prakṛtaśākhā*), they will be described here by extracting them from the *Nityāhṛdaya*, *Tantrarāja*, *Bindusūtra*, and other such sources, as they are required.
The venerable Guru is the power that is the cause of all. || 1 ||
Therefore, the body consists of nine apertures. || 2 ||
And this pair of statements is corroborated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The Guru should be the primordial Śakti; she is considered to consist of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The ninefold nature of his body manifests as the [nine] apertures."

Here, the phrase "the first ones" is an explanation of "being the cause of all," because a cause is designated as "first" due to its temporal priority to the effect. It is precisely discriminative discernment (*viveka*), arising through the grace of the Lord, which— by shattering all doubts and manifesting the potency of the mantra— [fulfills this role].
The Guru, designated by the term *vimarśa*, provides space for the ultimate categories of reality (*tāttvika-padārtha*);
he possesses apertures that are non-different from the Guru.
As stated by the author of the *Vārttika* on the *Śivasūtra*: "The Guru is the means."

"The Guru alone is the supreme Śakti, whose nature is the grace of the Lord; by granting space [for realization], she herself becomes the means. Because he knows the beginning and the end through the nature of the unartificial self-awareness of "I," the Guru possesses the status of the supreme means by virtue of his equality with the Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhin). Thus it is said.
In the *Mālinītantra* as well:
"That guru is declared to be equal to Me, the illuminator of the potency of mantra."
"Mantras devoid of their initial and final [syllables] would be like autumn clouds;
such is the characteristic of a Guru—that he should impart the initial and final [syllables].
Thus, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) delimited by such a mental state called discernment (viveka)—

The channel known as Suṣumnā, which culminates in the sporting of the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) and consists of pure reflective awareness (vimarśa), is so described. The venerable Guru possesses three forms according to the distinction between the divine, the perfected (siddha), and the human; each of these, moreover, is again threefold.

In the Tantra, its ninefold nature is well known through the distinction beginning with Prakāśānandanātha and ending with Subhagānandanātha. He states the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that [nature] with the word "tena" (by that). The instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive;
thus, "its" refers to that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose body—that is, its essential form—consists of the nine apertures.
There are two each for the ears, eyes, and nostrils; the tongue, genitals,
and anus are each one— thus, through these nine apertures, there occurs the discernment of their respective objects,
as well as the grasping of what is to be accepted and the instruction [on what is to be done], and the discarding of what is not to be accepted, and so forth.
Because they possess common characteristics such as "it exists" (*bhavati*) and so forth, they are indeed of the nature of deliberation (*vimarśa*).

In reality, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here despite the non-difference [of the parts from the whole], as in the expression *dhānyena dhanī* ("wealthy by means of grain"). The meaning is that one's own body possesses nine cavities that are non-different from those [deliberations]. Furthermore, in the *Tantrarāja*, the word "of that" (*tasya*) is construed only with the state of being nine (*navatva*), and not otherwise.

The connection is with the word "body" (*deha*). The meaning is that the Guru’s ninefold nature (*navatva*) shines forth by virtue of having nine apertures in the body. That is to say, the nine apertures located in one's own body are the nine Lords (*nātha*).
Among them, the two ears and the organ of speech constitute the Divine Current (*divyaugha*); the two eyes and the organ of generation [constitute the next current].
The tradition holds that the *siddhaugha* [is one stream], while the others constitute the *mānavaugha*.
The Suṣumnā channel itself is the root of this group of nine contemplations (*vimarśana*),
because at the base of the porous Suṣumnā, the channels of the ears and other senses are joined together.

Because it is precisely the power of consciousness (cicchakti), as delimited by the *suṣumnā*, that manifests various objects through the respective channels (*nāḍīs*). The manner in which the channels are situated is as follows:
from the center of the triangle located in the middle of the previously mentioned *mūlādhāra*.
The channel named Suṣumnā runs through the center of the spinal column, which is called the neck of the lute;

it extends from the head to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and measures twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose. The channel named Alambusā is said to originate from its base and extend down to the anus.
The channel named Kuhū, rising from the front of the triangle and reaching to the tip of the banner,
extends from its left and right sides to the Viśvodara and Vāraṇa channels, ending at the belly.
And likewise, the Sarvagā is said to be in the [anus], while the Hastijihvā and Yaśasvinī extend to the ends of the big toes. Similarly, the two, Iḍā and Piṅgalā,
reside at the two nostrils, and Gāndhārī and Pūṣā reside in the two eyes.
In the same manner, there are the two channels reaching the ears, namely Śaṅkhinī and Payasvinī;
and that which reaches the tip of the tongue, known as Sarasvatī—thus there are fourteen channels.
The sequence of the location of the channels (*nāḍī*) in the *mūlādhāra* is as follows:
In the center of the triangle at the *mūlādhāra*, there are both the *suṣumnā* and the *alambuṣā*, situated facing east and west respectively;
the other channels are positioned clockwise along the lines starting from the tip of the triangle.
Kuhū and Vāraṇā, Yaśasvinī and Piṅgalā, Pūṣā by name and Payasvinī; Sarasvatī and Śaṅkhinī, and after that Gāndhārī; Iḍā and Hastijihvā, and then the one called Viśvodarā.
"Those located in the apertures, the anus, the genitals, the remaining [orifices], the palate, the eyes,

and the ears— namely, the tongue, the ears, the eyes, the nose, the feet, and the interior of the stomach— make fourteen. Thus, by this, [the text refers to] the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the ninefold reflective awareness of their respective objects, which constitutes the function of the nine apertures.

Thus it is established that one should meditate [on them] as non-different from the Guru. Some, however, maintain that one should meditate on the non-difference of the various parts, such as the ears and so forth, and their respective channels (nāḍīs) from their respective Lords.
The Śrīcakra has the form of nine wheels. || 3 ||

The word "body" (deha) is understood to carry over from the previous context. One's own body alone is non-different from the Śrīcakra, which is the collective totality of the nine cakras beginning with the Trailokyamohana.
The internal division of the wheels (*cakras*), however, will become manifest through the locations of the presiding deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*).

And those locations have been explained according to the different branches (*śākhā*) precisely because of their secret nature. For this very reason, they were not mentioned even in the *Tantrarāja*, since they are explained in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.
This very point has been stated in the *Bindusūtra*:

"The secret of the method of discernment, obtained through the grace of a teacher who is expert in determining the location of the *vyākula* as proclaimed by Aparaśiva, is [this] 'Upahvara'. One Śiva is well known as the author of the Tantras.
Another Śiva is the Veda-puruṣa; by him, through the grace of a Guru capable of determining the locations taught in various branches of the Vedas due to their complexity,
was attained that form of body which is the secret of his own manifestation.

The meaning of the *Śrīcakra* as a secret among the means for direct realization (*aparokṣānubhava*) has been described by the teacher Padmapāda as "the invocation" (*upahvara*). This is illustrated by the word *śiva* in the verse from the *Mahābhārata*: "The lands have *aṭṭaśūlas*, and the crossroads have *śivaśūlas*."
It is easily stated that because [the practice] is performed solely through devotion to the Veda, it is by means of other Śivas, that is, by means of other recensional branches (śākhās).
Vārāhī is the mother, the deity of the ancestral offering (bali) who has the form of the ancestors, Kurukullā. || 4 ||
The goals of human endeavor are like oceans. || 5 ||
Within one's own body— in the sense organs, the organs of action, the intellect, and so forth— those specific portions derived from the father and mother, consisting of bone, flesh, and the rest,
should be meditated upon as Vārāhī and Kurukullā through the power of desire. [This refers to] Vārāhī.
Even though she is female, because her face possesses a masculine form, the status of being the Father (Pitṛ) is logically established.

The oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, and milk, situated in the directions from the west to the north, are the embodiments of the four human goals (puruṣārtha), beginning with Dharma. It is also stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The offering goddesses (balidevyas) are her own māyās; the fifth is the nature of the progenitor (janakātmikā). Kurukullā shall be the mother, and the oceans are the human goals (puruṣārthas).
Here, the first quarter-verse is based on another recensional branch (śākhāntara).
Even though there is unity of meditation according to the principle that all Vedānta texts convey the same meaning, there is no combination [of attributes] from one to the other,
because of the specific qualification of Kurukullā herself as the deity of the bali offering. This is because [the rule] regarding the cognition of one thing in what is not that...
The author of the *Manoramā* states that the powers which, having been produced, cause one to proceed along wrong paths are indeed designated by the term "one's own *māyā*."
The body is an island of nine jewels. || 6 ||
Endowed with the seven constituent elements beginning with skin, together with the body hair. || 7 ||
His intentions are wish-fulfilling trees; his splendor is a garden of world-destroying fires.

The term *tvagādi* (skin and so forth) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type; by this, it is established that there is a group of nine consisting of skin alone, and the seven [elements] beginning with blood and ending with bone, plus the body hairs—thus forming a "ninefold fragment" (*khaṇḍanavaka*) composed of the nine jewels. Herein lies the meaning obtainable through the oral tradition (*sampradāya*).
The sap, flesh, hair, skin, blood, semen, marrow, bone,

and fat take on the forms of fragments consisting of the nine gems— ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, coral, pearl, emerald, diamond, hessonite, and topaz— located in the directions starting from the west and ending with the northwest.
"One should contemplate them as situated in the middle" means [one should contemplate them] as being in the center.

According to the principles of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā, there is a single ritual action based on all Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya*), and likewise, there is a single meditative practice (*upāsana*) based on all Vedānta texts (*sarva-vedānta-pratyaya*).
Since the integration of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) is necessary,

the distinction of the nine deities beginning with Kālacakreśvarī mentioned in other branches [of the tradition] must also be meditated upon within these very elements (*dhātu*). The method for this is found in the *Prayogavidhi*.

This will be clarified: the mental trees of desire, such as the Kalpa-tree, are indeed specific volitions (saṅkalpa); for through engagement in actions preceded by volition, the attainment of desired fruits occurs. The light that serves as their substratum is the mind (manas).

Thus, the garden of the Kalpa tree; for, according to the usage of the Śruti in the passage, "The mind is the light" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.2), it is the mind itself— consisting of volition and conceptualization—
that is denoted here by the word "light."
The six seasons, consisting of the sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, astringent, and salty tastes, are to be experienced by the tongue. || 9 ||
When sweetness and other qualities are perceived by the sense of taste, then, with respect to those [qualities] as qualified by such being experienced, [the following applies].
The contemplation of the distinctions of the seasons, beginning with spring, must consist solely of those [seasons] themselves,
because if they were directed toward other objects non-different from themselves, it would result in the mind's outward-turning (*parāgvṛtti*);
for this contemplation consists in the practice of the inward-turning (*pratyagvṛtti*) of the mind.

Because it is impossible for anything other than that [the tongue] to be the locus of cessation, for this very reason, the qualification "consisting of the tongue" (*rasanābhāvyattva*) is employed. By this, the exclusion of those [faculties] residing in the skin and so forth is also achieved as a result. However, in the *Tantrarāja*, it is said:
"The body is an island of jewels, while its novelty consists of the skin and so forth; the volitions (*saṅkalpa*s)..."
The wish-fulfilling trees are their own support; they are known as the seasons.

Thus it has been said. Here, by the term "one's own support" (*svādhāra*), the six cakras situated within the *suṣumnā* are meant, which serve as the supports for the six wheels of the yoginīs, such as Ḍākinī and the others. Of the *suṣumnā*...

They explain that because the cakras situated therein possess the nature of the *kalās* (phases) as inferred from the conjunction of the moon and sun, which consist of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* [nadīs], it is logical for them to have the nature of the seasons (*ṛtu*).
However, in reality, in accordance with direct scriptural revelation, they refer exclusively to the essence being experienced within oneself.

It is appropriate for the term "one's own support" (*svādhāra*). Now, if it is argued that because the suffix *śānac* in the word "being cultivated" (*bhāvyamāna*) indicates the present tense, there would be an absence of the flavor being experienced at the time of meditation, we say no; for even then, the experiences themselves exist in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [and thus] one's own self [is the support].

Since it is more appropriate to understand the term *svādhāra* (one's own substratum) as referring to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), according to the etymological derivation "that which has [the impressions] as its inherent substratum" (*samavāyin*),
the word *sva* cannot refer to Ḍākinīs and the others, as they have not been previously introduced in this context.
