Because it is impossible to refer back to that [earlier statement], and because the medical treatises (*vaidyaka*) describe the determination of tastes according to the divisions of seasons, it is logical that there is no difference between the season and the transformation of taste (*rasa*). Furthermore, since this explanation is established in such a manner, there is no occasion for inferring that it is based on a different Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*). Here, regarding horses and elephants...
And there is a conclusion of the meditative cultivation regarding the moat and the pavilion.
Knowledge is the water of honor (*arghya*), the object of knowledge is the oblation (*havis*), and the knower is the priest (*hotṛ*);
the worship of the Śrīcakra is the contemplation of the non-difference between the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge. || 10 ||
And this is further elaborated in the *Tantrarāja*:

"The knower is one's own self; knowledge is the *arghya* offering; and the object of knowledge is the oblation (*havir*) situated externally. The worship of the *Śrīcakra* is said to be the unification of these."

The word *jñāna* refers to cognitions such as those of a jar and so forth; the word *arghya* refers to the materials for worship; and the word *jñeya* (or *bahiḥ*) refers exclusively to external objects.

Whatever constitutes this entire range of objects is prescribed in the Śruti as being fit for the oblation (havis), meaning it is to be offered as *naivedya*. For this very reason, the term *arghya* must be restricted to refer specifically to that which is other than such [offerings]. [The recipient] is worthy of worship.

The deity, being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is not mentioned because it is already well-known. The worshipper, who is the knower whose object is the sense of "I" (*ahantā*), is not explicitly mentioned in the scripture due to the context, yet he is indicated in the *tantra*.
[This refers to] those things perceived as distinct from the consciousness of one's own self...

In this context, it is prescribed that one should contemplate the knower, the knowing, and the known as being of the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra), preceded by a non-contemplation of their differentiating names and forms. In the Tantric system, however, the meaning of the word "worship" (pūjana)— derived from the root *pūj* with the suffix *lyuṭ*— is simply the non-duality of these three.

This is the contemplation of non-difference. For in the world, worship consists precisely in the relationship of offering—wherein the specific water for the arghya, the drops of water, the food offerings (naivedya), and one's own self are surrendered to the deity.
Likewise, in the present case as well, it is precisely the identity of these three with consciousness that constitutes [worship].
Such a state is appropriate; for it is an action (kṛti) conducive to that [state] which is here designated as "vibhāvana.

If "vibhāvana" itself were the meaning of the word "worship" (pūjana), then, due to the identity between "vibhāvana" and "worship," it would result in a different kind of "vibhāvanā. Therefore, the word is derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and this is the primary (śrauta) sense.
The term "pūjana" (worship) refers to an activity conducive to worship;
this is further clarified by the expression "unification."

Niyati consists of the aesthetic sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and so forth, the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, and the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī, which consist of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, merit, and demerit. || 19 ||
*Niyati* (destiny) and *prārabdha* (commenced karma) constitute one [power]. There are nine [rasas], beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the terrible (*bhayānaka*), the furious (*raudra*), the loathsome (*vībhatsa*), the comic (*hāsya*), the heroic (*vīra*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), and the tranquil (*śānta*) is intended.
These ten are, respectively, non-different from the ten supernatural powers (*siddhi*) beginning with *aṇimā*.

In this sequence, the source should be understood from the *Bindusūtra*, because it is appropriate to take the order of those [elements] included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)— beginning with *śṛṅgāra*— from elsewhere, as their sequence is not known here; however,
for the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) to be mentioned later, such as *Kāmākarṣiṇī* and the rest, the order follows the sequence of the text.

Because a definitive conclusion is possible, the reversal of order mentioned by Nidhikāra is not to be trusted until the root source is seen. Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of non-difference (*abheda*), as in expressions such as "the world is composed of Brahman" (*brahmamayaṃ jagat*). As for that which is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
In the Śrīcakra, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are proclaimed, along with the tastes (rasas) conjoined with Niyati; the waves (ūrmis),
merit and demerit (puṇya-pāpa), and the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are likewise remembered [to be located there].

Thus it has been stated; furthermore, in that context, the word "wave" (*ūrmi*) refers specifically to the group of six enemies beginning with desire (*kāma*), since we observe the use of the term "wave" for desire and the rest in certain Purāṇas. Therefore, the interpretation offered by others—taking [the waves] to mean hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death—is [incorrect].
It is not to be accepted because it contradicts direct Vedic revelation.
The nine supports are the powers of the mudrās. || 12 ||

Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, the generative organ, and the mind— these modifications of the mind are the sixteen powers, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī. || 13 ||

The six centers beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, the two thousand-petaled lotuses at the top and bottom, and the tip of the uvula (*lambikā*) constitute nine supports (*ādhāras*). Their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) constitutes one; thus, there are ten.
By these—
These are the non-dualities of the ten powers presiding over the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Trikhaṇḍā;
for in other tantras,
since there is no deity for the third line, [these correspond] to those mentioned in the Bindusūtra which follow that system.
The locations of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) are not included here. Others, however,

maintain that since the *Yoginīhṛdaya* also follows the *Kādimata*, those very locations should be accepted, because it describes the abiding of the seal-deities (*mudrādevatā*) within the limbs of the body.

Because the tradition of both the visualization of the deity as taught in this Upaniṣad and its dual nature as worship and ritual placement (*nyāsa*) has been maintained through the lineage of teachers beginning with Nidhikāra, some say that certain rules of *nyāsa* mentioned in the Tantras should be applied here. And those [rules] are:

The rules for the practical application, such as "one should place [the seed-syllables] starting from 'sama' onto the lines of the square and so forth," will be concluded in the section on the ritual procedure (*prayogavidhi*). Furthermore, the visualization of each individual *siddhi* and *mudrā* for every enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) will be prescribed later on.

The visualization of each respective Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), as taught elsewhere, should also be incorporated here. The five elements and the eleven sense organs are non-different from the deities residing in the Sarvāśāparipūraka-cakra; in this context, the word "modification" (*vikāra*) [is used].

It refers to the number sixteen. Alternatively, "manovikāra" may be treated as a single compound word meaning "the mind transformed," based on the grammatical principle that "an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix appears like a substance.
Therefore, there is no tautology with the phrase "the sugarcane-bow of the mind."
The eight [mental states] beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are called speech, grasping, movement, excretion, pleasure, rejection, acquisition, and equanimity. (14)
The objects of the organs of action are five, beginning with speech. Renunciation (*hāna*) means abandonment;

appropriation (*upādāna*) means grasping; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) means indifference. Together with these three types of cognition, there are eight. This very triad of cognitions is referred to by the word "defect" (*doṣa*) in the *Tantrarāja*:
Furthermore, the elements, the senses, and the mind are the eternal *kalās* in their respective order;
the organs of action, their objects, and their defects should be known as the eightfold *śaktis*.
Thus [it is said]. Others say that wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are the humors (doṣas).
[The channels are] Alambusā, Kuhū, Viśvodarā, Vāraṇā, Hastijihvā, Yaśovatī, Payasvinī, Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, Sarasvatī, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā.

And thus, there are fourteen channels (*nāḍī*), which are the fourteen powers (*śakti*) beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. The true nature of these channels was previously explained during the exposition of the nine Lords (*nātha*); the deities of the Mantra-group (*mantrāśra*) are non-different from them. Of these channels—
Furthermore, a considerable inversion of the previously mentioned sixteen elements beginning with earth is observed in the Nidhi treatise;
this is despite the absence of any direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) that would establish the sequence found here.
Since that which is free from affliction is impossible, the root cause for this must be investigated.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—these ten winds are the deities of the outer ten spokes, who bestow all perfections and other benefits. || 16 ||

(279) Due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts arising from contact with these various winds, the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) becomes fivefold through its primary function as the vital breath (prāṇa): namely, the expeller (recaka), the cooker (pācaka), the dryer (śoṣaka), the burner (dāhaka), and the saturator (plāvaka). || 17 ||
Kṣāraka, udgāraka, kṣobhaka, jṛmbhaka, and mohaka— these five types of [winds] residing in the bodies of humans, being preeminent among the nāgas,
digest the fivefold food consisting of that which is chewed (bhakṣya), eaten (bhojya), sucked (coṣya), licked (lehya), and drunk (peya).
These ten fire-powers (vahnikalās), beginning with Sarvajñā, are the deities residing within the inner ten-spoked [lotus].
The five great winds beginning with Prāṇa and the five secondary winds beginning with Nāga—
these ten as well— are non-different from the deities situated in the wheel that accomplishes all aims (sarvārthasādhakacakra).
Also in the *Tantrārāja*: "The fourteen channels beginning with Kṣobhiṇī are said to be the Śaktis; the ten winds are fully proclaimed to be the Śaktis beginning with Sarvasiddhi."

The fact that the single digestive fire (*audarya-agni*) possesses a conditioned nature (*aupādhikatva*) through its connection with the ten vital winds (*prāṇa* and so forth) is explained by two statements. By the third statement, its function as the "Cooker" (*pācaka*) is described.
By the fourth statement, its non-difference from the deities residing in the wheel (*cakra*) that accomplishes all purposes is stated.
Others maintain that fire is tenfold because it exists within the seven elements and the three defects; however, in the *Tantrarāja* (p.
The ten fires are proclaimed, as well as the powers beginning with Sarvajñā.
In this context, the meaning of the phrase "thus proclaimed" (*samproktāḥ*) in the Śruti is simply that the *recaka* and other [breath-controls] have been mentioned;
some, however, consider the word "proclaimed" (*prokta*) to refer to what is about to be explained. In that very chapter—
Agni is the bearer, the pure, the splendor, the radiance, the forest-fire, the crested one, the brilliance;
he is the burning, the devourer... ||

This is because the ten names will be mentioned later; however, in actual practice, it is only the Vedic name that is appropriate as a constituent of the mantra, according to the principle of the tenth book of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* (10.4.22): "When a word is part of a mantra, it must be the one prescribed by scripture."
Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and desire are the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; these, along with the eight powers beginning with *vaśinī*, constitute [the group]. || 20 ||

Cold and heat, pleasure and pain—these two pairs; desire, and the triad beginning with *sattva* (the three *guṇas*)—these eight are the forms of the eight goddesses of speech. As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and desire are indeed declared to be the qualities in their respective order."
The powers (śaktis) shall be Vaśinī and the others... [so it is said].
The five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound are the five flower-arrows. || 21 ||
The mind is a bow made of sugarcane. || 22 ||
Passion is the noose. || 23 ||
Hatred is the goad. || 24 ||

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are designated by the term *tanmātra*. These are sharp at the tip and harsh at the end; for this very reason, they are like arrows. But the unmodified mind is like a bow made of sugar-cane.
Because it impels the sense organs, which consist of the contact with objects; *rāga* is *prīti* (joy), which is included among the thirty-six [tattvas].

It is a specific reality (*tattvaviśeṣa*), not desire in its general sense. Therefore, there is no redundancy with the goddess Aruṇā, who resides at the end [of that category]. Because they are similar in their nature as bonders (*bandhaka*), it is not distinct from the *pāśa* (the fetter). Hatred is anger; of that...
She possesses the nature of a goad because she restrains those who are hateful. And it is said in the *Rahasyanāmasāhasra*:

"Adorned with the noose that is the very form of passion, radiant with the goad that is the appearance of anger, having the mind as her sugarcane bow, and possessing the five subtle elements as her arrows."
In the *Tantrarāja* as well:
"The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the flower-arrows;
the mind becomes the sugarcane bow; attachment is declared to be the noose; and hatred shall be the goad."
Thus it was declared in due order, O lady of excellent complexion.
The deities residing within the inner triangle are Avyakta (the Unmanifest), Mahat (the Great Principle), and Ahaṃkāra (the Ego), who are Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī respectively.
Here, the terms *mahat* and *avyakta* refer to the principles (*tattva*) of the Intellect (*buddhi*) and Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*). [This applies] to the three terms beginning with "Unmanifest."
This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). However, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) between the triads;

rather, according to the expansion of the Tantra (*tantrōpabṛṃhaṇa*), the goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī are the forms of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), Ego (*ahaṅkṛti*), and the Great Principle (*mahat*) in reverse order.
The latent impressions are in a state of disorder.
In this context, Lalitā is the primary substantive (mukhyaviśeṣya). Kāmeśvara is the delimiting property of that substantivity (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka).
These two possess the nature of red feet and white feet respectively; thus, they have red and white colors.
Between these very two, there exists a specific relation. Of that [relation] alone...

The threefold form consists of the gross, the subtle, and the mixed mode of conduct (*caraṇa*). The object of meditation is the worshipper as a qualifying attribute (*prakāra*); along with his primary substantive (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), their relationship, and the delimiting factor of that qualification (*prakāratā-avacchedaka*), there are eleven categories (*padārtha*).
He analyzes [the subject] through three statements beginning with "nirupādhikā" (p.
"The unconditioned consciousness itself is Kāmeśvara. (26)
For it is stated in the *Upabṛhmaṇa*: "The pure consciousness itself, free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is Kāmeśvara in the form of the Bindu; he is known as Saṃvitkāmeśvara."
The Supreme Deity Lalitā is one's own self, ever full and blissful. || 27 ||

By virtue of the qualification "unconditioned" (*nirupādhika*) applied to consciousness (*saṃvid*), the Supreme Deity—who resides within that [consciousness] as its mark—is to be worshipped as distinct from it merely by being characterized by some slight condition (*upādhi*). And such [a deity] is none other than one's own self; indeed, it is non-different from oneself.
The Supreme Deity, who possesses the primary status as the substantive (viśeṣya) defined by the specific forms of those proficient in her worship,
is designated by that very unique name, "Lalitā. Herein...

The phrase "Sadānandapūrṇa" (the one who is eternally blissful and full) is a statement of an epithet (*upādhi*). By this, that which is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not possess the nature of Lalitā, because such a thing falls within the category of the worshipper (*upāsaka*). For this very reason, it is called "one's own self" (*svātmā*), since its meaning is "the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) who is the self of oneself," i.e., the worshipper. And thus, [it is] one.
Thus, the Self, being conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), becomes the worshiper;
while Lalitā is the object of worship in her form distinguished by the three attributes of existence, consciousness, and bliss. [She is] that which is free from these three attributes...
The distinction is this: the mere substratum (dharmin) becomes Kāmeśvara, serving as the locus for the deity to be worshipped. As it is stated in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*:
"The single Brahman-consciousness is the dharma, which is eternal, free from even a trace of defect, and unsurpassed bliss."
The subject (*dharmin*) is the triad of divisions that has become separate through the power of *māyā*.

Therein, the attribute (*dharma*) is experience, which encompasses all objects; it is the power conforming to all effects, consisting of [the will] such as one's own desire (*svecchā*), and it alone is the substratum of the multitude of qualities (*guṇa*). Agency (*kartṛtva*)...

In this regard, the substrate (dharmī) performs the fivefold creative acts of the worlds, while the attribute (dharma), having assumed a male form, maintains the state of being the material cause of the entire universe; and having attained a female form,
it becomes the divine queen (mahiṣī) of its own substratum, the primordial creator— thus they are described.
"Even the various divisions of the Dharma are, for those who know the Vedas, like the Brahman itself, reaching unto the pinnacle of reality."
The redness of all this is its reflective awareness. || 28 ||

By the word *sarva* (all), the triad consisting of Kāmeśvara, Lalitā, and herself [the Goddess] is indicated. The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of this very triad is precisely their mutual interconnection (*anusandhāna*), which resides in the Goddess as redness (*lauhitya*), because everything is colored by attachment to her own self.
This is because passion (*rāga*) and redness (*lauhitya*) are non-different. And it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose form is the universe; redness is its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and this is the contemplation that constitutes worship."
In this regard, here is a secret to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru: by the use of the term "unconditioned" (*nirupādhika*) to express absolute oneness (*kevalatva*),

and by the terms "eternal bliss" and "fullness" to express the possession of attributes (*dharmaviśiṣṭatva*), it is shown that the qualified and the absolute are identical in nature, being inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) like a part and its whole.
The relationship is not of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or the like, which is constituted by difference; rather,
it is the relationship between the two gross forms consisting of the bodies of Tripurasundarī and Kāmeśvara,
expressed by the phrase "residing upon the lap of Kāmeśvara."

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) is that what is conventionally designated as Śiva is essentially the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, a specific kind of union like that between lac-dye and cloth; thus, it is only when one is entirely free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that one attains purity,
just as a crystal lacks the tinge of another color when it is in its natural state.
Since the state of being unblemished white culminates precisely in non-difference from pure crystal, there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the "white foot" in Kāmeśvara;
for this contemplation (*anusandhāna*) consists merely of a specific mental modification (*mānasavṛtti*) whose nature is the "I-self."
Because that objectivity either exists by way of the relation of objectivity,
or because it ultimately results in the mind itself being non-different from passion by way of the relation of occurrence,
there is an impression of "red feet" in that which is qualified by it; by the word "of everything," [it refers to] objectivity.

Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated with respect to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and their relationship (*tatsambandha*), it is indicated that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the "mixed foot" (*miśracaraṇa*)—which consists of the relationship characterized by the state of "equal flavor" (*samarasabhāva*) between the light of the feet and [the disciple]—is also suggested; this is the general direction. In the *tantra* verse, the Guru is the first.

The fourth quarter [of the verse] is intended to state that the continuous mental application (*anusandhāna*) of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) described in the passage beginning with "there would be power" (*bhavecchaktiḥ*) is what is denoted by the term "meditation" (*upāsti*). Alternatively, meditation itself also possesses three forms.
Worship of the form and so forth is the gross aspect; mental recitation is the subtle aspect; this meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the supreme aspect.
And accomplishment is attained through one-pointedness of mind. (29) Each [deity] belongs to a single enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
Each individual *siddhi* and *mudrā* is worshipped in the external sacrifice;
this scripture exists for the purpose of establishing that mental impression (*vāsanā*).
The instrumental case in *ananyacittatvena* signifies non-difference. The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of including the *mudrā*.
And thus it is augmented in the *Tantrarāja*:
Success consists in one-pointedness of mind; the mudrā is the meditation on the manifestation of power. Thus it is said.

The accomplishment residing in each respective veil (*āvaraṇa*) consists precisely in the mental cultivation of those deities of the various veils—though they have been meditated upon as non-different from specific parts of one's own body—as being non-other than one's own self. It is simply the realization: "These are not distinct from me."
"Success" (*siddhi*) means up to that point. Some maintain that the "state of success" (*siddhipada*) refers to the attainment of the fruit of worship (*upāsti*).

According to that view, worship (*upāsanā*) occurs because the non-distinction [of the object]—which is necessitated by the difference in the mode of being the object (*viṣayatāvailakṣaṇya*)—is not discarded within the meditation (*bhāvanā*) mentioned immediately prior.

The meaning is that it bears fruit. In reality, since the object of the propitiation (*tarpaṇa*) to be described hereafter is not distinct [from what precedes], this passage is intended solely for the sake of *siddhi* (accomplishment) and so forth. Their "vaibhava" is their omnipresence (*vibhutva*), which is their unlimitedness; the cultivation of that very state is what is meant.
The meaning is that the meditation on the mudrās situated within their respective coverings constitutes the ritual applications of meditation. || 30 ||
Regarding the aforementioned meditation on Lalitā as non-different from one's own self, its "actions" refer to their repeated performance— that is to say, continuous (dhārāvāhinī) meditations.
This is because the offering of ritual services (*upacāra*) is inherently constituted by duality, as follows:

The sense is that, according to the position which maintains the cultivation of [the deity] as possessing established fragrance and so forth, since there would be the consequence of forgetting the previously cultivated distinction, one should freely conceive metaphorical cultivations (*upacāra-bhāvanā*) that do not contradict that [established nature]. As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Even when there is movement, there is ritual conduct, because of being absorbed in that [state] and being heedful."
"Mobility" (*calatva*) is restlessness, the absence of stability in the contemplation of non-duality;

even while possessing such a nature and character, one should contemplate in such a way that there is no negligence regarding the aspect of being identical with Brahman, but rather the utmost vigilance.

The meaning of that [passage] is: "this is a figurative usage. Although the word *cala* (moving) has been explained in the *Manoramā* as referring to inevitable states such as negligence (*pramāda*) and sleep (*svapna*), nevertheless, by the force of the particle *api*, it refers to the waking state (*jāgrat*).
It should be understood that this statement by the other [author] refers solely to the necessity of vigilance (*sāvadhānatā*).
Such heedfulness is to be observed in the worship of Śiva as described in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*.
[This applies to] all the bliss of the self arising from the enjoyment of sense objects.
The continuous realization [of all things] as non-different from one's own Self (p.
285) acts to exhaust even the karma consisting of the pleasure and pain obtained through *prārabdha*.

The essential point therein is that because it brings about happiness upon its maturation—just like the massaging of one's limbs with substances that are pungent or astringent—the very form of worship consists in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
[This is expressed in verses such as: "May whatever playful activity of mine becomes a synonym for worship," and so forth.
The statements of Bhagavatpāda and others also express this same meaning;

however, since such worship is to be accomplished over the duration of a day and night, whereas the meditative visualization intended here is subsequently governed by rules regarding specific durations such as a *muhūrta*, [the two differ].
Because of contradiction, figurative applications must be conceived in a different manner. An example of that method is as follows:

"seated" (āsana) is the contemplation of being established in one's own glory; and according to the Śruti, "All beings are His foot" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12), [He is seated] upon the expansion of ether and so forth, which is of the nature of speech.

The water for washing the feet consists of the contemplation of the mere aspects of "existence," "luster," and "loveliness," which serves to cleanse the impurity of name and form; this is conceived through the superimposition of the non-distinction of being a single part of that very subtle phenomenal world, according to the method described.
The removal of impurity is the *arghya*. The swallowing of even the water of meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) is the *ācamana*.

The contact with the water of visualization through the non-differentiation of all limbs, such as being pure (*sattva*), conscious (*cit*), and blissful (*ānanda*), is the *snāna*. Regarding the [impurity] that has become attached to those very limbs by contact with the aforementioned water:
The garment is the contemplation of the state of being the object of the [Brahman’s] functional manifestation (vṛtti) as something concealed.
The ornament is the contemplation of those non-different attributes that constitute various marks of Brahman, such as being devoid of objects and being stainless.

By removing the inert portions of the earthy, ethereal, airy, and fiery elements contained within one's own body, as well as the inert portions of the lunar orb and its nectar, leaving only that which remains as pure existence, consciousness, and bliss;
The six services, beginning with fragrance and ending with betel, consist of the contemplation of [the deity] as being composed of Brahman.
As it is stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
"One should worship you with offerings such as food, which are themselves composed of you."
"The universe consists of the five elements, and she, the eternal one, consists of them. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, this hymn is a meditative visualization (*vibhāvanā*) wherein all the words belonging to the mantra that serves as a limb for the contemplation at hand—beginning with "Parā," "Paśyantī," and so forth—are dissolved into Brahman by means of their own *nāda*.

Pradakṣiṇa is the dissolving of the fluctuations of the mind— which are running hither and thither among sense objects— into Brahman, preceded by the removal of the dullness inherent in those objects;
it is the state of the mental modifications being solely inclined toward Brahman through their turning away from sense objects.
Regarding "namaskāra": although *āsana* is the state of the external and internal organs remaining in a single form (p.

Sentences such as these are also seen in some places in the root text (*mūla*); nevertheless, because certain among them lack conformity with the intended meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) at hand, because they are not found in many manuscripts, and because no expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of them is observed in the Tantras, [they have been omitted].
Those have not been attended to by us here.

The dissolution within the Self of conceptual constructions such as "I," "you," "existence," "non-existence," "that which is to be done," "that which is not to be done," and "that which is to be worshipped," is the oblation (homa). || 31 ||
There exist within the Śrīcakra other infinite powers as well, distinct from those previously described:
"But those other powers residing in the cakra on all sides are declared to be the causes of the manifold conceptual constructions of the universe."

These have been described in the Tantra by such passages as "ityādi. He states the underlying intention (*vāsanā*) for the fire-oblation (*homa*), which results in the realization of the non-difference between those [deities] and Tripurasundarī, beginning with the words "I am" (*aham*).
Consequently, the fire-oblation that is an ancillary part of the food offering (*naivedya*) is taught separately, rather than being included within the ritual services (*upacāra*).

There is no inconsistency. Thus, it follows that the three statements beginning with "I" (*aham*) are solely devoted to the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) consisting of the act of relinquishing (*visarjana*).

By the words "I" and "you" (*tvam*), the notions of "self" (*asmat-pratyaya*) and "other" (*yuṣmad-pratyaya*) are grasped. [The inquiry as to] whether [the self] exists or does not exist [is thus addressed].
By this [phrase], worldly injunctions and prohibitions—[expressed as] "that which ought to be done" and "that which ought not to be done"—are included;

by "that which is to be worshipped," the injunctions residing in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Vedas are grasped; and by "one should not worship," [the prohibition of the injunctions] residing in the Upanishads (*vedaśiras*) is grasped.
The non-mention of negation is precisely because it is not seen in the Upaniṣads. By this group of seven, the totality of the modes of being (*vṛtti-sāmagrī*) is indicated.
Even for such conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), the state of being the very nature of the Self is nothing other than the contemplation of the non-differentiation of the Self.
The cultivation of the fire offering.

"Man is firmly the setting of all conceptual constructions within his own self"— from such an expansion [of the teaching]. One should contemplate the dissolution of the entire collection of the powers that cause those conceptual constructions into the deity, preceded by their absorption through the absence of emergence.
The meaning of the commentary.
Meditation on the non-difference of objects is their satiation. || 32 ||

All the ritual elements (padārtha) described here, beginning with the venerable Guru and ending with the special fire-oblation (viśeṣahoma)— both those already contemplated and those yet to be contemplated— are to be understood through the contemplation of their mutual non-difference;
for even the contemplation of difference, which is occasioned by the distinctness of their respective objects, [must be transcended].

(287) By means of swallowing (*nigaraṇa*), one brings about the state of having the non-conceptual, fourth, indivisible reality as its object; then, by abandoning even that [object], the residual impression (*vāsanā*) of satiation remains as nothing but one's own Self. Although—
Betel, worship, hymn, libation, and prostration—

these are enumerated as distinct services (*upacāra*); nevertheless, since libation here takes the form of a service to the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadeva*), it is merely a single part of the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).

It is also "satisfying" (tarpaṇatā) because it brings about the cessation of the cultivation of anything other than itself. Regarding the statement in the *Tantrarāja*, "The mutual interpenetration of these is known as satisfying," the word "of these" (*eṣām*) refers in a restricted sense to the [three] acts of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblation (*homa*).
The explanation provided by Nidhikṛta is not to be accepted because it contradicts the Vedas.

Having, through this much of the treatise, explained that the Śrīcakra in the form of the body is nothing but one's own self, he now describes the dissolution of the phenomenal world— which possesses an external relationship with that [body]— into one's own self:
The observation of the transformation of time in the form of the fifteen lunar days constitutes the fifteen Nityās. || 33 ||
And that proliferation (*prapañca*) is threefold: consisting of time, consisting of space, and consisting of both.

Among these, the first is as follows: the days of the new moon (*darśa*), which are enumerated in such Vedic texts as "The new moon was seen, it was visible" (*tai. brā. 3.10.1*), and so forth, which exceed the *sādākhyakalā* residing within the lunar orb.

There are fifteen digits (*kalās*), which correspond to the lunar days (*tithis*) beginning with *pratipad* and ending with *pūrṇimā*; these very digits are non-different from the eternal goddesses (*nityās*) beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā. Lalitā, however, is eternally present. And of such [a cycle] that is constantly revolving...
The Śrīcakra exists within the wheel of the lunar days (*tithicakra*) which is the form of Time, and not outside it.
Just as Mount Meru is situated on the northern part of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*),
there are seven islands (*dvīpa*) to its south, known as Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālma, Aśmaka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara.

In the intervals between them are the six oceans of the terrestrial globe, ring-shaped, known as salt, sugarcane-juice, wine, clarified butter, honey, and milk; outside of Puṣkara is the seventh ocean, the Sweet-water Ocean (Madhuroda). Beyond that, to the south—
"Beyond the sky"— thus there are sixteen deities.
Within those [locations] beginning with Meru and ending with the Sky, the Nityās beginning with Lalitā and ending with Citrā reside in sequence.

In the first year of the pair, they remain stationary. In the second year, however, they travel from Jambūdvīpa up to the end of Meru. In the third year, they travel from the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇasāgara) up to the end of Jambūdvīpa; and so on, in this manner, until the sixteenth year.
The sixteen Nityās, beginning with Lalitā, reside in the regions starting from Paravyoma and extending to the Sweet Ocean (Madhurasamudra). Thus,
there is a rotation of one Nityā for each of the sixteen years.

Even for Śakra, who possesses such a form as this region, the Śrīcakra is within and not outside. Just as there are eight orbits—of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the stars—which encircle the terrestrial globe from above and below; that is the third [point].

The eight intermediate spaces between those [points] make sixteen locations that are of the nature of the Kālacakra. Within these places, the sixteen Nityās revolve in a sequence contrary to the rotation of the regions. Furthermore, the Śrīcakra is within this very wheel, not outside it. Of this...
The ultimate form of all three wheels is indeed the wheel of Nityā.

Since everything other than Brahman is non-different from it—being delimited by space and time—the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is of the very nature of Nityā. For here, the contemplation of their non-difference from one's own self is precisely what is intended.
It is prescribed:
Now, listen to the instruction on the internalization (*vāsanā*) of the sixteen *Nityās* as one's own self,
by which the realization of identity with them certainly becomes manifest.

Having begun with the words, "The Guru shall be the primordial Śakti," and so forth, and having explained the cultivation of the realization that Lalitā—with her limbs and sub-limbs—is one's own self, [the text] concludes at the end:
"The observation of the transformation of time in the form of lunar days; [these are] the Nityās."
Thus, fifteen other latent impressions (vāsanās) have been described.
This is because such a conclusion is seen in the *Tantrarāja*. Furthermore, that [conclusion] has as its fruit the withdrawal of the manifold (*prapañca*) by way of the lunar days (*tithi*);
thus, by means of indicating the threefold wheel, it refers to the supreme manifold. This is because [the conclusion] consists of the nature of the manifold.

The meaning is that the contemplation (*vibhāvana*) that "only Time has reached its transformation" is itself the contemplation of the other fifteen *Nityās*. Because their non-difference from Tripurasundarī is established, she is not mentioned separately.

This is because, according to the *Krīḍīkāra*, the meditation on non-duality has already been enjoined in the preceding statement regarding those [deities] mentioned by the term "objects of meditation" (*bhāvanāviṣaya*) and those yet to be described; or rather, in reality, all lunar days (*tithi*) are [equally objects of meditation].
They consist of time in the form of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths;
Lalitā possesses their collective body (samaṣṭi-vigraha), while the other fifteen exist individually through their specific distributive manifestations (vyaṣṭi).
They consist of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths;
the meaning is that one should meditate upon them in that manner. This is the meditation on these two positions.

Some maintain that [the worship] should be performed after the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), because in external worship the arrangement of locations is established right there, and since all [the previous] has been dissolved, there is no opportunity for another meditation. However, in reality, when the mind is stilled through being focused solely upon one's own self...

Since the stabilization of the breath is inevitable, and because the dissolution of the deity’s rays is appropriate only at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*), and since the subsequent injunction for the simultaneous stabilization of both mind and breath occurs later, it is improper to extract this [instruction] here as a meaningless statement.
Therefore, it should be understood that here, indeed, constant cultivation (bhāvanā) is appropriate.

Thus, emphasizing the necessity of maintaining a continuous stream of meditation day and night— preceded by the dissolution of the entire internal and external manifold, leaving only one's own self as the remainder— he describes three types [of practice] according to the distinction between superior, middling, and inferior practitioners who are unable to achieve that [highest state].
He states the rule regarding time:
"In this manner, by being intent on meditation for three muhūrtas, two muhūrtas, or even just one muhūrta, one becomes liberated while living; such a person alone is called a Śivayogin. (34)

By the word "thus" (evam), the non-conceptual mental state (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) previously described immediately before— which has as its object the self alone and is accompanied by the suspension of breath— is indicated.
One who is intent upon the cultivation of that [state] is "supreme," being fully absorbed in that very [state].
That is to say, one who is devoid of the activity of both cultivation and its opposite, and possesses a continuous flow of cultivation;
such a person becomes a partaker of the fruit in the form of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) very soon. These are those such as Jaigīṣavya and others who are designated as Śiva-yogins.
They too [are so called] precisely because they are permeated by such a cultivation;
thus, the meaning is that "such cultivation" is the ground for the application of that term.
The meditations on the internal wheels according to the Kādimata system have been explained. || 35 ||
He who knows this thus has studied the Atharvaśiras. || 36 ||

The three Vedas primarily expound external rituals; the Atharvaveda, however, extensively expounds internal rituals. And this Upanishad, which is the very head of that [Atharvaveda], expresses a realization that is even more internal than those.

290) The internal meditations on the wheels (*cakrabhāvanā*) described herein are according to the system of the Śakti known as Kādī, and not according to the Kaula doctrine. This is the secret teaching (*upaniṣad*) of this [tradition].

The meaning is this: he who knows that [the text] has the function of establishing such a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), both word by word and sentence by sentence, is alone one who has studied the *Atharvaśiras*, and not merely one who has studied the words alone;
for the purpose of the meditative cultivation, which has study as its instrument, is the realization of the meaning.

"Whoever knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness"— from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "all" (*sakala*) in this other Vedic text (*śrutyantara*), it is understood that even from the mere recitation of the words, some measure of auspiciousness indeed exists; may there be peace (*śivam*).
Thus Bhāskararāya has composed this commentary on the *Bhāvanopaniṣad* and the *Atharvaśiras*,
for the satisfaction of the learned and for those seeking liberation while living.
Thus ends the Bhāvanopaniṣad with its commentary.
[Now begins] the Śrī Devīstotrapañcaka: (1) Laghustuti.
Bearing a white radiance upon her forehead like that of Indra’s bow, and spreading a luster all around her head like the cool light of the moon, may this very Tripurā—
like the brilliance of the sun ever present within the heart— suddenly sever our bonds.
By three steps, she is composed of light and composed of speech. || 1 ||
We meditate upon that measure which resides eternally in your first seed-syllable (*vāgbīja*), rivaling the stability of the finest thread of a blue lotus fiber;
we recognize it as the power *Kuṇḍalinī*, whose efforts are ever-bound to the activity of generating the universe— having understood this, one [is liberated].
Furthermore, men again experience childhood within the womb of their mother.

O Giver of Boons! O Goddess! when even one who, upon suddenly seeing a startling object, has involuntarily uttered "Ai Ai! here—even without the vowel-bindu—becomes certain to receive Your grace swiftly once You have taken pity on him.
From his lotus-like mouth issue forth words that discharge the flowing essence of the nectar of eloquent speech.

O Eternal One! If some rare sage on earth understands that the next syllable of your mantra, *Kāmarāja*, is partless (*niṣkala*) and belongs to Sarasvatī; and if, at the beginning of each section (*parvan*), the twice-born recite the narrative of Satyatapas—
Having brought it to a state of intimacy with the locus of the Praṇava, they clearly utter it.
I bow in my mind to that third seed-syllable of yours, moon-bright, whose power is seen by the wise to instantly bring about the flow of speech;
and there is also the submarine fire, followed by Sarasvatī, and the word "cow" (go) on the mountain, for the destruction of the waters of dullness.
It proceeds with perfect certainty, bestowing accomplishment even without [the practice of] yoga. || 5 ||
O Goddess! Whichever one of your sinless seed-syllables— whether with its consonant or without its consonant, whether standing as a compound (kūṭastha),
or occurring separately in sequential order, or situated out of order— whichever [one it may be]...
Whichever method or by whatever rite it may be, when performed with desire, it constantly brings to fruition every single thought or recitation of men.

O Mother! Those who [meditate upon] You—holding a book in Your left hand and granting fearlessness, with Your right hand gracefully bestowing boons upon devotees while holding a rosary; radiant as camphor and the *kunda* flower; gazing with a gentle luster from eyes as beautiful as the petals of a blooming lotus; [they shall attain liberation].
They do not even contemplate them with their minds; how then could they possess poetic skill? || 7 ||
For those who meditate upon you stationed upon their heads— drenching their crowns with nectar-like fluids, your splendor as radiant and lovely as a cluster of white lotuses—
from the lotus of their mouths there issues forth, without ceasing, speech composed of formidable and distinct syllables and words.
O Bhāratī! O Bhāratī, you are like the restless, dancing waves of the surging billows of the celestial river.

Those who, with undistracted minds, behold for even a moment this primordial Earth— dusty with the pollen of vermilion and covered by Your splendor, as if submerged in a spreading expanse of molten lac— their fever of love shall fade like the exhaustion of a fawn’s young.
Invisible beings clearly become subject to one's will. || 9 ||
Those who, having made you firm in their minds, meditate upon you for even a moment— you who wear shimmering golden earrings and armlets, and are bound with girdles and flower garlands— for them,
the splendors within their dwellings shall expand daily for a long time through your grace.

Fortunes, as fickle as the flapping ears of elephants in rut, attain stability [only] through your fierce majesty— [stability found in] you, whose mass of matted hair is adorned with the crescent moon, who wears a garland of human skulls,
who are clothed in garments as red as the Bandhūka flower, and who sit upon the throne of a corpse. You...
They meditate upon her who has four arms and three eyes, whose breasts are full and high, and whose slender waist is marked by three folds, for the sake of realizing your form.

Though born into a family that was merely ordinary among kings and possessed of few attendants, he attained the status of a sovereign over the entire circle of the earth and became exalted by his majesty.
O Goddess! That he has become Śrīvatsarāja, whose feet are worshipped by hosts of vidyādharas, is the arising of grace born from prostrating at your lotus-feet. 12.
O Caṇḍī! Those whose hands have never acquired the calluses from the tips of thorns broken by the forceful plucking of bilva fruits and other offerings for the sake of worshipping Your lotus feet,
are born with hands marked by the staff, goad, discus, bow, thunderbolt, śrīvatsa, and fish.
How indeed [could they be compared] to the kings of the earth with their hands possessing the luster of lotuses? || 13 ||

O Goddess Tripura, consisting of both the supreme and the non-supreme, when Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and others have gratified You in the ritual of worship with milk, clarified butter, honey, and spirituous liquors,
whatever those of steady intellect may pray for, that very thing they certainly obtain.
They swiftly attain success, unhindered by obstacles. || 14 ||
In this world, you are called Vāgvādinī, the mother of all sounds;
from you clearly emerge even Keśava, Vāsava, and the other gods. You are she into whom Brahmā and the rest likewise dissolve at the end of a kalpa. You are that very one.
You are celebrated as the supreme power, whose majesty and form are inconceivable.

The triad of gods, the three Vedas, the three sacrificial fires, the triple power, the three vowels, the three worlds, the three steps, the three Puṣkaras, the threefold Brahman, and the three castes—
whatever object in the world is categorized in a triad, such as the three aims of life and so forth, all that [is contained within you].
O Blessed One, the name "Tripurā" truly corresponds to you in reality.
One should remember Lakṣmī in the royal court, Jayā on the battlefield, Kṣemaṅkarī on the road, Śabarī in the mountain fastnesses of the forest infested with carnivorous beasts,
elephants, and serpents, and Mahābhairavī when bewildered by the fear of ghosts, spirits, demons, and jackals.
They cross over misfortunes by means of Tripurā, and they cross over floods of water by means of Tārā.
Māyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Kriyā, Madhumatī, Kālī, Kalāmālinī, Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, Jayā, Bhagavatī, Devī, Śivā, and Śāmbhavī.

You are Śakti, the beloved of Śaṅkara; you are the three-eyed one, Vāgvādinī, Bhairavī, and Hrīṃkārī; you are Tripurā, consisting of both the supreme and the non-supreme; you are the Mother, the Virgin Kumārī. || 18 ||

O Consort of Bhairava! From those extremely secret names of Tripurā which arise from vowels joined with consonants beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'kṣa', arranged in pairs, triads, and so forth— both those starting with vowels and ending with consonants, as well as those starting with consonants and ending with vowels— [these names are formed].
Salutations to those beyond twenty thousand. || 19 ||
Having composed this praise, the wise should skillfully understand it with their minds fixed upon Tripurā; for in its first verse, she is clearly described by means of one,
two, and three words respectively, according to the number of syllables in her feet, with an undivided mind.
The procedure for extracting the mantra, together with its specific details and endowed with the authentic tradition. || 20 ||
Whether it be blameworthy or blameless— what is the use of this reflection? Surely,
that person who possesses devotion to you will recite this hymn,
even though a sense of personal insignificance arises firmly within them by force of their devotion to you.
For it was certainly composed by me as well, since I have been made eloquent [by him]. || 21 ||
Thus ends the first, the *Laghustava*. (2) The *Carcastava*:
O Tripurā, you who are the source of the playful grace of beauty and the wish-fulfilling trees for the realization of sovereignty over the worlds!
Victorious are these prostrations unto you, O Mother of the World! They are like full moons that awaken the multitude of night-lotuses of poetic genius. || 1 ||

O Goddess! Even those such as Vācaspati and others, whose minds are intent upon the composition of hymns of praise, become stupefied; therefore, who am I, naturally dull-witted, to offer a hymn to you here?
O wife of Tripuratāpana! [To] act... || 2 ||

O Mother! Nevertheless, for the sake of dispelling the intense heat of worldly existence, that helmsman of the great ocean of praise—held by the grasp of devotion to your lotus feet, O Bhavānī!—makes me somehow eloquent to offer you hymns. (3)
O Bhavānī! You give birth to the worlds, you sustain them, and you remain awake for their destruction;
you shatter delusion and you restrain it—this playful sport of yours is truly wondrous. || 4 ||

Upon whichever man you cast even a slight glance— sweet with favor and as fair as the petal of a fresh lotus— the continuous streams of eyes from women, pierced by the arrows of the bodiless Love-god, fall incessantly upon him. (5)
Even for that lord of the earth, Udayanaprabhava,
whose footstool was kissed by the prostrations of the Vidyādharas,
this very affection for the station of a universal emperor was born from a single grain of dust from your lotus feet.
Serene faith. || 6 ||

By certain eminent poets of great intellect and virtuous deeds, preceded by prostrations at the dust of your lotus feet, fame as white as milk, the moon, silk, or snow has been attained even throughout the three worlds. (7)

O Bhavānī! The Vidyādharas constantly play the lute for you, performing variegated worship fashioned from the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling tree and singing songs as dear to you as the affection of a lover.
In the cave-dwellings of the golden mountain.

O Goddess, may the grace born from your feet be victorious— the perfected mantra for the subjugation of Lakṣmī, the means for attracting passionate women, and the lamp that pierces the dense darkness of delusion. 9.

O Goddess! The rays from the jewels of your toe-nails, possessing the luster of fresh pearls, bring great joy; for during the prostrations of the celestial beauties in service, they act as clusters of flowers upon the parting lines of their hair.

O Mother! That light which blazes with the brilliance of the shimmering moon upon Your crown, which is variegated by the rays of the weapon of the gods between Your brows, and which kisses the heart-center while mimicking a spark of fire— that is Your true nature.
He who beholds upon your head the goddess of speech, white as the shimmering rays of the moon,
from him flow words sweet with grace, like a boundless cascade of the nectar of well-composed hymns.

O Mṛḍānī! Those fair-eyed women who, casting aside shame, gaze even for a moment upon the sky as if it were smeared with a mass of vermilion powder by your splendor, or upon the earth as if it were drenched in lacquer—those beautiful women pursue him. (13)
O Mother, he who remembers Your true form for even a moment— that form resembling a thread spreading through liquid lac— [attains liberation].

Young women, consumed by the god of love, meditate with undivided minds upon the quality of supreme beauty found in Pradyumna. This moon, which shines as a jewel in the ocean of the sky, is that very ancient Puruṣa who is the preceptor of gods and demons.
"O Goddess! You yourself are that very half-portion which belongs to the slayer of Andhaka"—thus they declare. || 15 ||

O You who draw forth excellence through qualities that correspond to Your will! When You touch and sustain him, then even Lord Śiva— the sole preceptor of the three worlds and the architect of the triple universe— shall be born.
O Hemavatī! Since you have been meditated upon by that one of stainless mind, whose splendor is as pure as the garland of rays of the moon,
O beautiful one, you shall create for him an unblemished and eternal world within a few days without delay.
The play of speech. || 17 ||
O Goddess, those whose radiant form— resembling a lotus stained with vermilion— flashes within their hearts by virtue of restraining the foundational breath (ādhāra-māruta),
meditate upon you here and attain the full wealth of their desired perfections. (18)

O Mother! those who meditate upon Your form, tawny like fresh liquid lac, situated in the center of the crimson orb [of the rising sun], their chests are forever pierced by the arrows of the flower-armed god, and the deer-eyed women remain under their control. (19)
O Bhavānī! Beholding you, who illuminate the expanse of the sky like a digit of the moon emerging from the region of the horizon, wise poets immediately [attain inspiration].
You are the wish-fulfilling cow for the lineage of those whose intellects are cultivated through meditation.
O Śarvāṇī! O you whose lotus-feet are worshipped by all people! O you whose beauty of eyes mocks the luster of lotus petals!
O royal swan in the minds of those whose forms are free from sin! You destroy manifold calamities.
Of the people. || 21 ||

O Tripura, radiant as molten gold! Purify my ancient mind and cut down the forest of my multitude of sins. For me, bound by shackles in this prison, the fetters instantly snap upon the mere remembrance of you.

O Goddess! They praise you as Vyāpinī, as Sumanā, as Kuṇḍalī; they praise you as Kāminī, as Kamalā, as Kalāvatī; they praise you as Mālinī, as Lalitā, as Aparājitā, as Vijayā, as Jayā, and as Umā. 23.

I bow to the Blessed Lady, who is like the fierce sun dispelling the sixfold transformations upon the lotus-thicket of the ultimate reality of unrestrained desire; she is the playful cave of the lion of awakening, intent upon the destruction of the lordly elephant of delusion.
I bow to Tripurā. || 24 ||

May Tripurasundarī, praised by Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka, accompanied by Rati and Kāma, seated upon the excellent throne of the enemy of Smara, joined with the arrows of the flower-bowed god, surrounded by the three Siddhas beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, and dwelling in the midst of the Kadamba forest, protect us. 25.
O Rudrāṇī! Those who meditate upon you— whose form is unique and whose luster is ruddy, like an image made of coral— to them, O lady with long-lashed eyes, come [and bestow your grace].
Young women forcibly embrace you, whose soft vine-like arms are clung to their necks.

Your eyes are bound by the affection of gazing solely upon your own form; your ears are colored by the passion of hearing the multitude of your virtues; and your mind is filled with the remembrance of you.
O Goddess, may my skill in worshipping Your feet remain in my two hands, may Your glory abide in my speech, and may my devotion to Your service never cease anywhere. 27.

Whosoever manifests that imperishable deity Madana, whose form is as red as a blooming pomegranate flower, him the young women regard as no different from the God of Love himself, even if he be devoid of physical beauty, for their broad hips and slopes gaze upon him.

O Vāgīśvarī! O Sovereign of the three worlds! O Mother of the universe! Salutations to you who are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Hari, the thousand-rayed Sun, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and Agni, and who have established your abode both within and without. 29.

Whoever recites this hymn to the Goddess every day—which brings about the highest good—or even listens to it, for him his desired goal bears fruit; he is honored by kings and becomes most beloved by women with intoxicating eyes. (30)
Thus ends the second hymn, the Carcā-stava. (3) The Ghaṭa-stava:
[I bow to Him] upon whose head the garland released by Indra, slow with joy, was forcibly placed.
May the lotus-foot of Ambikā, enchanting with the tinkling of her exquisite anklets, bring victory to me against Mahiṣāsura. || 1 ||
O Goddess! O Consort of Tryambaka! O Pārvatī! O Sati! O Mother of the Three Worlds!
O Śivā! O Śarvāṇī! O Tripurā! O Mṛḍānī! O Giver of Boons! O Rudrāṇī! O Kātyāyanī! O Bhīmā! O Bhairavī! O Caṇḍī! O Śarvarikalā! O Kālakṣayā! O Śūlinī!
Protect us, who are agitated and whose minds are focused on nothing other than devotion to your feet. || 2 ||
O Goddess! Even one who bows to you but once, the lords of the earth bow down to him, their millions of crowns rolling upon the surface of your footstool which has been shining since birth;
he who worships you is worshipped by the hosts of gods, and he who praises you is praised.
Distraught by the pain of love, those fair-browed women meditate upon him.

Those who meditate upon the Daughter of the Mountain King are truly blessed; they appear as if intoxicated, as if possessed by a planet, as if fainted from contact with poison, as if overcome by full-blown passion, as if seized by the pain of separation, or as if afflicted by distress. They alone stand foremost.
Those fair-browed women meditate upon them with minds whose passion has increased due to the abandonment of all external constraints. || 4 ||

O Tripura! Even those men who meditate upon you in their hearts for but a moment, though deprived of beauty, youth, and wealth, shine forth as the sole images painted upon the wall of the minds of women with lovely, long eyes. (5)

"Shall I drink him with my eyes? Or shall I enter his limbs with my own? Or shall I suddenly swallow him whole? Or shall I resort to madness?"—O Goddess, what is there that women will not do when they are thus rendered helpless by the playful intentions of their fickle imaginations?
In whose heart you dwell.

O Mother of the Three Worlds! Just as the term "Lord" (Īśvara) applies to the omnipresent [Being], so too the power of the word resides solely in You, the immovable pillar that has no other support; such is the true state of things. Thus...
O Goddess, it is a great marvel that although these minor ailments are capable of afflicting even those devoted to You, You do not destroy them with Your wrath. || 7 ||
O Bhavānī! Those embodied beings who meditate upon you— dwelling within the moon, possessing a charming luster like that of the moon,
seated upon a pale, blossoming lotus, with a complexion like a glistening lamp,
and raining down nectar— they [attain liberation].
Their enemies become free from affliction and abandon them from afar.

Those who meditate with faith upon your body, as if it were fashioned from fragments of the full moon, from abundant floods of nectar, from the massed waves of the Ocean of Milk, from lumps of the paste of ambrosia, or from masses of frost; [They attain the state of liberation.]
Those whose misfortunes, afflictions, and calamities are internalized within the mind possess true prosperity.

Those deer-eyed women who remember you— fickle yet suddenly bursting forth, piercing the five knots, red as the rising sun, and immersing the entire world in a deep-red ocean of passion— hold you within their hearts. (10)

O Bhavānī! O you of incomparable form, those deer-eyed women daily meditate within their hearts upon that man who is like the god of love himself—him whom they worship fervently with the lotuses of their eyes, as he is slender as a lotus fiber bathed in lac-dye. 11.
We praise you, the unmanifest Speech, who possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and who bears a garland of kadamba flowers hanging down as far as the soles of your feet.
On her head, she sits upon a white lotus-throne of the moon, possessing a brilliance as pale-white as frost;
she pours nectar into the mouth and the [other] apertures of the lotus-born Brahmā.
O beloved of the enemy of Smara, as I thus remember you— unbroken, enchanting, graceful, and exceedingly serene— my speech leaps forth in every direction.

She bestows desired enjoyments, destroys enemies, slays calamities, burns away mental anxieties, pacifies diseases, and extends happiness; she forcibly shatters inner suffering and grinds away the pain of separation from the beloved. What faultless thing, indeed, does the Goddess not accomplish for one who meditates upon her even once?
He performs [it]. || 14 ||

O beloved of Tryambaka! Prosperity never departs from the home of one who meditates upon you, knows you, attains you, chants your name, beholds you, contemplates you, follows you, practices your path, measures you, praises you, takes refuge in you, and honors you;
and he who listens with devotion to your virtues.
Vijaya runs ahead of him. || 15 ||
O Destroyer of the Danujas! What suffering does not perish when You are remembered?

O Lotus of the lineage! What fame is not proclaimed when You are praised? O Praise of the Best of Gods! What perfection is not attained when You are worshipped? And what yoga is not [attained] in You?
One accumulates [karma] when the mind has an object of focus. || 16 ||
O Goddess! those who stand within the jaws of the irresistible Kṛtānta; O Kālī! those who are tightly bound by the thick noose of Time; and O Caṇḍī!
those who are submerged in the ocean of fierce and heavy sin—you protect them, you liberate them, and you cause them to cross over.
It is indeed remembered. || 17 ||

Victorious for a long time are the dust-particles from your lotus-feet, which are like a powder for subjugating Lakṣmī; when they meet upon the foreheads of men through prostration, they erase the ill-fated letters inscribed there by destiny. 18.
O fools! Why is this body being needlessly tormented by asceticism, or why are other households being emptied by sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees?
If devotion to the two feet of the Blessed Goddess is imperishable, then Fortune—beautiful with the parasol of her blossoming lotus—will hasten before you. 19.

I beg nothing from anyone, I deceive no one, and I serve no one; with all poverty cast away, I wear fine garments, eat sweet food, and enjoy the company of beautiful women—for the Goddess, the wish-fulfilling cow of my lineage, flashes within my heart. (20)
I bow to Bhavānī, whose locks of hair are adorned by the crescent moon, and who is a river of nectar that extinguishes the fever of worldly existence. 21.
Thus ends the third hymn, the Ghaṭastava. (4) The Ambāstava:
She whom the sages declare to be the ancient primordial nature, and whom they call Vidya—
Those who know the secret of the Vedas declare this; I, having no other refuge, take refuge in that Goddess, whose form is the mudrā of Śaṅkara with half-a-pallava. || 1 ||
O Mother, in hymns to you, even the compositions of words become powerless, for they lack an author. May this praise of mine, though incoherent like that of a child,
gladden you whose heart is overwhelmed with maternal affection.
As the ether, as the point (bindu), as the sound (nāda), as the form of the crescent moon, as the body of the Vāgbhava syllable,
and as the Mother-Letter (mātṛkā)— O You whose nature is the flowing nectar of bliss and awakening, You shine forth in the minds of fortunate people. || 3 ||
With bodies whose horripilation constantly manifests,
with eyes from which tears perpetually flow, and with words—
O Mother! those in the worlds who worship Your feet with faltering words—they alone are blessed. || 4 ||

O Goddess! that mouth which is raised up for Your praise, O Mother! that head which bows to You, and that mind which has You as its supreme refuge—these belong to someone through certain specific austerities. || 5 ||

O Bhavānī! Having risen from the hollow of the root-basin and pierced through the six lotuses like a flash of lightning, you surely enter back into that same place in the form of the supreme nectar-water trickling from the moon of the Dhruva-maṇḍala. 6.
O Goddess, when that single Madana was burnt by you in many ways, your charming method of casting side-glances caused him to sprout anew; from that time forth, O Goddess,
the moon-crested Lord truly bears a third eye on his forehead, which remains closed as if out of shame.

O Daughter of the Mountain King, who indeed recognized Śambhu at the time of your auspicious marriage— him whose origin was unknown, whose lineage was unascertained, a naked mendicant bearing a skull-bowl, and without a companion?

O Girijā! The deer-skin garment, the smearing of the ashes of the dead, the wandering for alms, the dancing in the cremation ground, and the embracing of a multitude of Vetālas— all these bring splendor to Śambhu through his association with you.

O Mother! Even the fierce dances of the wielder of the broken axe (Śiva), though skilled in the playful acts of dissolving the cosmic ages, become tendered by your glance through its very nature as a graceful dance.
They transform for the sake of the world's prosperity. || 10 ||

O auspicious one! When the karma of a living being in his final birth becomes equalized, the initiation by the piercing of Śambhu— which severs the entire web of bonds— occurs in the twinkling of an eye through compassion, by relying upon the side-glance of the Teacher.

Adorned with pearls and possessing the luster of fresh coral, when you flash in my mind like the starry twilight, you alone— though devoid of five arrows— attain the state of Cupid among all the beauties of the three worlds. (12)

O Mother, those who meditate upon you, the Sovereign of Nectar, who nourishes the world with her streams of nectar-bearing rays, surely cross that boundary of Time which cannot be transgressed even by the foremost of gods, beginning with Brahmā.

O Mother! He who worships you in his heart—resplendent as the autumnal moon, seated upon a lotus, and with hands raised in the act of exposition, adorned with crystal rosaries, a book, and a water-pot—is a sovereign emperor among poets and logicians of the universe. 14.

I bow to you alone, the Śabara woman, the wife of the Śabara: you who possess a mass of hair adorned with peacock feathers, whose thick breasts are beautified by necklaces made of guñjā berries, who are dark-complexioned, whose face is like a young sprout, and whose hands are delicate. (15)
"O charming girl, what have you gained by trading this beautiful half of the fresh vine for this harsh half of the Lord?"— I believe these were the joking words of her friends.
O Goddess! By your gentle smile, [all beings] become as if frozen. || 16 ||

O Mother! This ocean of māyā, teeming with clusters of bubbles that are the cosmic eggs and possessing rows of waves that are the various principles (tattvas), is wondrously brought to instantaneous dissolution by the great submarine fire of the continuous stream of meditation upon You. 17.
As Dākṣāyaṇī, as Kuṭilā, as Kuhāriṇī, as Kātyāyanī, as Kamalā,
and as Kalāvatī— you who are truly one, O Blessed Lady, you appear in manifold forms even in the ultimate sense, like a dancer.
O Sovereign Lady, your form, characterized by bliss, has transformed into the nature of sound within the region known as the Unstruck (anāhata);
the fortunate ones, perceiving it with an inward-turned mind, proclaim it through tears and horripilation. 19.
You are the moonlight in the moon, you are the radiance in the sun; you are consciousness in the person, and you are strength in the wind. You are sweetness in water, and you are heat in fire;
if everything were devoid of you, it would indeed be utterly essence-less. (20)
That the luminaries move in the sky, that the atmosphere produces waters, that the serpent supports the earth, that the wind blows, and that the fire remains with its upward flame—
all this, O Mother, exists solely by Your command alone. 21.
O Girijā! When you wish to contract, you are then the ground of speech and logic, nameless and formless; and when you undergo expansion, then—
The enumeration of your names and forms becomes easy. || 22 ||

O Goddess! Having prostrated before you for the sake of enjoyment, the fortunate ones— having made the lotus-dwellers their servants with a mere glance of your eyebrows— delight for a long time in a pleasure-mountain fashioned from heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, within a grove of kalpa-trees.

O Sovereign, you alone are capable of removing the entire suffering of worldly existence for your subjects through your compassion; just as the very mass of rays belonging to the son of Vikartana is able to dispel its own heat by means of its own rain.

You are power, the body, the presiding deity, the inner self, knowledge, action, the instruments of perception, the web of the mind, will, sovereignty, the abode, and the veils; O Goddess, what is there that you are not of the one who bears the crescent moon?

Cessation is said to reside in the earth, stability in water, knowledge in fire, peace in the wind, and supreme splendor in space— those very powers which, it is said, sustain the universe; yet, O Mother, Your state is far more remote than they.

O refuge of the world! As long as Your pair of lotus feet do not take up residence within the hearts of people, so long will the planetary afflictions of logic—twisted in form and entangled with conceptual constructions—never come to an end for those bound by dogmatic tenets. (27)
Having abandoned the paths of the gods and the ancestors, some make their minds sovereign over the entire circle of the senses and establish them in meditation upon You.
O Pārvatī! the joints of the fivefold causes lead to the state of their own seat. || 28 ||

O Mother! Among the gross forms beginning with the earth, even that form whose majesty cannot be described by the Lord of Speech (Brahmā) himself—she too has indeed been praised by me; this must be forgiven. (29)
O Mother, those who meditate upon You— who possess the brilliance of ten million fires of cosmic dissolution during the purification of the six paths,
who pour down a rain of floods of nectar during the ritual ablutions, who are dark-hued with the slope of Your firm breasts,
and who have shattered all evils— truly become the teachers of the worlds. 30.

O Mother! Some call You the supreme knowledge (*vidyā*), some the ether (*ambaram*), some bliss alone, and others *māyā*; others say You are the universe itself, while we revere You as the very embodiment of the Guru, manifesting boundless compassion. 31.

With hair as dark and glossy as the petals of the blue water-lily, and with the slender waist of Your beloved woman weighed down by the burden of full breasts—O Mother, Mother of all beings! what need is there for many words here? Such is Your supreme form to us.
May it be continuously present. || 32 ||
Thus ends the fourth hymn to Ambā (5). The Hymn to the Mother of Lakṣmaṇa:
These beings, unaware [of the truth], go to destruction through their inevitable mutual quarrels within the knot of your Māyā.

O Mother of the World! O Moonlight to the darkness of the fear of the fever of birth! We, who bow to You, approach the Blessed One for refuge as You roll upon the ground, subduing those who follow the path of worldly convention. || 1 ||

Salutations always to that certain, charming, great Light, who is worshipped by Śiva and others, who is perpetually bowed down by the weight of his breasts, whose splendor rivals the blue lotus, and whose form is the awakening of the sovereign bliss of supreme natural consciousness that is inaccessible to speech or logic. 2.
O Goddess! Though you are the beloved of Śiva who delights in the rasa of beginningless and endless non-duality,

that you became his wife in the rite of marriage, and that you were born as the daughter of the Mountain and the mother of all beings— this is the prologue to the great drama of the manifestation of the world.
O Blessed One! Some declare the truth to be "existent," while others, O Mother, declare it to be "non-existent.
Other wise poets say that it is both existent and non-existent; yet others, O Goddess, maintain that none of this is so. Indeed, O Śivā, all of this is surely the play of Your Māyā.
Śiva, whose slender waist bends under the weight of breasts adorned with dangling clusters of *guñjā* berries,
and whose lotus-like face has its radiance enhanced by rising drops of perspiration;
may he grant you auspiciousness.
I seek refuge in Śabarī, who follows behind the auspicious goddess, her form multiplied by the guise of a hunt focused on protecting the son of Pṛthā. || 5 ||
The constructions of logic involve mutual seizing of hair by hair, beginning and ending in dispute;
the rules of the scriptures are objects of bowing with great faith and devotion.
Be gracious, O Daughter of the Mountain! Become manifest before me; grant refuge to this mind of mine, which is without support and tossing about in agitation. 6.

No one knows at any time, by whom, where, or how the food of dogs, of fire, or of the flocks of birds shall be; therefore, O mind, abandon all trust in this body and immediately take refuge in the Mother of All alone! 7.

I incessantly worship that indescribable Light, which has entered its own support—the dense thicket of the six knots—shattered by the brilliance of the light of ten million lightning flashes; which, once again, takes the form of a shower of nectar; and which, becoming fully manifest as the twenty-eight rays, shines forever.
Dark-complexioned, bent by the weight of her breasts, and with curly hair. || 8 ||

O Daughter of the Mountain, salutations to you who, having first passed through the four-petaled, then the six-petaled, and the vulva-shaped [lotuses], proceed through the three circles possessing the splendor of millions of lightning-flashes, fire-jewels, and suns, and then enter the hexagon, the ten-petaled, the twelve-petaled, the sixteen-petaled, and the double-triangle.

Some wise ones declare that *kula* is the body, while others say it is not; still others assert it to be their union, and yet others call it *kaula*. O Mahāmāyā! Others speak of something even above these four. How can we determine what your true nature is? (10)

Having reduced the forest of the six paths to ashes with a luster that rivals ten million suns at the time of dissolution, you—whose body possesses the splendor of a blue lotus—assume an indescribable Śaiva form; yet, as your devotees bow their heads before your lotus feet, you remain bowed by their breasts. Thus, your human exertion (puruṣakāra) triumphs! 11.
Having entered the middle path, unknown to both light and bliss, and swallowing this pair known as the sun and the moon;
Having attained the upward-sounding resonance (nāda) and having reduced his entire being to ashes in the fire of dissolution through your grace,
O Mother, this living being enters Śiva, the Akula.

Humans, animals, and gods— these three worlds are submerged in the ocean of existence, tossed about by millions of waves of the three *guṇas*. O Mother, if Your compassionate glance should fall upon anyone anywhere, that embodied being immediately attains the state of the body of supreme bliss.
Her body dark as the priyaṅgu creeper, her garments and tender shoots a deeper red, beautiful with an abundant adornment of shimmering pearls,
she is like a wish-fulfilling vine bent low by the heavy clusters of her pair of breasts.
For those who meditate upon you even once, you bestow the state of the Śiva-cintāmaṇi.

O Bhavānī! You flow as a fresh river of the nectar of supreme sound (*paranāda*) through the currents of the *krama*, with six supporting eddies, vast masses of waves of mantra, foaming with shimmering mudrās, and various moving deities for its fish.
She is the beloved of the nectar-ocean of Śiva’s consciousness. || 15 ||

O Mother! Though swallowed by your forms—the earth, water, fire, air, ether, moon, and sun—how small is their greatness? O Blessed One, these do not attain even the most minute state anywhere; yet in You, whose body is the supreme sky, they are contained.
They call her the digit, the command, wisdom, the observance, experience, the state of equal flavor,

the Guru, the lineage, discipline, instruction, the abode of Śiva, the means of knowledge, liberation, primordial nature, the overcoming [of obstacles], the supreme cave, the ritual procedure, and knowledge— verily, they say she alone is the Mother of all beings.
The sages. || 17 ||
